title: Auburn’s annual Auburn Farm Forest Tour
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DEAR SUN SPOTS: Auburn is home to many incredible farms, homesteads, forestry operations, and other agricultural gems. Please join Auburn’s Natural Products & Agricultural Working Group for the 3rd Annual Auburn Farm & Forest Tour on on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. . Walk trails, learn about our forests, meet farm animals, buy pumpkins, much more! This event is free and all are welcome.
Tour locations: Woodlot Trail Forestry Management, Hobart Road; Life Forest Whistle Ridge, 589 Trapp Road; Farmer’s Family Gardens, 150 Sopers Mill Road; Valley View Farm, 1176 Sopers Mill Road; Open Heart Farm , 304 Sopers Mill Road; WISH Farm & Shearing, 96 South Witham Road; Homestead and Family Farm, 736 South Witham Road; Community Forestry Board Tree Nursery, 115 North Auburn Road; Retreeus Orchard at Park Avenue School, 161 Park Ave.; Bell Farms Inc., 1552 Riverside Drive; Land Lab at Evergreen Outdoor Education, 45 Andrew Drive; Chestnuts Across Maine Grove, 24 Chestnut St., behind PAL; Pam’s Garden, 745 West Auburn Road.
Participants who visit six or more locations will be entered to win a local goodies raffle basket.
Special thanks to the Natural Products & Agricultural Working Group, Good Food Council of Lewiston-Auburn, and the School Based Food Hub for making this event possible. — No name, Auburn
ANSWER: This sounds like an excellent way to spend an autumn Saturday. Count me in! I encourage you to make a plan and of course, schedule extra time to stop at any other places along the way. It’s sure to be a day to remember.
DEAR SUN SPOTS: The United Methodist Church of Auburn, 439 Park Ave., is hosting a Bean Supper and Silent Auction on Saturday, Oct. 17. The menu includes beans, casseroles, hot dogs, and homemade pies.
Supper will be served at 5 p.m. and entertainment will begin at 4:30 p.m. with music by the Park Avenue Pickers.
We invite you to come and view all the great items in the silent auction and place
your bids. For more information, call 782-3792. — Steve, Auburn
ANSWER: Fun times are ahead with these suppers coming back for the season. Be sure to put them on your calendar and bring your friends.
DEAR SUN SPOTS: As the temperature drops, more homeowners are signing up for our food pantry at Trinity Jubilee Center at 123 Bates St. in Lewiston. That first heating oil bill has left a lot of people worried about how they will make ends meet this winter. If you’re in this situation, don’t be embarrassed to ask for help. Each week we have fruits and vegetables, meat, bread, and canned goods. You can also check out Healthy Androscoggin‘s list of local food resources at https://healthyandroscoggin.org/andro-county-food-resources. — No name, Lewiston
ANSWER: You can sign up for the food pantry online at https://trinityjubileecenter.org/our-work/food-pantry/ or in person during Trinity Jubilee’s distributions on Wednesdays from 7:45-10:45 a.m. If you have questions, call 782-5700.
This column is for you, our readers. It is for your questions and comments. There are only two rules: You must write to the column and sign your name. We won’t use it if you ask us not to. Please include your phone number. Letters will not be returned or answered by mail, and telephone calls will not be accepted. Your letters will appear as quickly as space allows. Address them to Sun Spots, P.O. Box 11349 Portland, ME 04101-7349. Inquiries can also be emailed to [email protected].

title: 'ENERGY CEASEFIRE:' Trump announces de-escalation in Russia-Ukraine war
text:
'ENERGY CEASEFIRE:' Trump announces de-escalation in Russia-Ukraine war
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump expressed frustration over Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries.
'ENERGY CEASEFIRE:' Trump announces de-escalation in Russia-Ukraine war
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump expressed frustration over Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries.
President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to pause attacks on energy infrastructure, but he provided no details about the terms in his initial social media post.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it," Trump said.
It comes one day after Trump suggested that Ukraine should "get a new leader." He accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of hindering a peace deal and driving up global diesel prices by striking Russia's oil refineries.
"He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel, because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world," Trump said. "We told him, do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel. There's a big problem, a big shortage, and what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel."
Experts say the Russia-Ukraine conflict has driven up fuel prices, but so has Trump's war with Iran.
Trump is pursuing several strategies to bring prices down ahead of the midterm elections, including his new deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump said Friday that Russia will immediately supply diesel to America and the global market.
The announcement marked a sharp pivot in U.S. policy, as America has banned Russian oil imports since Moscow first invaded Ukraine in 2022. Just last month, Congress passed a bipartisan law that aimed to choke off Russia's oil revenue.
Critics of Trump's deal warn that it will fund Russia's war effort and prolong the conflict.
In a social media post on Sunday before Trump announced the energy ceasefire, Zelenskyy said Russia alone is responsible for the war. He said Ukraine is ready to stop hitting Russian refineries, but only if Russia stops targeting its energy infrastructure too.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so," Zelenskyy said. "Any de-escalation steps must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees."
As for Trump's call for a new leader, Zelenskyy told ABC on Sunday that they would organize elections if Russia commits to a total ceasefire for 60 days. Zelenskyy also stressed that the decision is up to the people of Ukraine.

title: Obituary: Paul David Rea Jr.
text:
AUBURN – Paul D. Rea, Jr. passed away peacefully in his sleep at his home on Sept. 22, 2026.
He was born Nov. 12, 1941, in Albany, Ore. and grew up in Tangent, Ore. While in high school Paul played football and lettered in track. Paul then went on to join the United States Air Force and was extremely proud of serving.
Paul is survived by his wife Gail; daughter Liz, and son Herbert; grandchildren, Joshua, Delila, David, Nathan, Josiah, Caleb, Hadassah; great-grandchildren, Emilina, Izzabella, Kyle and Amelia; sister, Donna and brother, Richard; as well as family members’ spouses and partners and many more relatives.
Paul was predeceased by son, Paul (David) III; parents Paul Sr. and Ruby; and sister, Carmoletta.
Paul’s sense of humor will remain as fond memories to all who knew him.
For a full biography of Paul and to share online condolences and fond memories, please visit http://www.albert-burpee.com
Services will be held at a later date.
Arrangements are under the care of Albert & Burpee Funeral Home & Cremation Services, 253 Pine St., Lewiston, ME 04240, 207-782-7201.

title: Two years after Hurricane Helene, rivers in North Carolina still are littered with debris
text:
PVC pipes swept away by Hurricane Helene dominate cleanup of North Carolina river
They're piled on river banks, lodged in uprooted trees, embedded in sediment and jammed under logs. Many are tangled in mounds of debris up to two stories high.
Related video: Roof ripped off Pensacola hotel during Isaias
Two years after Hurricane Helene leveled forests, bulldozed houses and filled western North Carolina rivers with everything from cars to refrigerators, the work of cleaning up the debris goes on. And along the iconic French Broad River, known for its whitewater rapids, one item stands out among the rest: massive numbers of PVC pipes that washed away from a factory north of Asheville.
"Just the amount of time and energy that we put into removing all this pipe is exhausting," said Jon Stamper, operations director at MountainTrue, the nonprofit conducting cleanup on several rivers affected by Helene. "We still have stretches of river that haven't been touched."
MountainTrue estimates its crews have pulled hundreds of thousands of pipes from the river — most of which went to landfills — with an untold number still littering the river for 70 miles (113 kilometers), to a large lake at the Tennessee border.
Canada-based IPEX would not say how many pipes were stored at its Woodfin, North Carolina, site before the storm, or share results of a company-funded study of how much remains in the river, calling the information "commercially sensitive." Officials did say 60% of pipes stored outdoors at the site, sandwiched between railroad tracks and the river, were swept away in the 2024 flood, but most were recovered fairly quickly.
But the company acknowledged that the remaining debris was significant and has agreed to pay MountainTrue $500,000 toward continued cleanup on the French Broad, which will allow the organization to continue working into next year.
A $10 million state grant awarded to MountainTrue in 2025 to clean up debris in several western North Carolina rivers that was set to expire in December has been extended to February. The organization said there's still a long way to go, and estimates that it's spent 50,000 work-hours and over $1.5 million just on pipe removal, which is only in the French Broad.
PVC pipe comprises 80% of the debris in some areas, according to MountainTrue, posing risks to rafters and kayakers, changing water flow and altering the ecosystem.
"We understand the ongoing challenge," IPEX CEO Colleen Pritchett said. "We recognize that ... recovery efforts are complex: they're resource-intensive, and it's constantly shaped by the river conditions."
Hurricane Helene hit western North Carolina in late September 2024, dumping more than 30 inches (76 centimeters) of rain in some areas, triggering landslides, toppling trees, pushing buildings off their foundations and choking waterways.
At IPEX, an earthen berm was the only thing separating tall stacks of pipes from the French Broad River. Company officials said they expected a so-called 100-year flood — meaning it has a 1% chance of occurring in any given year — and moved pipes out of that flood zone.
But the flooding from Helene was 10 times worse.
"We secured the site as best we could and we sent people home a day before the flooding was expected," said Johnny Drummond, vice president of manufacturing. He said the company did not anticipate a 1,000-year flood, which has a 1-in-1,000 chance of occurring.
The company closed the factory for a couple of months afterward, with losses "well over $100 million," Pritchett said. It since has invested over $100 million to repair and strengthen the buildings, and now is studying ways to contain the pipes in future floods — something MountainTrue had publicly urged for months.
Though there's much more than IPEX debris still in the waterways, the pipes are so ubiquitous that "there are places where you go that it makes up almost everything that we remove," said Stamper, who formerly worked for a whitewater river outfitter and now oversees 10 cleanup crews totaling about 100 people — many of them former river or fishing guides who lost their livelihoods after the hurricane.
Removing the pipe is especially vexing because it binds with other debris and has become embedded in the river bottom, where fish and other creatures have taken up residence inside. Stamper said he also worries about long-term environmental and health effects from the pipe, which can degrade and become brittle, leaving microplastics in the river.
"We want to avoid that stuff sitting there forever and just slowly deteriorating and breaking into smaller and smaller pieces," said Stamper. "Some of the pipe that's been sitting out since Hurricane Helene that has been exposed to the sun all the time is getting to the point where you could crack it when you grab it."
Some of the pipes — both straight, rigid plastic and flexible coils that have unraveled — are under huge piles of tangled logs topped by other debris, often in mounds 20 feet (6 meters) high. Cleanup crews "just sort of picture it as a jungle gym" that they must climb and balance on as they clear the pile, said Jemima Filiss-Cook, who leads the cleanup in Madison County, where most of the pipe is concentrated.
She said many crew members were already cleaning up the river before MountainTrue hired them, as a way of "trauma bonding" over what had happened.
They include avid outdoors-people, including rock climbers, because the cleanup is "quite a tedious and technical process" that requires comfort with the rigors of the job, said Anna Alsobrook, MountainTrue's French Broad Riverkeeper.
Crews saw longer pipes into smaller chunks, load them on a boat, then take it downstream to a landing spot where they're loaded onto a truck. Almost all of the pipe goes to a landfill, though some in good condition are given to community members, because there are no good recycling options, MountainTrue said.
"I truly don't think anybody else could do this work except for our debris team members," said Alsobrook, noting they must be able to navigate whitewater rapids with a boat full of pipes and saws.
The first priority was removing pipes that could pose an immediate danger or entrapment hazard to tubers or kayakers, and much of the remaining debris stranded in flood plains and on banks, especially around riverbends and corners and vulnerable to being washed away in another flood, Stamper said.
But it becomes apparent that many pipes are still in the river whenever the water levels change, he said.
MountainTrue is applying for other grants to help extend its program after state and IPEX funding run out, Stamper said, because it could take years to remove all the debris.
"We're going to do our best as long as the funding allows," he said. "But there's going to be pipe out there that we can't get ever."
___
Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan.

title: American among 12 killed and more than 300 hurt in latest attack on Riyadh airport, authorities say
text:
CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
It was the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
A missile struck a King Khalid International Airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
Footage posted on social media following the attack and analyzed by The Associated Press shows emergency vehicles outside the airport.
Saudi civil aviation authorities on Saturday said airport operations were suspended. The closure was later extended by 24 hours until 9 p.m. Sunday, according to the flight tracking platform Flightradar 24.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels
The attack — the latest of several in the past week on the airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, U.S. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
Trump later Saturday said he planned to speak to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and said “what happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable.” Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” he said.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
The airport had a heavy police presence on Saturday, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, Flightradar24 said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Also Saturday, U.S. Central Command said a fighter jet struck and disabled a commercial cargo vessel with a precision munition in the Gulf of Oman, part of U.S. efforts to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica had departed an Iranian port and did not heed repeated warnings. The ship’s crew was unharmed, CENTCOM said.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key U.S. ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
While the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for the one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked dozens of ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Saudi flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.

title: Saudi-led coalition says a projectile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh airport
text:
CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war’s new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran’s most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels’ strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports, and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels’ use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
The toll rises on both sides
Earlier on Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday’s attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national.
Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety.
An expert says the Houthis’ tactics could backfire
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they’re pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution, and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels’ pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.”
___
A previous version of this report has been corrected to show that the Egyptian killed was a woman, not a man.
___
Frankel and Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington, Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut and Omar Albam in Maarat al-Numan, Syria, contributed to this report.

title: Maine Man Arrested Following Fatal Shooting In Indian Township Saturday Night
text:
One man is dead after a shooting Saturday night in Indian Township.
Maine State Police are Investigating a Fatal Shooting in Indian Township
Maine State Police have identified the victim as Cory Fields, 41, of Indian Island.
Officials say Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township is now charged with murder.
Stevens was taken to the Washington County Jail.
Indian Island, Maine Man Found Fatally Shot in Indian Township
The charge stems from an investigation that began at approximately 9:28 pm on Saturday, October 10, 2026.
The Indian Township Police Department received a report of a shooting at 312 Peter Dana Point Road in Indian Township.
Several agencies responded to the scene, including Indian Township Police and Fire-Rescue, the Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service, and the Washington County Sheriff's Office.
When officials arrived, they found Mr. Fields deceased.
Maine Man Charged With Murder for a Fatal Shooting in Indian Township
Maine State Police were called to investigate.
That investigation led to Stevens being arrested for murder.
Mr. Fields' body was taken to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, where an autopsy was performed.
As a result, the cause of death was determined to be gunshot wounds, and the manner of death was homicide.
Authorities have not commented on the circumstances that led up to the fatal shooting.
This incident remains under investigation.
We'll update this story as more details become available.

title: Schmidt Leads Katahdin as County Teams Earn Big Saturday Wins
text:
The County Scoreboard: Schmidt Powers Katahdin, Presque Isle and Caribou Earn Shutout Wins
Conor Schmidt turned in another big offensive performance for Katahdin, while Presque Isle and Caribou both earned shutout victories to highlight Saturday's Aroostook County high school soccer action.
Schmidt finished with three goals and two assists as the Katahdin boys rolled past Shead 8-0. Presque Isle's girls blanked Ellsworth 2-0, while the Caribou boys earned a 2-0 victory over Hermon.
Saturday also brought a double-overtime battle between Katahdin and Shead in girls soccer and another overtime result for the Presque Isle boys.
Here is a look at the County action.
Girls Soccer
Presque Isle 2, Ellsworth 0
Presque Isle picked up an important road victory Saturday, shutting out Ellsworth 2-0.
Carrlyn Buck and Peyton Boinske scored for the Lady Wildcats.
Delanie Cyr added an assist, and Sammi Argreaves with her 5th shutout of the season.
Presque Isle's defense did the rest, keeping Ellsworth off the scoreboard and adding another clean sheet to the Wildcats' season.
Fort Kent 4, Penobscot Valley 1
Fort Kent earned another strong victory Saturday, defeating Penobscot Valley 4-1.
Shead 2, Katahdin 1, 2OT
Katahdin and Shead needed two overtime periods to decide Saturday's matchup before Shead came away with a 2-1 victory.
Ashland 6, Schenck/Stearns 1
Ashland continued its strong late-season stretch with a 6-1 victory over Schenck/Stearns.
Hermon 10, Caribou 2
Hermon came away with a 10-2 victory over Caribou.
Carly Levesque and Peyton West scored the goals for the Lady Vikings.
Boys Soccer
Katahdin 8, Shead 0
Conor Schmidt led another offensive explosion for Katahdin with three goals and two assists in an 8-0 shutout victory over Shead.
Blake Rush added two goals and an assist.
Bryten Hartsgrove, Leighton Rodgerson and Gabe Landry each finished with a goal and an assist.
Gage Phillips made four saves in goal to preserve the shutout for the Cougars.
Caribou 2, Hermon 0
Caribou answered Hermon's win in the girls matchup by shutting out the Hawks 2-0 in boys action.
The victory gave the Vikings another important result as the Class B North regular season moves toward its final stretch.
Fort Kent 3, George Stevens Academy 1
Fort Kent picked up a 3-1 victory over George Stevens Academy on Saturday.
Ellsworth 2, Presque Isle 2
Presque Isle and Ellsworth could not be separated Saturday, finishing in a 2-2 draw.
Pruet Dionne and Jackson Greaves scored for the Wildcats.
Schenck/Stearns 5, Ashland 0
Schenck/Stearns earned a 5-0 victory over Ashland in boys action.
Lee Academy 3, Houlton 2
Houlton battled Lee Academy in a close contest before the Pandas came away with a 3-2 victory.

title: Patriots place WR Mack Hollins on injured reserve
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots were without their top performing receiver when they host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins was placed on injured reserve Saturday with a calf injury. Also sent to IR was fullback Reggie Gilliam, who is dealing with ankle and knee injuries.
Both players must sit out for at least the next four games. The moves came a day after starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck) were ruled out for Sunday’s game.
In Hollins the Patriots lose their leader in receptions (15) and yards (209). Patriots receiver A.J. Brown has been on injured reserve since suffering a high-ankle sprain in the season opener at Seattle. He is eligible to return to practice next week.

title: Vets say owners often miss this sign of dog dementia
text:
Signs your dog may have dementia, according to vets
It’s not fatal, but it can affect your pup’s quality of life.
Signs your dog may have dementia, according to vets
It’s not fatal, but it can affect your pup’s quality of life.
If you’ve ever had a family member or loved one who experienced dementia, then you know just how difficult it can be for them, their caregivers, and others around them. Canine dementia is much like that for our furry companions, says Cathy Alinovi, D.V.M., a veterinarian at Healthy Pawsibilities in Clearwater, Florida.
Related video above: Are Pets Protecting Our Brains as We Age?
Doggy dementia, or canine cognitive dysfunction (CCD), “really is a similar process,” says Alinovi. “In the elderly, regardless of the species, the brain doesn’t work as well as it did when the animal or human was young. And aging brains don’t process information as well, sometimes leading to confusion.” Remembering that dementia is essentially changes in brain function can help pet parents cope, she adds.
There is no exact cause known for dementia in dogs, aside from simply an aging brain, says Alinovi. That’s why it helps to watch for symptoms to manage them as they come.
Symptoms of dementia in dogs
Symptoms of CCD vary from dog to dog, but most pet parents tend to notice changes in their dog’s behavior or routine, says Sarah Amblard, D.V.M., veterinarian at Marathon Veterinary Hospital in Marathon, Florida.
The acronym DISHAAL can serve as a helpful reminder for common symptoms:
- Disorientation
- Abnormal Interactions
- Sleep/Wake Cycle Disturbances
- House Soiling
- Activity Changes
- Anxiety
- Learning or Memory Changes
Dementia symptoms in dogs can include getting stuck in corners or behind furniture, wandering, staring at the wall, or becoming extra clingy. Your pup may also begin pacing, whining, and barking at night, while sleeping less during the day.
“My childhood dog developed canine cognitive dysfunction as she got older, and one of the first signs we noticed was that she would pace and whine at night,” explains Amblard. “At first, it was easy to wonder if something else was bothering her or if she simply needed to go outside. As it became a recurring pattern, though, we realized that her sleep-wake cycle and nighttime behavior were changing. That experience really stuck with me because cognitive dysfunction can start with changes that seem relatively minor or easy to chalk up to just getting old.”
On the flip side, these symptoms don’t always signal dementia—sometimes it truly does mean your dog is just getting older. Alternatively, these same signs could indicate another problem, like pain, a neurologic condition, or urinary issues.
Is dementia in dogs fatal?
While not technically fatal, CCD is a progressive condition, says Amblard. Although dogs can live for years after the first signs of symptoms, the issues become more noticeable over time.
“As the disease progresses, cognitive decline can have a greater impact on a dog’s quality of life,” says Amblard. “Every dog progresses differently, so there is no specific timeline that applies to every dog with dementia.”
It ultimately comes down to paying attention to how your dog is behaving and their quality of life, as well as regularly chatting with their veterinarian, who can give insight into how far the disease may have progressed.
How to manage dementia in dogs
Sadly, there’s currently no cure for canine dementia, but there are strategies that can help you manage their symptoms. Veterinarians can prescribe selegiline, a medication that may help control some CCD symptoms, including sleep issues or disorientation, though not all dogs respond to it, says Amblard.
Diet can also help manage symptoms, says Alinovi. She suggests feeding your dog a brain-healthy diet of fresh food with high-quality ingredients, such as blueberries, mushrooms, fish, oil, coconut oil, and apples.
“Most people don’t realize their pet food contains many inflammatory ingredients and these ingredients are going to impair not only brain function, but body function,” she says.
Also try to keep your dog’s brain stimulated by continuing walks, getting them outdoors frequently, offering plenty of playtime, giving them scent-based tasks, and refreshing their basic commands.
“The more you interact with them, the more they will stay connected between their brain and their body,” says Alinovi. A dog with CCD can live a fulfilling life as long as they’re kept comfortable, engaged, and out of dangerous situations.

title: Maine is wrong to bring AI into early childhood education
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the mother of a soon-to-be toddler who does part-time daycare, I am incensed that the state Department of Health and Human Services gave a contract to train Maine’s childhood educators to an out-of-state, for-profit, private equity-backed firm that is going to use “artificial intelligence” to train childcare workers instead of actual experienced people.
And to add economic injury to insult, the contract was taken away from a local group, Maine Roads to Quality, which is part of the University of Southern Maine. This group is now looking at layoffs in the middle of the worst economy since 2008.
The University of Southern Maine? Where my dad got his teaching degree; the place that set the foundation for him being a damn good teacher. BlackRock? A giant multinational private equity firm that makes money from the suffering of innocent people through its investments in fossil fuels (climate change), the arms industry (school shootings), the Chinese military (Uyghur genocide) and the Israeli military (Gaza genocide).
Listen, I get that the economy sucks right now. My wife and I are arguing about when to turn the heat on just like everybody else. I’m sure the fact that the New York organization Shine Early Learning underbid everyone else by $2 million probably looked pretty good to DHHS decision-makers. (I’d also bet a sales person had a slick PowerPoint.)
But that $2 million doesn’t just vanish into thin air. The $2 million would have been invested in local Maine educators training childcare workers. It would be an investment in our literal future: Maine children, including my son. And these savings? They’re coming because Shine Early Learning admits it’s using AI to do a bunch of the work.
The way large language models (LLMs) work is they vacuum up enormous training sets of data and writing. Much of this is stolen without compensation or consent from writers like my mother, whose books were among those found in a database of stolen books that Meta and OpenAI fed to train its artificial intelligence programs, Muse and ChatGPT.
It takes enormous environmental resources to keep data centers humming. Those data centers emit noise and environmental pollution in any community they are housed in. Where AI data centers go, electricity prices spike. Every time I open the Press Herald’s website I see a headline about yet another town banning or putting a moratorium on data centers. And the DHHS thought, “You know what Mainers really want more of in their life? AI!”
LLMs are glorified word prediction machines. And they frequently make errors. Just this week I’ve had to explain to angry customers at work that Google’s AI gave them incorrect information about our company’s services; the AI bot cited a random Instagram post as a fact. It wasn’t.
Early childhood educators are constantly underpaid and disrespected, mostly because they are a female-dominated profession and, well, we’ve been battling sexism since time immemorial. Also, most people have their own children, so they tend to think of early childhood care as “anyone can do it.” But the idea that early childhood educators can just be trained by an environment-killing lie-generating theft-powered word machine?
The disrespect is so galling that I can’t use the words I want to use in print.
Who made this decision? Do they have children or grandchildren whose education and development they care about? Was it a bunch of men? This seems like a decision a bunch of men would make. “Let’s replace a bunch of local Maine professionals with the magic malarkey generating button! Great idea, team!”
My son’s daycare closes several days a year for mandatory staff training and development. While the schedule interruption is annoying, I’m grateful that they care about their workers’ education and want them to remain engaged, up to date and constantly learning (traits I hope my son develops). If only the DHHS contract team cared as much.
I don’t believe there’s a way for members of the public, like myself, to weigh in on this trash decision other than contacting their state representatives, which I will absolutely be doing. If you have young children in your life you care about, or you just want to stop private equity from burrowing its tentacles further into our state, I recommend you do the same.

title: Week Ahead in Washington: Oct. 11
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will travel to Ohio and Alaska this week to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, while Vice President JD Vance is set to campaign in Texas.
Trump heads to Youngstown, Ohio, on Monday. Trump won the state three times, including by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. The state has reclaimed its battleground status, as incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted is locked in a tight race with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in 2024 after serving three terms.
The governor’s race is also tight, with Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy facing former state health director Dr. Amy Acton.
After stumping for Husted and Ramaswamy, the president will head to Alaska Tuesday. He is going to Wasilla to campaign for Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R-Alaska) bid for a third term.
Sullivan is facing former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) in what has turned into a close race in a state that Trump won three times by double digits.
Also on Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance is set to campaign in Tyler, Texas. He is stumping for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate bid, as well as Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s bid for a fourth term leading the state. Paxton is facing state Rep. James Talarico. Abbott is facing state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

title: UMaine’s role in pay-to-play scheme deserves a closer look
text:
ProPublica’s investigation into Sen. Susan Collins’ pay-to-play practice raises serious concerns about complicity on the part of the University of Maine and damage to the university’s research mission.
In addition to wood composites, to what extent has research at Maine’s institution been dependent on the senator’s largesse and to what extent has this largesse been determined on the senator’s need for campaign funds? To what extent does the research that the university embraces reflect the senator’s priorities and to what extent are those priorities in the best interests of Maine people and Maine students? To what extent have the senator’s priorities corrupted the university?
It beggars belief that the university’s administration did not understand Sen. Collins’ pay-to-play strategy, and the university’s claim of innocence should be thoroughly investigated.
ProPublica has played its part, and Maine’s media should now play theirs.
Tony Brinkley
Professor of English (retired), University of Maine
Bangor

title: West Bethel Makerspace grows, offers more resources
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The old Newton Tibbetts wood mill in West Bethel has found new life as a low-cost work center for crafters, small businesses and homeowners with DIY projects. It also serves as a community gathering place.
The workshop is known as the West Bethel Makerspace, modeled on other centers under the worldwide “makerspace” banner.
Such centers provide workspace and both high- and low-tech tools for people at minimal cost, saving them from having to invest in specialized equipment themselves.
West Bethel Makerspace Executive Director Dustin Sysko, a software developer and native of Newry, first became involved in the makerspace while living in the Netherlands, and continued to lend a hand when he returned to the U.S., in Somerville, Massachusetts. He then lived in British Columbia for five years.
Sysko moved back to the Bethel area four years ago, and with other volunteers last year pursued bringing the makerspace here.
“I knew we needed a community workshop,” he said.
They partnered with the mill property owners, Chris Dagdigian and Diana Lamppu, to convert the former machine shop into a community workshop at the 10 Ferry Road site.
Sysko said the couple donated the renovation of the space, a very generous offer that was key to the project. Work on it began last summer. Space for a woodshop, digital fabrication lab, multipurpose assembly/loading bay and community lounge were created. The building was turned over to the local nonprofit Jan. 1 and the work to outfit it began.
Initial equipment included a fully-equipped woodworking shop, computer numerical control router and 3D printers, as well as traditional manual and power tools and work tables. A laser cutter/engraver machine came later this spring.
The makerspace then began to offer classes on use of the equipment and other related skill classes, as well as memberships at a monthly fee. The nonprofit is overseen by a board of five people.
Most of the makerspace users so far are people doing home improvement projects, said Sysko. For example, he said, “They are making planters, shelves, signs, conversion van parts, as well as fabricating parts for home renovations.”
Since opening in late April, the center has expanded its offerings and its plans. Volunteers have made improvements to the facility and acquired many more traditional tools for a tool library. Recent additions included the gift of new laser cutters and an extra-large format 3D printer, donated by friends of the Fay School in Southborough, Massachusetts, Sysko said.
The large printer will not be ready for public use for a while, he said, but plans are in the works to use it to print ceramics using porcelain, earthenware and clay. “I’m excited about it,” he said.
Overall, equipment comes primarily from a combination of donations and items purchased by others and on loan to the makerspace, according to Sysko.
The makerspace is also offering many more classes and events on a wide range of subjects. In addition to basic tool operation, there are CNC wood milling classes, bicycle maintenance classes and themed birthday parties featuring experiments and other learning events. After the annual used ski and snowboard equipment sale at Gould Academy in October, there will be classes “on how to tune equipment, cross-country ski maintenance, and ski and snowboard maintenance,” Sysko said.
Craft offerings include a monthly last-Friday craft event intended to bring families together for crafting projects for all ages. A recent one featured using the laser cutter to cut cardboard into shapes for kids to put together and color however they wish. Sysko said more craft teachers are welcome to get in touch if they would like to offer a class.
Every second Friday there is a workshop with the group Community Mending, which teaches and offers help “on anything that needs to be fixed,” said Sysko. “The Community Mending group offers a place and time for people to get together, where we fix things and share knowledge and ways to reuse otherwise discarded personal items.” They sometimes have a specific topic for the meeting, he said.
The group first started with a focus on clothing and fabric, but then expanded.
The monthly membership fee to use the space is $65. The public may take individual classes without paying the fee. For more on the West Bethel Makerspace go to westbethelmakerspace.org.
Alison Aloisio is a freelance writer.

title: Susan Collins among 6 senators demanding Trump cancel Russian diesel plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.
“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote.
The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there’s a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said.
Trump’s announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president’s action would be in violation of U.S. law.
“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”
He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.
“This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said.
Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

title: Sad pumpkins, embarrassed stop signs and why I owe Steve McQueen an apology
text:
My shame is great
I’ve never been so embarrassed. Last week, in a state of giddiness brought on by the Wide Load Thingy being transported from Jay to South Portland, I ranted about my plans to deem the massive thing “Newman” because it makes me think of that old B classic “The Blob” starring the great Paul Newman. It seemed such a solid plan. You just can’t imagine the level of my shame when an alert and nearly-sober reader pointed out that it was actually Steve McQueen, not Paul Newman, who starred in that great old film. I owe both of those men heartfelt apologies, and it’s not going to be easy because I’m pretty sure both of them are dead.
Yet more red-faced embarrassment
I once quipped that thieves in Lewiston-Auburn are so bold they’d steal the red off a stop sign. Nobody laughed. It was a really tough crowd that night. But anyway, it finally happened. Over the weekend, somebody sent me a picture of a stop sign in the Walmart parking lot that had been completely stripped of its former crimson glory. The thing was left with nothing but a dull gray face, leaving it standing practically naked out there with other traffic signs pointing and laughing. At least that’s how I fancy things in the strange world of traffic signage when I’m sitting at a city council meeting or something with nothing better to think about.
By the way …
Did you know that the retro-reflective shade of a standard stop sign corresponds approximately to the color Pantone 187 C, which is also known as Russian Red? Or that the hex code for this particular shade is #CC0202? Well, now you know all of that and I’m sure you’ll be the hit of the room when you bring it up at your next office party. Go get ’em, you hilarious freak!
Sad pumpkins
I was appalled recently to discover that Walmart sells pumpkins. Not those classic plastic pumpkins with painted-on faces, but real, live pumpkins they just cram into a giant box and sell for a couple bucks each. I just can’t imagine what kind of life that is for a pumpkin. One day you’re sprawled in a vast green field, embraced by motherly vines with the splendor of an autumnal sun shining upon you and then BAM! Suddenly you’re on display under bland fluorescent lights while people in pajamas wander around like zombies buying canned cat food and frozen dinners. I swear, the next time I’m out buying canned cat food and frozen dinners, I’m gonna free those poor souls and set them loose in the woods.
It was the thought that counts
I had the same thought not long ago about live lobsters imprisoned in glass cases at the grocery stores. I attempted to free those guys, too. Unfortunately, it turns out that crustaceans can’t survive in the woods.
Mark LaFlamme is an award-winning Sun Journal reporter and columnist. He’s covered the nighttime police beat since 1994, which is just grand because he doesn’t like getting out of bed before noon. He is the author of eight published novels and rides a dual sport motorcycle everywhere he goes. Unless it’s winter, in which case he just sulks a lot.

title: Obituary: Anthony E. “Tony” Morgan
text:
WEST GARDINER – Anthony E. “Tony” Morgan, 79, went home to the Lord and rejoined his wife on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, with his loving family by his side.
Tony was born in Gardiner on Jan. 11, 1947, the son of late Elmore E. and Leona E. (Malaney) Morgan. He attended local schools and graduated from Gardiner High School in the Class of 1966 and EMVTI in 1968 before enlisting in the United States Navy as a Seabee.
On Dec. 11, 1971, he married the love of his life, Sally A. Knowlton. Together they shared nearly 50 years of marriage before Sally’s passing in 2021.
Tony worked as a planner at Bath Iron Works for 39 years before he retired.
Tony enjoyed hunting and fishing, snowmobiling and spending time with family and friends at camp on Great Moose Lake in Hartland. His greatest love was the time he spent surrounded by his family, especially his grandchildren.
Tony was predeceased by his wife, Sally Morgan; brother, Rodney Morgan and brother-in-law, Scott A. Knowlton.
He is survived by his son, Darrin Morgan and his wife Katrina and their two children, Harbor and Nash of Hartland; brother, Ron and his wife Carol Morgan of Pittston, sister, Lynda and her husband Herb Moreshead of West Gardiner; many nieces and nephews; and special life long friends Mel Cole, John Black and Gerald Roy.
The family wishes to extend appreciation and gratitude for the loving care of Tony in his last years to the staff of Kennebec Assisted Living and Respite and Oak Grove Nursing Facility.
A graveside service will be held on Friday, Oct. 16, at 11 a.m. at Cherry Hill Cemetery in West Gardiner followed by a celebration of life at American Legion, Post 181, West Gardiner. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Staples Funeral Home & Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Ave., Gardiner. Condolences, memories and photos may be shared with the family by visiting the Staples Funeral Home website http://www.StaplesFuneralHome.com .

title: DOJ says it's investigating whether White House TV pool's coverage halt violated antitrust law
text:
DOJ says it's investigating whether White House TV pool's coverage halt violated antitrust law
The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
Video above: Judge rules Trump administration must restore access for banned news outlets
Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the department, said group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” she said.
The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that cover the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports — a type of free speech, a pillar of American democracy.
Video below: President Donald Trump on the new White House press secretary
Last month's developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over the dayslong ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organizations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.
Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration's decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”
Taxin contributed to this report from Santa Ana, California.

title: Troy Jackson, Bernie Sanders bring ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour to Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — With just over three weeks until the midterm elections, Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is touring Maine to shore up support with the help of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Sunday’s rally at the Agora Palace Events Center marked Jackson’s second stop on the weekend’s “Solidarity Forever” tour. He held a rally Saturday in Bangor, and will make his final stop in Biddeford on Sunday evening.
He and Sanders’ remarks relied on a plea to give Democrats control of the Senate. Both focused on healthcare and affordability issues, and on a mission to support working Mainers.
“Now Troy believes, and I believe not only that healthcare is a human right, but that we have got to move toward a Medicare for All system,” Sanders said, adding that he believes President Donald Trump is “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States.”
Jackson also focused on Sen. Susan Collins’ shortfalls in her 30 years as a senator, pointing to her tendency to side with Trump and recent pay-to-play allegations.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington. She tells us that she’s one of the most powerful people in the U.S. Senate. So I think that Maine has the right to ask, ‘Well, what the hell did you do with that time?’” Jackson said.
“Trump, and the cabinet that Collins voted for, start a trade war that makes everything cost more: groceries, clothes, cars, lumber, even the equipment that Maine workers need to do their jobs is more expensive,” he added.
Hundreds of Mainers attended the event, many carrying signs with Jackson’s name printed in bold navy letters.
Their voices boomed, booing at the mention of Collins. Several wore stickers denouncing road salt — a dig at Collins’ claim that she managed to exempt the material from tariffs.
“Well, senator, we can’t eat road salt,” Jackson said, echoing a one-liner he delivered during his and Collins’ second debate on Wednesday.
Joan Schwartz, a Newcastle resident, said she’s terrified for democracy. She’s relying on Jackson to help ease her worries, especially after losing a progressive advocate in Graham Platner.
“Troy came in like gangbusters,” Schwartz said, speaking to how quickly Jackson managed to build a platform before the election. “It really speaks to the hunger that Mainers have for social justice, economic justice, addressing healthcare issues, addressing housing issues, childcare issues. Troy stands for all the things that I believe Mainers really want.”
Schwartz and fellow Jackson supporter, Greg Tangen, of Lewiston, are excited about his platform, especially his stance on Medicare and women’s rights.
But both said they wished Jackson were more outspoken about the war in Gaza, though Sanders reassured voters during his speech that he and Jackson share a common goal to end U.S. aid to Israel.
Sunday’s lineup also included Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline, a nurse who was terminated from Central Maine Medical Center amid a unionization effort, Lewiston City Councilor Safiya Khalid and David Sullivan, vice president of the IAM Union, which serves workers at Bath Iron Works.
“Donald Trump will go down as the worst president ever. We’re sending Troy to help restore sanity to our country. But Troy can’t do it alone. As we vote for Troy, we need to vote for Democrats up and down the ticket,” Sheline said.

title: Obituary: Roger B. Ouellette
text:
AUGUSTA – Roger B. Ouellette, 94, of Augusta, passed away on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at the Maine Veterans home in Augusta.
Roger was born March 31, 1932, in Lewiston, Maine, the son of Albert and Bernadette (Bergeron) Ouellette and attended local schools. He was employed for many years at the former Knapp Shoe and then Phillips-Elmet. He was mobilized with the Second Tank Battalion for the Berlin Crisis in 1960 and served for over 35 years in the Army National Guard.
He was predeceased by his parents; brother Gerry, sister Theresa; wife Nancy (Sylvain); son, Michael; and grandson, Nicholas.
He is survived by his sisters Jeanine and her husband Leo, Lorraine, and his brother, Maurice. He is also survived by his children Linda (Jenkins), Ken, and Bryan; as well many grandchildren; and great-grandchildren.
The family appreciates the staff and the Maine Veterans home for their professionalism and compassion recently (during Roger’s most recent stay). We also want to thank the staff of Togus VA for their care and support during these past few years.
Funeral services honoring Roger’s life will be celebrated on Monday, Oct. 19, at 11 a.m. at The Fortin & Pinette Group in Auburn. Committal services will then follow at St. Peter’s Cemetery. title: Trump suggests renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean: Here’s what he said

“We could call it Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americans. Something like that ... We have to. We should have before I get out,” he said.
Last year, he renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. In August, he also renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America.

“He did a good job of setting up that sucker a long time ago,” he said.
The president also said he would not change the name of the Mississippi River.
“Now, I’m not changing the name of the Mississippi. I love Mississippi. We won that state by so much,” he said.
The president can use executive authority to rename bodies of water and other geographic features.

title: Indian Township man charged with murder after fatal shooting
text:
INDIAN TOWNSHIP, Maine (WABI) - A man has been taken into custody following a fatal shooting in Indian Township on Saturday night.
Police say Cory Fields, 41, of Indian Island, was found dead at a home on Peter Dana Point Road.
An investigation led to the arrest of Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township, according to Maine State Police.
He was charged with murder and taken to the Washington County Jail.
An autopsy determined Fields died from gunshot wounds; his death was ruled a homicide. The investigation is ongoing. Authorities have released no further information.
The Passamaquoddy and Penobscot Chiefs released a joint statement on the shooting, which reads in part: “As Chiefs, we stand together in mourning this loss and reaffirming our shared responsibility to protect the well-being of our people. Our strength has always come from family, community, peace, and love for one another. In this moment of sorrow, we must hold firmly to those values and work together toward healing, understanding, and a safer future for all our people.”
You can read the full letter here.
Fields’ cousin, Gabby Fields-Love remembered Corey as “a true friend who would drop whatever he was doing to support those he cared for,” adding he was “fiercely loyal” and loved his children. She expressed anger on behalf of the family that his life was taken.
“We want justice and peace,” Fields-Love said.

title: Maine State Police investigate homicide in Indian Township
text:
State and tribal law enforcement are investigating a weekend shooting on a Passamaquoddy reservation that left one man dead and another facing a murder charge.
Officials from the Indian Township police and fire departments responded just before 9:30 p.m. Saturday to reports of a shooting at 312 Peter Dana Point Road and found the body of 41-year-old Cory Fields, of Indian Island.
An investigation by the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit and evidence response team led to the arrest of 46-year-old Jeremy Stevens, of Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), according to a state police news release Sunday.
Stevens was charged with murder and taken to the Washington County Jail in Machias. Jail staff confirmed Monday he is being held without bail.
Fields’ body was taken to the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, which determined his death was a homicide. An autopsy performed Saturday concluded that his cause of death was gunshot wounds.
One of Fields’ friends described him Monday as a kind and caring father who worked as a roofer.
Becky Saulnier, 41, of Dedham, said in an interview that Fields loved music and being outdoors. She said she was shocked to hear about his death.
Chiefs from the Passamaquoddy Tribe and the Penobscot Nation on Sunday evening published a joint statement about the killing, saying that tribal law enforcement is working in coordination with state authorities as the investigation proceeds.
“We understand that this tragedy has raised difficult questions and that our communities are seeking answers. … We ask for patience as the investigation moves forward and for respect for the process as those involved work to determine what happened,” the chiefs wrote.
The letter was signed by Chief Amkuwiposhehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), Chief William Nichols Sr. of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk and Chief Kirk Francis of the Penobscot Nation.
“To the family and loved ones of the Penobscot citizen who was taken from us, we offer our deepest condolences,” their statement read. “We recognize that no words can take away the pain of losing someone you love. Please know that you are held in the hearts of our Nations, and that our communities stand with you as you face the difficult days ahead.”
Officials from the Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service and the Washington County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the scene Saturday, state police said.
The Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk, also known as Indian Township, is home to about 760 residents, according to census data. It’s one of the tribe’s two reservations in Washington County, along with the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point).
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 12 to add more details.

title: Maine is wrong to bring AI into early childhood education
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the mother of a soon-to-be toddler who does part-time daycare, I am incensed that the state Department of Health and Human Services gave a contract to train Maine’s childhood educators to an out-of-state, for-profit, private equity-backed firm that is going to use “artificial intelligence” to train childcare workers instead of actual experienced people.
And to add economic injury to insult, the contract was taken away from a local group, Maine Roads to Quality, which is part of the University of Southern Maine. This group is now looking at layoffs in the middle of the worst economy since 2008.
The University of Southern Maine? Where my dad got his teaching degree; the place that set the foundation for him being a damn good teacher. BlackRock? A giant multinational private equity firm that makes money from the suffering of innocent people through its investments in fossil fuels (climate change), the arms industry (school shootings), the Chinese military (Uyghur genocide) and the Israeli military (Gaza genocide).
Listen, I get that the economy sucks right now. My wife and I are arguing about when to turn the heat on just like everybody else. I’m sure the fact that the New York organization Shine Early Learning underbid everyone else by $2 million probably looked pretty good to DHHS decision-makers. (I’d also bet a sales person had a slick PowerPoint.)
But that $2 million doesn’t just vanish into thin air. The $2 million would have been invested in local Maine educators training childcare workers. It would be an investment in our literal future: Maine children, including my son. And these savings? They’re coming because Shine Early Learning admits it’s using AI to do a bunch of the work.
The way large language models (LLMs) work is they vacuum up enormous training sets of data and writing. Much of this is stolen without compensation or consent from writers like my mother, whose books were among those found in a database of stolen books that Meta and OpenAI fed to train its artificial intelligence programs, Muse and ChatGPT.
It takes enormous environmental resources to keep data centers humming. Those data centers emit noise and environmental pollution in any community they are housed in. Where AI data centers go, electricity prices spike. Every time I open the Press Herald’s website I see a headline about yet another town banning or putting a moratorium on data centers. And the DHHS thought, “You know what Mainers really want more of in their life? AI!”
LLMs are glorified word prediction machines. And they frequently make errors. Just this week I’ve had to explain to angry customers at work that Google’s AI gave them incorrect information about our company’s services; the AI bot cited a random Instagram post as a fact. It wasn’t.
Early childhood educators are constantly underpaid and disrespected, mostly because they are a female-dominated profession and, well, we’ve been battling sexism since time immemorial. Also, most people have their own children, so they tend to think of early childhood care as “anyone can do it.” But the idea that early childhood educators can just be trained by an environment-killing lie-generating theft-powered word machine?
The disrespect is so galling that I can’t use the words I want to use in print.
Who made this decision? Do they have children or grandchildren whose education and development they care about? Was it a bunch of men? This seems like a decision a bunch of men would make. “Let’s replace a bunch of local Maine professionals with the magic malarkey generating button! Great idea, team!”
My son’s daycare closes several days a year for mandatory staff training and development. While the schedule interruption is annoying, I’m grateful that they care about their workers’ education and want them to remain engaged, up to date and constantly learning (traits I hope my son develops). If only the DHHS contract team cared as much.
I don’t believe there’s a way for members of the public, like myself, to weigh in on this trash decision other than contacting their state representatives, which I will absolutely be doing. If you have young children in your life you care about, or you just want to stop private equity from burrowing its tentacles further into our state, I recommend you do the same.

title: Firefighter’s toddler son dies after he and his father hit by car while window-shopping
text:
GAINESVILLE, Ga. (ANF/Gray News) - A Georgia boy who was just shy of turning 2 died after he and his father were hit by a car while window-shopping in a shopping center parking lot, police say.
Samuel Skelton, a Gainesville firefighter, and his 22-month-old son, Knox Skelton, were window-shopping Wednesday at the Limestone Marketplace. A driver in a white SUV accidentally accelerated over a curb while parking and hit them, according to Gainesville Police.
“Samuel was there, holding his 22-month-old son, Knox. Had his back to everything, didn’t even know what was coming, didn’t see what was coming,” Police Capt. Kevin Holbrook said.
Knox suffered critical injuries and was flown to a hospital in Atlanta, where he later died. His father was also injured but did not need medical treatment, police say.
Holbrook said Samuel Skelton and his wife, Kiana Skelton, were able to get to Atlanta to say goodbye before Knox died.
“We typically compartmentalize. At some point, you can only keep that compartmentalized for so long,” Holbrook said. “And just like trying to get through this interview, it’s emotional, knowing that we lost a young child in this community.”
Fire department mourns with family
The Gainesville Fire Department released a photo of the Skelton family in a social media post Thursday that described Samuel Skelton and his wife as “humble, caring, and genuine people.”
The department said it is “heartbroken by this tragedy” and asked the community to “surround the Skelton family with love, prayers, and support as they navigate this incredibly difficult time.”
The department also said members of its staff who responded to the crash were faced with the realization that it involved one of their own.
“They, too, are carrying the weight of this tragedy,” the department said.
Members of the fire department have organized a fundraiser to support Samuel and Kiana Skelton. It had raised more than $65,000, as of early Sunday.
Investigation into crash continues
Police say the driver, a 68-year-old woman, stayed on the scene and cooperated with officers. She is not currently facing charges.
“This was just a tragic accident, altogether. You had an elderly female who did not intentionally do this,” Holbrook said.
Officials have the car as evidence and are investigating its brakes and tires. They will also review cellphone data.
Holbrook said that after the investigation, the case will be handed over to the district attorney or solicitor general, and it is only then that the driver could face criminal charges.
Holbrook said an answer on potential charges could come within weeks.
