title: Drake Maye’s big day leads Patriots past Raiders
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye didn’t have his top receiver, and the New England Patriots were missing both of their starting cornerbacks.
The third-year quarterback found plenty of other targets, and his defense still found a way to slow down Kirk Cousins and the Las Vegas Raiders.
Maye threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score, helping the Patriots pull away in the second half of a 45-17 victory on Sunday.
Maye was 26 of 34 for 374 yards passing in the second 300-yard game of his career. Two TDs went to Pop Douglas and one each to Hunter Henry and Kyle Williams.
Rhamondre Stevenson added a scoring run in a second consecutive victory after a sluggish start for the defending AFC champions.
With receiver Mack Hollins missing the first of at least four games with a calf injury, Maye had five players catch at least three passes, including Stevenson. Two pass-catchers who didn’t score — Efton Chism III and Eli Raridon — each had five catches for 57 yards.
“It was beautiful to be a part of today,” Maye said. “There’s still some out there.”
On a day the Patriots celebrated the 25th anniversary of the first of their six first Super Bowl championships, Maye became the first with back-to-back games of at least three TDs passing for New England since Tom Brady in 2018. It was also Maye’s first game this season without a turnover. He scored on a 3-yard run.
The Patriots (3-2) finished with season-high 536 yards, and the defense held Las Vegas under 26 points for the first time this season without injured cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III.
“That’s what it has to be,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “They realize when you get an opportunity, you do something with it.”
Cousins was 19 of 28 for 243 yards with a touchdown to Brock Bowers that pulled the Raiders (3-2) even early, but they were trailing by 28 points when they finally found the end zone again in the fourth quarter.
Cousins had limited time to operate throughout the game and was sacked three times.
“They did a nice job with their pressures, getting home quickly. Made it hard for us,” Cousins said.
Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said it’s clear there is work to do after back-to-back losses.
“We’re not happy with what happened today, and we’ve got to go do something about it,” Kubiak said.
No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza replaced Cousins with the game out of reach later in the fourth. Kubiak said Mendoza’s appearance doesn’t change the QB depth chart for now.
“Just wanted to get (Mendoza) some exposure,” Kubiak said.
Scoring quickly
Four of the Patriots seven scoring drives lasted less than three minutes. New England scored touchdowns on four of five trips inside the 20-yard line.
Fast start for Patriots
It didn’t take long for New England’s offense to get going.
After a quick three-and-out by the Raiders to open the game, New England needed just five plays to cap a 79-yard drive with a 35-yard TD pass from Maye to a wide-open Douglas.
The drive included a 16-yard pass to Romeo Doubs to get the Patriots into Las Vegas territory.
The Raiders responded on the next series. First, Cousins connected on long completions to Bowers and Coby White. He then capitalized on a pass interference call on Kevin Byard that set up a 13-yard scoring pass to Bowers, who had eight catches for 110 yards.
New England kept its momentum going after Bowers’ TD, scoring on a 5-yard run by Stevenson.
Las Vegas had a chance before halftime after Corey Kiner fumbled at the New England 37. But Matt Gay’s 49-yard field goal try hit the left upright, and the Patriots took a 14-point halftime lead on Maye’s 11-yard pass to Henry 24 seconds before the break.
Injuries
Raiders: DT Tonka Hemingway left in the first quarter with a neck injury and was ruled out. … DE Patrick Johnson (neck) left in the second quarter.
Patriots: RB TreVeyon Henderson limped to the locker room in the second quarter with an ankle injury. Two plays later, LT Will Campbell was helped off with a right knee injury. Neither returned. … CB Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Up next
Raiders: Host the Bills next Sunday.
Patriots: Host the Jets next Sunday.

title: Pennsylvania shooter who killed 8 was family’s patriarch, slain toddler’s dad says
text:
ERIE, Pa. (AP) — A man whose toddler was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, said Sunday that the gunman was a grandfather who never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary.
“I think that was a front for him,” Julius Windham said as he stood at a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting, including his 1-year-old daughter Amarianna, her pregnant mother and the woman’s 5-year-old son and unborn baby.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just — you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.
The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.
Those killed include 2 women outside the home
Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 p.m. Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words, “Forever In My Heart.”
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.
Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the 5-year-old boy and 1-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Police decline to discuss motive as investigation continues
Erie is about 120 miles (190 kilometers) north of Pittsburgh.
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”
Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, said they’ve known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything.”
“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie Mayor Daria Devlin addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.
“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier. … Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”

title: Death Notice: Normand R. Lamie
58th annual Fall Foliage Festival supports coastal Maine history
text:
BOOTHBAY, Maine (WABI) - There was lots of red, orange and gold at one coastal Maine this weekend with businesses from all over helping to support an important piece of history. Autumn colors were in full swing at the 58th annual Fall Foliage Festival, held at the Boothbay Railway Village Museum.
The 35-acre museum was founded in 1964 by Maine preservationist George McEvoy, who had a passion for locomotives.
“There is over 100 years of Maine history here. It’s not your average museum where families come and kids can’t run free. It’s there’s a lot of hands on and we do a ton of community events throughout the year,” said Lori Reynolds, Marketing and Event Coordinator for the Boothbay Railway Village Museum. much history from around the state that has ended up here for permanent archival.”
The festival helps to support the museum, with around a hundred vendors spanning from Boothbay to other regions of Maine.
“I have been coming here for 25 years with my pickles and jam. It’s been a lot of fun. I’m seeing a lot of familiar faces from over the years. A lot of people look for me specifically here, and it’s always great to see them come in and remember their favorite flavors,” said vendor Sarah Brewer of Slice O’Country.
“We like the historical context and hearing the train going around and seeing the steam and everything from the train,” said Renee Brown of Misty Mountain Farm, “We like looking at all of the different historical buildings and everything they have on display.”
“The Boothbay Town Hall is the real original Boothbay building town hall that was built in 1847, and they moved it here and they moved a lot of buildings here,” said Reynolds.
Organizers say it was also a great day for families to get out during peak foliage season.
“We’ve always had that beautiful foliage view while we’re enjoying the festival. Being outdoors in the nice crisp fall air, we have hot cider here, we have tons of great food, that whole vibe of just enjoying fall in New England,” said Reynolds.

Obituary: Selma Nelson
text:
LEWISTON – Selma Nelson, former, and formidable, English teacher at Lewiston High School, passed away at home on Sept. 29, 2026, at the age of 96.
Selma was born on Feb. 2, 1930, in Brooklyn, N.Y., the only child of Adolph Wagner and Rachel Lowenstein Wagner. She attended Brooklyn College where she earned her BA, and then went on to study for an MA in English Literature at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.
Born with a bold and adventurous spirit, Selma was on the road before Jack Kerouac made it popular. In her 20s she held a variety of jobs, from waitressing in the Catskills, to working retail in Manhattan or a carnival in California, to picking beans in Canada, though her sharp wit, and willingness to say what she felt, left her poorly suited for many such positions.
In 1957 Selma married David Nelson, a fellow graduate student at Cornell. Their daughter, Stephanie, was born the following year. They moved to Lewiston when David was offered a position in the English Department at Bates College. Their son, James, was born in Lewiston in 1962. The following year the Nelsons built their house on Franklin Street, a home Selma would occupy for the next 63 years.
In the mid-1960s Selma began teaching English, first at night school and then at Lewiston High School, where she found her true calling. For more than three decades she taught World Lit, British Lit, and courses of her own devising, such as Humor and Satire, and touched the lives of generations of high school students. More than a few of her former students attributed their success in college to the rigorous academic training they had received from Selma. Along with teaching, Selma supervised the literary magazine Collage, co-directed the senior play and for many years led the senior class trip to London (sometimes London and Paris), a city she knew well and loved.
In the 1980s Selma earned a master’s degree in Art History from the University of Maine. She retired from teaching in 1998.
Selma Nelson is survived by her daughter Stephanie, her son James and his wife Lisa; her four grandchildren, Elizabeth Lockard, Nathaniel Nelson, Jonathan Nelson, and Abigail Nelson; and her three great-granddaughters, Felicity Lockard, Victoria Lockard, and Penelope Lockard.
An open house/memorial gathering will be held on Oct. 17, 11 to 3 p.m. at Selma’s home, 101 Franklin St. in Lewiston. All are welcome to drop in during those hours and join in the celebration of her life.
Arrangements are in the care of The Fortin & Pinette Group, 305 Alfred A Plourde Parkway, Lewiston.
Condolences and memories may be shared with Selma’s family and friends on the obituary page of the funeral home website. http://www.dignitymemorial.com/3558

title: Agents tear-gas protesters after group blocks ICE vehicles
text:
SALEM, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A group of protesters confronted federal agents working with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Oregon on Saturday morning, according to police.
At 9:30 a.m., federal agents reported to the Salem Police Department that about 30 people had surrounded their vehicles and were blocking them in with cars near Lancaster Drive Northeast and Sunnyview Road Northeast.
While Salem officers were on their way to the area, agents told police they had cleared the crowd using tear gas and driven away.
Meanwhile, 911 received multiple calls about people suffering from tear gas-related medical issues, including difficulty breathing.
Once at the scene, police and crews with the Salem Fire Department gave people first aid and then began investigating the incident, according to police. That information will then be passed on to the Oregon Department of Justice and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
“Salem Police Officers had no prior knowledge of the activity in this incident and did not coordinate in any way with Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” Salem police said. “Our officers respond to disturbances such as this solely to de-escalate, provide medical aid when necessary, and collect evidence so that the appropriate oversight agencies can conduct their review.”
Congresswoman Andrea Salinas issued a statement on Saturday afternoon, in which she says ICE operations are not making Oregon communities safer.
“ICE’s actions today were reckless and needlessly endangered innocent people. As part of today’s operations, ICE deployed pepper spray, pepper balls, and smoke canisters against the elderly and children. They followed and harassed U.S. citizens, and they drove recklessly with a blatant disregard for the safety of other drivers. At one point, they shut down 99E and nearly caused several accidents,” Salinas said in her statement.
This comes after immigration rights groups and advocates reported a recent surge in detentions and arrests by federal agents across Oregon.

title: Overnight crash in Gray leaves one dead, others injured
text:
GRAY, Maine (WABI) - A person was killed after a crash on I-95 north in Gray Friday night.
It happened just before midnight on the northbound side of the interstate.
State Police say the driver, 31-year-old Megan Stuart of Auburn was driving north when she swerved to avoid a deer and lost control.
Another car driving north then crashed head-on into Stuart’s car.
Officials say Stuart was taken to a Portland hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
State Police say the passenger in Stuart’s car, 38-year-old Soda Mao of Auburn died at the scene.
We’re told the driver and passenger in the other car suffered minor injuries.

title: Trump: Russia and Ukraine agreed to an ‘energy ceasefire,’ specifics on terms unknown
text:
Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an ‘energy ceasefire’ but Kyiv says attacks continue
U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
Related video: Trump says Ukraine should "get a new leader" after striking diesel deal with Russia
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.”
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponizing winter.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin “had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet.’ We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world.”
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC’s “This Week.”
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
Trump spars with Zelenskyy
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
“Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
“With all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
Ukrainian strike on Russian data center triggers outages
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.
Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.
“I’d press the ‘call’ button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said. “There’s nothing I can do, so I’m just forced to cancel.”
Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said.
Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a “direct impact” and weren't just about “convenience.” He said they affected “healthcare, and everything else.”
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company’s major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.
Zaporizhzhia death toll rises to 23
Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, Ivan Fedorov, the former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council, said Sunday.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.
Morton reported from London.

title: It's not too late to cross the Fryeburg Fair off your fall bucket list
text:
Last weekend to get out to the Fryeburg Fair
The fairgrounds open at 7 a.m., but many buildings don't open until 9 a.m. The fair will stay open until 9 p.m.
Last weekend to get out to the Fryeburg Fair
The fairgrounds open at 7 a.m., but many buildings don't open until 9 a.m. The fair will stay open until 9 p.m.
This weekend is the last opportunity to see the Fryeburg Fair before it closes down again until next year, and there's still plenty to do and see.
The fairgrounds open every day at 7 a.m., but many buildings don't open until 9 a.m. The fair will stay open until 9 p.m.
Animals will still be seeing a lot of action on Sunday with shows, scooting contests, ox and horse pulling.
At 1 p.m. there is a chocolate chip cookie contest, and food stalls are all still open. The midway, with it's thrill rides and games, continues to be open.
For a full schedule of events, you can see the 2026 program here.
For those looking to show off their more crafty side, the flower show is holding several exhibits where spectators can watch florists design elaborate arrangements live. Afterward, the arrangements get auctioned off.
"We try to get that crowd involved and they tell us what they want. So, last year it was Halloween, Halloween, Halloween, which really kind of surprised me," said Rhoda Burke, one of the florists working at the fair.
The flower show is holding expos at 10 a.m., noon, and 2 p.m.
The arrangements aren't limited to live and artificial flowers. Many of their arrangements include items like statuettes, ornaments, stuffed animals-- one arrangement even used pillow stuffing to look like artificial snow.
Burke says it has become a community within the larger Fryeburg Fair community.
"It's amazing how they help us and they look forward to bringing back containers because we upcycle them. Or they'll bring us a set of something," Burke said. "They like to challenge us on a design and they have as much fun with us as we have with them."
Next year, the fair will be open from Oct. 3 to Oct. 10.

title: Dixfield man drowns while kayaking in Roxbury
text:
A Dixfield man died after apparently falling out of his kayak Saturday on Ellis Pond in Roxbury, officials said.
The Maine Warden Service was notified shortly after 4 p.m. of a possible drowning.
Shawn Noyes, 20, had been kayaking with his family, Lt. Dan Menard wrote Sunday in a Maine Warden Service news release.
Noyes was seen in the water attempting to swim to a nearby island, when he disappeared and was feared drowned.
The air temperature Saturday was in the mid-50s and the water temperature would have been even colder. A person entering water at such temperatures would experience cold water immersion syndrome, which can lead to a loss of motor control within minutes.
The Maine Warden Service conducted a search Saturday evening with the help of the Roxbury, Mexico and Rumford fire departments.
Noyes’s kayak and life jacket were recovered from the pond.
 On Sunday, the Maine Warden Service dive team recovered Noyes’s body; he was not wearing a life jacket. The Maine Warden Service said everyone should wear life jackets while recreating
on the water.

title: Death Notice: Doris L. Violette
Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove nodule on lung
text:
Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove nodular lesion on his lung
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery “in the coming days” to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate.
Related video: Pope Leo says he isn’t panicking over AI, but warns of its power
The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
The Vatican didn’t say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it.
A nodule can be benign or malignant
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
“Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.
"When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis,” he said.
If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview.
"It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, “doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it."
He thanked the faithful "for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”
Surgery to be at the pope's hospital
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Francis' illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope's health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days.
This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted.
A nodule doesn't mean cancer but should be investigated
Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn't mean lung cancer. And in fact “a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer."
But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. "The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule,” he said in an interview.
Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said.
"In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery,” he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications.
Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking.
Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage “the aim … is curative,” he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy’s private Sky TG24.
“When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere,” he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.
“Being physically fit and healthy is certainly an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery,” he added.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, for Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days.” In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.
—-
Barry reported from Milan; AP reporter Danica Kirka contributed from London.

title: A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Two years after his release from prison, Patrick Dewayne Smith spends Sundays with his family in a modest brick church with a white steeple in rural Tennessee. He works two jobs. He goes to ball games to cheer for nieces and nephews he had never met. After serving 13 years for a nonviolent drug conviction, he is trying to rebuild his life.
Now Smith could be sent back to prison for the rest of it.
A federal judge released him in 2024 under rules adopted after Congress passed the First Step Act, a landmark criminal justice law during President Donald Trump’s first term. But the Supreme Court ruled in May that people sentenced under older, harsher laws cannot rely on the disparity between their sentences and current penalties to seek early compassionate release.
“Every time I get a call, I’m hoping it’s some good news. Or, you know, at least not no bad news,” said Smith, a tall, soft-spoken 47-year-old whose beard is now flecked with gray.
Smith is among about a dozen people nationwide who could be returned to prison because of the ruling, according to FAMM, a sentencing reform group formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums. Without clemency from the White House, the group says, second chances could disappear for those people.
The First Step Act opened a path to freedom
The First Step Act was the most significant rewrite of federal sentencing laws in a generation. Among other changes, it reduced some lengthy mandatory minimum sentences, particularly for nonviolent drug crimes. Trump said the law would “make our communities safer and give former inmates a second chance at life after they have served their time.”
The law was championed by Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and senior adviser who had a personal connection to the issue: Kushner’s his father had spent time in federal prison when Kushner was younger.
Thousands of people have been released from prison in the years since the law was passed, but some recent Supreme Court rulings have made it harder for other people already serving long sentences to argue for their release. For Smith and others like him, competing interpretations have created a high-stakes legal limbo.
“They’re doing everything that they should be doing. They’re reestablishing relationships with families. They’re volunteering in their communities. They’re working,” said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM’s general counsel. “Having them reincarcerated is so unjust given that they have demonstrated their rehabilitation.”
Without a grant of clemency from the White House, Rifkin says their second chance could be snatched away.
Trump remains proud of signing the First Step Act, and the administration is actively reviewing developments, said a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorize to speak publicly on the issue.
Supreme Court ruling narrows options for people serving long sentences
In 2023, the U.S. Sentencing Commission adopted new rules for people serving unusually long sentences. Judges could sometimes consider changes to the law when deciding whether to grant compassionate release to inmates who had served at least 10 years.
Not everyone agreed.
The Department of Justice argued the new rules went beyond what the First Step Act allowed. Judges nevertheless agreed to free dozens of people across the country after considering legal changes and other factors, FAMM found.
The dispute eventually went all the way to the Supreme Court, which handed down a 6-3 decision in May. It found that sentencing disparities from decades past are not “extraordinary and compelling” reasons to grant compassionate release.
“It is hard to see how Congress’s deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that ‘warrant(s)’ a reduction,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for the conservative majority.
The decision was one of two during the last Supreme Court term that narrowed the options for people serving long sentences, said Daniel Harawa, a law professor at New York University. “I worry a lot about what this means for federal criminal justice reform,” he said.
For Smith and about a dozen other people around the country, it could mean they have to finish serving a sentence that would not be handed down today.
Prior convictions meant a life sentence
Smith grew up in a small town in rural northern Alabama and became addicted to drugs as a teenager, his lawyers said in court documents. At 17 he was arrested for twice selling crack cocaine to an informant. A pair of marijuana convictions followed a few years later. He served about three years in prison. After his release he worked as a construction worker and a janitor.
In 2010, he got involved with a drug ring selling crack cocaine and marijuana on the Tennessee-Alabama line, prosecutors said. Caught on phone calls recorded by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, he was convicted of drug conspiracy and money laundering after he pulled out of a plea deal that called for 12 years to 14 years in prison in exchange for his cooperation.
His lawyers called his involvement “unremarkable,” but the federal conviction combined with his prior record triggered a life sentence.
The judge questioned whether the punishment fit the crime, but said the laws tied her hands. It was the longest sentence linked to the 20-person case, exceeding even the ringleader’s.
Smith said he resolved to keep his head down behind bars, working prison jobs and avoiding infractions.
“What kept me sane was that faith, that belief in God,” he said.
He missed little things, like sleeping in a full-sized bed and taking a bath after a long day. He missed big things, too: His mother died during his first year in prison and he couldn’t ask his family to shoulder the $1,000 it would cost for him to travel home for the funeral.
After 13 years, Smith got his second chance
After the Sentencing Commission adopted its new compassionate release rules following the First Step Act, Smith asked a judge for a reduction to time served. It took nearly a year, but the court agreed he should go free.
He returned to Alabama and moved in with his sister and her daughter.
Last month, prosecutors filed court documents challenging his release and they pointed to the Supreme Court decision. They argued he would be subject to a mandatory-minimum sentence of 25 years, even under current laws, and called the judge’s decision to release him “difficult to justify.”
A Justice Department official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing case said Rutherford’s case means his release is no longer valid, and the department cannot agree to a sentence below what the law requires.
The prospect of a return to prison is a bitter pill for his father, James Smith, a mainstay at the Willow Grove Missionary Baptist Church.
“When you got rapists and murderers and you get this guy on a nonviolent case and you want him for life,” he said, “it doesn’t sit well with me.”
___
Associated Press video journalist Kristin M. Hall in Nashville, Tenn., contributed to this report.

title: Drake Maye’s big day leads Patriots past Raiders
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye didn’t have his top receiver, and the New England Patriots were missing both of their starting cornerbacks.
The third-year quarterback found plenty of other targets, and his defense still found a way to slow down Kirk Cousins and the Las Vegas Raiders.
Maye threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score, helping the Patriots pull away in the second half of a 45-17 victory on Sunday.
Maye was 26 of 34 for 374 yards passing in the second 300-yard game of his career. Two TDs went to Pop Douglas and one each to Hunter Henry and Kyle Williams.
Rhamondre Stevenson added a scoring run in a second consecutive victory after a sluggish start for the defending AFC champions.
With receiver Mack Hollins missing the first of at least four games with a calf injury, Maye had five players catch at least three passes, including Stevenson. Two pass-catchers who didn’t score — Efton Chism III and Eli Raridon — each had five catches for 57 yards.
“It was beautiful to be a part of today,” Maye said. “There’s still some out there.”
On a day the Patriots celebrated the 25th anniversary of the first of their six first Super Bowl championships, Maye became the first with back-to-back games of at least three TDs passing for New England since Tom Brady in 2018. It was also Maye’s first game this season without a turnover. He scored on a 3-yard run.
The Patriots (3-2) finished with season-high 536 yards, and the defense held Las Vegas under 26 points for the first time this season without injured cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III.
“That’s what it has to be,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “They realize when you get an opportunity, you do something with it.”
Cousins was 19 of 28 for 243 yards with a touchdown to Brock Bowers that pulled the Raiders (3-2) even early, but they were trailing by 28 points when they finally found the end zone again in the fourth quarter.
Cousins had limited time to operate throughout the game and was sacked three times.
“They did a nice job with their pressures, getting home quickly. Made it hard for us,” Cousins said.
Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said it’s clear there is work to do after back-to-back losses.
“We’re not happy with what happened today, and we’ve got to go do something about it,” Kubiak said.
No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza replaced Cousins with the game out of reach later in the fourth. Kubiak said Mendoza’s appearance doesn’t change the QB depth chart for now.
“Just wanted to get (Mendoza) some exposure,” Kubiak said.
Scoring quickly
Four of the Patriots seven scoring drives lasted less than three minutes. New England scored touchdowns on four of five trips inside the 20-yard line.
Fast start for Patriots
It didn’t take long for New England’s offense to get going.
After a quick three-and-out by the Raiders to open the game, New England needed just five plays to cap a 79-yard drive with a 35-yard TD pass from Maye to a wide-open Douglas.
The drive included a 16-yard pass to Romeo Doubs to get the Patriots into Las Vegas territory.
The Raiders responded on the next series. First, Cousins connected on long completions to Bowers and Coby White. He then capitalized on a pass interference call on Kevin Byard that set up a 13-yard scoring pass to Bowers, who had eight catches for 110 yards.
New England kept its momentum going after Bowers’ TD, scoring on a 5-yard run by Stevenson.
Las Vegas had a chance before halftime after Corey Kiner fumbled at the New England 37. But Matt Gay’s 49-yard field goal try hit the left upright, and the Patriots took a 14-point halftime lead on Maye’s 11-yard pass to Henry 24 seconds before the break.
Injuries
Raiders: DT Tonka Hemingway left in the first quarter with a neck injury and was ruled out. … DE Patrick Johnson (neck) left in the second quarter.
Patriots: RB TreVeyon Henderson limped to the locker room in the second quarter with an ankle injury. Two plays later, LT Will Campbell was helped off with a right knee injury. Neither returned. … CB Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Up next
Raiders: Host the Bills next Sunday.
Patriots: Host the Jets next Sunday.

title: Death Notice: Paul David Rea Jr.
Troy Jackson, Bernie Sanders bring ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour to Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — With just over three weeks until the midterm elections, Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is touring Maine to shore up support with the help of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Sunday’s rally at the Agora Palace Events Center marked Jackson’s second stop on the weekend’s “Solidarity Forever” tour. He held a rally Saturday in Bangor, and will make his final stop in Biddeford on Sunday evening.
He and Sanders’ remarks relied on a plea to give Democrats control of the Senate. Both focused on healthcare and affordability issues, and on a mission to support working Mainers.
“Now Troy believes, and I believe not only that healthcare is a human right, but that we have got to move toward a Medicare for All system,” Sanders said, adding that he believes President Donald Trump is “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States.”
Jackson also focused on Sen. Susan Collins’ shortfalls in her 30 years as a senator, pointing to her tendency to side with Trump and recent pay-to-play allegations.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington. She tells us that she’s one of the most powerful people in the U.S. Senate. So I think that Maine has the right to ask, ‘Well, what the hell did you do with that time?’” Jackson said.
“Trump, and the cabinet that Collins voted for, start a trade war that makes everything cost more: groceries, clothes, cars, lumber, even the equipment that Maine workers need to do their jobs is more expensive,” he added.
Hundreds of Mainers attended the event, many carrying signs with Jackson’s name printed in bold navy letters.
Their voices boomed, booing at the mention of Collins. Several wore stickers denouncing road salt — a dig at Collins’ claim that she managed to exempt the material from tariffs.
“Well, senator, we can’t eat road salt,” Jackson said, echoing a one-liner he delivered during his and Collins’ second debate on Wednesday.
Joan Schwartz, a Newcastle resident, said she’s terrified for democracy. She’s relying on Jackson to help ease her worries, especially after losing a progressive advocate in Graham Platner.
“Troy came in like gangbusters,” Schwartz said, speaking to how quickly Jackson managed to build a platform before the election. “It really speaks to the hunger that Mainers have for social justice, economic justice, addressing healthcare issues, addressing housing issues, childcare issues. Troy stands for all the things that I believe Mainers really want.”
Schwartz and fellow Jackson supporter, Greg Tangen, of Lewiston, are excited about his platform, especially his stance on Medicare and women’s rights.
But both said they wished Jackson were more outspoken about the war in Gaza, though Sanders reassured voters during his speech that he and Jackson share a common goal to end U.S. aid to Israel.
Sunday’s lineup also included Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline, a nurse who was terminated from Central Maine Medical Center amid a unionization effort, Lewiston City Councilor Safiya Khalid and David Sullivan, vice president of the IAM Union, which serves workers at Bath Iron Works.
“Donald Trump will go down as the worst president ever. We’re sending Troy to help restore sanity to our country. But Troy can’t do it alone. As we vote for Troy, we need to vote for Democrats up and down the ticket,” Sheline said.

title: The grave consequences of politicizing science
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Laura Ligouri is founder and chief external strategy officer of Mindbridge, a Maine-based nonprofit organization that uses psychology and neuroscience to support work on human rights and democratic resilience.
Democracy is more than a system for electing leaders. At its core, it is a system designed to protect human dignity and freedom by distributing power, safeguarding fundamental rights and holding those in authority accountable to the people they serve.
Democracies accomplish this not through elections alone, but through a network of independent institutions that help ensure decisions are guided by evidence, law and professional expertise.
Among these institutions are an independent judiciary, a free press, a professional civil service and an independent scientific enterprise. Each serves a distinct role, but together they make it more difficult for any individual or political movement to consolidate power by controlling how reality is defined, interpreted or communicated.
It’s no coincidence that a 2026 report by Freedom House warns that independent institutions are facing increasing political pressure both globally and within the United States. This is why the scientific community is right to be alarmed by the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules.
The concern is not simply that political actors may exert greater influence over scientific funding decisions. The deeper concern is the political capture of institutions that produce knowledge.
The proposed changes to federal research funding are often framed as a dispute over science. In reality, they reflect something much broader: a struggle over power. Throughout history, political movements have sought not only to win elections, but to shape the institutions that determine how society understands truth, expertise and reality itself.
Political power, however, is rarely consolidated through coercion alone. More often, power is secured by persuading ordinary citizens that independent institutions no longer deserve their trust. As the OECD notes, declining trust in public institutions undermines democratic governance by weakening citizens’ confidence in the institutions responsible for informing, protecting and representing them.
Appeals to patriotism, morality, tradition or partisan allegiance transform institutional disputes into questions of identity — framing universities, scientists, journalists or judges not as independent arbiters, but as adversaries in a larger political struggle.
This strategy is effective not because people abandon reason, but because it taps into psychological processes that have shaped human survival for thousands of years. We like to think of ourselves as rational decision-makers, carefully weighing evidence before reaching conclusions. In reality, we are motivated reasoners. Our brains evolved not primarily to discover objective truth, but to help us survive within groups.
For most of human history, survival depended on remaining connected to trusted communities. As a result, our emotions, identities and group affiliations often shape what we believe long before conscious reasoning begins. Under conditions of uncertainty or perceived threat, these tendencies become even more pronounced. We increasingly look to those we identify with for cues about whom to trust, what to fear and which version of reality to accept.
Once scientific questions become tied to political identity, evidence itself begins to function differently. It is no longer evaluated primarily for its accuracy, but for what accepting or rejecting it communicates about who we are and where we belong. Scientific claims become badges of group membership rather than invitations to inquiry.
Viewed through this lens, the debate over the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules is about far more than research funding.
Here in Maine, Sen. Susan Collins recently expressed concern that the proposal would allow political appointees to override scientific merit review, undermining the longstanding principle that federally funded research should be evaluated on scientific merit.
When political ideology begins shaping which scientific questions receive support and which findings receive legitimacy, science ceases to function as an independent check on power.
The deeper concern is that proposals like this risk embedding those dynamics within the institutions themselves, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which political influence further erodes public trust, and declining trust becomes justification for even greater political influence. Any and all guardrails that intervene on such processes from taking place are no longer present.
Democracies depend upon citizens having access to trusted sources of information and shared mechanisms for evaluating competing claims. In an era of social media, misinformation and declining institutional trust, that premise can feel increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet that is precisely why independent institutions committed to evaluating evidence through transparent, accountable processes have never been more important.
For states like Maine, where scientific research serves small and rural communities and supports major regional employers, the consequences extend well beyond academia. Federal research funding helps drive discoveries that lead to new medical treatments, fuels Maine’s growing life sciences economy, creates high-skilled jobs and trains the next generation of scientists, physicians and innovators at institutions such as the University of Maine, The Jackson Laboratory, MaineHealth, MDI Biological Laboratory and the University of New England.
Research leaders have warned that growing uncertainty surrounding federal funding threatens not only scientific discovery, but also the economic vitality, workforce development and medical advances upon which communities across Maine increasingly depend.
Importantly, history suggests that democratic institutions are rarely weakened all at once. More often, they are gradually reshaped through a series of changes that each appear limited in scope, administrative in nature or justified by immediate political concerns. Viewed in isolation, any one change may seem relatively insignificant. Viewed together, they can fundamentally alter how democratic societies determine what is true.
This is why the debate surrounding the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions matters, even to those who will never apply for a federal research grant. The proposal is not simply about science funding. It is about whether one of democracy’s most important safeguards — the independent evaluation of evidence — remains insulated from political loyalty or becomes increasingly subject to it.
Protecting scientific independence is about far more than protecting science. It is about safeguarding one of democracy’s most essential foundations: our collective ability to distinguish evidence from ideology, truth from propaganda and scientific process from political loyalty.

title: Saudi-led coalition says a projectile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh airport
text:
CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said one person, described as a Pakistani national, was killed, and 11 were injured in the latest attack on the domestic terminal complex at King Khalid International Airport.
The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war’s new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran’s most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels’ strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports, and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels’ use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
The toll rises on both sides
Earlier on Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday’s attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The government has previously said the dead also include four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, one Palestinian, one American, one Jordanian and one Sudanese national.
Early Monday, Saudi Arabia released videos of the moment of the strike captured by security cameras. They show people, many dressed in the white robes of Mecca-bound pilgrims, standing in line in a busy hall, while others scroll phones in a nearby seating area before a fireball erupts, following by people throwing themselves to the floor and running for safety.
An expert says the Houthis’ tactics could backfire
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they’re pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution, and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels’ pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.”
___
A previous version of this report has been corrected to show that the Egyptian killed was a woman, not a man.
___
Frankel and Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington, Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut and Omar Albam in Maarat al-Numan, Syria, contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Judy Marie (Strout) Rosenhek
text:
PORTLAND – Judy Marie (Strout) Rosenhek of Raymond passed away on Sept. 27, 2026, in Portland after a long illness.
Judy was born in Portland on July 7, 1955, to Willis G. Strout Jr. and Betty M. (Babbidge) Strout. Raised in Westbrook, she attended public schools and graduated with the Class of 1974.
Independent and adventurous from the start, Judy grew up enjoying the company of family and friends, both two- and four-legged. The tales told of her pre-teen years are all truths. She suffered a broken collarbone courtesy of the family horse, raised and sold award-winning rabbits with her father, solely navigated the shoreline of Little Sebago in a motorboat, and led the family procession along the shores of Moosehead while on the way to camp, sporting the ash basket backpack bought just for her at The Indian Store in Greenville.
In November of 1976, she married Mark Rosenhek. The couple settled in Newburyport, Mass., where they both worked, and where life in the quaint coastal community was good. In the Fall of 1978, they moved to New Jersey for new jobs, with their rough collie, Sanda, in tow.
With her husband often working away from home, and with no relatives nearby or other reliable support system, Judy’s ingrained independence and perseverance shone through. She raised three children, worked at a veterinary hospital, kept her household running, and cared expertly for her cherished cats, collies, shelties, golden retrievers and the myriads of other animals that made their way to their home.
Always aspiring to return, in August of 1994 Judy and her family moved back to Maine, where all three children attended, as Judy did, Westbrook High School. Judy enjoyed being closer to extended family and working locally as an independent animal care professional in an environment that only Maine can provide.
Judy is survived by her husband, Mark; her sons Matthew and Justin (Danielle), her daughter, Elise Gould; and her grandchildren, Jeremiah Gould and Cara Gould; her siblings, Raymond Strout (Stephanie) and Sharon Davenport (Burt), her brother-in-law, Seth Rosenhek (Edell); and her longtime family friend, Bethany Fulton.
A celebration of life will be held on Oct. 18, at the Old Robie School, 668 Gray Rd., Gorham, ME 04038 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
To share memories of Judy please visit, http://www.cascobaycremation.com
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation of your time, consumables or funds made in Judy’s name to the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland, as we know that Judy had many companions patiently waiting for her at the Rainbow Bridge.

title: Sen. Collins opposes diesel deal with Russia
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sen. Collins opposes diesel deal with Russia
Sen. Collins joined in a bipartisan letter opposing President Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia
Sen. Collins opposes diesel deal with Russia
Sen. Collins joined in a bipartisan letter opposing President Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, joined in a bipartisan letter opposing President Donald Trump's agreement to purchase diesel from Russia. It calls for the Trump administration to "immediately reverse course" on the plan.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia. I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following," Collins said in a statement to Maine's Total Coverage.
The U.S. senators joining Collins in the letter are Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-New Hampshire, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Connecticut. The senators say the administration did not consult with Congress or give any explanation for the decision.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the senators write.
This comes after Sen. Angus King called the deal "fraud" on Saturday.
On Friday, Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. He said Russia agreed to immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel "to the American and Global Marketplace," with 500,000 tons to follow in November, and another 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
In a post on Truth Social Sunday morning, Trump said Russia and Ukraine reached an "energy ceasefire," but did not give any details of the deal. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded, saying the country "welcomed" the agreement.

title: An 18-year investment pays off: Maine’s first ‘Alfond babies’ head to college
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gregory W. Powell is executive chairman of the Harold Alfond Foundation.
Eighteen years ago, the Harold Alfond Foundation made an investment of $500 in hundreds of babies born in central Maine. In so doing, we invited their families to invest along with us.
This fall, that long-term investment is paying off as these “Alfond babies,” now young
adults, are stepping onto college campuses and into postsecondary training programs for
the first time.
This milestone moment affirms something we at the Harold Alfond Foundation have long believed: that even a modest investment in a child’s future can fundamentally change their aspirations and trajectory.
Our founder, Harold Alfond, believed that every Maine child deserved an opportunity to
excel in life and that higher education in all its various forms would enhance each child’s
future. And along with it, our state. 
Harold knew, what the research now confirms and our federal government has come to realize, that children with higher education savings, no matter how modest, are more likely to enroll in and complete higher education. And that investing early in life was best as it strengthened the aspirations for success in life of parents and their children as the value of their financial investment grew over time.
And so, in 2008, we established the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, and with its terrific help began investing $500 in a college savings account for every child born in a handful of
central Maine communities whose parents opened a NextGen 529 savings account.
Building on the success of that early pilot, we then took the program statewide in 2009. Today, every baby born in Maine automatically receives a $500 Alfond Grant, which is invested on their behalf in the state’s NextGen 529 college savings program.
Since the program’s inception, our $500 grants have been awarded to and invested for more than 184,000 Maine children. Thanks to the stock market, together with our grants and the contributions of Maine families who opened their companion accounts, and matching grants by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME), total savings for higher education now exceeds $813 million.
For our oldest and first grant recipients who have started college this fall, that $500 grew to nearly $2,500. That’s five times the original grant, funds that they are now using tax-free for higher education expenses whether for a Harvard degree or trade certifications,
apprenticeships or licensing exams.
But $500, even with compound investment returns over time, was never meant to single-
handedly fund higher education. Rather, the Alfond Grant was intended as a spark to build aspirations and confidence as well as to inspire every family to join us and start actively saving for their children’s futures.
Today, a third of Maine families with an Alfond Grant have joined us and taken the critical step of opening their own companion NextGen 529 account where they are investing additional funds for their child’s education. That is where I want to focus our attention here.
If your child has received our $500 grant and you have not yet opened a NextGen 529 account, we encourage you to join us and do so. You do not need to start big. You can open a NextGen account for your child alongside the Foundation’s $500 Alfond Grant without making an initial contribution. And you can invest money into your child’s account when you are ready and in many cases receive generous additional contributions from FAME, our state’s nationally recognized NextGen 529 provider.
In the last autumn of Harold Alfond’s life, I sat with him at his camp as he looked over the lawn and lake where his great grandchildren, now off to school, had played and swam in the summer sun. We imagined how the future of every Maine child might be shaped with a $500 investment for higher education. And how with even the most modest of family contributions and the compounding of investment returns over 18 years, our children and our state would be better for it.
Harold knew he would never meet the young adults, once newborns, who headed off to college this fall. But he loved this state and he said, “Let’s do it.”
So this fall, we are celebrating the first of our Alfond babies, now young adults off to college. We are celebrating with their families, who had the foresight to open a NextGen 529 account for their children.
To those students and their families: congratulations! And to the families whose children
will follow, we hope the Alfond Grant and saving for higher education will be part of your
journey, too. An investment in your children today that opens the door to their greater
opportunity tomorrow.

title: Morgan Geyser granted restraining order against ‘true crime collector’
text:
Morgan Geyser, known for Slender Man stabbing, granted restraining order against ‘true crime collector’
A judge in Winnebago County, Wisconsin, on Tuesday granted Morgan Geyser a four-year restraining order against a South Milwaukee man she described as a self-proclaimed “true crime collector.”
Geyser was 12 in 2014 when she and a friend stabbed a classmate after a sleepover in Waukesha, Wisconsin, in an attempt to please the fictional character Slender Man.
In a petition filed Sept. 16, Geyser said the man contacted her three years ago and that they began communicating.
She said she ended the communication after learning how he was talking about her and that he was “selling things belonging to me online.”
Geyser said the man “collects and sells memorabilia related to my criminal case.” She also alleged that after she stopped communicating with him, he posted a video online showing him stabbing a photograph of her.
In the petition, Geyser said the man “collects knives and torture devices” in his home.
Sister station WISN spoke by phone with the man after Geyser filed the petition. We are not identifying him because he has not been charged with a crime.
“I hope Morgan gets out and lives a productive life, but I can’t be part of it 100%. I cannot be part of her life,” the man said.

title: Nearly 396,000 without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north to Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Hurricane Isaias swept through as the storm’s remnants caused flooding in North Carolina on Sunday, while powerful Pacific Ocean waves stirred up by Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California.
In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. It said tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina as well as dangerous surf and rip current conditions along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts.
At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north.
In Florida’s Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city’s fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Heavy rains cause problems in North Carolina
In Burke County, North Carolina, an unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton.
In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks.
Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The weather service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible.
Dealing with Isaias aftermath in Florida
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out.
With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it’s hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies.
While her home didn’t suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. “The biggest thing is our food going bad,” she said.
About 226,000 customers remained without power Sunday evening in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama, according to poweroutage.com. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he expected nearly everyone to have it restored by Tuesday night.
Rachel brings wind and rain to southern California and the Southwest
Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing unusually big waves to Southern California.
Waves battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September.
“This area is completely shattered and vulnerable,” Jack Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said.
The Pacific Ocean is abnormally warm, about 7 to 8 degrees F warmer than normal for this time of year, due to the El Niño weather pattern, said Joe Sirard of the weather service in Oxnard, California
“When we have this warm water, it actually causes the ocean to rise above the normal predicted tide levels,” Sirard said. That’s affected by Rachel’s ocean swells and wind gusts. The City of Long Beach placed dozens of 3,000-pound (1,360-kilogram) sandbags along the stretch of peninsula where waves tore apart the historic boardwalk and smashed against coastal homes.
Jazmin Evers, a 37-year-old mother who runs a pottery business from her Long Beach rental home, said the community is on edge. “Every time the tide goes down everyone just kind of takes a breath — except, of course, the people whose buildings are being destroyed,” she said. “When the tide comes back up, everybody’s nerves kind of ramp back up.” Rachel dissipated over Las Vegas as it drenched deserts across the Southwest. An inch (2.4 centimeters) of rain fell in the city Sunday, leading to gushing water and flooded streets on the Las Vegas Strip.
In the Pacific, Hurricane Simon was a Category 4 storm as it pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. ___
Brumback reported from Atlanta. Walker reported from New York. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, Jack Brook in New Orleans and Josh Kelety in Phoenix also contributed.
