title: Bernie Sanders joins Troy Jackson for ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour in Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With Election Day about three weeks away, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is in Maine this weekend, drumming up support for Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson.
The three-stop ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour kicked off in Bangor Saturday night at the Cross Insurance Center.
“Whether Troy wins or not can determine who controls the Senate and the future of the United States of America,” said Sanders during his remarks. “So, I am running around the country and others are doing the same for two goals. Number one, we’ve got to stop Trump. We got to make sure Democrats gain control over the House and the Senate, but that is not enough. We got to make sure that when Democrats do have control over the House and the Senate, they have the guts to stand up to their campaign contributors and fight for an agenda that works for working families.”
Former Maine Senate President Jackson said his priorities include protecting and expanding Social Security, supporting unions and schools, and Medicare for All.
“Look, I’ve had the honor of having some power in Maine. And for 20 years, I’ve tried to remember one thing: It was never mine. You gave it to me. My job was to use it for you. And if you send me the United States Senate, that’s exactly what I’m going to do,” Jackson said during Saturday’s rally.
Jackson responded to criticism from Collins’ campaign, saying: “They’re not going to make me ashamed of where I’ve come from. They’re not going to make me ashamed of my family. They’re not sure as hell going to stop me for fighting for yours.”
He also addressed the current senator’s record and allegations of corruption.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington. She claims to be one of the most powerful people in the Senate. And what I know is where were you when we needed you the most?” Jackson questioned. “I don’t take corporate PAC money or trade tax dollars for donations, and unlike our senator, I don’t owe Donald Trump anything.”
Speakers joining Jackson and Sanders at Saturday’s rally included Erin Oberson, co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association, and Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance.
Saturday night’s rally marked the first stop of the Solidarity Forever tour. Jackson and Sanders are scheduled to travel to Lewiston and Biddeford on Sunday.

title: Obituary: Abigail Sanborn
text:
GORHAM – Abigail Sanborn, a beacon of inexhaustible curiosity and compassion, died of cancer on Oct. 5, 2026, at home at Wilson Farm in Gorham, surrounded by family and friends. She was 73 years old.
In a favorite poem of Abigail’s – “When Death Comes” by Mary Oliver – Oliver declares that “when it’s over, I want to say: all my life / I was a bride married to amazement, / I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms.” These lines now seem an apt description of Abigail’s remarkable life, which was defined as much by her fascination with the world as her sure-handed support of just about everyone lucky enough to have known her.
Born to Patricia and Parker Sanborn in Augusta, Maine, on March 18, 1953, Abigail grew up on Woodside Farm in Sidney with her younger siblings Kate and Wilson. She took naturally to the role of big sister, exhibiting from an early age a couple of lifelong hallmarks: her generosity of spirit and her unassuming respect for others, no matter their age — or species. Young Abigail doted on her beloved Jersey cow, Odolfawn, and cherished her work with 4-H, including a winning collaboration with Kate they evocatively titled “A Cow’s Makeup Kit.”
Abigail studied at Bates College and Michigan State University, between which she spent a formative interlude with the Peace Corps in Belize. After obtaining her graduate degree at MSU, she joined her beau from Bates, Scott Balcomb, who was teaching at Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire. For nearly a decade they lived in the school dorms, where, true to form, Abigail earned a reputation as an adored surrogate parent to many homesick boarding students.
Yet the call of home couldn’t be denied. Despite living at Exeter, N.H., Abigail and Scott returned to Woodside Farm for their wedding in 1980. And as she neared the 1987 due date of her older daughter Theo, Abigail came north to Portland expressly so her first-born would enter the world a bonafide Mainer. Abigail and her family returned to Maine for good a couple of years later. They settled at Wilson Farm, where her uncle Hubbard still maintained a working dairy farm as her mother’s line had done for generations before them. Hallie, their younger daughter, rounded out the farm’s newest generation when she was born in 1992.
Ever the tireless caregiver, Abigail nursed Hubbard and cousin Miriam in their old age, taught Sunday School at the United Church of Christ, dropped in regularly at the public library, kept up with close friends from Bates, and worked at the Social Security Administration, where she braved the paperwork labyrinths that separated claimants from their benefits. For more than three decades her work brought her into homes, hospitals, and correctional facilities, where she often found herself comforting, and advocating for, people during their darkest hour. Such was her steadfast service, the state legislature commemorated her 2016 retirement with a formal commendation for her “long and dedicated commitment to the people of Maine.”
When her daughters returned as adults to Wilson Farm and Portland, with their own growing families in tow, Abigail embraced a new mantle: Abba, the term bestowed by her two grandchildren, who seemed to understand instinctively that “grandmother” couldn’t do justice to their singular connection. Otherwise, she was often traveling, reading, and watching sports – though in truth, she was less interested in the activities themselves than the relationships they nurtured. The destinations didn’t matter as much as the friends there to greet her; a fresh book always offered an opportunity for discussion with old friends; and the exact teams mattered less than the joy a big win could bring a loved one.
A lodestar for her community until the very end, Abigail was usually busy in her apron, at the stove or making guests comfortable. The day before her stage 4 cancer diagnosis, Abigail made 15 pounds of coleslaw for the church’s beanhole bean supper. Later faced with her doctor’s incredulity, Abigail answered with trademark succinctness: “It was damn good coleslaw.”
Abigail is survived by her husband, Scott; siblings Kate and Wilson and sister-in-law Sally; daughters Theo and Hallie and their spouses, Colin and Sam, respectively; two grandchildren, including Hallie’s son, Arthur; nieces Molly and Rose and Rose’s husband, Kyle; and Liliane, Kenane, and Cooper, who became family in every respect but blood.
Those hoping to help are encouraged to make their memorial donations directly to the North Gorham Public Library, where you may also dedicate books or other special recognitions in her honor. For more information, contact [email protected] or 207-892-2575.

title: Obituary: Theresa I. (Lewis) Chamard
text:
WESTBROOK – Theresa I. (Lewis) Chamard, of Westbrook, passed away on Oct. 5, 2026, in her hometown of Westbrook. She was born on April 1, 1933, in Westbrook, the last living child of the late Arthur P. and Edesse Clara (Thuotte) Lewis and remained deeply connected to the Westbrook community she loved throughout her life. She was the wife of the late Robert A. Chamard Sr., who passed away on Oct. 10, 2017.
Theresa was devoted, loving, and full of life. She built a life centered on family, hard work, and caring for others, and she brought warmth and energy wherever she went. Her days were filled with the things she loved most: knitting, cooking and baking, gathering with family, and enjoying cribbage and other card games. She especially loved holding babies, a simple joy that reflected her gentle, nurturing spirit.
One of Theresa’s most meaningful accomplishments was founding Hilltop Kindergarten in Westbrook. For 25 years, she ran the kindergarten with dedication and pride, creating a place that became an important part of many lives. She even had her own fleet of buses, maintained by her husband, a detail that spoke to the commitment and teamwork behind the life they built. She also worked for several years in the bakery at Jordan Marsh, where her care and industrious nature were well suited to the work. After that, she continued to stay involved by helping with the family printing business.
Theresa also gave generously of herself to her community. She was very active as a member of the Red Hats and the Eagles, and she served as president of the Westbrook Senior Citizens for numerous years. She also volunteered for several years as a poll worker, another reflection of her steady commitment to the people and civic life of her city.
Among Theresa’s happiest times were the summers spent at the family camp on Sebago Lake. Those days became cherished family traditions, marked by togetherness and the expectation that everyone should be there. If someone did not show up on Sunday, a phone call would surely follow. That loving vigilance captured so much of who Theresa was: attentive, deeply connected, and always keeping her family close.
She loved to laugh and have fun, whether it was telling a joke or playing a prank on a family member. It was fitting, after all her birthday was April 1.
She is survived by her daughter, Cindy L. Wilson and her husband David of Yarmouth, and her son, Robert A. Chamard Jr. and his wife Patricia of Portland. She also leaves behind four grandchildren, Carl “CJ” and his wife Mori-Ann, Christopher and his wife Patricia, Destiny and her husband Jeovani and Samantha; and her seven great-grandchildren, Joshua, Lindsey, Marissa, Logan, Andrew, Ezekiel and Zion; as well as several nieces and nephews. In their lives, and in the lives of all who shared in her love, her presence will continue to be felt in family meals, in handmade gifts, in laughter around card tables, and in the enduring comfort of being cared for well.
Theresa will be remembered with love for her devotion to family, her generous spirit, and the joyful energy she brought to her home and community. Her life was a blessing, and her memory will be treasured.
A private burial was held on Thursday, Oct. 8, at Woodlawn Cemetery, Westbrook.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend a celebration of a life fully lived at Bruno’s Restaurant, 33 Allen Ave., Portland, on Saturday, Oct. 24, from 12:30 to 3 p.m.
Please visit http://www.DolbyBlaisSegee.com to sign Theresa’s guestbook and leave memories and condolences for the Chamard family.

The festival will be running from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tickets are $5 per person.
There's only a narrow window every year to see the trees turn from green to yellow and red before the leaves fall off. One spot that has become a sightseeing tradition is the Railway Village Museum in Boothbay.
Sunday, Oct. 11 is the last day of the Fall Foliage Festival. The festival will be running from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Tickets are $5 per person. It's a separate $5 to ride the museum's steam train.
According to the museum's website, the festival will include live music, food, drinks and a maker fair with more than 85 vendors.
Organizers say the train ride is a great way to see the foliage, but it's not complete without seeing all of the museum's historical buildings.
"A lot of people maybe think it's just a train ride, and it is a wonderful train ride, but we have so much history here," said Lori Reynolds, one of the Fall Festival's organizers. "There's just so much to learn. But at the same time, you're having fun while you're doing it."

title: Fire damages convenience store in New Gloucester
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New Gloucester variety store considered a total loss after fire
Link's Variety will be closed until further notice as it rebuilds after the fire
New Gloucester variety store considered a total loss after fire
Link's Variety will be closed until further notice as it rebuilds after the fire
A convenience store in New Gloucester is considered a total loss following an early Sunday morning fire, according to the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office.
Authorities say just after 2 a.m., fire crews were dispatched to a structure fire at Link's Variety. Crews from several fire departments spent around five hours and used about 5,000 gallons of water putting out the fire. Officials say no one was injured.
In an update Monday, the Maine State Fire Marshal's Office said investigators believe the fire originated in or around the furnace area, where multiple boxes were located.
Officials said the store and its contents sustained extensive damage and are considered a total loss. The exact cause of the fire remains undetermined and the investigation is ongoing.
Fire officials and the store thank a passerby who saw the fire and quickly called 911. The store says it was her fast response that saved the store from "completely engulfing in flames."
Link's Variety is asking customers to avoid coming to the store as the investigation and cleanup continue. In a post on Facebook, the staff said, "We will rebuild. We will be back."

title: Death Notice: Claire Delisle Levine
Maine State Police investigate homicide in Indian Township
text:
State and tribal law enforcement are investigating a weekend shooting on a Passamaquoddy reservation that left one man dead and another facing a murder charge.
Officials from the Indian Township police and fire departments responded just before 9:30 p.m. Saturday to reports of a shooting at 312 Peter Dana Point Road and found the body of 41-year-old Cory Fields, of Indian Island.
An investigation by the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit and evidence response team led to the arrest of 46-year-old Jeremy Stevens, of Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), according to a state police news release Sunday.
Stevens was charged with murder and taken to the Washington County Jail in Machias. Jail staff confirmed Monday he is being held without bail.
Fields’ body was taken to the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, which determined his death was a homicide. An autopsy performed Saturday concluded that his cause of death was gunshot wounds.
One of Fields’ friends described him Monday as a kind and caring father who worked as a roofer.
Becky Saulnier, 41, of Dedham, said in an interview that Fields loved music and being outdoors. She said she was shocked to hear about his death.
Chiefs from the Passamaquoddy Tribe and the Penobscot Nation on Sunday evening published a joint statement about the killing, saying that tribal law enforcement is working in coordination with state authorities as the investigation proceeds.
“We understand that this tragedy has raised difficult questions and that our communities are seeking answers. … We ask for patience as the investigation moves forward and for respect for the process as those involved work to determine what happened,” the chiefs wrote.
The letter was signed by Chief Amkuwiposhehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), Chief William Nichols Sr. of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk and Chief Kirk Francis of the Penobscot Nation.
“To the family and loved ones of the Penobscot citizen who was taken from us, we offer our deepest condolences,” their statement read. “We recognize that no words can take away the pain of losing someone you love. Please know that you are held in the hearts of our Nations, and that our communities stand with you as you face the difficult days ahead.”
Officials from the Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service and the Washington County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the scene Saturday, state police said.
The Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk, also known as Indian Township, is home to about 760 residents, according to census data. It’s one of the tribe’s two reservations in Washington County, along with the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point).

title: Republicans want Abdul El-Sayed to be the main character of the midterms. He's happy to oblige
text:
PORT HURON, Mich. (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed, holding a handheld mic and wearing his signature V-neck black shirt, slowly shook his head as a woman at his town hall described how she burned through her savings after undergoing emergency brain surgery.
“I’m really sorry for your experience, and I hope that you’re on the mend,” said El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, after outlining proposals for guaranteed health care and paid leave.
Later that night, while talking to reporters in the basement below the theatre, his tone was far different. El-Sayed called his Republican opponent Mike Rogers a “coward,” said President Donald Trump was “afraid” to visit the state and dismissed as “dumb” a question about whether Iran or Israel posed a greater threat to the United States.
The exchanges captured two sides of a candidate who is the central figure in one of the nation’s most consequential Senate races. El-Sayed would be the country’s first Muslim senator, and he’s crisscrossing the state to counter a Republican effort, fueled by tens of millions of dollars, to portray him as a dangerous radical. But he has also embraced his confrontational side by mocking and taunting Trump and Rogers.
“If they want to make me the main character in the midterms, I’m not shying away from it,” El-Sayed said in an interview. “Run against me. See how well that works out for you.”
El-Sayed’s brash, swaggering confidence rubbed some Democrats the wrong way during a divisive primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. The former public health official has shown little interest in toning it down, remaining unapologetic about his progressive agenda and adversarial approach, emboldening supporters who believe he’s the right candidate for an angry electorate that has lost faith in the political establishment.
But his doubters fear he’ll cost Democrats control of the Senate by failing to unite his party’s disparate factions ahead of November.
“If you want their votes, you have to make nice with those people, and he’s not really doing that,” said Michigan political strategist Adrian Hemond, who supported Stevens. “Maybe he doesn’t have to. The entire theory of this candidacy has been he can remake what the electorate looks like.”
Republicans target El-Sayed
Even though Michigan backed Trump twice in his three presidential campaigns, no Republican has won a Senate race in the state since 1994.
The political landscape is no friendlier this year. Trump started an unpopular war with Iran, leading to higher gas prices. Rogers has opted for a low-key campaign with fewer public events than El-Sayed as he tries to make the race all about his Democratic opponent.
As of Oct. 10, Republicans had outspent Democrats by $78 million to $63 million in the Michigan Senate race, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. Around $40 million in Republican spending has gone toward negative advertisements, compared to only around $20 million from Democrats.
The ads portray El-Sayed as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme,” highlighting his past calls to defund the police and relax immigration enforcement. Others tie him to Hasan Piker, a popular online streamer with whom El-Sayed has appeared and who has drawn criticism for past comments, including saying that “America deserved 9/11.”
On Friday, Rogers appeared alongside Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy, who told reporters that El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey.” Rogers laughed.
Vice President JD Vance has called him “evil.” In one social media post, Trump shared a photo of himself with first lady Melania Trump alongside a photo of El-Sayed and his wife, who wears a hijab, with the caption: “Two VERY DIFFERENT America’s.”
Late Wednesday, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” and said he “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”
El-Sayed has hardly backed down. At the campaign stop in Port Huron, he taunted Trump to visit Michigan, suggesting Rogers and other Republicans were afraid the president would hurt their chances.
“Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man,” El-Sayed said.
And he responded to Kennedy’s attack by suggesting the Republican is in the KKK.
“That’s rich coming from someone who wears his bed sheets out at night,” El-Sayed posted on social media.
El-Sayed uses a personal touch with voters
Before the Port Huron town hall, El-Sayed worked his way down a line of people who couldn’t fit inside the theater, shaking hands, taking photos and stopping for conversations.
Jeff Petrucella and his wife Alice traveled from Macomb County to see El-Sayed. They described themselves as politically “middle of the road” and said they had voted Republican in the past.
“I’m pretty done with the Republicans right now,” Jeff said.
Alice said she was “looking for a change that is better for my granddaughters,” pointing to El-Sayed’s support for Medicare for All. Nor was she put off by his more confrontational appearances on Fox News.
“I think he expresses himself well. You can tell he’s a well-spoken, educated man,” she said.
Pat Kreiner was among those who waited nearly an hour to see El-Sayed. Her children had persuaded her to support him in the Democratic primary.
“My son said to me, ‘I have been living with this trickle-down economy since the day I was born,’” Kreiner said. “‘It doesn’t work for me.’”
Kreiner also expressed anger about Trump’s trade war with Canada, just across the river from Port Huron.
“We are heartsick about our neighbors,” she said. “They used to come over a lot. We don’t see them now.”
Visiting smaller towns such as Port Huron has become central to El-Sayed’s campaign, with his team recently saying he’s held more than 500 events in over 100 cities across the state.
“Go everywhere. Talk to everyone. That’s what we do,” El-Sayed said in an interview.
The personal approach has not erased all the skepticism surrounding El-Sayed, including within his own party.
His criticism of Israel and association with Piker have raised concerns among some Jewish Democrats. El-Sayed has held a series of private gatherings with undecided Jewish voters as he works to win their support.
He has also sought to strengthen his standing with Black voters. In the Democratic primary, Stevens drew more support in Wayne County, home to Detroit and its large Black population.
Ahead of Thursday’s debate, El-Sayed attended two events with Black leaders before stopping at a Black barbershop, where he moved from chair to chair talking with customers. He stopped at one point to speak with a pregnant woman, congratulating her and asking when her baby was due.
“November 8th?” El-Sayed joked. “Make sure you vote early, huh?”
The race has become about more than just Michigan
While El-Sayed has spent much of his campaign trying to win over Michigan voters, his candidacy has taken on significance far beyond the state. Republicans have made him a symbol of what they warn is an increasingly radical Democratic Party, while progressives see his campaign as a chance to prove their politics can win in a closely divided state.
At a New York City fundraiser on Oct. 5, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez cast his campaign as a test for progressives nationwide.
“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” said the New York Democrat, a potential presidential candidate.
Ocasio-Cortez plans to campaign with El-Sayed in Michigan next week, followed by former President Barack Obama on Oct. 24.
The national stakes have also drawn renewed opposition. United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with AIPAC, disclosed an initial $94,000 expenditure against El-Sayed on Friday, after spending nearly $30 million to oppose him in the Democratic primary.
And El-Sayed, despite insisting the election should focus on Michigan voters and their economic struggles, has embraced the larger implications of his candidacy.
“I am grateful for your support,” he told the audience at the New York fundraiser, according to remarks obtained by The Associated Press. He said he had two goals — “pick up a U.S. Senate seat” and “change the nature of our politics for the better.”

title: County Runners Capture Four Team Titles in Big Saturday of Cross Country
text:
County Cross Country: Houlton, Caribou and Presque Isle Bring Home Team Titles
Aroostook County runners put together a dominant Saturday on two different courses, bringing home four team championships along with several individual victories at the Red Riot Challenge in Orono and the Pendale’s meet in Hermon.
Houlton/GHCA captured both the varsity boys and JV girls team titles at the Red Riot Challenge. At Pendale’s, Caribou won the varsity boys competition and Presque Isle claimed the varsity girls title.
Individually, Houlton/GHCA’s Malachi Witmer, Caribou’s Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves all crossed the finish line first in their respective varsity races.
Red Riot Challenge
Houlton Boys Put Four Runners in the Top Five
Houlton/GHCA controlled the varsity boys 4,000-meter race, placing four runners among the first five finishers and winning the team championship with 35 points.
Malachi Witmer led the way, winning the race in 13:22.20.
Wyatt Quint finished third in 13:39.71, Logan Witmer was fourth at 13:40.40 and Brayden Drake followed in fifth with a time of 13:41.60.
Stephen Cormier completed Houlton/GHCA's scoring five in 23rd place at 15:59.20.
The Shires finished 17 points ahead of second-place George Stevens Academy. Orono was third with 61.
Lucas McPhee added a 29th-place finish for Houlton/GHCA in 16:59.80.
Fort Kent's Jaxson Saucier was 30th overall with a time of 17:00.30.
Houlton JV Girls Earn Perfect Team Score
Houlton/GHCA also swept the scoring positions in the JV girls race to finish with a perfect 15 points.
Charlotte Estabrook won the 4,000-meter race in 20:00.94.
Dalylah Mincey finished second at 22:48.95, Kaley Whitman was fourth at 25:09.28, Alaina Locker finished sixth at 25:48.28 and Sandra Quinlan rounded out the scoring in eighth.
Burlock Leads County JV Boys
Houlton/GHCA's Victor Burlock was the top County finisher in the JV boys race, placing fourth in 18:53.38.
Pendale's Meet
Caribou Goes 1-2-3 to Win Boys Team Championship
Caribou grabbed the first three individual places in the varsity boys 5,000-meter race and went on to win the team title with 33 points.
Pierce Gorneault took the individual victory in 16:45.00.
Tewolde Stewart followed in second at 17:24.95, while Peyton Gorneault completed the Vikings' 1-2-3 sweep with a third-place finish in 18:00.59.
Xander Jamieson finished 13th and Alex Searles was 14th to complete Caribou's scoring five.
Micah Menifield finished 17th and Isaac Brissette was 20th.
Caribou finished 36 points ahead of second-place Presque Isle.
Presque Isle Boys Take Second
Presque Isle packed four runners into the top 12 on the way to second place with 69 points.
Jeremy Charette led the Wildcats with a fourth-place finish in 18:02.30.
Connor Meile placed ninth at 18:28.24, Geonni Guevara was 11th in 18:58.76 and Henry Clayton finished 12th at 19:01.52.
Matthew Demarest completed the Wildcat scoring in 35th place.
Central Aroostook freshman Carlson Rolon also turned in a strong race, finishing 26th in 21:36.85.
Graves Wins, Presque Isle Claims Girls Team Title
Caribou's Emma Graves earned the individual victory in the varsity girls 5,000-meter race, crossing the line in 19:23.22.
Presque Isle then used a deep pack behind Graves to win the team championship.
Aleah Rideout led the Wildcats with a runner-up finish in 19:58.19, followed immediately by Lillian Johnson in third at 20:06.15.
Taylor York placed seventh in 20:55.44 and Marie Johnston was 10th at 22:19.55.
Meredith House finished 16th to complete Presque Isle's scoring five and give the Wildcats 31 points.
Caribou finished second with 42 points.
Behind Graves, Jenna Strid placed fifth, Isabella Albert was eighth, Gloria Dionne finished 17th and Anna Haley was 23rd.
Jade Clayton finished 18th for Presque Isle, while Lydia Bragdon was 26th.
Caribou Sweeps Top Four in JV Boys
Caribou also dominated the front of the JV boys race.
Isaac Goodwin won in 19:46.29, followed by teammates Emerson Langworthy in second, Wesley Thomas in third and Jimmy Norelli in fourth.
Presque Isle Places Two in JV Girls Top Four
Presque Isle freshmen Ashton Hughes and Macyn Morton finished third and fourth in the JV girls race.
Hughes crossed the line in 25:17.55, with Morton just behind at 25:21.86.
Washburn's Eleanora Streeter finished fifth in 26:51.15, while Presque Isle's Ellie Blackstone and Grace Hilton placed seventh and eighth.
Saturday's results gave County runners a strong finish to another busy weekend, with team championships for Houlton/GHCA, Caribou and Presque Isle and individual victories from Witmer, Gorneault, Graves, Estabrook and Goodwin.

title: Obituary: Richard A. Webster
text:
WARNER, N.H. – Richard A. Webster, 91, a resident of Fayette, Maine, and Warner, N.H., passed away, Friday, Aug. 14, 2026.
He was born on Dec. 27, 1934, in Livermore Falls, to Frank Erle and Doris (Hibbs) Webster and spent his youth on the family farm in Fayette. He was a graduate of Livermore Falls High School, Class of 1954, where he was active in Future Farmers of America, 4-H, and band playing the trumpet.
After graduation, he served in the USAF as a clerk for four years during the Cold War being stationed in Canada and New Mexico. Upon his discharge, he married Nancy Hannah Mee on Aug. 3, 1958, at 4 p.m. in South Acton, at South Acton Baptist Church. They met at a State 4-H Conference during their high school years and were married for 65 years. In the early 1960s, they moved their young family from Maine to Derry, N.H., where they resided for the next 45-plus years.
Richard was employed as a diesel mechanic and truck driver with moving/freight haulers commuting to nearby Massachusetts. He was active in his community as a Freemason and Shriner; St. Mark’s Lodge #44 F.&A.M.- Past Master, Bektash Shrine-Scottish and York Rite.
Richard and Nancy loved to travel and explore new places visiting numerous sites in North America and Europe by land, sea and air. Upon retirement, they returned to the family farm in Fayette where Richard enjoyed the company of family and friends, attending Norland Grange and North Livermore Baptist Church, and keeping himself busy tinkering on various projects.

title: Foodie Calls Are the New Booty Calls
text:
Forget late-night texts asking you to come over. Apparently, some people are swiping right for the dinner reservation.
It's called a "foodie call," and it's exactly what it sounds like: accepting a date primarily because someone's picking up the tab.
Romance is alive and well. Your free entrée? Even better.
According to a recent DatingAdvice survey of 1,016 U.S. adults, 30% said they've accepted a date primarily for free food or drinks.
READ MORE: Woman Questions Boyfriend’s Motives After He Admits Marriage Would Help His Finances
Cupid might be working overtime, but apparently, so is the dinner menu.
What Is a Foodie Call?
Think of it as the culinary cousin of a booty call — except instead of a late-night text, the main event is a dinner reservation.
A study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science defined a foodie call as accepting a date without romantic attraction simply to get a free meal.
And yes, there's a difference between being open to a little dinner-date chemistry and treating someone like a walking gift card.
Alexandra Foglia, a doctor of marriage and family therapy, describes foodie calls as existing "on a continuum of intent," ranging from genuine curiosity about another person to outright opportunism.
READ MORE: What To Do When Someone Ghosts You in a Relationship
In other words, being unsure about someone but willing to see where dinner goes isn't quite the same as having absolutely zero interest and showing up for the steak.
Who's Accepting Dates for the Free Food?
According to the DatingAdvice survey, women reported accepting foodie calls slightly more often than men, at 32% compared with 26%.
Gen Z and younger millennials reported the highest rate overall, with 32% saying they'd accepted a date primarily for free food or drinks.
READ MORE: Love Off the Rocks! Navigating Sober Dating (EXCLUSIVE)
But don't go blaming the kids just yet: Among respondents ages 65 and older, 26% said they'd done it, too.
In fact, at least one in four respondents in every generation reported accepting a date primarily for the meal or drinks.
So, while younger daters led the survey, the behavior isn't exactly a Gen Z invention. Turns out, a free dinner has cross-generational appeal.

title: Man attacked, killed by tiger after entering wildlife park enclosure
text:
LONDON (AP) - A man died Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said.
Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1:35 p.m., but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement.
The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said.
The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its “Land of the Tigers” attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter (yard) raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or playing in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

title: Obituary: Ann Marie (Hollywood) McDonough
text:
PORTLAND – Ann Marie (Hollywood) McDonough, 88, passed away peacefully on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, surrounded by her family and loving friends. She was born in Portland on April 23, 1938, daughter of the late Peter “Jimmy” and Sarah “Sally” Hollywood.
Ann attended Portland schools and graduated from St. Josephs Academy in 1956. It was during her time at St. Joe’s that she met the boy who would become the love of her life at a party where she asked him to dance. He said no. They subsequently married on Aug. 9, 1958. They lived together through fair weather and stormy seas in a wonderfully chaotic and loyal love affair for 62 years until her Joey passed away in 2018.
As a young mother, Ann achieved her dream of becoming a nurse by juggling her nursing training and raising her first two babies. She began her storied nursing career at Maine Medical Center, eventually becoming head nurse of the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit. Ann finished her career as head nurse of the Family Practice Center on India Street. Her closest colleagues say she extended the same immense level of compassion and acceptance to her coworkers as she did to her patients.
Ann was instrumental in initiating the innovative Family Medicine Residency Program, which taught young doctors the art of treating an entire extended family in addition to the patient, resulting in more successful outcomes for all. She was passionate about serving her Munjoy Hill community with love and acceptance and strove to make healthcare readily accessible to families in the area. She removed barriers to care by sparing them the need to travel to the big hospital.
When Ann decided to become an athlete in her late 30s, she began with Bonnie Pruden exercise videos on TV, transitioning seamlessly to becoming a serious racquetball player and medal winning runner. At the age of 60, she completed the Bermuda Marathon, winning first place in her age group. She proudly remembered being called to the stage as “Ann McDonough from the United States of America!” Ann participated in several Tri for a Cure triathlons, well into her 70s, raising money for cancer research.
Ann’s children and grandchildren will attest to her natural and intuitive connection with babies. She mesmerized even the crankiest of little ones with storytelling and singing. She led the children on walks in the woods and on the beaches she loved. Her 14 grandchildren are now experts in sea glass collecting. Nothing was better than a boat ride on Casco Bay or Sebago Lake with her family on board. No one loved a sunset more than Ann, who stopped everything, daily, to watch the sky turn orange and red over the lake.
The family would like to extend their heartfelt gratitude to all the staff at Cedars Sam Cohen Household for the loving and compassionate care they gave to Ann in her final days. Additionally, our immeasurable thanks to Marcelle Landry, RN, the angel who dropped into our lives when Ann needed her, bringing laughter, dancing, and love.
Predeceased by her husband, Chief Joseph E. McDonough; and daughter, Monica Ann McDonough.
She is survived by her children, Maria Kilbride, Melissa and her husband Jim Allen, and John and his wife Sara McDonough; grandchildren, Erin Kilbride and her wife Alicia Seda, Maggie Kilbride and her husband Dan O’Connell, Seamus, Keegan, and Chloe Kilbride, Amanda Nurse, Ashley and her husband Ryan Kent, Amy Allen, Meaghan and her husband Joe Phillips, Gabriella Martin, Joey, MacEllen, and Maddie McDonough, Murphy and her husband Cody Trybus; great-grandchildren, Kieran and Tiegan O’Connell, Riley and Addie Nurse, Jimmy and Tommy Kent, Harlon and Josie Phillips, Cooper Trybus; sister, Pam and her husband Wayne Webster.

title: South Bristol Residents Question DOT Decision to Fill Culvert at the Gut
text:
The South Bristol Select Board was joined by representatives from the Maine Department of Transportation at its Thursday, Oct. 1 meeting to discuss residents’ concerns about the filling of a culvert on Route 129.
In September, DOT filled the culvert located in the area known as The Gut at the bridge. At the Oct. 1 meeting, DOT representative Mackenzie Kersbergen said the department was notified at the end of July that there were concerns about a 3-foot hole in the culvert and later had a meeting to discuss options moving forward.
At the meeting, she said DOT was notified again that the road was continuing to fail on Sept. 13, and were sent out to review the situation. After considering several options, including replacing the culvert or slip lining it, the department chose to fill in the culvert based on engineering and environmental recommendations.
“We looked at the road, the culvert, public safety, taxpayer dollars, and how much it costs to maintain the culvert and lining it,” Kersbergen said. “We went through our process, our engineers, our hydrologists, our environmental for fish passage, and we followed our programmatic agreements.”
Since the work was completed, residents of the property abutting the now-blocked culvert have said it has caused problems with the flow of water in the area.
Bradley Fiske said there are also concerns about how the filled culvert would affect the working waterfront, including Parlin’s Lobster Wharf, at 2104 Route 129.
“We were all under the impression that it was going to be replaced rather than filled in,” said Christian Cotz, one of the nearby landowners.
Fiske said he saw the Maine Department of Environmental Protection was photographing the culvert this summer. The DEP said they did not plan on eliminating the culvert when Fiske asked, only relining it, he said.
When Fiske asked Kersbergen if the DOT considered speaking to the nearby homeowners when the decision was made to fill the culvert, she said it was within the department’s right of way.
“We did not go outside of our right of way,” Kersbergen said, “There are a lot of exemptions for existing culverts if you’re doing maintenance to them, this was a maintenance activity.”
Fiske also asked about whether the DOT acquired the correct permitting to continue with their work. DOT representative Joshua Brown said the department did not need a permit from the DEP because the filling was considered a maintenance activity. Because of the nearby bridge, he said the DOT were also exempt from permitting regarding fish passage.
Historically, Fiske said South Bristol residents have opposed the removal of the culvert. He cited a similar situation in the 1950s, when the bridge was taken out and there were considerations of filling the culvert. Residents opposed the idea and it was left open.
“There must be precedent setting,” Fiske said.
Cotz and Fiske said they mostly wanted to find out if the work on the culvert was final and if anything could be done to replace it. Kerbergen said the project is considered complete and DOT does not plan to go back and look at it.
Cotz then asked if anything could be done at the town level. Kersbergen said the culvert is in the state’s jurisdiction and if the residents wanted another opinion, she recommended going up the “chain of command.”
“I don’t know how far that would go,” Kersbergen said. “It’s a tricky situation and I don’t know what the best course of action for you guys is and I don’t want to speak much more out of turn because I don’t know.”
At the end of the meeting, South Bristol Select Board Chair Bruce Farrin said the town could potentially write a letter to the state to consider reevaluating the process of reinstalling the culvert. He said the town had invited state Rep. Holly Stover, D-Boothbay, and Sen. Cameron Reny, D-Bristol, to the meeting, but the two were unable to make it.
Farrin said the next steps for the select board will be discussing the letter with member Adam Rice, who was out of town during the meeting. Farrin also encouraged residents to write to the DOT regarding the issue.
The South Bristol Select Board will meet next at 6 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 8 at the town office, at 470 Clarks Cove Road in Walpole. For more information, call 563-3977 or go to sbristolme.gov.

Family and friends always knew what games were playing based on the messages they received from Michael. He was our built-in sports broadcaster.

title: Troy Jackson’s sound bites won’t be enough
text:
Jacob Posik is the political director of Maine Civic Action and the director of legislative affairs of Maine Policy Institute.
There is a fundamental difference between sounding like you know what you’re talking about and knowing what you’re talking about. In last week’s first U.S. Senate debate, Troy Jackson brought the sound bites. Sen. Susan Collins brought the substance.
This likely wasn’t shocking to anyone who’s used to hearing Jackson fumble over his words or make a fool of himself while commanding the Maine Senate.
For much of the debate, while Jackson seemed determined to land the next punch, deliver the next rehearsed line or manufacture the next campaign clip, Collins did something much less flashy but far more important. The senator demonstrated that she, unlike Jackson, understands how government works, how policy is made and the responsibilities of the office she holds.
As the debate went on, this distinction became impossible to ignore. Jackson was quick with accusations but thin on details. And when the conversation moved beyond simple political rhetoric and into the mechanics of how policy is made, his lack of substance and shallow intellectual depth became painfully obvious. The contrast was striking.
Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly returned to familiar attacks against President Donald Trump and Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Regardless of the question, he seemed more interested in delivering his next rehearsed one-liner than offering substantive answers about the challenges facing Maine families.
This kind of political rhetoric might generate applause at a campaign rally comprised of a small smattering of Graham Platner leftovers, but it’s hardly a substitute for knowledge or competence when it comes to a U.S. Senate debate.
Perhaps the most embarrassing moment came during an exchange about healthcare, when Jackson appeared to confuse the responsibilities associated with Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement.
Jackson criticized Collins for failing to increase Medicaid reimbursement rates for Maine hospitals, suggesting that her position as chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee magically gave her the authority to address the issue.
The problem? Jackson revealed he fundamentally misunderstands how the program operates and which level of government is in charge of reimbursement.
Collins correctly explained that Medicaid reimbursement rates are established by states within federal requirements. Maine has the authority to adjust those rates, meaning Jackson was criticizing Collins for something that falls substantially within the responsibilities of state government. Hopefully the irony isn’t lost on anyone.
Jackson has spent the better part of 20 years as a fixture in Augusta politics. He served as president of the Senate for six years, one of the most powerful positions in state government, helping to oversee the very legislative institution responsible for determining Maine’s healthcare policies and funding priorities.
Instead of increasing those rates to help the people he pretends to care about, Jackson and his allies went on bloated spending sprees in budget after budget. They provided oodles in subsidies to their friends in the “affordable” housing and “clean” energy worlds. They gave out “free” community college on your dime and “free” school lunches to the children of millionaires.
Yet there he stood, trying to blame Collins for a responsibility that largely belongs to the state government he once led for six years. For someone seeking promotion to the U.S. Senate, that’s an embarrassing display of ignorance.
This exchange also exposed a broader weakness of Jackson’s. It’s easy to criticize Washington for the problems Maine faces; it’s much more difficult to explain how we should solve those problems.
Based on Jackson’s statements during the debate, all of Maine’s problems would cease to exist overnight if Trump was no longer president or Brett Kavanaugh no longer served on the Supreme Court. His performance suggested he believes political outrage can substitute for legislative effectiveness.
To be clear, Collins’ record is not beyond criticism. Her decisions deserve scrutiny, and all Maine voters are entitled to question her judgment on any vote she’s cast while serving as our senator.
But meaningful criticism requires more than repeating the same accusations, delivering rehearsed insults or hoping the audience overlooks the absence of substantive policy knowledge.
More than anything, the debate demonstrated why experience and competence matter. Collins came prepared to discuss the responsibilities of government and defend her legislative record. Troy Jackson came prepared to attack Trump, Kavanaugh and deliver campaign slogans.
One candidate demonstrated the knowledge necessary to govern. The other demonstrated a meager ability to campaign.
If Jackson hopes to convince Mainers that he belongs in the U.S. Senate, he will need to offer considerably more than political theater.
Susan Collins didn’t just win the first debate. She gave Maine’s former Senate president a much-needed lesson in how government actually works.

title: Electing Troy Jackson would be tragic for Maine, America
text:
Watching the Democratic Party’s recent U.S. Senate candidate selection process makes you wonder what the party stands for. It’s obvious that little thought went into choosing a challenger to Sen. Collins. Graham Platner went from “wonderful” to “horrible,” revealing that a minimum of vetting took place. Quickly, a replacement was found to comply with Maine state law, and now we have Troy Jackson.
Looking at Jackson, it’s obvious why he wasn’t chosen initially. Watching his rather empty TV ads, you find logging experience and a mother’s love for her son, but not much more. Other personal testimonials from Jackson supporters are a steady stream of vindictiveness. The same down-in-the-mouth fatalism is seen in Senate leaders like Chuck Schumer, who spews uncooperative childishness every time he steps to the podium. What is happening to this once proud, capable party?
I believe replacing Sen. Collins with Jackson would be a tragedy for Maine and for the United States. By any reasonable measure, compared to Susan Collins, Jackson is not qualified to be a United States senator.
Please don’t let raw emotion be your guiding light by voting for Jackson. A vote for Susan Collins is a vote for an extremely hardworking, intelligent Mainer who for many years has poured her heart and soul into the state she loves and serves. Susan Collins deserves to continue as our U.S. senator.
Jon Kuhl
Camden

title: Kansas GOP Sen. Roger Marshall pays off 6-year-old campaign cookie bill
text:
Kansas GOP Sen. Roger Marshall pays off 6-year-old campaign cookie bill
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall settled his debts this weekend with a bakery in Kansas after a bill for hundreds of treats his campaign ordered for a 2020 event sat unpaid for six years.
Related video above: How the 2026 midterms could determine control of Congress
Holly Thomas, the owner of the shop that made cookies, brownies and cupcakes for Marshall's primary election watch party, said in a social media post on Friday that she will not vote for the senator in this year's election, where he is facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, after he failed to pay the $678.75 he owed her small business.
"This isn't about political parties or policy disagreements. It's about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments," Thomas said. "That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote."
Thomas said she reached out several times but never heard back, noting that the lack of payment came as her business was just beginning and at the height of the coronavirus pandemic.
"Six years later, I haven't forgotten," she said.
Marshall posted a screenshot of a payment for $1,300 on Saturday, showing that he had paid the half-a-decade-old cookie bill, and then some.
"We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double," Marshall said on social media.
Thomas confirmed a few hours later that she can "finally mark the invoice paid."
The Republican senator is facing a competitive reelection race this fall, with voters' strong disapproval of President Donald Trump and widespread economic anxiety raising the possibility that Kansas could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly a century. A recent poll by The New York Times and Siena University showed Marshall tied with Hamilton at 45% among likely voters.
The repayment of the bakery bill comes as Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist, has faced criticism over a report last month that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical debt.
The New York Times found that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills and at least 81 of those individuals were arrested for missing court dates. Democrats have leaned on the story in ads, accusing Marshall of disregarding people's concerns about healthcare costs.
A spokesperson for Marshall told the Times that the longtime doctor spent many years treating patients regardless of their ability to pay.
"Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors," spokesperson Payton Fuller said in a statement to the outlet.

title: Agents tear-gas protesters after group blocks ICE vehicles
text:
SALEM, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A group of protesters confronted federal agents working with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Oregon on Saturday morning, according to police.
At 9:30 a.m., federal agents reported to the Salem Police Department that about 30 people had surrounded their vehicles and were blocking them in with cars near Lancaster Drive Northeast and Sunnyview Road Northeast.
While Salem officers were on their way to the area, agents told police they had cleared the crowd using tear gas and driven away.
Meanwhile, 911 received multiple calls about people suffering from tear gas-related medical issues, including difficulty breathing.
Once at the scene, police and crews with the Salem Fire Department gave people first aid and then began investigating the incident, according to police. That information will then be passed on to the Oregon Department of Justice and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
“Salem Police Officers had no prior knowledge of the activity in this incident and did not coordinate in any way with Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” Salem police said. “Our officers respond to disturbances such as this solely to de-escalate, provide medical aid when necessary, and collect evidence so that the appropriate oversight agencies can conduct their review.”
Congresswoman Andrea Salinas issued a statement on Saturday afternoon, in which she says ICE operations are not making Oregon communities safer.
“ICE’s actions today were reckless and needlessly endangered innocent people. As part of today’s operations, ICE deployed pepper spray, pepper balls, and smoke canisters against the elderly and children. They followed and harassed U.S. citizens, and they drove recklessly with a blatant disregard for the safety of other drivers. At one point, they shut down 99E and nearly caused several accidents,” Salinas said in her statement.
This comes after immigration rights groups and advocates reported a recent surge in detentions and arrests by federal agents across Oregon.

title: Death Notice: Selma Nelson
The grave consequences of politicizing science
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Laura Ligouri is founder and chief external strategy officer of Mindbridge, a Maine-based nonprofit organization that uses psychology and neuroscience to support work on human rights and democratic resilience.
Democracy is more than a system for electing leaders. At its core, it is a system designed to protect human dignity and freedom by distributing power, safeguarding fundamental rights and holding those in authority accountable to the people they serve.
Democracies accomplish this not through elections alone, but through a network of independent institutions that help ensure decisions are guided by evidence, law and professional expertise.
Among these institutions are an independent judiciary, a free press, a professional civil service and an independent scientific enterprise. Each serves a distinct role, but together they make it more difficult for any individual or political movement to consolidate power by controlling how reality is defined, interpreted or communicated.
It’s no coincidence that a 2026 report by Freedom House warns that independent institutions are facing increasing political pressure both globally and within the United States. This is why the scientific community is right to be alarmed by the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules.
The concern is not simply that political actors may exert greater influence over scientific funding decisions. The deeper concern is the political capture of institutions that produce knowledge.
The proposed changes to federal research funding are often framed as a dispute over science. In reality, they reflect something much broader: a struggle over power. Throughout history, political movements have sought not only to win elections, but to shape the institutions that determine how society understands truth, expertise and reality itself.
Political power, however, is rarely consolidated through coercion alone. More often, power is secured by persuading ordinary citizens that independent institutions no longer deserve their trust. As the OECD notes, declining trust in public institutions undermines democratic governance by weakening citizens’ confidence in the institutions responsible for informing, protecting and representing them.
Appeals to patriotism, morality, tradition or partisan allegiance transform institutional disputes into questions of identity — framing universities, scientists, journalists or judges not as independent arbiters, but as adversaries in a larger political struggle.
This strategy is effective not because people abandon reason, but because it taps into psychological processes that have shaped human survival for thousands of years. We like to think of ourselves as rational decision-makers, carefully weighing evidence before reaching conclusions. In reality, we are motivated reasoners. Our brains evolved not primarily to discover objective truth, but to help us survive within groups.
For most of human history, survival depended on remaining connected to trusted communities. As a result, our emotions, identities and group affiliations often shape what we believe long before conscious reasoning begins. Under conditions of uncertainty or perceived threat, these tendencies become even more pronounced. We increasingly look to those we identify with for cues about whom to trust, what to fear and which version of reality to accept.
Once scientific questions become tied to political identity, evidence itself begins to function differently. It is no longer evaluated primarily for its accuracy, but for what accepting or rejecting it communicates about who we are and where we belong. Scientific claims become badges of group membership rather than invitations to inquiry.
Viewed through this lens, the debate over the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules is about far more than research funding.
Here in Maine, Sen. Susan Collins recently expressed concern that the proposal would allow political appointees to override scientific merit review, undermining the longstanding principle that federally funded research should be evaluated on scientific merit.
When political ideology begins shaping which scientific questions receive support and which findings receive legitimacy, science ceases to function as an independent check on power.
The deeper concern is that proposals like this risk embedding those dynamics within the institutions themselves, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which political influence further erodes public trust, and declining trust becomes justification for even greater political influence. Any and all guardrails that intervene on such processes from taking place are no longer present.
Democracies depend upon citizens having access to trusted sources of information and shared mechanisms for evaluating competing claims. In an era of social media, misinformation and declining institutional trust, that premise can feel increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet that is precisely why independent institutions committed to evaluating evidence through transparent, accountable processes have never been more important.
For states like Maine, where scientific research serves small and rural communities and supports major regional employers, the consequences extend well beyond academia. Federal research funding helps drive discoveries that lead to new medical treatments, fuels Maine’s growing life sciences economy, creates high-skilled jobs and trains the next generation of scientists, physicians and innovators at institutions such as the University of Maine, The Jackson Laboratory, MaineHealth, MDI Biological Laboratory and the University of New England.
Research leaders have warned that growing uncertainty surrounding federal funding threatens not only scientific discovery, but also the economic vitality, workforce development and medical advances upon which communities across Maine increasingly depend.
Importantly, history suggests that democratic institutions are rarely weakened all at once. More often, they are gradually reshaped through a series of changes that each appear limited in scope, administrative in nature or justified by immediate political concerns. Viewed in isolation, any one change may seem relatively insignificant. Viewed together, they can fundamentally alter how democratic societies determine what is true.
This is why the debate surrounding the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions matters, even to those who will never apply for a federal research grant. The proposal is not simply about science funding. It is about whether one of democracy’s most important safeguards — the independent evaluation of evidence — remains insulated from political loyalty or becomes increasingly subject to it.
Protecting scientific independence is about far more than protecting science. It is about safeguarding one of democracy’s most essential foundations: our collective ability to distinguish evidence from ideology, truth from propaganda and scientific process from political loyalty.

title: Obituary: Capt. George B. Pressly
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH – Capt. George B. Pressly passed away on Sept. 30, 2026. George was the fourth child of William C. and Harriet Byrne Pressly. He was born on Nov. 18, 1933, in Raleigh, N.C.
He is survived by his sister, Dorothy Fulghum of Vaux sur Vienne, France, and his brother, James M. Pressly of Huntsville, Ala.
He was predeceased by his older brother, Billy and his older sisters Harriet and Mary Lou.
He is also survived by his wife, Judy Potter of Cape Elizabeth; and his three children, Patti Bradbury and her husband Craig of Sandwich, Mass., George Jr. of Nashua, N.H., and retired Col. Robert F. Pressly, USMCR and his wife Amy of Rexford, N.Y. He also leaves behind his stepdaughters Molly Dall of Cape Elizabeth, and Sarah Fleischer of Montpelier, Vt.; and his six grandchildren; one great-granddaughter; and four step-grandchildren.
George attended Needham Broughton High School in Raleigh, N.C., where he was student manager of the football team and a member of three state championship swimming teams. He received a NROTC scholarship to Duke University from where he graduated in 1955.
He was commissioned upon graduation and began his 24-year naval career. He served in four surface ships, the last being the heavy cruiser, USS Newport News, the flagship of the Commander of the Quarantine Force in the Cuban Missile Crisis.
His additional assignments were in the naval intelligence field. He lived for three years each in Stockholm, Sweden, Rota, Spain, and London, England, with his wife, Barbara, and his three children, Patti, George, and Bob. While living in these countries, he served in various naval intelligence positions.
He considered his most distinguished accomplishment was founding the Fleet Ocean Surveillance Facility in Rota, Spain. Under his guidance, the organization pioneered new methods for providing operational intelligence to the fleet—innovations that later were a Navy-wide standard for a generation.
Following his retirement from the navy, George spent a decade at Sanders Associates (now BAE Systems) working in advanced defense technology and intelligence solutions.
After retiring a second time, George founded Nashua Meds and Meds for Manchester, organizations which, along with their offshoots, secured millions of dollars’ worth of free or low-cost prescription medications for hundreds of low-income citizens in New Hampshire.
George met Judy Potter, a lawyer and law professor, in 2002. He moved to Cape Elizabeth and married Judy in 2008. They enjoyed the “Maine life,” the Red Sox, the Patriots and the Celtics, numerous cruises, many days in Venice, Italy, and most of all, their blended family. He also played many rounds of golf and enjoyed weekly lunches with Richard, Bob, Fred, Kerry, Phil and Tony.
No public services are planned.

title: Pope Leo XIV says he will undergo surgery in the coming days. Here’s why
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery “in the coming days” to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate.
The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo’s expected recovery time from surgery would be a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
The Vatican didn’t say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it.
A nodule can be benign or malignant
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
“Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.
“When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis,” he said.
If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview.
“It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It’s unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, “doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it.”
He thanked the faithful “for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”
Surgery to be at the pope’s hospital
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Francis’ illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope’s health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days.
This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted.
A nodule doesn’t mean cancer but should be investigated
Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn’t mean lung cancer. And in fact “a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer.”
But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. “The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule,” he said in an interview.
Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said.
“In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery,” he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications.
Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking.
Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage “the aim … is curative,” he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy’s private Sky TG24.
“When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere,” he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.
“Being physically fit and healthy is certainly an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery,” he added.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, for Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days.” In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.
—-
Barry reported from Milan; AP reporter Danica Kirka contributed from London.

title: A cold start today, then pleasant until Tuesday, then wet and chilly
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It was a chilly start across the state with temps in the 30s across the board with a few 20s. Some clouds will move in throughout the day as the remnants of Isaias stay off to our south later but it will still be a very comfortable fall day. A few light showers associated with it may work their way along the coast. Monday will be mainly clear with the chance of a shower or two possible far up north. Another system moves in Tuesday that may bring our first wintry precip to northern locations.
Sunday: Sun and clouds mixed with warmer temperatures
The winds will swing around to the SW and bring some warmth with them. More clouds will move into the region as well with the remnants of Isaias which will eventually slide out to sea to our south but may bring a few showers later in the day on Sunday especially for southern regions of the state. Highs will fall mainly in the 60s. Winds will again be somewhat gusty perhaps as high as 25 mph or so.
Sunday night: Slight chance of a weak shower, otherwise overcast
There is a slight chance for a stray shower Sunday night but it will otherwise be mainly overcast and warmer than previous nights. Lows will only probably drop into the 40s for most with some areas further south barely getting below 50. Winds will be light out of the SW at 5-10 mph.
Monday: A very pleasant, partly sunny day, a chance of a shower in the far north
The work week will start off comfortably with highs in the 60s and very little wind. A few showers may work their way into the far northern tier of the state but they will be scattered and light in nature.
Monday night and beyond:
Temps will drop quickly Monday evening into the 40s and 30s and a developing low likely slides into the region early Tuesday and brings some cold Canadian air with it and there is a possibility some of the coldest spots may see some wintry mix early on Tuesday. But a cold rain is possible for most on Tuesday. It will likely bring a half inch to an inch for most with some areas possibly seeing more than inch. The system likely sticks around into Wednesday before finally clearing Wednesday afternoon.
There is another chance at a storm later in the week as well, possibly Friday into Saturday bringing more rain and possibly some wintry precip as well. Still a lot of details to be worked out with this system however.
Sunday: Partly sunny with highs back into the 60s. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: More clouds and a slight chance of a shower. Winds SW at 5-10 mph
Monday: Warmer with a few breaks of sun. Highs in the upper 60s. Winds light.
Monday night: Chance of showers move in and chilly. Lows in the 30s and 40s.
Tuesday: Rainy and chilly. Highs only in the 40s and 50s. Winds E at 5-10 mph.

title: Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television commercials paid for with millions of dollars in taxpayer money to promote his political message, a federal judge ordered Sunday night, even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads and called them an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order.
“Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment Sunday night. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.”
The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that ran afoul of a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other federal laws. The Homeland Security money tapped for the ads comes from a $175 million package Congress gave to the department as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have done to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs. One of the ads is a near replica of a 2024 ad that Trump ran during his presidential reelection campaign.
