title: Nearly 396,000 without power in Florida and Alabama as Isaias moves north to Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Hurricane Isaias swept through as the storm’s remnants caused flooding in North Carolina on Sunday, while powerful Pacific Ocean waves stirred up by Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California.
In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. It said tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina as well as dangerous surf and rip current conditions along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts.
At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north.
In Florida’s Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city’s fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Heavy rains cause problems in North Carolina
In Burke County, North Carolina, an unhoused male and female were camping when floodwaters from the Catawba River caught them off guard. They were rescued, along with their dog, according to a spokesperson for the county emergency management agency. Separately, a woman trapped inside her car in floodwaters was freed outside of Morganton.
In McDowell County, North Carolina, just west of Burke County, first responders said they dealt with five landslides and voluntary evacuations overnight Saturday into Sunday as they responded to flooded roads and streams overflowing their banks.
Nearly a dozen local weather stations in the western North Carolina county reported torrential 24-hour rainfall totals from about 5 inches (13 centimeters) to as much as 9.57 inches (24 centimeters) at the fire/rescue station in Enola. The weather service said rainfall was diminishing in the area but that rapid river rises and flooding remained possible.
Dealing with Isaias aftermath in Florida
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
At a church in Pensacola where the United Cajun Navy was distributing supplies Sunday morning, a line of hundreds of cars stretched around the block. Yvette Haro said she arrived at 5 a.m. after being turned away the previous day because supplies had run out.
With a 10-year-old son and a 5-year-old daughter at home, she said it’s hard to go to stores and wait in long lines. She was looking for water, paper towels, toilet paper and cleaning supplies.
While her home didn’t suffer any damage, the loss of electricity was making things difficult, Haro said. “The biggest thing is our food going bad,” she said.
About 226,000 customers remained without power Sunday evening in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama, according to poweroutage.com. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said he expected nearly everyone to have it restored by Tuesday night.
Rachel brings wind and rain to southern California and the Southwest
Rachel became a post-tropical cyclone overnight, bringing unusually big waves to Southern California.
Waves battered a century-old wooden boardwalk on the Long Beach peninsula and forced homeowners to evacuate. The strip of multimillion-dollar oceanfront properties, along with much of the Southern California coastline, was already reeling from Hurricane Marie in September.
“This area is completely shattered and vulnerable,” Jack Gordon, a Long Beach real estate agent, said.
The Pacific Ocean is abnormally warm, about 7 to 8 degrees F warmer than normal for this time of year, due to the El Niño weather pattern, said Joe Sirard of the weather service in Oxnard, California
“When we have this warm water, it actually causes the ocean to rise above the normal predicted tide levels,” Sirard said. That’s affected by Rachel’s ocean swells and wind gusts. The City of Long Beach placed dozens of 3,000-pound (1,360-kilogram) sandbags along the stretch of peninsula where waves tore apart the historic boardwalk and smashed against coastal homes.
Jazmin Evers, a 37-year-old mother who runs a pottery business from her Long Beach rental home, said the community is on edge. “Every time the tide goes down everyone just kind of takes a breath — except, of course, the people whose buildings are being destroyed,” she said. “When the tide comes back up, everybody’s nerves kind of ramp back up.” Rachel dissipated over Las Vegas as it drenched deserts across the Southwest. An inch (2.4 centimeters) of rain fell in the city Sunday, leading to gushing water and flooded streets on the Las Vegas Strip.
In the Pacific, Hurricane Simon was a Category 4 storm as it pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. ___
Brumback reported from Atlanta. Walker reported from New York. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, Jack Brook in New Orleans and Josh Kelety in Phoenix also contributed.

title: 'Something like that': Trump suggests renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Oceans
text:
'Something like that': Trump suggests renaming the Atlantic or Pacific oceans during campaign rally
President Donald Trump brought up the idea of renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific Oceans during a campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee.
Watch video in the play finder above
"We've got the Gulf, we've got a beautiful lake, and now someone said 'you need a river,' so, I don't wanna change the name of the Hudson River," Trump said during the Oct. 10 rally. "So, we need a river, we need an ocean. So, I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific. We call it Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americans, something like that."
Trump's midterm rally comes just two weeks after his last stop in Tennessee gained attention after he barred CNN from boarding Air Force One.
CNN contributed to this report.

title: Pets of the Week: Chad and Plunger
Firefighter’s toddler son dies after he and his father hit by car while window-shopping
text:
GAINESVILLE, Ga. (ANF/Gray News) - A Georgia boy who was just shy of turning 2 died after he and his father were hit by a car while window-shopping in a shopping center parking lot, police say.
Samuel Skelton, a Gainesville firefighter, and his 22-month-old son, Knox Skelton, were window-shopping Wednesday at the Limestone Marketplace. A driver in a white SUV accidentally accelerated over a curb while parking and hit them, according to Gainesville Police.
“Samuel was there, holding his 22-month-old son, Knox. Had his back to everything, didn’t even know what was coming, didn’t see what was coming,” Police Capt. Kevin Holbrook said.
Knox suffered critical injuries and was flown to a hospital in Atlanta, where he later died. His father was also injured but did not need medical treatment, police say.
Holbrook said Samuel Skelton and his wife, Kiana Skelton, were able to get to Atlanta to say goodbye before Knox died.
“We typically compartmentalize. At some point, you can only keep that compartmentalized for so long,” Holbrook said. “And just like trying to get through this interview, it’s emotional, knowing that we lost a young child in this community.”
Fire department mourns with family
The Gainesville Fire Department released a photo of the Skelton family in a social media post Thursday that described Samuel Skelton and his wife as “humble, caring, and genuine people.”
The department said it is “heartbroken by this tragedy” and asked the community to “surround the Skelton family with love, prayers, and support as they navigate this incredibly difficult time.”
The department also said members of its staff who responded to the crash were faced with the realization that it involved one of their own.
“They, too, are carrying the weight of this tragedy,” the department said.
Members of the fire department have organized a fundraiser to support Samuel and Kiana Skelton. It had raised more than $65,000, as of early Sunday.
Investigation into crash continues
Police say the driver, a 68-year-old woman, stayed on the scene and cooperated with officers. She is not currently facing charges.
“This was just a tragic accident, altogether. You had an elderly female who did not intentionally do this,” Holbrook said.
Officials have the car as evidence and are investigating its brakes and tires. They will also review cellphone data.
Holbrook said that after the investigation, the case will be handed over to the district attorney or solicitor general, and it is only then that the driver could face criminal charges.
Holbrook said an answer on potential charges could come within weeks.

title: Obituary: Steven Jones
text:
BEALS – Steven Jones, 84, passed away Oct. 1, 2026, at his home on Beals Island. He was born Dec. 24, 1941, the son of Clarence and Dorothy (Stevens) Jones.
Steve grew up in Flagstaff until CMP flooded the town to create Flagstaff Lake, prompting his family to relocate their home—house and all—to Eustis. He attended Stratton schools, graduated in 1959, and graduated from Southern Maine Technical College. During his 50-year career in the automotive industry, Steve worked for Morton Motor Co. in Farmington, owned a garage in New Sharon, and later worked for Forest City Chevrolet in Portland and Peter Brown in Saco. He received numerous awards and accolades for his knowledge and skill. After retiring in 2006, Steve and his wife moved to Bingham, to care for his father.
Steve loved hunting, fishing, and sharing outdoor adventures with his dad and uncle, Perly Stevens. He climbed Bigelow Mountain at just 7 years old and shot his first deer at 12. He was also a devoted fan of country and bluegrass music and cherished his “bluegrass family.” An avid reader, Steve especially enjoyed the novels of Louis L’Amour. With a lifetime of rich experiences, he could always be counted on to share a good story.
Steve is survived by his wife Elizabeth (Nichols); daughter, Crystal and husband Darrel Gregor of Livermore Falls, son, Kenneth of Jacksonville, N.C.; three stepsons, Craig, Clark and Chris Leach; brother, Larry and his wife Stephanie, sister-in-law, Insowa; nephews, Travis, Mattthew, and Christopher, niece, Nicole.
Steve was predeceased by his parents; brother, Tom, sister, Marilyn (Rogers-Bull), and brother-in-law, Frank Rogers.
Funeral service will be held at 2 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, at the Flagstaff Memorial Chapel, in Eustis.
Arrangements have been entrusted to the care of Bragdon-Kelley Funeral Home, Machias, where online condolences may be shared: http://www.bragdonkelley.com.

title: Officer with questionable past becomes city’s top cop, fires detective who investigated him
text:
RIVERVIEW, Mo. (First Alert 4/Gray News) - First Alert 4 Investigates has been digging into allegations regarding the police officers in charge of public safety in one town and the governments that employ them.
On Sept. 10, Riverview’s City Hall and Police Department were furloughed, but money issues aren’t where the problems end for the department.
A First Alert 4 investigation has revealed Riverview’s chief of police has a history of allegations of excessive use of force, has fired a detective who investigated him and was handpicked by a man sitting in the St. Louis County jail.
Three incidents, caught on camera, show Riverview Police Chief Brandin Neil allegedly using excessive force, including punches to the head, against people who do not appear to be resisting. Two of these incidents resulted in court actions against Neil.
A former Riverview detective, who says he did Neil’s background check for Riverview, alleges the chief fired him for an investigation that stemmed from that check.
Jailhouse calls obtained by First Alert 4 Investigates show the decision to hire Neil into the department’s top brass came from the city’s now-former mayor, Michael Cornell Jr., while he was in the St. Louis County jail awaiting trial for alleged sex crimes.
Now, Neil is one of two remaining commissioned officers in Riverview following the furlough, according to state records.
Neil sent a written statement for this story that reads in part:
“Since my return to the Riverview Police Department, I have utilized the past 5 months to bring this department into state compliance, foster working relationships with our neighboring departments and elected officials, and attending as many community events as possible. The betterment of this city and the protection of it’s residents is my ultimate goal, and I will continue to do so, both as transparently and efficiently as possible.”
In an on-camera interview, Neil told First Alert 4 Investigates he did speak with the former mayor while he was in jail, but said he could not speak about why the former detective had been fired, due to it being a personnel issue.
Neil faced court action, misconduct reports while an SLMPD officer
On the morning of Aug. 8, 2019, Neil is seen on video walking into a St. Louis City gas station and getting in line to buy something. At the time, he was a St. Louis City police officer, and he was off duty as he was heading into work, court records say.
Inside that gas station, security footage obtained by First Alert 4 in 2019 showed Neil get into an argument with a man, attempt to tase him and then repeatedly punch him in the head with his handcuffs.
That man, Bryan Boyle, spoke to First Alert 4 in 2019 after the gas station incident. During that interview, he said that he had asked Neil a question.
“‘What are you?’ That’s all I asked because I was interested in doing private security and private bodyguard work,” Boyle said during that 2019 interview.
A St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department (SLMPD) Employee Misconduct Report of the incident obtained by First Alert 4 Investigates reports that Boyle said Neil never identified himself as a police officer during the incident.
Neil was charged with third-degree assault in the case, a class-E felony. In September 2021, Neil had a bench trial, which waives a defendant’s right to a jury trial and allows a judge to make the ruling of guilty or not guilty.
A judge found Neil not guilty following a single-day trial, court records show.
Eusef Robin Huq, now a defense attorney, had tried the case against Neil in 2021.
He says the prosecutor’s office argued Neil had no reason for the response he had to Boyle, and he had escalated the situation.
“Essentially, we argued that there was no reason for the aggressive response by Brandin Neil,” he said. “We had witnesses testify that he was the aggressor in the situation.”
In 2021, Boyle sued Neil in federal court, accusing him of Fourth and 14th Amendment rights violations.
Boyle’s attorney filed to drop the lawsuit in April of 2024 after Boyle was shot dead in his car while waiting at a red light in St. Louis City’s Vandeventer neighborhood. The man police say shot Boyle died inside of the St. Louis City Justice Center before going to trial.
Neil, when asked about this incident with Boyle, wrote in a statement, “As far as Mr. Boyle, who is unfortunately deceased, all matters of that case are public record.”
According to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, before the incident with Boyle, Neil was already being investigated for a different internal affairs complaint.
In May of 2019, Neil was accused of tackling Billy Busch’s daughter, Abbey Busch, and her boyfriend to the ground inside a South City bar. The Post-Dispatch reported this incident was under investigation by both St. Louis City Police internal affairs and the circuit attorney’s office.
First Alert 4 Investigates filed multiple records requests with SLMPD regarding any potential internal affairs investigation into Neil from this incident with Busch. SLMPD says under Missouri law, internal affairs investigations into police officers are closed records.
Neil was never criminally charged with anything related to this May incident inside a bar, but he did ultimately leave the department in September that same year. Whether an officer is fired or resigns is not an open record under Missouri law. Records show he was with SLMPD for less than three years.
“The alleged incident involving Ms. Busch, is exactly as stated, an alleged incident that was investigated and found to not be factual,” Neil said when asked about these allegations.
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Busch for comment, and as of publication time, we have not heard back. First Alert 4 has not been able to independently verify the alleged incident between Neil and Busch.
Huq says he was surprised to hear Neil is now a police chief, but hopes he’s changed for the better.
“Maybe 2021 and that trial was a wake-up call,” Huq said. “Maybe a mentor had a word with him and said, ‘Hey Brandin, you’ve got to do things different, because you got lucky this time. If you keep pulling stuff like that, it’s going to catch up with you.’”
Potential misconduct seen on video, again
More recently, in 2025, Neil was seen on video arresting former Riverview Alderwoman Regina Davis during a town hall meeting.
Davis told First Alert 4 at the time she had gone to a meeting to ask then-Mayor Cornell about a lawsuit accusing him of sexual misconduct with a city employee. She was charged with assault, accused of biting Neil during the arrest. Those charges have since been dropped against Davis.
Davis has now filed a lawsuit against Neil and the city of Riverview over the arrest. Davis’ lawsuit claims the force used by Neil specifically was excessive and unwarranted.
When asked about Davis’ lawsuit, Neil said he would not comment on active litigation.
This year, a video was circulated on social media showing Neil in a police uniform punching a man in the head while he was on the ground outside of a St. Louis City nightclub.
A former Riverview detective says the video is from March 14 and that the man seen throwing the punch is Neil.
When asked about this video, Neil said in a statement, “I only ask that you share the entirety of the video that is approximately 25 minutes long, as it depicts the attempted de-escalation of a group of subjects, assault of officers, and the resisting of arrest that followed.”
First Alert 4 asked Neil to share this additional video with us. As of publication time, we have not received it.
Potential investigation by a state agency, jail calls suggest
A recorded jail call conversation between the now-former Riverview mayor and now-former Riverview Alderwoman Judy Jones in April suggests Neil may have been under investigation by Missouri Peace Officer’s Standards and Training (POST) from an incident during his time with the Moline Acres Police Department.
Neil was with Moline Acres from Dec. 1, 2025, until April 23, 2026, the department said.
Jones, who Riverview confirms recently resigned from the board of aldermen, is heard in the call asking then-Mayor Cornell about POST.
“What’s up with this... St. Louis City POST? Is it an organization or what is that?” Jones asked during an April 17 call.
Jones tells Cornell that POST is “coming against” Neil.
“This person is not even where we are yet. They’re still at the other place,” Jones said. Neil, at the time of the call, was still with Moline Acres. “And they’re cool, they’re good with it. They’re good with it. They look at the stuff that whatever occurred, and they don’t have no problem.”
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Jones to get comment for this story. Jones responded by text, asking not to be contacted and telling us to reach out to Riverview’s city attorney instead.
Riverview’s city attorney, when asked about a potential investigation into Neil by POST, said, “The city has no comment regarding this matter, as it predates the current administration’s depth and breadth of knowledge regarding the topic.”
Missouri law prohibits the Missouri Department of Public Safety, which oversees POST, from commenting on any investigation. First Alert 4 reached out to the Missouri Attorney General’s Office, which files complaints against peace officer licenses based on POST investigations. As of publication time, the attorney general’s office has not provided information regarding any possible action against Neil’s license.
Former detective alleges being fired for investigating Chief Neil before his appointment
Since Neil was appointed the chief of police for Riverview, he told First Alert 4 Investigates he has fired three officers.
All three officers, he said, were fired for policy violations. One of those officers, according to Neil, is being investigated for a non-specified non-violent felony. A court records check shows no charges have been filed against any of the three officers who were fired from the department since Neil’s appointment.
Former Riverview Detective Corporal Maurico Wilson says he believes he is the officer Neil is investigating for a felony.
“Ultimately, I was fired for investigating him and uncovering other crimes,” Wilson alleged.
According to Wilson, he was in charge of doing Neil’s background check before he was rehired into the department. During the background check, Wilson says he learned of accusations made against Neil while he was working secondary employment as security at a North County grocery store.
Wilson says the incident he was investigating happened during a time when Neil wasn’t working for any police department, which, under Missouri law, would prevent him from legally working secondary employment.
First Alert 4 Investigates confirmed with the Moline Acres Police Department that Neil worked for them from Dec. 1, 2025, until April 23, 2026. Wilson says Neil was rehired into the Riverview Police Department and made chief on May 5.
Wilson says the incident he was investigating allegedly happened on April 26, while Neil was not employed by either police department.
Wilson said because Neil was not with any department at the time, he began investigating him for impersonation of a police officer.
A “wanted” was put out for Neil on May 4 for impersonating a police officer, according to Wilson. A “wanted” is not a warrant, but an internal note for police, flagging Neil for questioning or possible arrest.
Neil started working for Riverview the next day.
“The wanted had got issued out on [May 4],” Wilson said, “So you see how it became a sticky situation.”
Wilson and his supervisor were both fired the next month, he said. Neil confirmed Wilson and his supervisor had been fired when asked directly by First Alert 4 Investigates.
“All I can honestly, legally, say is that they were terminated,” Neil said. “With that being a personnel matter, I can’t go any further into it.”
Wilson also shared with First Alert 4 Investigates a written reprimand document he says was written by Neil.
The document reads:
“Upon notification from police officers from surrounding agencies, it was made aware that Interim Chief of Police Neil, DSN 375, had an active “Wanted” for “Impersonating A Police Officer” through the Riverview Police Department. Further investigation revealed the “Wanted” was authorized by Detective/Corporal Maurico Wilson, DNS 414, on 5/04/2026.
“Upon review of the report, it was discovered the report was blank, containing very vague and fictitious pedigree information and there was additionally no narrative.”
In the document written to reprimand Wilson, it says Neil was not a member of the Riverview police department when the “wanted” was issued against him.
The document says that Wilson was not acting ethically after he issued “a wanted on citizen of Riverview for a supposed crime that did not take place in Riverview’s venue and by leaving the wanted ‘Active’ after the citizen was appointed to Interim Chief of Police.”
Wilson says he had a right to conduct his investigation because Neil had applied to work for the department, and he was in charge of background checks.
According to Wilson’s termination paperwork, which he also shared with First Alert 4 Investigates, he was fired for “multiple blatant violations of Police Department and City policies, as well as alleged criminal conduct.”
Wilson says he didn’t violate department policies or do anything criminal. He says he believes he was fired for investigating Neil.
“Who’s above the law? Nobody, right? We all should be held accountable,” Wilson said.
Jailed mayor handpicks Neil for Riverview’s top brass
Neil had previously worked for the Riverview Police Department as a Sergeant. He left the department in 2025, telling First Alert 4 Investigates shortly after then-Mayor Cornell was arrested that he had quit because of Cornell’s behavior.
“I was just tired of the mayor and his antics; the foolishness is usually how I refer to it as,” Neil said in his Jan. 23 interview with us.
During this interview, Neil said he had suspicions that a lot of things Cornell had done were criminal.
“We felt a lot of things that he did were criminal,” he said. “We just couldn’t put our fingers on it or prove that these things were happening. I’m not really surprised about how you flaunt your authority and your power over people and stuff like that. That mentality you have. But to hear that it was, underage men and the child pornography and stuff like that. That was surprising to me.”
When asked if he was surprised by Cornell’s arrest, Neil said, “No, I’d honestly been waiting on it.”
Two months after this interview with First Alert 4 Investigates, Neil is on a recorded jailhouse call with Cornell and Alderwoman Jones.
“What would that look like if he’s not on board?” Neil asked Jones about then-acting Police Chief Toreyon Times.
“I don’t know,” Jones responded, “this is perpetual existence of government. You know, push, pull in, pull out, change up, to make sure that the government continues.”
Neil also said the board would need to post the job opening on the front door of Riverview City Hall.
“That way, even if it came down to, ‘Hey, we know we want you for the position, we’re going to select him,’ you’ve given other people the opportunity, so it doesn’t seem like an unfair hiring practice,” Neil said.
Neil mentioned Wilson’s supervisor would likely apply for the position and might file a lawsuit if he isn’t given a chance to apply.
“This is not an opening,” Cornell said. “This is more like my appointment thing. It is not an opening, so it doesn’t matter.”
First Alert 4 Investigates asked Neil after the press conference on his department being furloughed if he had heard from the former mayor since his January arrest.
“I would prefer not to answer that or involve that,” he said. “I have not contacted him directly, but I have heard.”
First Alert 4 Investigates pressed Neil on why he would need to speak with Cornell after his arrest.
“Again, since I have been in this position with the city of Riverview, I have not spoken to him,” he said. “Preemptive conversations before I return to Riverview is another story. However, since I have been here, there has been no communication or contact.”
Neil worked ‘protection detail’ for Cornell, was paid for trips to Metro East strip clubs
When Neil was first with the Riverview Police Department, he said he was assigned to work frequently with Cornell.
“He had what he called the mayor’s protection detail,” Neil said in January. " So, I was assigned to that. So, the majority of the time I was like his driver, but he always goes somewhere with police officers as his security and different things."
Neil said a part of the job of being a part of Cornell’s protection detail was joining him on nights out.
“The mayor would come into the police department and say, ‘Hey, I’m going out tonight. I need you, you, you. You’re going to go clock out, go on to secondary duty, go on to the special patrol, mayor’s detail,’ whatever the case might be,” Neil said.
Neil said the protection detail would join Cornell on trips to Illinois, as well.
“There’s been a time before where, I mean, we bounced to multiple clubs, and now we’re over in East St. Louis because he wanted to go to a strip club,” Neil recounted.
Neil said officers would be in their Riverview police uniforms on these outings, “and even if we were in plain clothes, he wanted your gun and badge to be displayed.”
Neil said when he would go out to these clubs with Cornell, he was supposed to be paid for it.
“That would go to the comp time,” he said.
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Cornell’s attorney for comment on these alleged trips. As of publication time, we have not heard back.
Days after Cornell’s arrest, Neil filed a lawsuit against Riverview claiming the city did not pay out his accrued “comp” hours, along with holiday and vacation hours.
The court dropped Neil’s lawsuit after he did not show up to a hearing in May, records show.
During his interview in January, Neil said nobody ever stood up against Cornell.
“He’s the mayor. He runs everything in this city,” he said. “Who are you going to call? Who are you going to tell on?”
The Riverview Police Department furlough is expected to last until December. During the press conference about the furlough, Neil said he would still be working for Riverview as a civilian employee and would be assisting the St. Louis County Police Department when they respond to calls in the city.
Chief Neil’s full written statement:
“At this time, I will have to deny the request for the on-camera interview in regards to the aforementioned topics. Three of the incidents have no correlation with my tenure with the City of Riverview.
“As far as Mr. Boyle, who is unfortunately deceased, all matters of that case are public record.
“The alleged incident involving Ms. Busch, is exactly as stated, an alleged incident that was investigated and found to not be factual.
“As to the video you were provided, I only ask that you share the entirety of the video that is approximately 25 minutes long, as it depicts the attempted de-escalation of a group of subjects, assault of officers, and the resisting of arrest that followed.
“Lastly, in regards to Ms. Davis, who was lawfully arrested, I will not comment on any current litigation of the City and would recommend any information request be directed to our City’s attorney.
“In closing, since my return to the Riverview Police Department, I have utilized the past 5 months to bring this department into state compliance, foster working relationships with our neighboring departments and elected officials, and attending as many community events as possible. The betterment of this city and the protection of it’s residents is my ultimate goal, and I will continue to do so, both as transparently and efficiently as possible.”
Karla Vasquez Mejia contributed to this report.

title: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
text:
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
The hurricane’s center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened Sunday to 120 mph (195 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.
That’s not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
By Sunday afternoon, Simon’s eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.
Forecasters say powerful winds will sweep from Mexico’s western coast to the Sierra Madre
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon’s center, meaning the entire area between Mexico’s western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.
“We’re expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect,” Papin said. “They’re also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that’s likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells.”
The hurricane center on Sunday said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.
“Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco,” the center said in its latest advisory. “This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any on-going flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain.”
Mexico’s president urges residents to stay sheltered
As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
“Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety,” she wrote.
Hotel worker says residents learned from major hurricane in 2002
Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people’s concerns about the hurricane comforting.
“It happened to us before. It hit us years ago,” Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. “People didn’t expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we’re different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won’t let it happen again.”
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.
Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city’s boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
“The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!” police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco’s capital.
“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” Villarreal said. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

This article has been edited to correct the spelling of Philippe Papin’s name.

title: The UMaine System is becoming an ‘AI leader.’ Some students and staff are wary.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For Jared Fairfield, enrolling in graduate school at the University of Southern Maine this fall was a big personal and financial decision, one he said he’s still wrestling with.
That’s why the 36-year-old social work student was so jarred when he received artificial intelligence-generated feedback from a professor on the first assignment in his psychology methods course.
“For the person who is supposed to be the authority, the intellectual guide, to use ChatGPT, was very disorienting,” Fairfield said.
But when Fairfield raised concerns about what he saw as unethical AI use, he said his professor responded candidly that he had used it, and pointed to a recent announcement from the university system’s leader about its investment in an AI tool that would “help strengthen teaching and research.”
That interaction came shortly after the University of Maine System, to which USM belongs, rolled out access to ChatGPT Edu for all students, staff and faculty through a $1.4 million, two-year contract with the company OpenAI. The tool is now available to 30,000 individuals across the system, although “whether and how they use it will be entirely up to them,” per the system’s announcement.
His professor’s behavior, as Fairfield came to understand it, was fine. The professor later sent an email to every student in Fairfield’s class, telling them to expect that all responses would be “augmented with AI.”
“In a commonsense way, that’s probably not a good thing to be doing in a graduate-level course,” Fairfield said. “But he wasn’t doing anything that he couldn’t do.”
As of Oct. 8, more than 3,700 people across the system have signed up for an account, which comes with data privacy protections and cannot be used to train OpenAI’s models. Leaders describe the contract as a success, and critical to “preparing students for the modern workforce.”
But many in the system, including students, staff and faculty, seem skeptical of the deal — and AI’s place in higher education broadly.
As the technology becomes more ubiquitous in workplaces and universities across the country, the University of Maine System has embraced its place in the technological transition and describes itself as a “national AI leader.”
Ryan Low, formerly the system’s chief financial officer, received an additional title of Vice Chancellor of AI Integration last year and has taken the helm of that transformation. He said there haven’t been any surprises so far with the rollout, and that there has been strong interest in the ChatGPT Edu trainings offered by the system.
But some individual faculty and staff members have concerns about the impact on student learning, and many have raised issues with the purchase, which was made with unbudgeted funds, amid financial struggles in the university system.
“To see the system prioritize software contracts while cutting the hours and jobs of the human beings who keep these universities running sends a deeply troubling message about UMS fiscal priorities,” said Sara Abronze, president of the system’s professional staff union.
HOW THE CONTRACT CAME TO BE
In fall 2024, the system convened an AI Working Group — made up of university presidents, administrators, one trustee, one professor and one student — to develop a strategy on artificial intelligence’s implementation in the system.
Their final report, released in August 2025, concludes that, “strategic, deliberate investment now” will determine whether the system becomes a leader in the AI transformation or is “left reacting to it.” The group offered several recommendations, including that the system purchase a single AI tool that could be accessible to everyone.
People across the system were already using AI through personal, less-secure accounts. More than 12,600 students, 700 faculty members and 1,335 staff members already had a free or paid ChatGPT account, according to system data about the number of sign-ups associated with an @maine.edu email address.
Faculty surveys conducted by the working group at the flagship University of Maine and the University of Maine at Presque Isle found that a majority of professors were willing to use AI tools if they were easily accessible.
The system put out a public request for proposals in the early spring, and received four: one from OpenAI, and three from Gemini, Google’s chatbot product, from different sellers.
“It was a really easy decision that had nothing to do, in this case, with the difference between ChatGPT and Claude or Gemini, and really just came down to cost,” Low said.
Although the working group recommended paying for the tool with a per-credit hour fee of $18 to $20, faculty had concerns, and the system decided to pay instead with unbudgeted investment income.
The system announced the deal in May, and began rolling it out as an option for faculty, staff and students before the start of the semester. As of Oct. 8, about 8.8% of students, 22% of faculty and 30% of staff have made ChatGPT Edu accounts through the system.
Low said things are playing out roughly as anticipated, and he expects the numbers to increase throughout the semester.
SOME SKEPTICAL, SOME EXCITED
Americans are now more skeptical about AI than they are excited about it, according to an August study from the Pew Research Center. This is increasingly true of young people, 55% of whom now say they’re more concerned than excited about AI’s growing use in daily life, amid shocking headlines about leaders warning of the potential dangers of the technology.
At the same time, Americans increasingly use AI at work. More than half of U.S. employees say they use AI on the job, according to a July survey by Gallup, and 65% of employees at organizations that have implemented AI say it has improved their productivity and efficiency.
While many faculty members are excited about AI, others feel the university is jumping on the latest trendy bandwagon in higher education.
The union representing professional staff surveyed its members anonymously this summer, and out of 137 responses, about 69% disagreed that ChatGPT would have a positive impact on their work or productivity. More than 80% were extremely dissatisfied with the way the university communicated with staff about the contract, and nearly 90% said they were dissatisfied with the decision to spend $1.4 million on the product.
Paula Gerstenblatt, a professor of social work at USM, said AI has no place in her classroom. She said she’s invested in walking students through the iterative process of learning.
“I need to know where they are in their writing, in their critical thinking,” Gerstenblatt said. “If you’re using a tool like AI, it’s going to polish it up, and I don’t know where you are.”
She also doesn’t buy the system’s argument that AI familiarity is critical for entering the workforce; in her field, she said, employers want multi-faceted and civically engaged thinkers.
But the sentiment ranges across disciplines. Amir Kordijazi, an industrial engineering professor at USM who studies AI’s applications in manufacturing, said he supports the contract because he wants higher education to be at the forefront of AI innovation, and make sure the technology is developed in ways that benefit the public.
“Given the pace of this transformation, I don’t believe our educational institution can afford to remain on the sidelines,” Kordijazi said. “In fact, I believe they have a responsibility to take a leading role.”
Kordijazi said all of his students are using AI, so he has a responsibility to educate them on how to use it.
That’s not the situation for Erin Bertoni, a social work grad student at UMaine, who said there’s universal skepticism among her cohort.
Bertoni said she’s not anti-AI, but does have concerns about the specific deal (she cited OpenAI being sued for violating copyrights and investigated for allegedly misleading shareholders) and the system’s communications around it.
“We’re paying a lot of money for education, and we’re getting watered down education,” Bertoni said. “I think it really hinders academic integrity and learning, the capacity to learn.”
Bertoni said she’s not sure she would have chosen UMaine today, following the contract.
The editorial board of The Maine Campus, the university’s student newspaper, called for greater transparency in the AI acquisition process in a September piece, and said the contract calls into question the system’s concern for academic integrity.
“To the professors who have strict AI policies in their classes and view using it as cheating, this program could seem like an endorsement for that behavior by the university,” the board wrote.
UNIVERSITY SYSTEM BULLISH ON DEAL
Low said from his perspective, the deal has been “a very, very transparent process.” The working group gave regular public updates to the board of trustees, which were livestreamed, and held a public request for proposals.
Samantha Warren, the system’s spokesperson, said the system never received critical public comments about AI from students during trustee meetings, and have heard less pushback than expected. Low said the student representatives to the board, and to individual university AI task forces, didn’t share any concerns.
Warren said she can’t think of another voluntary resource that has been adopted by so many students so quickly.
Faculty seem to be adapting to the change, too. Just last week, after many rounds of discussion, USM’s faculty senate passed a policy that, among other things, will require professors to disclose all AI use to students, and permit students to opt out of being graded with AI.
It was a controversial debate and took several rounds of voting to resolve, said Shelton Waldrep, the faculty senate member who drafted the policy.
The proposal will go to the president and provost now, who have 30 days to approve it, before it can take effect.
There is no system-wide policy; it’s up to each individual university to set its own guidelines.
FUTURE OF CONTRACT UNKNOWN
UMS is not the first nor the largest university system to invest in AI on this scale.
The California State University System paid $17 million in 2025 to give all 523,000 of its students, faculty and staff access to ChatGPT Edu amid a financial crisis; this year, faculty asked the system not to renew the contract, but it did. The University of Colorado reached a three-year, $2 million-per-year agreement for its 100,000 students, staff and faculty, which has also garnered pushback.
But UMaine, the flagship university, is facing a $19 million budget shortfall. Faculty and staff reacted with apprehension about the new expenditure given that they have been told to expect layoffs to address the school’s financial woes.
“I see that and I think: How many of my colleagues could we retain for a million and a half a year?” biology and ecology professor Jacquelyn Gill said at the time. “Which of those is more important?”
Abronze, the staff union president, said many in her unit have serious fears that the system will replace their jobs with AI. She sent a letter to Low in May, sharing those worries and requesting more information about the contract. They met over the summer, but she was disappointed by his answers.
Warren, the spokesperson, said the system’s investments have won them national recognition. The system expects the contract will allow the universities to recruit students and faculty, and anticipates it will draw increased philanthropic and federal funding. She cited an ongoing application to the National Science Foundation for UMaine and other partners to expand AI literacy across the state.
Low said it’s too early to know if the system will extend the agreement with Open AI, or how they might fund it if so. He said they’ll do a survey this fall, and another at the end of the two-year period, and present those findings to trustees to decide if they will continue.
The contract includes options for three additional one-year extensions, the first of which would cost $693,665. Any financial process would happen publicly in board of trustee meetings. But if the system does extend the contract, it may need to look at funding it through a fee to students.

title: Inside a Maine moose hunt that didn’t go as planned
text:
This was originally published Oct. 1, 2025.
I’ve seen a lot of hunters get discouraged and misled by social media. They see guides, hunters and friends always posting their successes and rarely their failures — often thinking those successes come with ease. Here’s a look at the work that went into a hunt last week, one that ended with the first moose tag we’ve ever eaten.
First off, the week spent with Matt and Sydney Boyer was unmatched. This father-daughter duo is what makes guiding hunts memorable and worth it. Hands down, they’re the best people you could ever spend a week hunting alongside, and I’m forever grateful for the friendship we built.
I knew this hunt was going to be a challenge when the sign we were seeing locally was in small pockets, mostly around water. I started scouting in mid-August, logging 12 full days and nearly 50 miles on foot before the hunt. With several promising areas and a dozen cameras deployed, I felt confident.
As the hunt approached, my confidence grew when five “shooters” appeared on camera in three different areas. One of those was a deadwater we had hunted many times before and taken a few big bulls from. That deadwater was holding resident cows and likely some of our target bulls from the cuts above. The cuts, however, showed no cow activity leading up to the hunt.
Anyone who knows moose hunting understands that during the breeding phase, you need to hunt close to the cows to maximize your chances at a bull. Knowing the deadwater was holding cows, I figured it would be our ace in the hole — or so I thought.
Monday morning, we paddled upstream and found a cow along the bank. After setting up and calling, a bull quickly responded. It wasn’t a shooter, and certainly not on the first day. Half an hour later, we called in a second small bull who put on a little show. After joking that we were looking for his father, we got back in the canoe to see what else might answer.
Half a mile upstream, Matt heard a grunt and pointed right. I looked up to see antlers poking through a patch of alders. The bull came through the maples on the treeline like a rutting buck, head low and grunting every step. He looked like a bull anyone would be happy with. We got to shore and set up to call.
To my surprise, our calls were ignored. The bull kept moving away, grunting, never to be seen again. Maybe he was trailing a cow we didn’t notice.
We hunted hard into Thursday, only seeing a cow and calf Tuesday morning.
That Thursday, before we reached the canoe, we spotted a cow and small bull standing on the opposite bank. Sydney got her gun on the sticks and her crosshairs on the bull, but we agreed it was still early. He was one of the smaller bulls from Monday morning.
That evening, a trail camera showed a bull and cow at our setup — less than an hour after we left.
Friday came with hopes that the rain the night before might kick the rut into gear and bring in one of the big bulls. We now had help from my brother Charles and his client, Zach, who had shot a bull early Wednesday. But Friday was also quiet.
That evening, Charles and Zach scouted a deadwater for the final day. At this point, any bull would have been a shooter. They saw plenty of game, including a cow moose and two more unidentified moose that bolted as they paddled upstream in the dark.
We started Saturday on the new deadwater Charles and Zach had scouted. Thanks to Thursday night’s rain, the river was navigable again — before that, it had been too low from drought. We made the long trip down and back, portaging over beaver dams and dragging the canoe where the river was too shallow. Our only sighting was a buck bedded along the river.
With just a few hours left, we decided to finish in an area that had several small bulls and some of the only wallows we’d found all week. As our calls echoed into the fading light, the Boyers’ hunt came to a close.
As unfortunate as an unpunched tag may be, the Boyers left in high spirits after a weeklong hunt where we logged more than 50 miles paddling deadwaters and more than 40 miles on foot.
As a guide, this one stings. I worked harder scouting for this hunt than I normally would. I felt confident we could get Sydney the bull she wanted. But at the end of the day, there are two things you absolutely cannot control in moose hunting: the moose and the weather. Zone 28 is tough even in a good year, and this past week the success rate was 25%, compared to 70% during the same week last year.
Leading up to this hunt, nine out of the last 11 moose hunts I guided ended within 24 hours. The two that went longer were both my personal hunts — one in New Brunswick and one in Maine. Four topped 50 inches, and four more measured 47 to 50.
I share these stats because I’ve ridden the highs of moose hunting the past few years. This week was a humbling reminder that success isn’t guaranteed, even with preparation.

title: Nonpartisan state Supreme Court elections are being put to the test in Montana
text:
Support for nonpartisan judicial elections is being put to the test in Montana, the latest location in a nationwide battle for bench seats that can determine the fate of consequential state laws.
After a series of recent court rulings on abortion, voting and climate change displeased Republicans, GOP officials have tried to inject more partisanship into Montana’s officially nonpartisan Supreme Court elections. Citizen activists have responded by forcing a statewide vote on an amendment to enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution.
That’s resulted in an unusual November election. While voters are deciding whether to mandate nonpartisan elections, they also will be choosing between two officially nonpartisan candidates for the state Supreme Court — one backed by the Republican Party, the other by organized labor and a Democratic-aligned group.
The battle around the Montana Supreme Court ranks among the most intense of the roughly two dozen states holding November elections for their highest courts. Millions of dollars are being spent, continuing a recent trend in Montana and elsewhere and underscoring the elevated importance of top state judicial offices.
Last year, a record amount over $100 million was spent on a pivotal Wisconsin Supreme Court race that — while officially nonpartisan — kept liberals in narrow control of the court. Since gaining control in 2023, the liberal court majority has struck down an abortion ban law and overturned state legislative districts that benefited Republicans, putting partisan control of both chambers in play in this year’s election.
No state Supreme Court contest is expected to cost even close to that much this year, because no single seat is perceived as that essential to control a court. But interest groups nonetheless are focusing on court races in several states with a goal of positioning themselves for bigger races in 2028.
“State supreme courts are really, really important — increasingly important — arbiters of rights and liberties,” said Deirdre Schifeling, chief political and advocacy officer for the American Civil Liberties Union, which is spending $5.5 million on Supreme Court races in Michigan, Montana and North Carolina.
The organization said it also spent over $1 million on Supreme Court races earlier this year in Georgia and Wisconsin.
Republicans target Montana court after big rulings
Montana’s Supreme Court race features Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson, both currently district court judges in Flathead County. Eddy edged Wilson by fewer than 8,000 votes out of around 270,000 cast in a June primary for the state Supreme Court. But because they were the only candidates, both advanced to a rematch in the general election.
In recent years, the Montana Supreme Court struck down laws restricting abortion and limiting voter registration on Election Day. It also upheld a landmark ruling that the state was violating residents’ constitutional rights to a clean environment by permitting oil, gas and coal projects without regard for global warming.
Eddy, serving as a fill-in Supreme Court judge, was part of the majority that ruled the state’s abortion laws violated individual privacy rights in the state constitution.
Frustrated Republicans, who hold legislative majorities, have proposed numerous bills aimed at the judiciary. One new law effective for this year’s election allows political parties to contribute money to judicial candidates. Legislation to require partisan judicial elections passed the Senate but failed in the House.
Citizen activists responded to that attempt by gathering petition signatures to place an amendment on the November ballot that would enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution. The ACLU has contributed $2.1 million to that campaign, according to finance reports filed at the end of September.
The ACLU also has mailed flyers touting Eddy’s support for abortion rights and her decision not to accept money from political parties. The Democratic-aligned group Defend Our Courts also has backed Eddy. Wilson, meanwhile, has received funding from various Republican Party committees and spoke earlier this year at a GOP event.
Eddy said accepting money from political parties “undermines the public’s trust that the judicial branch can be impartial.”
Wilson, noting Eddy’s donations from lawyers, said “that’s more dangerous and corrosive to the objectivity of judges.”
Changes in court control can affect state laws
The focus on Montana’s high court comes after similar campaigns in other states.
In August, Kansas voters overwhelmingly defeated a Republican-backed proposal to elect Supreme Court judges instead of appointing them.
In North Carolina, the Republican-led state Legislature passed a law restoring partisan elections beginning in 2018, after Democratic-leaning judges won a majority on the state’s officially nonpartisan Supreme Court. That change paved the way for Republicans to reclaim control of the court in the 2022 elections. And that quickly led to more changes. A few months later, the new conservative majority reversed its predecessors by upholding a voter photo identification law and tossing out a ruling against a Republican-drawn congressional map.
In Ohio, the Republican-led Legislature passed a law in 2021 requiring partisan labels for Supreme Court judges on general election ballots. Since then, Republicans have expanded their narrow court majority into a dominant one.
Both the Ohio and North Carolina courts remain targets for the progressive group Alliance for Justice Action, which hopes to build momentum toward one day flipping control of those courts.
“It has been a slow process of losing judicial support in those spaces. It will be a slow process to regain it,” said Tish Gotell Faulks, the group’s state courts director.
Democrats are defending one Supreme Court seat in North Carolina this year, and each party is defending a seat in Ohio. Montana’s race will replace a retiring judge who has sometimes been a swing vote.
“What happens in this year’s races will determine how likely it is that the ideology of the court flips in 2028, when that is in fact at stake,” said Douglas Keith, deputy director of the judiciary program at the Brennan Center for Justice.

title: Trump suggests renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean: Here’s what he said
text:
(Gray News) - President Donald Trump on Saturday suggested renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean.
“We could call it Trump Ocean or Ocean of the Americans. Something like that ... We have to. We should have before I get out,” he said.
Last year, he renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. In August, he also renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America.
In his remarks at the rally in Tennessee, Trump said he would not change the name of the Hudson River, which is named for explorer Henry Hudson.
“He did a good job of setting up that sucker a long time ago,” he said.
The president also said he would not change the name of the Mississippi River.
“Now, I’m not changing the name of the Mississippi. I love Mississippi. We won that state by so much,” he said.
The president can use executive authority to rename bodies of water and other geographic features.

title: Man attacked, killed by tiger after entering wildlife park enclosure
text:
LONDON (AP) - A man died Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said.
Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1:35 p.m., but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement.
The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said.
The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,” the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its “Land of the Tigers” attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter (yard) raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or playing in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.

title: Patriots place WR Mack Hollins on injured reserve
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots were without their top performing receiver when they host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins was placed on injured reserve Saturday with a calf injury. Also sent to IR was fullback Reggie Gilliam, who is dealing with ankle and knee injuries.
Both players must sit out for at least the next four games. The moves came a day after starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck) were ruled out for Sunday’s game.
In Hollins the Patriots lose their leader in receptions (15) and yards (209). Patriots receiver A.J. Brown has been on injured reserve since suffering a high-ankle sprain in the season opener at Seattle. He is eligible to return to practice next week.

title: Indian Township man charged with murder after fatal shooting
text:
INDIAN TOWNSHIP, Maine (WABI) - A man has been taken into custody following a fatal shooting in Indian Township on Saturday night.
Police say Cory Fields, 41, of Indian Island, was found dead at a home on Peter Dana Point Road.
An investigation led to the arrest of Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township, according to Maine State Police.
He was charged with murder and taken to the Washington County Jail.
An autopsy determined Fields died from gunshot wounds; his death was ruled a homicide. The investigation is ongoing. Authorities have released no further information.
The Passamaquoddy and Penobscot Chiefs released a joint statement on the shooting, which reads in part: “As Chiefs, we stand together in mourning this loss and reaffirming our shared responsibility to protect the well-being of our people. Our strength has always come from family, community, peace, and love for one another. In this moment of sorrow, we must hold firmly to those values and work together toward healing, understanding, and a safer future for all our people.”
You can read the full letter here.
Fields’ cousin, Gabby Fields-Love remembered Corey as “a true friend who would drop whatever he was doing to support those he cared for,” adding he was “fiercely loyal” and loved his children. She expressed anger on behalf of the family that his life was taken.
“We want justice and peace,” Fields-Love said.

title: Maine is wrong to bring AI into early childhood education
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As the mother of a soon-to-be toddler who does part-time daycare, I am incensed that the state Department of Health and Human Services gave a contract to train Maine’s childhood educators to an out-of-state, for-profit, private equity-backed firm that is going to use “artificial intelligence” to train childcare workers instead of actual experienced people.
And to add economic injury to insult, the contract was taken away from a local group, Maine Roads to Quality, which is part of the University of Southern Maine. This group is now looking at layoffs in the middle of the worst economy since 2008.
The University of Southern Maine? Where my dad got his teaching degree; the place that set the foundation for him being a damn good teacher. BlackRock? A giant multinational private equity firm that makes money from the suffering of innocent people through its investments in fossil fuels (climate change), the arms industry (school shootings), the Chinese military (Uyghur genocide) and the Israeli military (Gaza genocide).
Listen, I get that the economy sucks right now. My wife and I are arguing about when to turn the heat on just like everybody else. I’m sure the fact that the New York organization Shine Early Learning underbid everyone else by $2 million probably looked pretty good to DHHS decision-makers. (I’d also bet a sales person had a slick PowerPoint.)
But that $2 million doesn’t just vanish into thin air. The $2 million would have been invested in local Maine educators training childcare workers. It would be an investment in our literal future: Maine children, including my son. And these savings? They’re coming because Shine Early Learning admits it’s using AI to do a bunch of the work.
The way large language models (LLMs) work is they vacuum up enormous training sets of data and writing. Much of this is stolen without compensation or consent from writers like my mother, whose books were among those found in a database of stolen books that Meta and OpenAI fed to train its artificial intelligence programs, Muse and ChatGPT.
It takes enormous environmental resources to keep data centers humming. Those data centers emit noise and environmental pollution in any community they are housed in. Where AI data centers go, electricity prices spike. Every time I open the Press Herald’s website I see a headline about yet another town banning or putting a moratorium on data centers. And the DHHS thought, “You know what Mainers really want more of in their life? AI!”
LLMs are glorified word prediction machines. And they frequently make errors. Just this week I’ve had to explain to angry customers at work that Google’s AI gave them incorrect information about our company’s services; the AI bot cited a random Instagram post as a fact. It wasn’t.
Early childhood educators are constantly underpaid and disrespected, mostly because they are a female-dominated profession and, well, we’ve been battling sexism since time immemorial. Also, most people have their own children, so they tend to think of early childhood care as “anyone can do it.” But the idea that early childhood educators can just be trained by an environment-killing lie-generating theft-powered word machine?
The disrespect is so galling that I can’t use the words I want to use in print.
Who made this decision? Do they have children or grandchildren whose education and development they care about? Was it a bunch of men? This seems like a decision a bunch of men would make. “Let’s replace a bunch of local Maine professionals with the magic malarkey generating button! Great idea, team!”
My son’s daycare closes several days a year for mandatory staff training and development. While the schedule interruption is annoying, I’m grateful that they care about their workers’ education and want them to remain engaged, up to date and constantly learning (traits I hope my son develops). If only the DHHS contract team cared as much.
I don’t believe there’s a way for members of the public, like myself, to weigh in on this trash decision other than contacting their state representatives, which I will absolutely be doing. If you have young children in your life you care about, or you just want to stop private equity from burrowing its tentacles further into our state, I recommend you do the same.

title: Drake Maye’s big day leads Patriots past Raiders
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Drake Maye didn’t have his top receiver, and the New England Patriots were missing both of their starting cornerbacks.
The third-year quarterback found plenty of other targets, and his defense still found a way to slow down Kirk Cousins and the Las Vegas Raiders.
Maye threw four touchdown passes and ran for another score, helping the Patriots pull away in the second half of a 45-17 victory on Sunday.
Maye was 26 of 34 for 374 yards passing in the second 300-yard game of his career. Two TDs went to Pop Douglas and one each to Hunter Henry and Kyle Williams.
Rhamondre Stevenson added a scoring run in a second consecutive victory after a sluggish start for the defending AFC champions.
With receiver Mack Hollins missing the first of at least four games with a calf injury, Maye had five players catch at least three passes, including Stevenson. Two pass-catchers who didn’t score — Efton Chism III and Eli Raridon — each had five catches for 57 yards.
“It was beautiful to be a part of today,” Maye said. “There’s still some out there.”
On a day the Patriots celebrated the 25th anniversary of the first of their six first Super Bowl championships, Maye became the first with back-to-back games of at least three TDs passing for New England since Tom Brady in 2018. It was also Maye’s first game this season without a turnover. He scored on a 3-yard run.
The Patriots (3-2) finished with season-high 536 yards, and the defense held Las Vegas under 26 points for the first time this season without injured cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III.
“That’s what it has to be,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “They realize when you get an opportunity, you do something with it.”
Cousins was 19 of 28 for 243 yards with a touchdown to Brock Bowers that pulled the Raiders (3-2) even early, but they were trailing by 28 points when they finally found the end zone again in the fourth quarter.
Cousins had limited time to operate throughout the game and was sacked three times.
“They did a nice job with their pressures, getting home quickly. Made it hard for us,” Cousins said.
Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said it’s clear there is work to do after back-to-back losses.
“We’re not happy with what happened today, and we’ve got to go do something about it,” Kubiak said.
No. 1 overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza replaced Cousins with the game out of reach later in the fourth. Kubiak said Mendoza’s appearance doesn’t change the QB depth chart for now.
“Just wanted to get (Mendoza) some exposure,” Kubiak said.
Scoring quickly
Four of the Patriots seven scoring drives lasted less than three minutes. New England scored touchdowns on four of five trips inside the 20-yard line.
Fast start for Patriots
It didn’t take long for New England’s offense to get going.
After a quick three-and-out by the Raiders to open the game, New England needed just five plays to cap a 79-yard drive with a 35-yard TD pass from Maye to a wide-open Douglas.
The drive included a 16-yard pass to Romeo Doubs to get the Patriots into Las Vegas territory.
The Raiders responded on the next series. First, Cousins connected on long completions to Bowers and Coby White. He then capitalized on a pass interference call on Kevin Byard that set up a 13-yard scoring pass to Bowers, who had eight catches for 110 yards.
New England kept its momentum going after Bowers’ TD, scoring on a 5-yard run by Stevenson.
Las Vegas had a chance before halftime after Corey Kiner fumbled at the New England 37. But Matt Gay’s 49-yard field goal try hit the left upright, and the Patriots took a 14-point halftime lead on Maye’s 11-yard pass to Henry 24 seconds before the break.
Injuries
Raiders: DT Tonka Hemingway left in the first quarter with a neck injury and was ruled out. … DE Patrick Johnson (neck) left in the second quarter.
Patriots: RB TreVeyon Henderson limped to the locker room in the second quarter with an ankle injury. Two plays later, LT Will Campbell was helped off with a right knee injury. Neither returned. … CB Charles Woods exited in the third quarter with a shoulder injury.
Up next
Raiders: Host the Bills next Sunday.
Patriots: Host the Jets next Sunday.

title: Van carrying Epstein files on tour through the U.S.
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WMTW)— A van carrying tens of thousands of pages of released Jeffrey Epstein files is on a nationwide tour.
The vehicle, called the Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Bookmobile, is traveling the country with the documents on board.
Survivor describes advocacy work
Dani Bensky, who was abused by Jeffrey Epstein, has spent recent years advocating for accountability, including speaking to lawmakers in Washington, D.C.
“We used to really live in isolation and think that we were buried in our own shame and really be locked into our own stories,” Bensky said. “But once we found each other and we started talking about how many of us there were, we’re talking about numbers of over 1,000. We think the number is closer to 1,400 at this point, of survivors and victims just within the Epstein and Maxwell case. So, just remembering how big this is. And it’s oddly, like, validating to see this much paperwork.”
Bensky said files released on Dec. 19 did not include all documents, and some redactions were missed.
“When the files were released on December 19th, we didn’t get all of the files. We got some. And we already started to see missed redactions. Right. My name was showing up there. And then in January we got this document dump that, expose over 100 of us and, like really in-depth information that was given to the FBI. And it should have been protected while perpetrators are then the ones being protected,” Bensky said.
Bensky said redaction errors occurred repeatedly.
“It feels like incompetence is the strategy here. Because so many times we would say, okay, this was not redacted properly. Can you go and fix this from our, you know, our lawyers would contact DOJ and then the document would be taken down, it would be redacted, put back up, but was still searchable,” Bensky said.
Candidate calls for policy changes
Bensky was joined by Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate running for a seat in the U.S. House.
Dunlap said if elected, he will prioritize more thorough investigation, removing the statute of limitations, and addressing law enforcement’s ability to not bury allegations.
“It’s just an extraordinary story of how, you know, simple authority that we derive from the electorate as public officials can be abused and to power over people, change their lives, traumatized them and dues, and kept anonymous, kept quiet. And it shouldn’t be quiet,” Dunlap said.
To see all locations of the bookmobile, visit their website.
