title: Fugitive businessman taken into US custody in Venezuela bribery case
text:
MIAMI (AP) — A businessman wanted for years in the U.S. for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.
Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and State Department had been offering a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido was taken into U.S. custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations agencies, Nicole Navas Oxman, a Homeland Security Task Force spokesperson, said Sunday.
Oxman didn’t say how Pulido ended up in U.S. custody but said he will make his initial court appearance Tuesday in Miami.
Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge acting President Delcy Rodríguez faces appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the U.S., sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.
The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro’s vice president. She took over as Venezuela’s acting president following the U.S. military’s ouster of Maduro in January.
Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.
Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the U.S. by Rodríguez in May. Last month, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195 million in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington.

title: 2-year-old ‘fighting for her life’ after suspect stabs toddler, her mom in random attack
text:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WJAR) - A 2-year-old Rhode Island girl is fighting for her life after she and her mother were stabbed in an attack police say was completely random.
Amaalia Javier and her 2-year-old daughter were waiting for the girl’s siblings to get off a school bus Wednesday afternoon when Providence Police say 46-year-old Nelson Blanco attacked them. The incident was caught on surveillance cameras.
Jessie Palmer, a certified nursing assistant, was also waiting for the school bus in a car with her own child when she heard a scream and saw the suspect attacking the victims. She claims Blanco went after the toddler first, and Javier tried to step in.
“He pushed her out of the way because she tried to shield the baby with her body, and he pushed her out of the way and stabbed her and then went back to the baby,” Palmer said.
Palmer and other bystanders intervened before the suspect ran off. While some people chased after him, Palmer worked to keep the 2-year-old alive.
“I helped the baby out the carriage, and when I saw she was bleeding, I put her to the floor and was putting pressure,” Palmer said. “Another lady… came and helped me apply the pressure, and then, the baby stopped breathing. So, we had to stop performing CPR and breathing for the baby until the ambulance came.”
The toddler remained in intensive care Thursday, and Providence Police Col. Oscar Perez said she is “fighting for her life.” Her mother has been released from the hospital and is focused on her daughter’s condition, friends say.
Blanco was arraigned Thursday on several charges stemming from the stabbing, including felony assault with a dangerous weapon. Police say he admitted to the attack, which they say was completely random. There was no known connection between the suspect and the victims.
“That man’s evil and what he did was wrong, and I don’t even think jail’s enough punishment for him,” Palmer said.
Court records show Blanco’s criminal history dates back decades and includes a 2003 case in which he was charged with stabbing two 7-year-old children.

title: Oklahoma upsets No. 1 Texas
text:
Oklahoma upsets No. 1 Texas on Tate Sandell's game-ending 47-yard field goal
Tate Sandell kicked a 47-yard field goal on the final play and Oklahoma overcame its continued offensive ineptitude with touchdowns on special teams and defense in a 27-24 win over No. 1 Texas in the Red River rivalry game on Saturday.
Video above: Red River Rivalry upset
The Sooners (3-2, 1-1 Southeastern Conference) beat a No. 1 team for the first time since a 38-17 win over Missouri in 2007. They had been 0-4-1 when facing a top-ranked Texas team.
“It was really a classic game of two really good programs in an incredibly intense environment,” Sooners coach Brent Venables said.
Arch Manning threw three touchdowns for the Longhorns (4-1, 1-1), but both of his interceptions were costly.
Texas had two late chances, but Gianni Spetic was wide right on a 53-yard field goal attempt with 1:55 left. After the Sooners went three-and-out for the seventh time in the game, Manning’s last pass was intercepted by Courtland Guillory with 19 seconds left.
“It’s obviously a level of disappointment, there’s a level of anger and frustration because we know we have issues that need to be fixed and we’re working on those issues and trying to get them fixed,” Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said. “But they reared their ugly head today against a quality team.”
The late pick had the Sooners at their 39 and, instead of settling for overtime, John Mateer completed passes of 13 and 20 yards to Isaiah Sategna on opposite sides of the field and both were upheld on replay review.
Oklahoma then ran a play to set up the kick by Sandell, who earlier had made a 53-yarder and missed another from the same distance.
Dakoda Fields recovered a blocked punt in the end zone and Peyton Bowen returned an interception 42 yards for a touchdown for the Sooners, who in their previous game two weeks earlier lost 41-13 at No. 2 Georgia.
“I want these guys to experience victory, certainly in this game, (it) was incredibly important,” Venables said. “People questioning the commitment and the coaches can’t coach and the players stink, it comes with the arena. But at the same time, sometimes that fuels you.”
Video below: Oklahoma Head Coach Brent Venables, QB John Mateer talk upcoming season
The pick-6 by Bowen came after Manning was scrambling away from pressure and throwing toward Cam Coleman, who had an earlier touchdown. But the ball instead went to the Oklahoma safety, whose return with 10:07 left put the Sooners up 24-17.
Texas responded with a tying 75-yard drive and Manning's third TD pass, a 15-yarder to Jermaine Bishop Jr. with 6:32 left.
Manning finished 19-of-31 passing for 260 yards.
Mateer completed 18 of 26 passes for 155 yards. The Sooners had only 238 total yards, well below their average of 321 coming into the game that was last in the SEC.
Texas didn’t have a first down on its first four drives, and it wasn’t until the first play after a short punt that Coleman made a leaping catch in the back of the end zone for a 41-yard score for a 7-0 lead with 6:56 left in the first quarter.

title: Troy Jackson’s sound bites won’t be enough
text:
Jacob Posik is the political director of Maine Civic Action and the director of legislative affairs of Maine Policy Institute.
There is a fundamental difference between sounding like you know what you’re talking about and knowing what you’re talking about. In last week’s first U.S. Senate debate, Troy Jackson brought the sound bites. Sen. Susan Collins brought the substance.
This likely wasn’t shocking to anyone who’s used to hearing Jackson fumble over his words or make a fool of himself while commanding the Maine Senate.
For much of the debate, while Jackson seemed determined to land the next punch, deliver the next rehearsed line or manufacture the next campaign clip, Collins did something much less flashy but far more important. The senator demonstrated that she, unlike Jackson, understands how government works, how policy is made and the responsibilities of the office she holds.
As the debate went on, this distinction became impossible to ignore. Jackson was quick with accusations but thin on details. And when the conversation moved beyond simple political rhetoric and into the mechanics of how policy is made, his lack of substance and shallow intellectual depth became painfully obvious. The contrast was striking.
Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly returned to familiar attacks against President Donald Trump and Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Regardless of the question, he seemed more interested in delivering his next rehearsed one-liner than offering substantive answers about the challenges facing Maine families.
This kind of political rhetoric might generate applause at a campaign rally comprised of a small smattering of Graham Platner leftovers, but it’s hardly a substitute for knowledge or competence when it comes to a U.S. Senate debate.
Perhaps the most embarrassing moment came during an exchange about healthcare, when Jackson appeared to confuse the responsibilities associated with Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement.
Jackson criticized Collins for failing to increase Medicaid reimbursement rates for Maine hospitals, suggesting that her position as chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee magically gave her the authority to address the issue.
The problem? Jackson revealed he fundamentally misunderstands how the program operates and which level of government is in charge of reimbursement.
Collins correctly explained that Medicaid reimbursement rates are established by states within federal requirements. Maine has the authority to adjust those rates, meaning Jackson was criticizing Collins for something that falls substantially within the responsibilities of state government. Hopefully the irony isn’t lost on anyone.
Jackson has spent the better part of 20 years as a fixture in Augusta politics. He served as president of the Senate for six years, one of the most powerful positions in state government, helping to oversee the very legislative institution responsible for determining Maine’s healthcare policies and funding priorities.
Instead of increasing those rates to help the people he pretends to care about, Jackson and his allies went on bloated spending sprees in budget after budget. They provided oodles in subsidies to their friends in the “affordable” housing and “clean” energy worlds. They gave out “free” community college on your dime and “free” school lunches to the children of millionaires.
Yet there he stood, trying to blame Collins for a responsibility that largely belongs to the state government he once led for six years. For someone seeking promotion to the U.S. Senate, that’s an embarrassing display of ignorance.
This exchange also exposed a broader weakness of Jackson’s. It’s easy to criticize Washington for the problems Maine faces; it’s much more difficult to explain how we should solve those problems.
Based on Jackson’s statements during the debate, all of Maine’s problems would cease to exist overnight if Trump was no longer president or Brett Kavanaugh no longer served on the Supreme Court. His performance suggested he believes political outrage can substitute for legislative effectiveness.
To be clear, Collins’ record is not beyond criticism. Her decisions deserve scrutiny, and all Maine voters are entitled to question her judgment on any vote she’s cast while serving as our senator.
But meaningful criticism requires more than repeating the same accusations, delivering rehearsed insults or hoping the audience overlooks the absence of substantive policy knowledge.
More than anything, the debate demonstrated why experience and competence matter. Collins came prepared to discuss the responsibilities of government and defend her legislative record. Troy Jackson came prepared to attack Trump, Kavanaugh and deliver campaign slogans.
One candidate demonstrated the knowledge necessary to govern. The other demonstrated a meager ability to campaign.
If Jackson hopes to convince Mainers that he belongs in the U.S. Senate, he will need to offer considerably more than political theater.
Susan Collins didn’t just win the first debate. She gave Maine’s former Senate president a much-needed lesson in how government actually works.

title: Obituary: E. Brooks Bornhofft
text:
CAPE ELIZABETH – Elias Brooks Bornhofft, known throughout his life as Brooks, died unexpectedly on Sept. 29, 2026, at the age of 49.
Brooks grew up in Prides Crossing, Mass., and made Cape Elizabeth home with his wife, Emily Calise, and their two young sons, Elias and Alden. He was the son of Nancy Daly Church and the late J. Eric Bornhofft, and the brother of Eric Bornhofft.
Brooks attended Shore Country Day School, The Governor’s Academy, and Colgate University, where he was a member of Sigma Chi fraternity and the rowing team. He later earned an M.B.A. from Boston University School of Management and worked for over 20 years in technology. He was a member of Boston’s Union Boat Club.
He had an extraordinary knowledge of and passion for the natural world. Active, kind, curious, engaging, and with a clever wit, Brooks had an energy that was entirely his own. He tackled life’s adventures, big and small, such as climbing Mt. Kilimanjaro with his mother and brother and building mountain biking trails with his sons.
An expert birder, Brooks shared his passion in his popular column in The Cape Courier. Since 2018 he brought biweekly field observations, natural history, and anecdotes, often including Elias and Alden, together for his readers in the “Local Birding Report.” The poetic column is a lasting record of his love of birds, natural spaces, and family. Brooks volunteered with BirdSafe Maine and was on the board of the Cape Elizabeth Land Trust.
Above all, Brooks cherished his family. He was a devoted husband to Emily and a superb and loving father to Elias and Alden. He was unique and admirable in his attentiveness to his sons and his ability to enter their worlds rather than just observe from the outside. He loved sharing his favorite place, Annisquam, Mass., with his sons, Emily and extended family.
Brooks leaves a legacy in his writing, environmental work, family, and relationships with the community, and those that knew him will continue to carry Brooks in each changing season.
A celebration of life will be held in Annisquam, Mass., in Summer 2027. For more information visit hobbsfuneralhome.com.
In lieu of flowers donations can be made to the Cape Elizabeth Land Trust.

title: Carr crash radio appearance by Sen. Collins
text:
When I lived in Maine, I worked hard against Susan Collins’ election to the United States Senate. Over the years, however, I have come to grudgingly admire her avowed commitment to avoiding name-calling and personal attacks. Collins is a dignified presence in an arena that is increasingly undignified. It was disappointing, therefore, to hear her on “The Howie Carr Show,” broadcast from Gorham on Sept. 25.
Carr, as anyone who listens regularly to his show knows, revels in name-calling and personal attacks. He often refers to immigrants as “cholos,” describes foreign countries as “Third-World hellholes,” and rates women on their looks. Indeed, in a segment that aired just before Collins appeared, he made some very misogynistic comments about the lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, who apparently does not meet his beauty standards.
Carr has been around for many years, and everyone is aware of his shtick. Collins should be ashamed of appearing on this show.
David Scannell
Bedford, N.H.

title: Obituary: Doris L. Violette
text:
LEWISTON – With hearts full of gratitude and sorrow, we announce the passing of our beloved mother, Doris L. Violette.
Doris was a fun-loving and selfless mother of four, who enjoyed laughter, playing games, solving puzzles, and time spent with family and friends. Doris was deeply devoted to her husband of 58 years, Roland L. Violette, who together with Doris were amazing and inseparable. She always made the right decisions for her family, and we are eternally thankful to her for that. Doris’ joyful nature and good humor were enjoyed by all who knew her, and her laughter was the center piece of every gathering, which will be forever missed but cherished in our hearts.
Doris was a life-long learner, and after raising her children she went back to school to get her college degree. Doris was great with words and numbers, and following her talents, she then had a long and fulfilling career as a proof-reader.
Doris possessed incredible strength and resolve, and was able to survive life’s many challenges, including breast cancer. Doris died of natural causes on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, surrounded and comforted by her family and her loving husband Roland.
Doris is survived by Roland; her son Dan Violette and his wife Cindy, her son Steve Violette and his fiancé Kristine Logan, and her daughter Amy St. Pierre and her husband Richard. She is also survived by three grandchildren, Matt St. Pierre, Ally Nichols, and Joey Violette; and their eight great-grandchildren.
Doris was predeceased by her son Theodore “Ted” Violette; and her grandson, Ben St. Pierre.
Condolences and fond memories may be shared with family and friends at http://www.albert-burpee.com
A Liturgy of the Word will be held on Monday Oct. 26, at Saint Peter’s Cemetery Mausoleum on Deer Road, Lewiston, at 11 a.m.
Arrangements are under the care of Albert & Burpee Funeral Home & Cremation Services, 253 Pine St., Lewiston, 207-782-7201.
In lieu of flowers,
donations made in
Doris’ name to:
Susan G. Komen Foundation for Breast Cancer at http://www.komen.org
would be appreciated by Doris and her family

title: Obituary: Carolyn (Boothby) McConnell
text:
SACO – Carolyn (Boothby) McConnell, 88, of Saco and formerly of Kennebunk, Maine and Harwinton, Conn., passed away on Oct. 2, 2026 in Biddeford following a short illness and a rich life full of experiences.
Carolyn was the daughter of Ronald Waterhouse Boothby and Edna Mae Philbrick both of York, Maine. She was the youngest of three children of which she always appreciated her big brother Herbert’s sense of humor and shared a passion for antiques and history with her sister, Shirley. Carolyn graduated from Kennebunk High School in 1956 where she was a majorette and very active with school activities. Researching the history of Maine was an area of interest, passion, and expertise for her. She was extremely proud of her heritage as a descendant of Maine pioneers and English lineage of which she researched inexhaustibly and quite thoroughly as evidenced by her notes and annotations that could fill a library. In addition to this research, she extensively studied Egyptology which was a constant interest throughout her life.
Carolyn married her high school sweetheart, David Marshall McConnell on Feb. 23, 1957, and they settled in Harwinton, Conn. and raised a family of four children who possessed a variety of talents of whom she was very proud. In Harwinton, Conn., as a lifetime lover of books, she volunteered for the Goshen and Harwinton libraries. When her husband began his career at Lewis S. Mills High, she created scrap books with newspaper clippings and photos of every basketball game he coached from the early 1960s through the early 1980s. Carolyn managed all the projects involved in maintaining a home. When her husband decided to pursue a doctoral degree at Boston University in the late 1980s, Carloyn was his editor in chief for his papers and dissertation. Upon relocating to support David in finishing his work in Boston, Mass., her children joked that she was off to college. David always recognized that she was essential in helping him earn his doctorate. During the summer months, she relished returning and residing at Kennebunk Beach to connect with relatives and provide behind the scenes support for her husband who was Executive Director of the Kennebunk Improvement Association for 32 years. Carolyn was an avid supporter of the Portland Sea Dogs and often took her mother-in-law Marie (Soule) McConnell to games at Hadlock Field and on other coastal Maine excursions.
In 1990, Carolyn returned to reside permanently in Kennebunk Beach when David accepted a headmaster position at their alma mater at Kennebunk High School. Returning home was deeply fulfilling for Carolyn. She attended many school events, including Rams football games where she recalled and shared her experiences with other locals and students there. During this period of life, Carolyn traveled to France to further her creative interests and talents in the visual arts and ancient history. She traveled to Montana to participate and train with paleontologists to excavate and preserve dinosaur bones. Using that experience, and her training, she was invited to join a team of archaeologists from the Maine State Museum to excavate a Mastodon excavation in Scarborough. She was a lover of music to the benefit of her children. In her homes one would commonly hear music from such genres as vocal jazz, country, sock hop, soft rock, and musicals. During the winters, she and David resided in Vero Beach, Fla. enjoying many outings with friends to professional baseball games during spring training, zoos, flea markets, and to launches at the Kennedy Space Center.
Since 2022, Carolyn has resided at Atlantic Heights in Saco. She enjoyed the activities, the company of residents, and especially the wonderful staff members who provided care in her later years. The family is grateful to all of them for their care and friendship over her four years at the Inn.
Carolyn is predeceased by her husband, Dr. David M. McConnell; a brother, Herbert Boothby and his wife Betty; a sister, Shirley LeBarge and her husband George and her nephew, Jason LeBarge.
The members of her surviving family whom she was blessed to see grow and succeed in all their endeavors include her sons James E. McConnell (Sheilah) of West Simsbury, Conn., USMC First Sergeant (Ret.) Mark D. McConnell (Amalia) of Yuma, Ariz., and Brian S. McConnell (Tracy) of East Granby, Conn., a daughter, Sharon L. McConnell-Dickerson (David) of Columbus, Miss.; three grandchildren, Keith J. McConnell of Simsbury, Conn., Maeve McConnell of East Granby, Conn., and Gavin McConnell (Carly) of Southwick, Mass.; one great-grandchild, Marshall McConnell of Southwick, Mass.; and five nieces, Deborah Soule (Thomas), Mary Kittrick (Leo), Susan Gorman (Harold), Georgeann Tudisco (Daryl), and Jennifer LeBarge Seabrooke.
They are all grateful that she has been reunited with her ancestors, parents, siblings, and friends as well as the many pets she cared for including dogs, “Rebound” and Big “Red” Cowens and cats, “Ming”, “Ernie”, and “Howard”.
Friends are invited to gather at 9 a.m. on Saturday Oct. 17, followed by a funeral service starting at 10 a.m. at Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk. A private family graveside service will be held immediately after at Hope Cemetery in Kennebunk.
To share a memory or leave a message of condolence, please visit Carolyn‘s Book of Memories Page at http://www.bibberfuneral.com.
Arrangements are in the care of Bibber Memorial Chapel, 67 Summer St., Kennebunk.
In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation in Carolyn’s memory to The Dr. David and Carolyn McConnell Memorial Scholarship Fund, a 501(c)(3) benefiting students at both Lewis S. Mills High School (Connecticut) and Kennebunk High School (Maine).
The fund is managed at
Bank of America
240 W Main St.
Avon, CT 06001
Please make checks payable to the “Dr. David and Carolyn McConnell Memorial” and reference “Account 385027179752” in the memo line.

title: DOJ says it’s investigating whether White House TV pool’s coverage halt violated antitrust law
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that cover the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports — a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.
Last month’s developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organizations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.
Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”
___
Taxin contributed to this report from Santa Ana, California.

title: UMaine’s role in pay-to-play scheme deserves a closer look
text:
ProPublica’s investigation into Sen. Susan Collins’ pay-to-play practice raises serious concerns about complicity on the part of the University of Maine and damage to the university’s research mission.
In addition to wood composites, to what extent has research at Maine’s institution been dependent on the senator’s largesse and to what extent has this largesse been determined on the senator’s need for campaign funds? To what extent does the research that the university embraces reflect the senator’s priorities and to what extent are those priorities in the best interests of Maine people and Maine students? To what extent have the senator’s priorities corrupted the university?
It beggars belief that the university’s administration did not understand Sen. Collins’ pay-to-play strategy, and the university’s claim of innocence should be thoroughly investigated.
ProPublica has played its part, and Maine’s media should now play theirs.
Tony Brinkley
Professor of English (retired), University of Maine
Bangor

title: Maine’s elections are getting crazy expensive. Where does the money go?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The most expensive advertisement of Maine’s campaign season so far begins like this: “Augusta politician Troy Jackson: While his family cashed in, you paid the price.”
A man narrates for 30 tensely soundtracked seconds over quotes pulled from years-old news articles, blaming the former Maine Senate president and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate for higher taxes. It’s a classic attack ad.
At the end, the narrator lowers and hastens his voice.
“Pine Tree Results PAC is responsible for the content of this advertising” — all $2.2 million of it, according to a federal campaign finance filing.
A different group, SRCP Media Inc., developed the spot and bought space on the airwaves for it — not Pine Tree Results PAC.
This is a pretty normal arrangement. SRCP Media is one of the premier conservative campaign advertising firms in the country. It’s based in a waterfront office building in Alexandria, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.
This year in Maine, with a potentially Senate-tilting election at the top of the ballot, plus a hotly contested House race and an open governor’s seat to boot, campaigns and outside groups have dropped hundreds of millions of donor dollars to persuade voters to fill in their preferred ballot bubble.
So far, the eye-watering total exceeds $300 million, according to the ad tracking service AdImpact. But little of the campaign money meant to convince Maine’s electorate is actually being spent on Maine companies.
Not all of the cash spent this cycle has shown up in federal financial reports, which are filed quarterly. But as of the last reports from late September, it’s clear that a relatively small percentage of campaign spending comes home to Maine broadcasters or other advertisers.
Instead, well over half is going to D.C.-area consultants and firms like SRCP Media, a Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram analysis of the data found. Only about 8% is spent in Maine.
Between a relative lack of locally based campaign expertise and the explosion of money available to campaigns and PACs, the modern election has turned into an expensive game of D.C.-area consultant chess, experts say.
Ben Coolidge Gagnon, a veteran of two Maine gubernatorial campaigns, said this small state’s campaigns can only grow so big before they run out of places to spend money. Sara Gideon’s record-fundraising 2020 U.S. Senate campaign, he noted, still has millions left in the bank.
“So where does all that money go in the future?” Coolidge Gagnon said. “More consultants.”
WHERE THE MONEY GOES
While they can sometimes get candidates in trouble, donations are the backbone of modern campaigns. Without millions from donors, candidates wouldn’t be able to pay staff, and outside groups couldn’t buy ads.
Most of those donations come from outside of Maine. In federal races this cycle, about 83% of Maine candidates’ donations have come from other states, according to the campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets.
The spending of that money mostly happens outside of Maine, too.
This year, more than $67 million has gone to Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia, where media firms and PACs operate in close proximity to Washington’s halls of power. Pennsylvania-based firms have raked in another $10.5 million.
In federal races, only 3.4% of the money has been spent in Maine. About a quarter of consulting costs went to Maine, and a staggeringly low 0.2% of advertising costs went to Maine firms.
Money is also flowing out of Maine even in the races for governor and state Legislature, where representatives are sent to Augusta, not Capitol Hill.
About 37% of electioneering spending for state offices has gone to the nation’s capital or its bordering states, while about 20% has gone to Maine-based companies.
Generally, campaigns were most likely to keep their money in Maine when paying for food, events and travel. Polling and advertising spending happened almost entirely outside of this state.
THE ELECTIONS BUSINESS
Coolidge Gagnon got his start in politics in 2014 on Mike Michaud’s gubernatorial campaign, and later worked for the Maine Democratic Party and on the finance team in Janet Mills’ first gubernatorial run.
He’s watched the elections industry explode in recent years, jet-fueled by the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision, which has allowed super PACs to independently raise and spend without limits.
Maine has mostly been left on the outside of that boom, Coolidge Gagnon said, and the reason is simple: this state only has three statewide elections, for governor and its two U.S. senators. It’s difficult to get experience here, and it’s not particularly lucrative to stay.
Massachusetts, by contrast, elects six executive officers and its two U.S. Senators in statewide elections. New York has six statewide elections. North Carolina has 34.
Consulting firms based elsewhere have more races to draw from, Coolidge Gagnon said, and political operatives “will hop state to state anyway” to follow big campaigns and big money.
Richard Schlackman, who has been in political advertising and consulting all over the country since the 1970s, said spending tens of millions of dollars across state lines is par for the course. All of the incentives point toward spending more.
“What you have to understand — if things are going well, your side gives you more money to keep it going well,” he said. “If things are going bad, your side gives you money to destroy the other side.”
It’s simply more profitable to center on Washington, D.C., or New York, Schlackman said — that’s where all of the power players are, and the big names with connections.
Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican nominee for that state’s competitive U.S. Senate seat, said outright that D.C. consultants had taken control of his message during a fundraiser this last month, Politico reported: “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.”
“They get more of that money,” Schlackman said of D.C. operatives. “That doesn’t mean you’re getting a better ad.”
WHO GETS THE MONEY?
There’s a scene in the early 2000s television series, The West Wing, where the fictional president’s chief of staff and prospective campaign manager, Bruno Gianelli, negotiate Gianelli’s pay.
“Fifteen percent of the ad buys,” Gianelli says. “You’re gonna say 10, so why don’t we just say 13?”
That scene holds pretty true to how campaign advertising consultants get paid today, Schlackman said — consultants develop the ad and charge a percentage of the total cost to place the ad on TV. For some, there’s a monthly retainer fee.
That makes consultants some of the biggest winners of expensive election seasons like this one in Maine.
“The money’s in the buy for these TV consultants,” Schlackman said.
In Maine’s state elections, campaigns and PACs regularly report their books to the Maine Ethics Commission. Federal races have similar requirements. But those public reports don’t always tell the whole story, Coolidge Gagnon said, especially on advertising.
State filings show less than $600,000 has been spent on advertising, but gubernatorial candidates’ spots have been blasting through TVs and radios for months.
While the state campaign finance guidebook recommends that groups record the final vendor — for an ad, that’s usually a TV station or social media company — campaigns and PACs often only report the first payee: the media consulting firm they used to develop and place the ad.
“They want to give the least amount of information as they legally have to,” Coolidge Gagnon said. “There’s a competitive advantage of people knowing where the buys are going.”
Campaigns and other groups can subscribe to services like AdImpact, which track ad spending, to get a bit more information. But those services cost thousands of dollars, and the Press Herald analysis didn’t find any Maine campaigns had subscribed to AdImpact.
The election cycle has long been a boon to TV and radio stations that get paid to air candidates’ ads, said Tim Moore, the CEO and president of the Maine Broadcasters Association, in an interview this summer. This year’s been no different, he said. Anyone watching or listening can vouch for that.
But while that money does help stations pay their employees and support a healthy broadcasting ecosystem, it also ebbs and flows. Off years don’t produce the same kind of political spending.
Plus, he said, stations sometimes have to hand over profits to their owners, wherever they may be.
New York-based Democratic political consultant Roy Moskowitz said Maine is a relatively cheap state to advertise in, especially compared with where he operates. Maine only has two congressional districts and three TV markets, where customers get the same channels and ads. New York City has more than a dozen congressional districts and two dozen cable advertising zones.
On the one hand, that means it’s pretty easy to buy advertising space here, he said. On the other, the relatively low cost, Moskowitz said, means there are fewer Maine-based media firms because it’s not worth it for businesses to set up shop here.
Plus, the advertising landscape is changing.
While Maine voters, who skew older, are easy to reach on broadcast television, Moskowitz said consultants see streaming services like Hulu and Apple TV and social media as the most effective forms of political advertising. It’s easier to target specific consumers based on their beliefs and habits through those platforms, he said.
More streaming-based advertising only promises to further shift money away from Maine and toward D.C.-based consulting firms and California-based media conglomerates.
And at some point, Coolidge Gagnon said, there’s only so much advertising to buy and so many people to hire.
When Maine’s ad breaks fill up and rosters bloat, there’s still millions left over.

title: Maine State Police investigate homicide in Indian Township
text:
State and tribal law enforcement are investigating a weekend shooting on a Passamaquoddy reservation that left one man dead and another facing a murder charge.
Officials from the Indian Township police and fire departments responded just before 9:30 p.m. Saturday to reports of a shooting at 312 Peter Dana Point Road and found the body of 41-year-old Cory Fields, of Indian Island.
An investigation by the Maine State Police Major Crimes Unit and evidence response team led to the arrest of 46-year-old Jeremy Stevens, of Motahkomikuk (Indian Township), according to a state police news release Sunday.
Stevens was charged with murder and taken to the Washington County Jail in Machias. Jail staff confirmed Monday he is being held without bail.
Fields’ body was taken to the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, which determined his death was a homicide. An autopsy performed Saturday concluded that his cause of death was gunshot wounds.
One of Fields’ friends described him Monday as a kind and caring father who worked as a roofer.
Becky Saulnier, 41, of Dedham, said in an interview that Fields loved music and being outdoors. She said she was shocked to hear about his death.
Chiefs from the Passamaquoddy Tribe and the Penobscot Nation on Sunday evening published a joint statement about the killing, saying that tribal law enforcement is working in coordination with state authorities as the investigation proceeds.
“We understand that this tragedy has raised difficult questions and that our communities are seeking answers. … We ask for patience as the investigation moves forward and for respect for the process as those involved work to determine what happened,” the chiefs wrote.
The letter was signed by Chief Amkuwiposhehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik (Pleasant Point), Chief William Nichols Sr. of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk and Chief Kirk Francis of the Penobscot Nation.
“To the family and loved ones of the Penobscot citizen who was taken from us, we offer our deepest condolences,” their statement read. “We recognize that no words can take away the pain of losing someone you love. Please know that you are held in the hearts of our Nations, and that our communities stand with you as you face the difficult days ahead.”
Officials from the Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service and the Washington County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the scene Saturday, state police said.
The Passamaquoddy Reservation at Motahkomikuk, also known as Indian Township, is home to about 760 residents, according to census data. It’s one of the tribe’s two reservations in Washington County, along with the Passamaquoddy Reservation at Sipayik (Pleasant Point).
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 12 to add more details.

title: Coast to coast with Ford & Brinkley, Part II
text:
Day six of our cross-country adventure on the Mother Road finds us at the Illinois State Fairgrounds in Springfield, for the second night. So far, the tall tales and the folklore surrounding the most widely known road in the world has met our expectations — as well as some of the schtick. After two-and-a-half days of pushing through eight states, resting at night in campgrounds next to freeways, listening to trains, planes and automobiles at all hours, we arrived outside Chicago, close to Joliet in a publicly owned park/campground that offered great opportunity, but desperately needed more attention.

title: Maine’s elections are getting crazy expensive. Where does the money go?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The most expensive advertisement of Maine’s campaign season so far begins like this: “Augusta politician Troy Jackson: While his family cashed in, you paid the price.”
A man narrates for 30 tensely soundtracked seconds over quotes pulled from years-old news articles, blaming the former Maine Senate president and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate for higher taxes. It’s a classic attack ad.
At the end, the narrator lowers and hastens his voice.
“Pine Tree Results PAC is responsible for the content of this advertising” — all $2.2 million of it, according to a federal campaign finance filing.
A different group, SRCP Media Inc., developed the spot and bought space on the airwaves for it — not Pine Tree Results PAC.
This is a pretty normal arrangement. SRCP Media is one of the premier conservative campaign advertising firms in the country. It’s based in a waterfront office building in Alexandria, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.
This year in Maine, with a potentially Senate-tilting election at the top of the ballot, plus a hotly contested House race and an open governor’s seat to boot, campaigns and outside groups have dropped hundreds of millions of donor dollars to persuade voters to fill in their preferred ballot bubble.
So far, the eye-watering total exceeds $300 million, according to the ad tracking service AdImpact. But little of the campaign money meant to convince Maine’s electorate is actually being spent on Maine companies.
Not all of the cash spent this cycle has shown up in federal financial reports, which are filed quarterly. But as of the last reports from late September, it’s clear that a relatively small percentage of campaign spending comes home to Maine broadcasters or other advertisers.
Instead, well over half is going to D.C.-area consultants and firms like SRCP Media, a Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram analysis of the data found. Only about 8% is spent in Maine.
Between a relative lack of locally based campaign expertise and the explosion of money available to campaigns and PACs, the modern election has turned into an expensive game of D.C.-area consultant chess, experts say.
Ben Coolidge Gagnon, a veteran of two Maine gubernatorial campaigns, said this small state’s campaigns can only grow so big before they run out of places to spend money. Sara Gideon’s record-fundraising 2020 U.S. Senate campaign, he noted, still has millions left in the bank.
“So where does all that money go in the future?” Coolidge Gagnon said. “More consultants.”
WHERE THE MONEY GOES
While they can sometimes get candidates in trouble, donations are the backbone of modern campaigns. Without millions from donors, candidates wouldn’t be able to pay staff, and outside groups couldn’t buy ads.
Most of those donations come from outside of Maine. In federal races this cycle, about 83% of Maine candidates’ donations have come from other states, according to the campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets.
The spending of that money mostly happens outside of Maine, too.
This year, more than $67 million has gone to Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia, where media firms and PACs operate in close proximity to Washington’s halls of power. Pennsylvania-based firms have raked in another $10.5 million.
In federal races, only 3.4% of the money has been spent in Maine. About a quarter of consulting costs went to Maine, and a staggeringly low 0.2% of advertising costs went to Maine firms.
Money is also flowing out of Maine even in the races for governor and state Legislature, where representatives are sent to Augusta, not Capitol Hill.
About 37% of electioneering spending for state offices has gone to the nation’s capital or its bordering states, while about 20% has gone to Maine-based companies.
Generally, campaigns were most likely to keep their money in Maine when paying for food, events and travel. Polling and advertising spending happened almost entirely outside of this state.
THE ELECTIONS BUSINESS
Coolidge Gagnon got his start in politics in 2014 on Mike Michaud’s gubernatorial campaign, and later worked for the Maine Democratic Party and on the finance team in Janet Mills’ first gubernatorial run.
He’s watched the elections industry explode in recent years, jet-fueled by the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision, which has allowed super PACs to independently raise and spend without limits.
Maine has mostly been left on the outside of that boom, Coolidge Gagnon said, and the reason is simple: this state only has three statewide elections, for governor and its two U.S. senators. It’s difficult to get experience here, and it’s not particularly lucrative to stay.
Massachusetts, by contrast, elects six executive officers and its two U.S. Senators in statewide elections. New York has six statewide elections. North Carolina has 34.
Consulting firms based elsewhere have more races to draw from, Coolidge Gagnon said, and political operatives “will hop state to state anyway” to follow big campaigns and big money.
Richard Schlackman, who has been in political advertising and consulting all over the country since the 1970s, said spending tens of millions of dollars across state lines is par for the course. All of the incentives point toward spending more.
“What you have to understand — if things are going well, your side gives you more money to keep it going well,” he said. “If things are going bad, your side gives you money to destroy the other side.”
It’s simply more profitable to center on Washington, D.C., or New York, Schlackman said — that’s where all of the power players are, and the big names with connections.
Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican nominee for that state’s competitive U.S. Senate seat, said outright that D.C. consultants had taken control of his message during a fundraiser this last month, Politico reported: “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.”
“They get more of that money,” Schlackman said of D.C. operatives. “That doesn’t mean you’re getting a better ad.”
WHO GETS THE MONEY?
There’s a scene in the early 2000s television series, The West Wing, where the fictional president’s chief of staff and prospective campaign manager, Bruno Gianelli, negotiate Gianelli’s pay.
“Fifteen percent of the ad buys,” Gianelli says. “You’re gonna say 10, so why don’t we just say 13?”
That scene holds pretty true to how campaign advertising consultants get paid today, Schlackman said — consultants develop the ad and charge a percentage of the total cost to place the ad on TV. For some, there’s a monthly retainer fee.
That makes consultants some of the biggest winners of expensive election seasons like this one in Maine.
“The money’s in the buy for these TV consultants,” Schlackman said.
In Maine’s state elections, campaigns and PACs regularly report their books to the Maine Ethics Commission. Federal races have similar requirements. But those public reports don’t always tell the whole story, Coolidge Gagnon said, especially on advertising.
State filings show less than $600,000 has been spent on advertising, but gubernatorial candidates’ spots have been blasting through TVs and radios for months.
While the state campaign finance guidebook recommends that groups record the final vendor — for an ad, that’s usually a TV station or social media company — campaigns and PACs often only report the first payee: the media consulting firm they used to develop and place the ad.
“They want to give the least amount of information as they legally have to,” Coolidge Gagnon said. “There’s a competitive advantage of people knowing where the buys are going.”
Campaigns and other groups can subscribe to services like AdImpact, which track ad spending, to get a bit more information. But those services cost thousands of dollars, and the Press Herald analysis didn’t find any Maine campaigns had subscribed to AdImpact.
The election cycle has long been a boon to TV and radio stations that get paid to air candidates’ ads, said Tim Moore, the CEO and president of the Maine Broadcasters Association, in an interview this summer. This year’s been no different, he said. Anyone watching or listening can vouch for that.
But while that money does help stations pay their employees and support a healthy broadcasting ecosystem, it also ebbs and flows. Off years don’t produce the same kind of political spending.
Plus, he said, stations sometimes have to hand over profits to their owners, wherever they may be.
New York-based Democratic political consultant Roy Moskowitz said Maine is a relatively cheap state to advertise in, especially compared with where he operates. Maine only has two congressional districts and three TV markets, where customers get the same channels and ads. New York City has more than a dozen congressional districts and two dozen cable advertising zones.
On the one hand, that means it’s pretty easy to buy advertising space here, he said. On the other, the relatively low cost, Moskowitz said, means there are fewer Maine-based media firms because it’s not worth it for businesses to set up shop here.
Plus, the advertising landscape is changing.
While Maine voters, who skew older, are easy to reach on broadcast television, Moskowitz said consultants see streaming services like Hulu and Apple TV and social media as the most effective forms of political advertising. It’s easier to target specific consumers based on their beliefs and habits through those platforms, he said.
More streaming-based advertising only promises to further shift money away from Maine and toward D.C.-based consulting firms and California-based media conglomerates.
And at some point, Coolidge Gagnon said, there’s only so much advertising to buy and so many people to hire.
When Maine’s ad breaks fill up and rosters bloat, there’s still millions left over.

20-year-old dead after drowning in Ellis Pond

A 20-year-old man is dead after drowning in Ellis Pond in Roxbury.
Authorities say Shawn Noyes, 20, of Dixfield, was kayaking with family when he fell out. He was seen trying to swim to a nearby island, and after a few minutes he disappeared and was feared drowned.

title: Van carrying Epstein files on tour through the U.S.
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WMTW)— A van carrying tens of thousands of pages of released Jeffrey Epstein files is on a nationwide tour.
The vehicle, called the Donald J. Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Bookmobile, is traveling the country with the documents on board.
Survivor describes advocacy work
Dani Bensky, who was abused by Jeffrey Epstein, has spent recent years advocating for accountability, including speaking to lawmakers in Washington, D.C.
“We used to really live in isolation and think that we were buried in our own shame and really be locked into our own stories,” Bensky said. “But once we found each other and we started talking about how many of us there were, we’re talking about numbers of over 1,000. We think the number is closer to 1,400 at this point, of survivors and victims just within the Epstein and Maxwell case. So, just remembering how big this is. And it’s oddly, like, validating to see this much paperwork.”
Bensky said files released on Dec. 19 did not include all documents, and some redactions were missed.
“When the files were released on December 19th, we didn’t get all of the files. We got some. And we already started to see missed redactions. Right. My name was showing up there. And then in January we got this document dump that, expose over 100 of us and, like really in-depth information that was given to the FBI. And it should have been protected while perpetrators are then the ones being protected,” Bensky said.
Bensky said redaction errors occurred repeatedly.
“It feels like incompetence is the strategy here. Because so many times we would say, okay, this was not redacted properly. Can you go and fix this from our, you know, our lawyers would contact DOJ and then the document would be taken down, it would be redacted, put back up, but was still searchable,” Bensky said.
Candidate calls for policy changes
Bensky was joined by Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate running for a seat in the U.S. House.
Dunlap said if elected, he will prioritize more thorough investigation, removing the statute of limitations, and addressing law enforcement’s ability to not bury allegations.
“It’s just an extraordinary story of how, you know, simple authority that we derive from the electorate as public officials can be abused and to power over people, change their lives, traumatized them and dues, and kept anonymous, kept quiet. And it shouldn’t be quiet,” Dunlap said.

title: UK prime minister say it's 'clear' Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum
text:
UK prime minister say it's 'clear' Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham says it is clear that Russia interfered with Britain’s vote to leave the European Union, adding it was important to put Moscow’s tampering on the record because countries across Europe are facing the same threat.
In excerpts from “The Rest is Politics’’ podcast released Sunday, Burnham said that when he became prime minister in July, he asked his advisers whether Russia had interfered with the 2016 referendum. The full podcast is scheduled to drop on Monday.
Related video above: Trump says Ukraine should "get a new leader" after striking diesel deal with Russia
“I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,’’ Burnham said. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Russia has long said it does not meddle in other countries’ elections or referendums.
Burnham’s comments come as U.K. intelligence agencies warn about the increasing threat of Russian interference in Britain’s democratic institutions. The intervention is believed to be the first time a British prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russian interference in the Brexit vote.
Burnham said he spoke to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin.
“You know he was saying to me that the AfD are clearly linked to Russia, funded, I believe,” Burnham said. “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” he added.
Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government failed to fully assess the impact Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have had on the EU referendum.

title: Pre-workout powder recalled over illegal stimulant. Here’s what it is and how to get a refund
text:
(CNN) - A popular pre-workout powder is being recalled because it contains an illegal ingredient that can raise blood pressure and lead to cardiovascular problems.
During testing, Food and Drug Administration officials found that Rapture Pre-workout contained DMAA, a derivative of amphetamine.
Three flavors of Rapture Pre-workout are included in the voluntary recall: Rainbow Twist, Electric Lemonade and Berry Mojito.
The product was sold at retailers and online between January and May.
Consumers who have the product should stop using it immediately and return it for a full refund.
Manufacturer Leader Formulas LLC says there have been no reports of adverse reactions.

title: Maine Sen. Susan Collins signs letter to Trump opposing Russian diesel imports
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Sen. Susan Collins has joined five other senators Sunday in signing a letter to President Donald Trump opposing the purchase of Russian diesel amid rising fuel costs.
Trump announced Friday in a social media post that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin struck a deal over the phone that would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia to the United States. An additional 500,000 tons would be supplied in November, with an addition 4 million to follow, Trump wrote.
Three Republican senators — Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, John Curtis of Utah and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — also signed the letter with Collins. Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and and Connecticut’s Richard Blumenthal also signed.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia,” Collins said in a statement provided Sunday by a spokesperson. “I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following.”
Trump’s announcement came a few weeks after Congress passed legislation in an effort to cut revenue Russia receives from oil and gas to finance its war against Ukraine. The legislation imposes tariffs on some Russian oil and natural gas importers, with exceptions for countries that import 15% or less.
The six lawmakers also noted in the letter that Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the lawmakers wrote. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”

title: Susan Collins among 6 senators calling on Trump to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.
“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote.
The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there’s a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said.
Trump’s announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president’s action would be in violation of U.S. law.
“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”
He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.
“This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said.
Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

Sunday will be mostly cloudy with temperatures reaching the low 60s. Rain and moisture from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will push towards Maine this evening, and showers will move across coastal areas tonight. Showers will linger in the early morning hours on Monday.

Tuesday will also have widespread showers lasting throughout the day. Rain will arrive before sunrise on Tuesday and may even linger into Wednesday morning. Some areas may see moderate rainfall at times from the system, but showers will become lighter on Wednesday.
Thursday will kick off a cooler trend of high temperatures, and we're watching another round of scattered showers as we head into the weekend.

text:

Woman scammed twice after trying to report fraud
A Pennsylvania woman fell victim to two scams after trying to report fraud on Facebook Marketplace, leaving her waiting for replacement cards for 13 accounts.
A tractor listing catches her attention
Donna Shaak said she was scrolling through Facebook Marketplace when she saw a seller near her offering various items.
"Farm equipment, four-wheelers, tractors, lawnmowers, go-karts, all just outdoor fun activity stuff," Shaak said.
One item caught her attention — a small Kubota tractor.
"So I saw the tractor, and I thought, oh, that would be nice for my hubby," Shaak said.
A $200 deposit leads to trouble
Shaak reached out to the seller, who was Facebook friends with two of her family members, and sent a $200 deposit. Shortly after, the seller stopped communicating, and their profile disappeared.
"And, I thought this happened on Facebook, so I'm going to call Facebook right now and report her," Shaak said.
A fake customer service number
Shaak searched for a Facebook customer service number on Google and called it. However, Facebook does not have a customer service phone number, and users must seek help through its website. Someone answered the number Shaak called, claiming to be with Facebook.
Video below: Lawsuit challenges 'no sugar' claim in some Dunkin' drinks
The person told Shaak that the seller might have accessed everything on her phone.
"He kept repeating, I'm going to help you. I'm going to help you clarify this. I may even get your $200 back," Shaak said.
Scammer gains access to 13 accounts
The caller then instructed Shaak to gather all her credit cards and account numbers, warning her that the seller might have the ability to access and use them.
"But what you're going to have to do is get all your credit cards and your account numbers. Depending on what she did on your phone, she might have the ability to get to those numbers and use them," Shaak said.
To protect her accounts, Shaak was told to provide her Social Security number and all her account details. She complied, sharing information for 13 different accounts.
"The caller asked us to go through all the cards that we had, read the numbers, and said he's going to go in and cancel them," Shaak said.
However, instead of canceling the cards, the caller stole the information. Shaak is now waiting for all her cards to be replaced.
How to avoid similar scams
Consumer investigator Brian Roche explained that Shaak was the victim of two separate scams: first through Facebook Marketplace and then by scammers who posted a fake customer service number online.
Roche advised that when buying items through social media sites, it is always best to deal with the seller in person.

title: I’m outraged by the Trump administration
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As I read the Sept. 30 paper, I found myself experiencing outrage at what is happening in our country. In particular, there were two articles that should be causing outrage across America.
The first was the Supreme Court allowing quick deportations to Third World countries while it weighs the Trump administration’s policy. How can it be legal to send immigrants, who are not violent or criminals, to a country they have never been in and have no connections to? Then they hide them so family members can’t find them.
The second article talked about Homeland Security using millions of dollars of taxpayer funds for pro-Trump ads. Our country is in a financial mess. Here in Maine, people can’t afford groceries, gas and heating oil while they blatantly use our taxpayer dollars to support ads for a criminal.
I hope that people are watching and come out to vote in record numbers. There must be an end to this.
Virginia Starbird
Lisbon

title: Longtime school bus driver fired after stopping to let student rescue injured kitten
text:
HARFORD COUNTY, Md. (WJZ) - Parents in a rural Maryland community are rallying behind a school bus driver who was fired after she stopped to let a student rescue an injured kitten.
Cynthia Morgan, 67, worked as a school bus driver in the Harford County Public Schools district for 11 years. She was recently removed from her route after she let a North Harford Elementary School student get off the bus to pick up an injured kitten. Morgan says being fired devastated her.
Parents like Carolyn Kalambihis say they understand the safety concerns but believe removing Morgan from her route was excessive. Video recorded on the rural Heaps School Road shows little traffic, a detail parents say is important to understanding what happened.
“We live in North Harford, so it’s very rural back here. She wouldn’t have done it, you know, let a child get off the bus to get a kitten if it was a more high-traffic road,” Kalambihis said.
She says Morgan has been driving her kids to school for five years, and they absolutely love her.
“She is an angel. She’s the most caring person. Every year at the beginning of the school year, she buys every child on the bus school supplies. She buys them gifts for Christmas, every holiday, birthdays. She’s given them birthday cards, all out of her own pocket,” Kalambihis said.
Now, Kalambihis and other Harford County parents are circulating a petition that calls for Morgan to be allowed to return to her route.
“We just feel the way that it was handled was not appropriate,” Kalambihis said. “We feel that termination was a little excessive, an overreaction by the Department of Transportation through HCPS. I think it could have been handled in a lot of other ways.”
Kalambihis said she believes Morgan understands that allowing a student off the bus was a mistake.
“It’s definitely a concern for safety. There is no question that it was a mistake,” Kalambihis said. “It shouldn’t have happened. I believe she knows that and understands and, looking back, knows she made a mistake and should not have done what she did.”
Harford County Public Schools said Morgan was employed by an independent contractor, not directly by the school district. However, the district is responsible for certifying drivers who transport students for its schools.
“Certification and decertification are not always based on a single factor but often involve consideration of multiple circumstances and requirements,” the district said in a statement. “Student safety remains our top priority, and all certification decisions are made with that responsibility in mind.”
The district declined to comment on Morgan’s specific situation.
