title: The UMaine System is becoming an ‘AI leader.’ Some students and staff are wary.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For Jared Fairfield, enrolling in graduate school at the University of Southern Maine this fall was a big personal and financial decision, one he said he’s still wrestling with.
That’s why the 36-year-old social work student was so jarred when he received artificial intelligence-generated feedback from a professor on the first assignment in his psychology methods course.
“For the person who is supposed to be the authority, the intellectual guide, to use ChatGPT, was very disorienting,” Fairfield said.
But when Fairfield raised concerns about what he saw as unethical AI use, he said his professor responded candidly that he had used it, and pointed to a recent announcement from the university system’s leader about its investment in an AI tool that would “help strengthen teaching and research.”
That interaction came shortly after the University of Maine System, to which USM belongs, rolled out access to ChatGPT Edu for all students, staff and faculty through a $1.4 million, two-year contract with the company OpenAI. The tool is now available to 30,000 individuals across the system, although “whether and how they use it will be entirely up to them,” per the system’s announcement.
His professor’s behavior, as Fairfield came to understand it, was fine. The professor later sent an email to every student in Fairfield’s class, telling them to expect that all responses would be “augmented with AI.”
“In a commonsense way, that’s probably not a good thing to be doing in a graduate-level course,” Fairfield said. “But he wasn’t doing anything that he couldn’t do.”
As of Oct. 8, more than 3,700 people across the system have signed up for an account, which comes with data privacy protections and cannot be used to train OpenAI’s models. Leaders describe the contract as a success, and critical to “preparing students for the modern workforce.”
But many in the system, including students, staff and faculty, seem skeptical of the deal — and AI’s place in higher education broadly.
As the technology becomes more ubiquitous in workplaces and universities across the country, the University of Maine System has embraced its place in the technological transition and describes itself as a “national AI leader.”
Ryan Low, formerly the system’s chief financial officer, received an additional title of Vice Chancellor of AI Integration last year and has taken the helm of that transformation. He said there haven’t been any surprises so far with the rollout, and that there has been strong interest in the ChatGPT Edu trainings offered by the system.
But some individual faculty and staff members have concerns about the impact on student learning, and many have raised issues with the purchase, which was made with unbudgeted funds, amid financial struggles in the university system.
“To see the system prioritize software contracts while cutting the hours and jobs of the human beings who keep these universities running sends a deeply troubling message about UMS fiscal priorities,” said Sara Abronze, president of the system’s professional staff union.
HOW THE CONTRACT CAME TO BE
In fall 2024, the system convened an AI Working Group — made up of university presidents, administrators, one trustee, one professor and one student — to develop a strategy on artificial intelligence’s implementation in the system.
Their final report, released in August 2025, concludes that, “strategic, deliberate investment now” will determine whether the system becomes a leader in the AI transformation or is “left reacting to it.” The group offered several recommendations, including that the system purchase a single AI tool that could be accessible to everyone.
People across the system were already using AI through personal, less-secure accounts. More than 12,600 students, 700 faculty members and 1,335 staff members already had a free or paid ChatGPT account, according to system data about the number of sign-ups associated with an @maine.edu email address.
Faculty surveys conducted by the working group at the flagship University of Maine and the University of Maine at Presque Isle found that a majority of professors were willing to use AI tools if they were easily accessible.
The system put out a public request for proposals in the early spring, and received four: one from OpenAI, and three from Gemini, Google’s chatbot product, from different sellers.
“It was a really easy decision that had nothing to do, in this case, with the difference between ChatGPT and Claude or Gemini, and really just came down to cost,” Low said.
Although the working group recommended paying for the tool with a per-credit hour fee of $18 to $20, faculty had concerns, and the system decided to pay instead with unbudgeted investment income.
The system announced the deal in May, and began rolling it out as an option for faculty, staff and students before the start of the semester. As of Oct. 8, about 8.8% of students, 22% of faculty and 30% of staff have made ChatGPT Edu accounts through the system.
Low said things are playing out roughly as anticipated, and he expects the numbers to increase throughout the semester.
SOME SKEPTICAL, SOME EXCITED
Americans are now more skeptical about AI than they are excited about it, according to an August study from the Pew Research Center. This is increasingly true of young people, 55% of whom now say they’re more concerned than excited about AI’s growing use in daily life, amid shocking headlines about leaders warning of the potential dangers of the technology.
At the same time, Americans increasingly use AI at work. More than half of U.S. employees say they use AI on the job, according to a July survey by Gallup, and 65% of employees at organizations that have implemented AI say it has improved their productivity and efficiency.
While many faculty members are excited about AI, others feel the university is jumping on the latest trendy bandwagon in higher education.
The union representing professional staff surveyed its members anonymously this summer, and out of 137 responses, about 69% disagreed that ChatGPT would have a positive impact on their work or productivity. More than 80% were extremely dissatisfied with the way the university communicated with staff about the contract, and nearly 90% said they were dissatisfied with the decision to spend $1.4 million on the product.
Paula Gerstenblatt, a professor of social work at USM, said AI has no place in her classroom. She said she’s invested in walking students through the iterative process of learning.
“I need to know where they are in their writing, in their critical thinking,” Gerstenblatt said. “If you’re using a tool like AI, it’s going to polish it up, and I don’t know where you are.”
She also doesn’t buy the system’s argument that AI familiarity is critical for entering the workforce; in her field, she said, employers want multi-faceted and civically engaged thinkers.
But the sentiment ranges across disciplines. Amir Kordijazi, an industrial engineering professor at USM who studies AI’s applications in manufacturing, said he supports the contract because he wants higher education to be at the forefront of AI innovation, and make sure the technology is developed in ways that benefit the public.
“Given the pace of this transformation, I don’t believe our educational institution can afford to remain on the sidelines,” Kordijazi said. “In fact, I believe they have a responsibility to take a leading role.”
Kordijazi said all of his students are using AI, so he has a responsibility to educate them on how to use it.
That’s not the situation for Erin Bertoni, a social work grad student at UMaine, who said there’s universal skepticism among her cohort.
Bertoni said she’s not anti-AI, but does have concerns about the specific deal (she cited OpenAI being sued for violating copyrights and investigated for allegedly misleading shareholders) and the system’s communications around it.
“We’re paying a lot of money for education, and we’re getting watered down education,” Bertoni said. “I think it really hinders academic integrity and learning, the capacity to learn.”
Bertoni said she’s not sure she would have chosen UMaine today, following the contract.
The editorial board of The Maine Campus, the university’s student newspaper, called for greater transparency in the AI acquisition process in a September piece, and said the contract calls into question the system’s concern for academic integrity.
“To the professors who have strict AI policies in their classes and view using it as cheating, this program could seem like an endorsement for that behavior by the university,” the board wrote.
UNIVERSITY SYSTEM BULLISH ON DEAL
Low said from his perspective, the deal has been “a very, very transparent process.” The working group gave regular public updates to the board of trustees, which were livestreamed, and held a public request for proposals.
Samantha Warren, the system’s spokesperson, said the system never received critical public comments about AI from students during trustee meetings, and have heard less pushback than expected. Low said the student representatives to the board, and to individual university AI task forces, didn’t share any concerns.
Warren said she can’t think of another voluntary resource that has been adopted by so many students so quickly.
Faculty seem to be adapting to the change, too. Just last week, after many rounds of discussion, USM’s faculty senate passed a policy that, among other things, will require professors to disclose all AI use to students, and permit students to opt out of being graded with AI.
It was a controversial debate and took several rounds of voting to resolve, said Shelton Waldrep, the faculty senate member who drafted the policy.
The proposal will go to the president and provost now, who have 30 days to approve it, before it can take effect.
There is no system-wide policy; it’s up to each individual university to set its own guidelines.
FUTURE OF CONTRACT UNKNOWN
UMS is not the first nor the largest university system to invest in AI on this scale.
The California State University System paid $17 million in 2025 to give all 523,000 of its students, faculty and staff access to ChatGPT Edu amid a financial crisis; this year, faculty asked the system not to renew the contract, but it did. The University of Colorado reached a three-year, $2 million-per-year agreement for its 100,000 students, staff and faculty, which has also garnered pushback.
But UMaine, the flagship university, is facing a $19 million budget shortfall. Faculty and staff reacted with apprehension about the new expenditure given that they have been told to expect layoffs to address the school’s financial woes.
“I see that and I think: How many of my colleagues could we retain for a million and a half a year?” biology and ecology professor Jacquelyn Gill said at the time. “Which of those is more important?”
Abronze, the staff union president, said many in her unit have serious fears that the system will replace their jobs with AI. She sent a letter to Low in May, sharing those worries and requesting more information about the contract. They met over the summer, but she was disappointed by his answers.
Warren, the spokesperson, said the system’s investments have won them national recognition. The system expects the contract will allow the universities to recruit students and faculty, and anticipates it will draw increased philanthropic and federal funding. She cited an ongoing application to the National Science Foundation for UMaine and other partners to expand AI literacy across the state.
Low said it’s too early to know if the system will extend the agreement with Open AI, or how they might fund it if so. He said they’ll do a survey this fall, and another at the end of the two-year period, and present those findings to trustees to decide if they will continue.
The contract includes options for three additional one-year extensions, the first of which would cost $693,665. Any financial process would happen publicly in board of trustee meetings. But if the system does extend the contract, it may need to look at funding it through a fee to students.

title: Carr crash radio appearance by Sen. Collins
text:
When I lived in Maine, I worked hard against Susan Collins’ election to the United States Senate. Over the years, however, I have come to grudgingly admire her avowed commitment to avoiding name-calling and personal attacks. Collins is a dignified presence in an arena that is increasingly undignified. It was disappointing, therefore, to hear her on “The Howie Carr Show,” broadcast from Gorham on Sept. 25.
Carr, as anyone who listens regularly to his show knows, revels in name-calling and personal attacks. He often refers to immigrants as “cholos,” describes foreign countries as “Third-World hellholes,” and rates women on their looks. Indeed, in a segment that aired just before Collins appeared, he made some very misogynistic comments about the lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, who apparently does not meet his beauty standards.
Carr has been around for many years, and everyone is aware of his shtick. Collins should be ashamed of appearing on this show.
David Scannell
Bedford, N.H.

title: American among 12 killed and more than 300 hurt in latest attack on Riyadh airport, authorities say
text:
CAIRO (AP) — The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured over 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.
It was the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, whose fronts have expanded to include the recent surge in fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.
A missile struck a King Khalid International Airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
Footage posted on social media following the attack and analyzed by The Associated Press shows emergency vehicles outside the airport.
Saudi civil aviation authorities on Saturday said airport operations were suspended. The closure was later extended by 24 hours until 9 p.m. Sunday, according to the flight tracking platform Flightradar 24.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels
The attack — the latest of several in the past week on the airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack on Saturday afternoon, U.S. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
Trump later Saturday said he planned to speak to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and said “what happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable.” Asked if the U.S. might get involved, Trump responded, “We’ll find out.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” he said.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a “fully-fledged war crime” and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
The airport had a heavy police presence on Saturday, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed. Flights diverted elsewhere, Flightradar24 said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Also Saturday, U.S. Central Command said a fighter jet struck and disabled a commercial cargo vessel with a precision munition in the Gulf of Oman, part of U.S. efforts to maintain a naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica had departed an Iranian port and did not heed repeated warnings. The ship’s crew was unharmed, CENTCOM said.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key U.S. ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
While the Houthis have said they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for the one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked dozens of ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.
Saudi Arabia has run low on interceptors, officials say
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.
On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of “supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions” in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.
Saudi flight disruptions are growing
The Houthis this week warned global airlines “for the last time” about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a “greater focus on aviation infrastructure.”
The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts “create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft,” it said.
Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.
Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that “filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability.”
___
Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington and Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut contributed to this report.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: Man who planned attack on Polish Prime Minister Tusk has been arrested, interior minister says
text:
WARSAW, Poland (AP) — A man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country’s interior minister said Sunday.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned.
Poland has been on high alert following a series of school stabbings this week, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
“The man who threatened an attack was detained,” Tusk wrote on X. “Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action.”
Poland’s police had said earlier on Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
“We take this matter extremely seriously,” said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland’s intelligence services. He said authorities considered there was a “high probability” the threats would be carried out.
Dobrzyński was speaking after an emergency meeting of security services, police and representatives of the Interior Ministry on Sunday. He said information about the threat first reached the state protection service, which then passed it to the police.
He gave no other information about the reported plot, but said the intelligence services were receiving an increasing number of various threats with every month.
Government spokesperson Adam Szłapka told Polish media Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that, even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was “exceptionally concerning.”
Three attacks at schools in Mazovia province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children.
In September, Tusk warned about likely intensified hybrid attacks by Russia on NATO’s eastern flank. He said Russia was planning strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland, with the goal of weakening Western support for Kyiv’s fight against the Russian invasion. Moscow has denied any such plans.
___
A previous version of the story corrected the day to Sunday.

title: Death Notice: Roger B. Ouellette
An 18-year investment pays off: Maine’s first ‘Alfond babies’ head to college
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gregory W. Powell is executive chairman of the Harold Alfond Foundation.
Eighteen years ago, the Harold Alfond Foundation made an investment of $500 in hundreds of babies born in central Maine. In so doing, we invited their families to invest along with us.
This fall, that long-term investment is paying off as these “Alfond babies,” now young
adults, are stepping onto college campuses and into postsecondary training programs for
the first time.
This milestone moment affirms something we at the Harold Alfond Foundation have long believed: that even a modest investment in a child’s future can fundamentally change their aspirations and trajectory.
Our founder, Harold Alfond, believed that every Maine child deserved an opportunity to
excel in life and that higher education in all its various forms would enhance each child’s
future. And along with it, our state. 
Harold knew, what the research now confirms and our federal government has come to realize, that children with higher education savings, no matter how modest, are more likely to enroll in and complete higher education. And that investing early in life was best as it strengthened the aspirations for success in life of parents and their children as the value of their financial investment grew over time.
And so, in 2008, we established the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, and with its terrific help began investing $500 in a college savings account for every child born in a handful of
central Maine communities whose parents opened a NextGen 529 savings account.
Building on the success of that early pilot, we then took the program statewide in 2009. Today, every baby born in Maine automatically receives a $500 Alfond Grant, which is invested on their behalf in the state’s NextGen 529 college savings program.
Since the program’s inception, our $500 grants have been awarded to and invested for more than 184,000 Maine children. Thanks to the stock market, together with our grants and the contributions of Maine families who opened their companion accounts, and matching grants by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME), total savings for higher education now exceeds $813 million.
For our oldest and first grant recipients who have started college this fall, that $500 grew to nearly $2,500. That’s five times the original grant, funds that they are now using tax-free for higher education expenses whether for a Harvard degree or trade certifications,
apprenticeships or licensing exams.
But $500, even with compound investment returns over time, was never meant to single-
handedly fund higher education. Rather, the Alfond Grant was intended as a spark to build aspirations and confidence as well as to inspire every family to join us and start actively saving for their children’s futures.
Today, a third of Maine families with an Alfond Grant have joined us and taken the critical step of opening their own companion NextGen 529 account where they are investing additional funds for their child’s education. That is where I want to focus our attention here.
If your child has received our $500 grant and you have not yet opened a NextGen 529 account, we encourage you to join us and do so. You do not need to start big. You can open a NextGen account for your child alongside the Foundation’s $500 Alfond Grant without making an initial contribution. And you can invest money into your child’s account when you are ready and in many cases receive generous additional contributions from FAME, our state’s nationally recognized NextGen 529 provider.
In the last autumn of Harold Alfond’s life, I sat with him at his camp as he looked over the lawn and lake where his great grandchildren, now off to school, had played and swam in the summer sun. We imagined how the future of every Maine child might be shaped with a $500 investment for higher education. And how with even the most modest of family contributions and the compounding of investment returns over 18 years, our children and our state would be better for it.
Harold knew he would never meet the young adults, once newborns, who headed off to college this fall. But he loved this state and he said, “Let’s do it.”
So this fall, we are celebrating the first of our Alfond babies, now young adults off to college. We are celebrating with their families, who had the foresight to open a NextGen 529 account for their children.
To those students and their families: congratulations! And to the families whose children
will follow, we hope the Alfond Grant and saving for higher education will be part of your
journey, too. An investment in your children today that opens the door to their greater
opportunity tomorrow.

title: Officer with questionable past becomes city’s top cop, fires detective who investigated him
text:
RIVERVIEW, Mo. (First Alert 4/Gray News) - First Alert 4 Investigates has been digging into allegations regarding the police officers in charge of public safety in one town and the governments that employ them.
On Sept. 10, Riverview’s City Hall and Police Department were furloughed, but money issues aren’t where the problems end for the department.
A First Alert 4 investigation has revealed Riverview’s chief of police has a history of allegations of excessive use of force, has fired a detective who investigated him and was handpicked by a man sitting in the St. Louis County jail.
Three incidents, caught on camera, show Riverview Police Chief Brandin Neil allegedly using excessive force, including punches to the head, against people who do not appear to be resisting. Two of these incidents resulted in court actions against Neil.
A former Riverview detective, who says he did Neil’s background check for Riverview, alleges the chief fired him for an investigation that stemmed from that check.
Jailhouse calls obtained by First Alert 4 Investigates show the decision to hire Neil into the department’s top brass came from the city’s now-former mayor, Michael Cornell Jr., while he was in the St. Louis County jail awaiting trial for alleged sex crimes.
Now, Neil is one of two remaining commissioned officers in Riverview following the furlough, according to state records.
Neil sent a written statement for this story that reads in part:
“Since my return to the Riverview Police Department, I have utilized the past 5 months to bring this department into state compliance, foster working relationships with our neighboring departments and elected officials, and attending as many community events as possible. The betterment of this city and the protection of it’s residents is my ultimate goal, and I will continue to do so, both as transparently and efficiently as possible.”
In an on-camera interview, Neil told First Alert 4 Investigates he did speak with the former mayor while he was in jail, but said he could not speak about why the former detective had been fired, due to it being a personnel issue.
Neil faced court action, misconduct reports while an SLMPD officer
On the morning of Aug. 8, 2019, Neil is seen on video walking into a St. Louis City gas station and getting in line to buy something. At the time, he was a St. Louis City police officer, and he was off duty as he was heading into work, court records say.
Inside that gas station, security footage obtained by First Alert 4 in 2019 showed Neil get into an argument with a man, attempt to tase him and then repeatedly punch him in the head with his handcuffs.
That man, Bryan Boyle, spoke to First Alert 4 in 2019 after the gas station incident. During that interview, he said that he had asked Neil a question.
“‘What are you?’ That’s all I asked because I was interested in doing private security and private bodyguard work,” Boyle said during that 2019 interview.
A St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department (SLMPD) Employee Misconduct Report of the incident obtained by First Alert 4 Investigates reports that Boyle said Neil never identified himself as a police officer during the incident.
Neil was charged with third-degree assault in the case, a class-E felony. In September 2021, Neil had a bench trial, which waives a defendant’s right to a jury trial and allows a judge to make the ruling of guilty or not guilty.
A judge found Neil not guilty following a single-day trial, court records show.
Eusef Robin Huq, now a defense attorney, had tried the case against Neil in 2021.
He says the prosecutor’s office argued Neil had no reason for the response he had to Boyle, and he had escalated the situation.
“Essentially, we argued that there was no reason for the aggressive response by Brandin Neil,” he said. “We had witnesses testify that he was the aggressor in the situation.”
In 2021, Boyle sued Neil in federal court, accusing him of Fourth and 14th Amendment rights violations.
Boyle’s attorney filed to drop the lawsuit in April of 2024 after Boyle was shot dead in his car while waiting at a red light in St. Louis City’s Vandeventer neighborhood. The man police say shot Boyle died inside of the St. Louis City Justice Center before going to trial.
Neil, when asked about this incident with Boyle, wrote in a statement, “As far as Mr. Boyle, who is unfortunately deceased, all matters of that case are public record.”
According to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, before the incident with Boyle, Neil was already being investigated for a different internal affairs complaint.
In May of 2019, Neil was accused of tackling Billy Busch’s daughter, Abbey Busch, and her boyfriend to the ground inside a South City bar. The Post-Dispatch reported this incident was under investigation by both St. Louis City Police internal affairs and the circuit attorney’s office.
First Alert 4 Investigates filed multiple records requests with SLMPD regarding any potential internal affairs investigation into Neil from this incident with Busch. SLMPD says under Missouri law, internal affairs investigations into police officers are closed records.
Neil was never criminally charged with anything related to this May incident inside a bar, but he did ultimately leave the department in September that same year. Whether an officer is fired or resigns is not an open record under Missouri law. Records show he was with SLMPD for less than three years.
“The alleged incident involving Ms. Busch, is exactly as stated, an alleged incident that was investigated and found to not be factual,” Neil said when asked about these allegations.
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Busch for comment, and as of publication time, we have not heard back. First Alert 4 has not been able to independently verify the alleged incident between Neil and Busch.
Huq says he was surprised to hear Neil is now a police chief, but hopes he’s changed for the better.
“Maybe 2021 and that trial was a wake-up call,” Huq said. “Maybe a mentor had a word with him and said, ‘Hey Brandin, you’ve got to do things different, because you got lucky this time. If you keep pulling stuff like that, it’s going to catch up with you.’”
Potential misconduct seen on video, again
More recently, in 2025, Neil was seen on video arresting former Riverview Alderwoman Regina Davis during a town hall meeting.
Davis told First Alert 4 at the time she had gone to a meeting to ask then-Mayor Cornell about a lawsuit accusing him of sexual misconduct with a city employee. She was charged with assault, accused of biting Neil during the arrest. Those charges have since been dropped against Davis.
Davis has now filed a lawsuit against Neil and the city of Riverview over the arrest. Davis’ lawsuit claims the force used by Neil specifically was excessive and unwarranted.
When asked about Davis’ lawsuit, Neil said he would not comment on active litigation.
This year, a video was circulated on social media showing Neil in a police uniform punching a man in the head while he was on the ground outside of a St. Louis City nightclub.
A former Riverview detective says the video is from March 14 and that the man seen throwing the punch is Neil.
When asked about this video, Neil said in a statement, “I only ask that you share the entirety of the video that is approximately 25 minutes long, as it depicts the attempted de-escalation of a group of subjects, assault of officers, and the resisting of arrest that followed.”
First Alert 4 asked Neil to share this additional video with us. As of publication time, we have not received it.
Potential investigation by a state agency, jail calls suggest
A recorded jail call conversation between the now-former Riverview mayor and now-former Riverview Alderwoman Judy Jones in April suggests Neil may have been under investigation by Missouri Peace Officer’s Standards and Training (POST) from an incident during his time with the Moline Acres Police Department.
Neil was with Moline Acres from Dec. 1, 2025, until April 23, 2026, the department said.
Jones, who Riverview confirms recently resigned from the board of aldermen, is heard in the call asking then-Mayor Cornell about POST.
“What’s up with this... St. Louis City POST? Is it an organization or what is that?” Jones asked during an April 17 call.
Jones tells Cornell that POST is “coming against” Neil.
“This person is not even where we are yet. They’re still at the other place,” Jones said. Neil, at the time of the call, was still with Moline Acres. “And they’re cool, they’re good with it. They’re good with it. They look at the stuff that whatever occurred, and they don’t have no problem.”
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Jones to get comment for this story. Jones responded by text, asking not to be contacted and telling us to reach out to Riverview’s city attorney instead.
Riverview’s city attorney, when asked about a potential investigation into Neil by POST, said, “The city has no comment regarding this matter, as it predates the current administration’s depth and breadth of knowledge regarding the topic.”
Missouri law prohibits the Missouri Department of Public Safety, which oversees POST, from commenting on any investigation. First Alert 4 reached out to the Missouri Attorney General’s Office, which files complaints against peace officer licenses based on POST investigations. As of publication time, the attorney general’s office has not provided information regarding any possible action against Neil’s license.
Former detective alleges being fired for investigating Chief Neil before his appointment
Since Neil was appointed the chief of police for Riverview, he told First Alert 4 Investigates he has fired three officers.
All three officers, he said, were fired for policy violations. One of those officers, according to Neil, is being investigated for a non-specified non-violent felony. A court records check shows no charges have been filed against any of the three officers who were fired from the department since Neil’s appointment.
Former Riverview Detective Corporal Maurico Wilson says he believes he is the officer Neil is investigating for a felony.
“Ultimately, I was fired for investigating him and uncovering other crimes,” Wilson alleged.
According to Wilson, he was in charge of doing Neil’s background check before he was rehired into the department. During the background check, Wilson says he learned of accusations made against Neil while he was working secondary employment as security at a North County grocery store.
Wilson says the incident he was investigating happened during a time when Neil wasn’t working for any police department, which, under Missouri law, would prevent him from legally working secondary employment.
First Alert 4 Investigates confirmed with the Moline Acres Police Department that Neil worked for them from Dec. 1, 2025, until April 23, 2026. Wilson says Neil was rehired into the Riverview Police Department and made chief on May 5.
Wilson says the incident he was investigating allegedly happened on April 26, while Neil was not employed by either police department.
Wilson said because Neil was not with any department at the time, he began investigating him for impersonation of a police officer.
A “wanted” was put out for Neil on May 4 for impersonating a police officer, according to Wilson. A “wanted” is not a warrant, but an internal note for police, flagging Neil for questioning or possible arrest.
Neil started working for Riverview the next day.
“The wanted had got issued out on [May 4],” Wilson said, “So you see how it became a sticky situation.”
Wilson and his supervisor were both fired the next month, he said. Neil confirmed Wilson and his supervisor had been fired when asked directly by First Alert 4 Investigates.
“All I can honestly, legally, say is that they were terminated,” Neil said. “With that being a personnel matter, I can’t go any further into it.”
Wilson also shared with First Alert 4 Investigates a written reprimand document he says was written by Neil.
The document reads:
“Upon notification from police officers from surrounding agencies, it was made aware that Interim Chief of Police Neil, DSN 375, had an active “Wanted” for “Impersonating A Police Officer” through the Riverview Police Department. Further investigation revealed the “Wanted” was authorized by Detective/Corporal Maurico Wilson, DNS 414, on 5/04/2026.
“Upon review of the report, it was discovered the report was blank, containing very vague and fictitious pedigree information and there was additionally no narrative.”
In the document written to reprimand Wilson, it says Neil was not a member of the Riverview police department when the “wanted” was issued against him.
The document says that Wilson was not acting ethically after he issued “a wanted on citizen of Riverview for a supposed crime that did not take place in Riverview’s venue and by leaving the wanted ‘Active’ after the citizen was appointed to Interim Chief of Police.”
Wilson says he had a right to conduct his investigation because Neil had applied to work for the department, and he was in charge of background checks.
According to Wilson’s termination paperwork, which he also shared with First Alert 4 Investigates, he was fired for “multiple blatant violations of Police Department and City policies, as well as alleged criminal conduct.”
Wilson says he didn’t violate department policies or do anything criminal. He says he believes he was fired for investigating Neil.
“Who’s above the law? Nobody, right? We all should be held accountable,” Wilson said.
Jailed mayor handpicks Neil for Riverview’s top brass
Neil had previously worked for the Riverview Police Department as a Sergeant. He left the department in 2025, telling First Alert 4 Investigates shortly after then-Mayor Cornell was arrested that he had quit because of Cornell’s behavior.
“I was just tired of the mayor and his antics; the foolishness is usually how I refer to it as,” Neil said in his Jan. 23 interview with us.
During this interview, Neil said he had suspicions that a lot of things Cornell had done were criminal.
“We felt a lot of things that he did were criminal,” he said. “We just couldn’t put our fingers on it or prove that these things were happening. I’m not really surprised about how you flaunt your authority and your power over people and stuff like that. That mentality you have. But to hear that it was, underage men and the child pornography and stuff like that. That was surprising to me.”
When asked if he was surprised by Cornell’s arrest, Neil said, “No, I’d honestly been waiting on it.”
Two months after this interview with First Alert 4 Investigates, Neil is on a recorded jailhouse call with Cornell and Alderwoman Jones.
“What would that look like if he’s not on board?” Neil asked Jones about then-acting Police Chief Toreyon Times.
“I don’t know,” Jones responded, “this is perpetual existence of government. You know, push, pull in, pull out, change up, to make sure that the government continues.”
Neil also said the board would need to post the job opening on the front door of Riverview City Hall.
“That way, even if it came down to, ‘Hey, we know we want you for the position, we’re going to select him,’ you’ve given other people the opportunity, so it doesn’t seem like an unfair hiring practice,” Neil said.
Neil mentioned Wilson’s supervisor would likely apply for the position and might file a lawsuit if he isn’t given a chance to apply.
“This is not an opening,” Cornell said. “This is more like my appointment thing. It is not an opening, so it doesn’t matter.”
First Alert 4 Investigates asked Neil after the press conference on his department being furloughed if he had heard from the former mayor since his January arrest.
“I would prefer not to answer that or involve that,” he said. “I have not contacted him directly, but I have heard.”
First Alert 4 Investigates pressed Neil on why he would need to speak with Cornell after his arrest.
“Again, since I have been in this position with the city of Riverview, I have not spoken to him,” he said. “Preemptive conversations before I return to Riverview is another story. However, since I have been here, there has been no communication or contact.”
Neil worked ‘protection detail’ for Cornell, was paid for trips to Metro East strip clubs
When Neil was first with the Riverview Police Department, he said he was assigned to work frequently with Cornell.
“He had what he called the mayor’s protection detail,” Neil said in January. " So, I was assigned to that. So, the majority of the time I was like his driver, but he always goes somewhere with police officers as his security and different things."
Neil said a part of the job of being a part of Cornell’s protection detail was joining him on nights out.
“The mayor would come into the police department and say, ‘Hey, I’m going out tonight. I need you, you, you. You’re going to go clock out, go on to secondary duty, go on to the special patrol, mayor’s detail,’ whatever the case might be,” Neil said.
Neil said the protection detail would join Cornell on trips to Illinois, as well.
“There’s been a time before where, I mean, we bounced to multiple clubs, and now we’re over in East St. Louis because he wanted to go to a strip club,” Neil recounted.
Neil said officers would be in their Riverview police uniforms on these outings, “and even if we were in plain clothes, he wanted your gun and badge to be displayed.”
Neil said when he would go out to these clubs with Cornell, he was supposed to be paid for it.
“That would go to the comp time,” he said.
First Alert 4 Investigates reached out to Cornell’s attorney for comment on these alleged trips. As of publication time, we have not heard back.
Days after Cornell’s arrest, Neil filed a lawsuit against Riverview claiming the city did not pay out his accrued “comp” hours, along with holiday and vacation hours.
The court dropped Neil’s lawsuit after he did not show up to a hearing in May, records show.
During his interview in January, Neil said nobody ever stood up against Cornell.
“He’s the mayor. He runs everything in this city,” he said. “Who are you going to call? Who are you going to tell on?”
The Riverview Police Department furlough is expected to last until December. During the press conference about the furlough, Neil said he would still be working for Riverview as a civilian employee and would be assisting the St. Louis County Police Department when they respond to calls in the city.
Chief Neil’s full written statement:
“At this time, I will have to deny the request for the on-camera interview in regards to the aforementioned topics. Three of the incidents have no correlation with my tenure with the City of Riverview.
“As far as Mr. Boyle, who is unfortunately deceased, all matters of that case are public record.
“The alleged incident involving Ms. Busch, is exactly as stated, an alleged incident that was investigated and found to not be factual.
“As to the video you were provided, I only ask that you share the entirety of the video that is approximately 25 minutes long, as it depicts the attempted de-escalation of a group of subjects, assault of officers, and the resisting of arrest that followed.
“Lastly, in regards to Ms. Davis, who was lawfully arrested, I will not comment on any current litigation of the City and would recommend any information request be directed to our City’s attorney.
“In closing, since my return to the Riverview Police Department, I have utilized the past 5 months to bring this department into state compliance, foster working relationships with our neighboring departments and elected officials, and attending as many community events as possible. The betterment of this city and the protection of it’s residents is my ultimate goal, and I will continue to do so, both as transparently and efficiently as possible.”
Karla Vasquez Mejia contributed to this report.

title: A chilly night with sun tomorrow. Rain possible Tuesday and Wednesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It will be a chilly overnight with mainly clear skies. Some clouds may filter in overnight as the remnants of Isaias stay off to our south later Sunday but it will still be a very comfortable fall day. Monday will be mainly clear before another system moves in Tuesday that may bring our first wintry precip to northern locations.
Tonight: A chilly but clear night
The wind will die off substantially and go basically calm and without the clouds temps will drop easily in the 30s for most. Some of the coldest areas may even drop into the 20s once again.
Sunday: Sun and clouds mixed with warmer temperatures
The winds will swing around to the SW and bring a warmer day with them. More clouds will move into the region as well with the remnants of Isaias which will eventually slide out to sea to our south but may bring a few showers later in the day on Sunday especially for southern regions of the state. Highs will fall mainly in the 60s. Winds will again be somewhat gusty perhaps as high as 25 mph or so.
Sunday night: Slight chance of a weak shower, otherwise overcast
There is a slight chance for a stray shower Sunday night but it will otherwise be mainly overcast and warmer than previous nights. Lows will only probably drop into the 40s for most with some areas further south barely getting below 50. Winds will be light out of the SW at 5-10 mph.
Monday and beyond: A very pleasant, partly sunny day Monday... Rain or even a wintry mix far north Tuesday
The work week will start off comfortably with highs in the 60s and very little wind. Temps will drop quickly Monday evening into the 40s and 30s and a developing low may slide into the region early Tuesday and bring some cold Canadian air with it and there is a possibility some of the coldest spots may see some wintry mix early on Tuesday. But a cold rain is possible for most on Tuesday.
Today: Sunny and breezy with highs in the 50s for most. Winds NW at 10-20 mph.
Tonight: Chilly and clear with lows in the middle to low 30s. Winds light.
Sunday: Partly sunny with highs back into the 60s. Winds SW at 10-15 mph.
Sunday night: More clouds and a slight chance of a shower. Winds SW at 5-10 mph
Monday: Warmer with a few breaks of sun. Winds light.
Monday night: Chance of showers move in and chilly. Lows in the 30s and 40s.

title: Pre-workout powder recalled over illegal stimulant. Here’s what it is and how to get a refund
text:
(CNN) - A popular pre-workout powder is being recalled because it contains an illegal ingredient that can raise blood pressure and lead to cardiovascular problems.
During testing, Food and Drug Administration officials found that Rapture Pre-workout contained DMAA, a derivative of amphetamine.
Three flavors of Rapture Pre-workout are included in the voluntary recall: Rainbow Twist, Electric Lemonade and Berry Mojito.
The product was sold at retailers and online between January and May.
Consumers who have the product should stop using it immediately and return it for a full refund.
Manufacturer Leader Formulas LLC says there have been no reports of adverse reactions.

title: Man who planned attack on Polish Prime Minister Tusk has been arrested, interior minister says
text:
WARSAW, Poland (AP) — A man suspected of threatening and planning to attack Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk was arrested, the country’s interior minister said Sunday.
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński gave no details about the identity of the man nor the type of attack planned.
Poland has been on high alert following a series of school stabbings this week, as well as fears of a possible Russian hybrid attack to weaken Western support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
“The man who threatened an attack was detained,” Tusk wrote on X. “Thanks to the police for fast and decisive action.”
Poland’s police had said earlier on Sunday they received information about a possible plot to attack Tusk and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.
“We take this matter extremely seriously,” said Jacek Dobrzyński, spokesperson for the minister overseeing Poland’s intelligence services. He said authorities considered there was a “high probability” the threats would be carried out.
Dobrzyński was speaking after an emergency meeting of security services, police and representatives of the Interior Ministry on Sunday. He said information about the threat first reached the state protection service, which then passed it to the police.
He gave no other information about the reported plot, but said the intelligence services were receiving an increasing number of various threats with every month.
Government spokesperson Adam Szłapka told Polish media Tusk learned about the threat first thing on Sunday morning. He said that, even if officials do occasionally get threats, this one was “exceptionally concerning.”
Three attacks at schools in Mazovia province in central Poland took place within four days this week, leaving one dead and many wounded, including children.
In September, Tusk warned about likely intensified hybrid attacks by Russia on NATO’s eastern flank. He said Russia was planning strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland, with the goal of weakening Western support for Kyiv’s fight against the Russian invasion. Moscow has denied any such plans.
___

title: Dixfield man drowns while kayaking in Roxbury
text:
A Dixfield man died after apparently falling out of his kayak Saturday on Ellis Pond in Roxbury, officials said.
The Maine Warden Service was notified shortly after 4 p.m. of a possible drowning.
Shawn Noyes, 20, had been kayaking with his family, Lt. Dan Menard wrote Sunday in a Maine Warden Service news release.
Noyes was seen in the water attempting to swim to a nearby island, when he disappeared and was feared drowned.
The air temperature Saturday was in the mid-50s and the water temperature would have been even colder. A person entering water at such temperatures would experience cold water immersion syndrome, which can lead to a loss of motor control within minutes.
The Maine Warden Service conducted a search Saturday evening with the help of the Roxbury, Mexico and Rumford fire departments.
Noyes’s kayak and life jacket were recovered from the pond.
 On Sunday, the Maine Warden Service dive team recovered Noyes’s body; he was not wearing a life jacket. The Maine Warden Service said everyone should wear life jackets while recreating
on the water.

title: Can’t find a deer you shot in Maine? These dogs can help
text:
This story was originally published Nov. 4, 2025.
If you shoot a deer in Maine this hunting season and can’t locate it, whether it wandered a short distance or ran several miles after being shot, a network of licensed dog trackers can help you recover your game quickly, safely and legally.
Each year, the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife licenses trained handlers who use leashed dogs to track wounded or dead deer. These trackers operate across the state and often volunteer their time to help hunters recover animals that might otherwise be lost.
One of the most experienced trackers is Susanne Hamilton of South Montville. She has been tracking since 2002, serves as president of the nationwide organization United Blood Trackers and has completed nearly 800 recoveries. Hamilton covers much of the midcoast, including Waldo and parts of Kennebec counties. She travels for the expanded deer season as well as for bear and moose, and she can be reached at 207‑249‑8078.
Downeast, another well-known tracker is Lindsay Ware of Ellsworth, who can be reached at 207-812-1366. Ware and her tracking dogs have helped recover many deer in Hancock, Washington and Penobscot counties and often respond the same day.
Joanne Greer covers the Bath area (603‑479‑7953), while further south inland, Scot Clontz (207‑831‑0872) covers the Lewiston region.
In central Maine, Ryan Cote tracks the Fairfield, Waterville and Skowhegan area (207‑313‑0202), while Tyler Turffs covers central Maine, including Windsor, and the Jackman area in western Maine (207‑214‑3867). Brian Hatch covers Penobscot County, rounding out central and northern coverage (207‑745‑3543).
In southern Maine on the border with New Hampshire, the couple Bethany Slack and Joey Badger work throughout the region, assisting hunters with deer recovery. Bethany can be reached at 603‑667‑7195, and Joey can be reached at 207‑608‑0870. Both are licensed to track in Maine and New Hampshire.
Many of these listed trackers have completed apprenticeship training under Hamilton. She notes that hunting is a big undertaking. “The preparation that goes into it until the shot is taken is absolutely enormous,” she said. “But when something goes wrong, the field behind the shot is just as enormous.”
Hamilton emphasizes that tracking a deer is more complicated than it might seem.
“There’s so much to ensure the recovery of wounded large game, than just taking a dog and running after it,” she said. “There’s so much to consider and handle carefully.”
Inexperienced trackers may push a gut shot deer tracking it too soon. It’s also very unsafe to run around with a loaded weapon, she said.
If you think your deer is still alive, contact a licensed tracker as soon as possible. Time, temperature and rain can all affect a dog’s ability to follow a blood trail. Be ready to describe where and when you shot the deer, the direction it ran and what kind of sign you found, such as blood, hair or tracks.

title: Obituary: Edite Kroll
text:
SACO – Edite Kroll, 87, died peacefully at home on Sept. 23, 2026, with her husband, Keith Walker, lovingly at her side. Edite had been struggling with mesothelioma for several months.
Born in Blasheim, Germany, in 1939, Edite was the daughter of Luise and Fritz Niedringhaus. She grew up in the shadow of World War II, and learning about the Holocaust in high school changed her life. She became a lifelong pacifist and a strong advocate for women’s rights and human rights. She was a courageous person who stood up for what she believed was right, without hesitation or regret.
After high school, she left Germany because, like many women, she did not receive support to attend college. She went first to Paris and then to London, where she began her life in book publishing. She worked for major publishers in London and New York, where she moved in 1965. She specialized in children’s books and especially loved working with artists who wrote. As assistant executive editor of Harper Junior Books, she later negotiated contracts for more than a hundred children’s titles for a retail publishing venture. The experience convinced her that she wanted to work directly with authors and use her gifts as an editor and expertise in contracts to be a literary agent.
In 1981, she founded the Edite Kroll Literary Agency in New York. It was her passion for the rest of her life. She loved working with authors and artists and helping transform their ideas into wonderful books. She helped bring hundreds of children’s books, works of fiction, and works on women’s studies into being. Drawing on her expertise in foreign publishing, she helped her authors’ work reach readers in dozens of countries around the world.
Edite met Keith in North Carolina in 1980. After several years in New York City, N.Y., they moved to Maine, where Edite had lived previously. She successfully transplanted her agency and continued to travel frequently to New York, Frankfurt, and Bologna.
No one loved books and reading more than Edite. Even after spending hours reading and editing manuscripts, she could happily curl up with a mystery to unwind. But mostly and always, Edite loved people. She had a huge heart and was an incredibly generous friend. She was loyal and dependable and could not be outworked. She loved good food, good white wine, conversation, and the occasional intense exchange of opinions. Her exuberant presence—her voice, her smile, her laughter, and her spirit—lit up every room.
Exceptionally smart and well-informed, Edite began each morning with coffee and the Times. She had strong moral and ethical standards and held herself, and those she loved and respected, to those same high standards. She loved working in her garden and watching her perennials grow and blossom.
After moving from Portland to Saco in 2004, Edite became involved with the Unitarian Universalist Church of Saco and Biddeford, serving on the board and chairing the membership committee, where she warmly welcomed visitors and newcomers.
Edite continued to visit her family in Germany every year. She lost her only sibling, her brother, Udo Niedringhaus, in July 2025, after spending several weeks with him when he was ill. She remained close to his former wife, Irina, their children Ole, Ulf, and Britta, and grandchildren Liv and Luke. She also cherished Christmases in North Carolina with Keith’s sister, Martha, and his niece Katie, her husband John, and their children Luke and Eve.
Edite had a special knack for choosing gifts for children, from baby clothes to books, and her choices became treasured favorites.
The gift of the last months was that Edite came to realize not only how much she loved others, but how much others truly loved her.
A memorial celebration of Edite’s life will be held on Saturday, Oct. 17, at 11 a.m. at the Unitarian Universalist Church, 60 School St., Saco.

title: Death Notice: Steven Jones
Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an ‘energy ceasefire’ but Kyiv says attacks continue
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.”
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump’s ceasefire post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponizing winter.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin “had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet.’ We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world.”
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC’s “This Week .”
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
Trump spars with Zelenskyy
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
Zelenskyy said in response to Trump’s comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
“Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
“With all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
Ukrainian strike on Russian data center triggers outages
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company’s services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.
Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.
“I’d press the ‘call’ button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said. “There’s nothing I can do, so I’m just forced to cancel.”
Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said.
Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a “direct impact” and weren’t just about “convenience.” He said they affected “healthcare, and everything else.”
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company’s major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.
Zaporizhzhia death toll rises to 23
Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia’s Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.
___
Blann reported from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Morton reported from London.
___
