title: Troy Jackson, Bernie Sanders bring ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour to Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — With just over three weeks until the midterm elections, Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson is touring Maine to shore up support with the help of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.
Sunday’s rally at the Agora Palace Events Center marked Jackson’s second stop on the weekend’s “Solidarity Forever” tour. He held a rally Saturday in Bangor, and will make his final stop in Biddeford on Sunday evening.
He and Sanders’ remarks relied on a plea to give Democrats control of the Senate. Both focused on healthcare and affordability issues, and on a mission to support working Mainers.
“Now Troy believes, and I believe not only that healthcare is a human right, but that we have got to move toward a Medicare for All system,” Sanders said, adding that he believes President Donald Trump is “the most dangerous president in the history of the United States.”
Jackson also focused on Sen. Susan Collins’ shortfalls in her 30 years as a senator, pointing to her tendency to side with Trump and recent pay-to-play allegations.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington. She tells us that she’s one of the most powerful people in the U.S. Senate. So I think that Maine has the right to ask, ‘Well, what the hell did you do with that time?’” Jackson said.
“Trump, and the cabinet that Collins voted for, start a trade war that makes everything cost more: groceries, clothes, cars, lumber, even the equipment that Maine workers need to do their jobs is more expensive,” he added.
Hundreds of Mainers attended the event, many carrying signs with Jackson’s name printed in bold navy letters.
Their voices boomed, booing at the mention of Collins. Several wore stickers denouncing road salt — a dig at Collins’ claim that she managed to exempt the material from tariffs.
“Well, senator, we can’t eat road salt,” Jackson said, echoing a one-liner he delivered during his and Collins’ second debate on Wednesday.
Joan Schwartz, a Newcastle resident, said she’s terrified for democracy. She’s relying on Jackson to help ease her worries, especially after losing a progressive advocate in Graham Platner.
“Troy came in like gangbusters,” Schwartz said, speaking to how quickly Jackson managed to build a platform before the election. “It really speaks to the hunger that Mainers have for social justice, economic justice, addressing healthcare issues, addressing housing issues, childcare issues. Troy stands for all the things that I believe Mainers really want.”
Schwartz and fellow Jackson supporter, Greg Tangen, of Lewiston, are excited about his platform, especially his stance on Medicare and women’s rights.
But both said they wished Jackson were more outspoken about the war in Gaza, though Sanders reassured voters during his speech that he and Jackson share a common goal to end U.S. aid to Israel.
Sunday’s lineup also included Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline, a nurse who was terminated from Central Maine Medical Center amid a unionization effort, Lewiston City Councilor Safiya Khalid and David Sullivan, vice president of the IAM Union, which serves workers at Bath Iron Works.
“Donald Trump will go down as the worst president ever. We’re sending Troy to help restore sanity to our country. But Troy can’t do it alone. As we vote for Troy, we need to vote for Democrats up and down the ticket,” Sheline said.

title: Trump administration approves emergency crude oil exchange to limit disruptions from Isaias
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump administration approves emergency crude oil exchange to limit disruptions from Isaias
Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the move will protect access for American families and businesses. 
Trump administration approves emergency crude oil exchange to limit disruptions from Isaias
Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the move will protect access for American families and businesses. 
The U.S. Department of Energy approved an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude oil from America's strategic reserves amid concerns that Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, could lead to price increases.
“With this emergency exchange, the Energy Department is acting swiftly to help maintain refinery operations, limit disruptions to fuel supplies, and ensure American families and businesses continue to have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright in a statement on Saturday.
The announcement is part of the ongoing federal response to Isaias, which came ashore as a Category 2 Hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida. The storm has since weakened, but several eastern states are still facing heavy rainfall and the risk of flooding this weekend, according to the National Weather Service.
As of Sunday morning, at least four deaths had been reported in connection with the storm, and hundreds of thousands were without power.
President Donald Trump has approved emergency declarations so far for Florida, Alabama, and Georgia to free up federal disaster assistance.
In preparation for the storm, FEMA pre-positioned supplies and staff throughout the region, such as Incident Management Assistance teams and National Urban Search and Rescue teams.

title: Obituary: Normand R. Lamie
text:
LEWISTON – Normand R. Lamie, of Lewiston, passed away on Sept. 30, 2026, following a challenging battle with pancreatic cancer.
Norm was born in Lewiston on March 21, 1952, the son of Armand and Rose (Morin) Lamie.
Norm married the love of his life, Susan D. Flagg, on Oct. 11, 1975 in Nobleboro, Maine.
Norm’s devotion to his family was at the heart of everything he did. He instilled the importance of hard work and good education in his children. His loving nature and generous spirit will be deeply missed by family and many friends. Norm especially enjoyed spending time with his seven grandchildren, Madelyn and Aidan Adams of Otisfield, Maine, Avah and Ethan Lamie of White River Junction, Vt., Austin McGregor of Litchfield, Emma McGregor of Sabattus, and Kody McGregor of Lewiston. He also enjoyed great-grandson Kingston McGregor of Litchfield, Maine.
He is survived by his wife, Susan Lamie; his daughter Kathryn Adams of Otisfield and her husband Ryan, son Nathan Lamie of White River Junction, Vt. and his wife Sara, his daughter Kimberly McGregor of Lewiston; and his sister Denise Powell and her husband Bill of South China, Maine. He is also survived by many nieces and nephews for whom he cared very much.
He was predeceased by his parents; his brother Larry Lamie, and his sister Lorraine Roberge.
Norm’s career included working for the City of Lewiston Public Works Department, Auburn Water & Sewer District, and as Chief Engineer with the State of Maine Drinking Water Program. He was President of the Maine Water Utilities Association in 1994 and President of the New England Water Works in 2005. He closed out his nearly 50-year career in the drinking water profession working as an independent contractor helping small water utilities in Maine with financial and operational issues with the Maine Rural Water Association.
Norm enjoyed nearly 40 years of professional networking and fellowship with Rotary. He became a charter member of the Auburn Lewiston Rotary Breakfast Club in 1991. He served as Club President in 1994 and as Club Treasurer since 2016.
Norm’s interest in genealogy came about in later years. His genealogy research uncovered many interesting facts about ancestors and historical connections that he freely shared with extended family. Norm was able to trace his ancestry back many generations to France. He served on the Board of Directors and Treasurer of the Maine Franco-American Genealogical Society since 2022. In the years to come, future generations will recognize the impact of having Norm in their family tree and feel a sense of pride.
The family extends a heartfelt thanks to the compassionate and talented medical team who cared for Norm during his illness, especially Dr. Daniel Rausch of Cancer Care Enter at Central Maine Medical Center, the talented and caring team of staff and doctors at Infusion Care, and the caring professionals from Hospice & Palliative Care Service provided by Andwell Health Partners.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend a Celebration of Life for Normand on Monday, Oct. 12, from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. at The Fortin & Pinette Group, 217 Turner St., Auburn, ME 04210.
In lieu of flowers, a donation in Norm’s memory would be welcomed by the
Maine Franco-American Genealogical Society,
217 Turner St.,
Auburn ME 04210, or the
Auburn Lewiston Rotary Breakfast Club, Scholarship Endowment Fund,
P.O. Box 3425
Auburn, ME 04210

title: Patriots place WR Mack Hollins on injured reserve
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — The New England Patriots were without their top performing receiver when they host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins was placed on injured reserve Saturday with a calf injury. Also sent to IR was fullback Reggie Gilliam, who is dealing with ankle and knee injuries.
Both players must sit out for at least the next four games. The moves came a day after starting cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez (shoulder) and Carlton Davis III (neck) were ruled out for Sunday’s game.
In Hollins the Patriots lose their leader in receptions (15) and yards (209). Patriots receiver A.J. Brown has been on injured reserve since suffering a high-ankle sprain in the season opener at Seattle. He is eligible to return to practice next week.

title: A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
text:
A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
"They're reestablishing relationships with families. They're volunteering in their communities. They're working."
A freed man faces life back in prison after a Supreme Court ruling on the First Step Act
"They're reestablishing relationships with families. They're volunteering in their communities. They're working."
Two years after his release from prison, Patrick Dewayne Smith spends Sundays with his family in a modest brick church with a white steeple in rural Tennessee. He works two jobs. He goes to ball games to cheer for nieces and nephews he had never met. After serving 13 years for a nonviolent drug conviction, he is trying to rebuild his life.
Now Smith could be sent back to prison for the rest of it.
A federal judge released him in 2024 under rules adopted after Congress passed the First Step Act, a landmark criminal justice law during President Donald Trump's first term. But the Supreme Court ruled in May that people sentenced under older, harsher laws cannot rely on the disparity between their sentences and current penalties to seek early compassionate release.
"Every time I get a call, I'm hoping it's some good news. Or, you know, at least not no bad news," said Smith, a tall, soft-spoken 47-year-old whose beard is now flecked with gray.
Smith is among about a dozen people nationwide who could be returned to prison because of the ruling, according to FAMM, a sentencing reform group, formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums. Without clemency from the White House, the group says, second chances could disappear for those people.
The First Step Act was the most significant rewrite of federal sentencing laws in a generation. Among other changes, it reduced some lengthy mandatory minimum sentences, particularly for nonviolent drug crimes. Trump said the law would "make our communities safer and give former inmates a second chance at life after they have served their time."
The law was championed by Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser who had a personal connection to the issue: Kushner's father had spent time in federal prison when he was younger.
Thousands of people have been released from prison in the years since the law was passed, but some recent Supreme Court rulings have made it harder for other people already serving long sentences to argue for their release. For Smith and others like him, competing interpretations have created a high-stakes legal limbo.
"They're doing everything that they should be doing. They're reestablishing relationships with families. They're volunteering in their communities. They're working," said Shanna Rifkin, FAMM's general counsel. "Having them reincarcerated is so unjust given that they have demonstrated their rehabilitation."
Without a grant of clemency from the White House, Rifkin says their second chance could be snatched away.
Trump remains proud of signing the First Step Act, and the administration is actively reviewing developments, said a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the issue.
In 2023, the U.S. Sentencing Commission adopted new rules for people serving unusually long sentences. Judges could sometimes consider changes to the law when deciding whether to grant compassionate release to inmates who had served at least 10 years.
Not everyone agreed.
The Department of Justice argued the new rules went beyond what the First Step Act allowed. Judges nevertheless agreed to free dozens of people across the country after considering legal changes and other factors, FAMM found.
The dispute eventually went all the way to the Supreme Court, which handed down a 6-3 decision in May. It found that sentencing disparities from decades past are not "extraordinary and compelling" reasons to grant compassionate release.
"It is hard to see how Congress's deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that 'warrant(s)' a reduction," Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote for the conservative majority.
The decision was one of two during the last Supreme Court term that narrowed the options for people serving long sentences, said Daniel Harawa, a law professor at New York University. "I worry a lot about what this means for federal criminal justice reform," he said.
For Smith and about a dozen other people around the country, it could mean they have to finish serving a sentence that would not be handed down for the same crime today.
Smith grew up in a small town in rural northern Alabama and became addicted to drugs as a teenager, his lawyers said in court documents. At 17 he was arrested for twice selling crack cocaine to an informant. A pair of marijuana convictions followed a few years later. He served about three years in prison. After his release, he worked as a construction worker and a janitor.
In 2010, he got involved with a drug ring selling crack cocaine and marijuana on the Tennessee-Alabama line, prosecutors said. Caught on phone calls recorded by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, he was convicted of drug conspiracy and money laundering after he pulled out of a plea deal that called for 12 years to 14 years in prison in exchange for his cooperation.
His lawyers called his involvement "unremarkable," but the federal conviction combined with his prior record triggered a life sentence.
The judge questioned whether the punishment fit the crime, but said the laws tied her hands. It was the longest sentence linked to the 20-person case, exceeding even the ringleader's.
Smith said he resolved to keep his head down behind bars, working prison jobs and avoiding infractions.
"What kept me sane was that faith, that belief in God," he said.
He missed little things, like sleeping in a full-sized bed and taking a bath after a long day. He missed big things, too: His mother died during his first year in prison and he couldn't ask his family to shoulder the $1,000 it would cost for him to travel home for the funeral.
After the Sentencing Commission adopted its new compassionate release rules following the First Step Act, Smith asked a judge for a reduction to time served. It took nearly a year, but the court agreed he should go free.
He returned to Alabama and moved in with his sister and her daughter.
Last month, prosecutors filed court documents challenging his release and they pointed to the Supreme Court decision. They argued he would be subject to a mandatory-minimum sentence of 25 years, even under current laws, and called the judge's decision to release him "difficult to justify."
A Justice Department official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing case said Rutherford's case means his release is no longer valid, and the department cannot agree to a sentence below what the law requires.
The prospect of a return to prison is a bitter pill for his father, James Smith, a mainstay at the Willow Grove Missionary Baptist Church.
"When you got rapists and murderers and you get this guy on a nonviolent case and you want him for life," he said, "it doesn't sit well with me."
Associated Press video journalist Kristin M. Hall in Nashville, Tenn., contributed to this report.

title: 'She didn't even make it to 2': Family, friends mourn Pennsylvania mass shooting victims
text:
'She didn't even make it to 2': Family, friends mourn Pennsylvania mass shooting victims
Eight people, including a pregnant woman and two children under 6, were killed in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday.
'She didn't even make it to 2': Family, friends mourn Pennsylvania mass shooting victims
Eight people, including a pregnant woman and two children under 6, were killed in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday.
Nine people, including the gunman, a pregnant woman and two children under 6, were killed in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday.
"It was horrific. It was the worst scene I have ever experienced," said Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah.
A candlelight vigil was held Saturday evening in front of the home on Perry Street where the tragedy occurred. Loved ones gathered to honor the victims, lighting candles, leaving balloons and placing stuffed animals at the growing memorial.
"How do you go home and tell your kids like, hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?" said Lisa Simmers, a family member.
Erie police said the shooter was a 45-year-old man who was a family member of the victims. Officials have not yet released the names of the shooter or the eight victims.
Julius Windham shared that his 1-year-old daughter, Amari’anna, and Amari'anna's mother, Angelina, were among those killed.
"She was the person that I could always talk to, and she would listen, instead of a person that you tell her something and they say every time, 'I understand.' She would just sit there and listen to me and be quiet," Windham said, describing Angelina as a "star" in his life and a "beautiful person."
Simmers, Windham’s sister, said her brother is grieving the loss of his daughter.
"That was the only child, and she didn’t even make it to 2. She didn’t get to live her life because somebody dimmed her light out," Simmers said.
The shooting occurred just before 5 p.m. on Friday. A ShotSpotter alert detected two gunshots outside the home, and officers arrived to find two women dead.
"My son heard the first shot go off, and then we heard the screaming, and then we heard the next three that went off as well. So it was quite frightening for us to experience," said neighbor Candice Delange.
Police surrounded the home and forced their way inside after securing a warrant. Seven people, including the gunman, were found dead inside. Officials said the gunman died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Some family members expressed frustration, believing more could have been done to intervene.
"We were here. We heard the shots. We heard everything go down, step by step. We were here while we couldn’t run into the house and help the babies," Simmers said.
Investigators are currently reviewing evidence and video from the scene. The memorial outside the home continues to grow as the community mourns. Police said the investigation remains active.

title: Passenger terminal at Saudi Arabian capital's airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
text:
Passenger terminal at Saudi Arabian capital's airport is struck again, a day after 12 were killed
A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4, serving domestic flights. The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.
The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday.
India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.
The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes.
At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi crown prince
There was no sign Sunday that Trump had followed up on plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance against the war-hardened rebel group that is currently Iran's most dynamic proxy.
A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government, has been trying to seize them back.
The rebels' strikes against Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities highlight a problem. The kingdom is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the Iran war.
Some airlines have suspended flights serving Saudi airports, and some embassies have cautioned citizens about the risks of using them, after multiple Houthi warnings about the rebels' use of Saudi airspace.
Sunday’s attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time,” the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.
He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.
The toll rises on both sides
Earlier on Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims, as fighting in Yemen surges after a major military offensive was launched against the Houthis a week ago.
Inside Saudi Arabia, identities emerged for some of those killed in Saturday's attack in Riyadh, including an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widow living in the kingdom.
The U.S. citizen has not been publicly identified.
An expert says the Houthis' tactics could backfire
The Houthis until recently had been largely on the Iran war’s sidelines. They have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran’s most powerful allies. Now they're pressuring its regional rival and a key U.S. ally.
Late Sunday, Saudi Arabia and Iran said their foreign ministers had spoken by phone. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he warned against insisting on a military approach and ignoring a political solution, and said Tehran was ready to help start a dialogue between the Saudis and the Houthis.
The Saudis and Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.
The attack revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The rebels declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Now the Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse Houthi territorial gains.
But the rebels' pressure tactics could backfire, said Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst for Yemen: “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign.”

title: Obituary: Byron L. West
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Byron “By” West, a modernist architect, community leader, and loving family man, died Oct. 4, 2026, in Scarborough. He was three weeks short of his 94th birthday.
Born on the east side of Toledo, Ohio, By showed an exceptional talent for music at an early age. Before he was old enough to drive, By was playing band jobs in dance halls, clubs, and VFW posts throughout the city. As a freshman in the University of Michigan’s marching band, he played in the 1950 “Snow Bowl” victory over Ohio State in Columbus, and, following the band’s cross-country train trip, Michigan’s 1951 Rose Bowl win over California. By also spent a season traveling with a band that accompanied Bob Hope.
By met Laura Wales Hoffman, the love of his life, as a freshman at Michigan in 1950. Little did the couple know that they would be together for 76 years, including a 70-year marriage. The family often noted, with affection, that Laura earned two degrees in social work during the six years it took By to earn his first degree in architecture, after changing his major from physics in his sophomore year.
After By and Laura married in January 1956, By’s graduate studies took the young couple to Chicago, where he studied at the Illinois Institute of Technology under Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the renowned architect and former director of Germany’s Bauhaus.
By and Laura returned to Toledo, where By soon commenced his 47-year career in architecture. Joining Samborn Steketee Otis & Evans (now SSOE) as a young architect, By quickly rose within the ranks and in 1981 was named Chairman and Chief Executive Officer. Along the way, he designed some of Toledo’s most iconic buildings and oversaw SSOE’s expansion and diversification, including the growth of its business with Honda. In 1982, the firm designed Honda’s first U.S. manufacturing plant in Marysville, Ohio.
By had an unwavering community commitment. In Toledo he served as the chair of Child and Family Services and WGTE public television as well as a trustee for the Toledo Symphony Orchestra, the Arts Commission of Greater Toledo, the Toledo Modern Art Group, and the Boy Scouts. He also served on the advisory boards for architecture schools at both the University of Michigan and Ohio State.
During his years in Toledo, By developed a passion for sailing, first on Lake Erie and then on the upper Great Lakes. On his beloved Shanghai Rooster, he skippered several Port Huron to Mackinac races and cruises with Laura and friends on Lake Michigan and Lake Huron.
During his years of sailboat racing, By and Laura fell in love with Harbor Springs, Mich. There they bought a lakefront cottage that has become a mecca for many generations of the family. By and Laura especially cherished the vibrant summer social life of Harbor Springs, which became the place they always considered home during their retirement years. They made many winter trips to Costa Rica and later to Sanibel Island, Fla., where By, well into his 80s, played in Island Jazz’s outdoor Sunday afternoon concerts. Their travels also included Russia, South America, and Western Europe. As a wine connoisseur and member of the Chevaliers du Tastevin, he made several trips to the Château du Clos de Vougeot with Laura and friends.
In 2015, By and Laura began dividing their time between Harbor Springs, Mich. and Maine, bringing them closer to their children, grandchildren, and (recently) great-granddaughter. The family is grateful for the care provided to By and Laura by Piper Shores in Scarborough.
By is survived by his brother Robert West (Tania) of Waltham, Mass.; son, Brent West (Tina) of Yarmouth, daughter, Lisa West Alpert (Mark) of New York City, N.Y.; grandchildren, Tommy Alpert, Sarah Alpert, Jacob Merrill; Molly West Dearing (Danny) and great-granddaughter, Blake Danielle Dearing.
He was predeceased by his wife Laura, whose death in July after 76 years of togetherness was particularly tough.
The family warmly requests that anyone wishing to share condolences or memories send them to [email protected]. A memorial service is planned for Summer 2027 in Harbor Springs, Mich.
In lieu of flowers, memorial contributions may be made to the Little Traverse Conservancy, the Greater Toledo Community Foundation, or the Portland (Maine) Symphony Orchestra.

title: Man has broken leg after being struck by ICE vehicle in parking lot
text:
Man has broken leg after being struck by ICE vehicle in parking lot
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer struck a man with an SUV in a west Houston parking lot Saturday morning, leaving the man with a broken leg after he fled from a vehicle immigration agents were trying to stop.
The crash was captured on video by at least one business’ security camera. The business owner, who provided the video to the Houston Chronicle, asked not to be identified for fear of retribution from authorities.
He said the video had also been shared with the sheriff’s office. The sheriff’s office, which is investigating the crash, did not confirm.
In a statement released Saturday evening, attributed to an unnamed spokesperson, ICE claimed the injured man, Miguel Parra-Hernandez, “ran in front of the vehicle and was struck.”
The moment the unmarked Jeep Cherokee hit Parra-Hernandez is obscured in the video. It shows that the ICE agent driving the SUV — who has not been identified — turned in Parra-Hernandez’s direction before the collision.
Parra-Hernandez was being treated at a Katy-area hospital and was in ICE custody, according to the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. His leg was broken in three places and required surgery, according to FIEL, the immigrant rights group.
In its statement, the ICE spokesperson said Parra-Hernandez is in the U.S. without permission. The spokesman said that agents had been trying to arrest another man in the vehicle, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who had a history of arrests, convictions and deportations, and had an active final deportation order.
Mendoza-Cervantes fled on foot after the crash and was not immediately arrested, officials said.
What the video shows
The six-minute video begins at 7:28 a.m. The camera points north toward Clay Road and shows a two-lane road within the strip center, a post office box and a pair of dumpsters. At the beginning of the video, a dark blue Dodge Ram pickup truck is seen driving slowly toward Clay Road and then stopping near the dumpsters.
Beyond it, a white pickup truck, which police said Mendoza-Cervantes was driving, is seen driving about 200 feet in the wrong lane of traffic on Clay Road before stopping at the curb.
About eight seconds after the white pickup stops, Mendoza-Cervantes and Parra-Hernandez emerge and run south toward the camera. Mendoza-Cervantes runs toward a gas station and disappears from view.
Parra-Hernandez takes a different route and runs in the direction of the dumpster and the Ram. Behind him, the Jeep Cherokee turns left off Clay Road, jumps the curb in the median and enters the parking lot.
The Cherokee comes up on Parra-Hernandez’s right, moves past him and stops. The Ram obscures the view of a collision, but a moment later it moves out of the way and Parra-Hernandez can be seen lying on the ground.
The Cherokee didn’t appear to have any visible flashing emergency lights as it entered the parking lot.
Moments after Parra-Hernandez was hit, another SUV, this one with its emergency lights activated, rolls up to the scene. Two other vehicles show up less than a minute later. At least five people appear to check on Parra-Hernandez as he was on the ground.
ICE agents can be seen moving the white pickup truck out of the traffic lane.
The two latest-arriving vehicles drive away from the scene before the video ends, and it doesn’t show an ambulance or sheriff’s office investigators arriving.
The sheriff’s office announced its investigation into the crash in a post on X at about 9:15 a.m. The agent behind the wheel of the Cherokee stayed at the scene and spoke to deputies, officials said.
Local officials react with condemnation
The crash drew immediate criticism from local elected officials, who called for transparency surrounding the federal operation. Investigators from both the sheriff’s office and the Harris County District Attorney’s Office were at the scene through Saturday afternoon.
Sheriff’s office officials called the investigation typical of what happens after a crash involving law enforcement and a pedestrian. The agency was notified after the ICE agents called 911 to request an ambulance for Parra-Hernandez, officials said. No charges have been announced.
The crash comes in the wake of the fatal July shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during an ICE pursuit involving unmarked vehicles in Houston’s East End.
The fallout from the Salgado shooting contributed to some policy changes by ICE, including a renewed promise to equip agents with body cameras and new rules governing high-speed pursuits. But local officials who commented on Saturday’s crash said they distrusted the agency.
U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia said in a social media post that she had been in contact with the sheriff’s office and was continuing to monitor the situation.
“We need to know exactly what happened, and ICE’s word alone is not enough,” Garcia wrote.
Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones also condemned the incident in a statement Saturday, calling for federal authorities to cooperate with the investigation and release any video evidence.
“I am horrified to learn that an ICE vehicle struck a man on Clay Road this morning in Precinct 4,” Briones said. “While we wait to learn more, my prayers are with his family.”
Briones also criticized the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, saying ICE has brought “chaos and destruction” to communities across the country.
“ICE must cooperate fully with the Harris County Sheriff’s Office and release all video evidence of this incident,” she said. “We demand full transparency, accountability, and respect for the rule of law.”
Cesar Espinosa, the executive director of FIEL, called on ICE to identify the agents involved in the operation.
“We must hold all parties accountable and demand a thorough, transparent investigation,” Espinosa said. “We have more questions than answers. The biggest question we have is why does this keep happening?"

title: A tiger kills man who entered big cat enclosure at wildlife park
text:
A tiger kills a man who entered the big cat enclosure at an English wildlife park
A man died Saturday after he entered the tiger enclosure at a wildlife park in northern England and was attacked by one of the animals, police said.
Video above: Newborn tiger cub at Oklahoma City Zoo
Emergency medical personnel responded to the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near the city of Doncaster after the incident was reported at about 1:35 p.m., but the victim died at the scene, South Yorkshire Police said in a statement.
The tiger was not injured and remained inside the enclosure during the incident, the force said.
The wildlife park was evacuated after the attack and officers remained at the scene Saturday night as they investigated.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened,’’ the wildlife park said in a statement posted on its website.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park began operations in 2009, with its “Land of the Tigers” attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers. The enclosure includes a 300-meter (yard) raised walkway that allows visitors to watch the big cats roam through woodlands and grasslands or play in a waterfall pool, the park says on its website.
The Associated Press contributed to this report

text:
'What a survivor': Hawk pulled from storm drain amid dangerous weather conditions
A red-shouldered hawk is on the mend after being pulled from a storm drain during dangerous weather conditions in Florida.
St. Johns County Fire Rescue shared video of the hawk being rescued as heavy rain and rising water created dangerous conditions in the area.
The hawk was transferred to animal control for treatment and care.
Ark Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation posted an update on the hawk's condition days following the rescue, saying the animal was nearly hypothermic and very weak after his ordeal.
The animal rescue said that despite the obstacles, the hawk has stabilized and is now eating on his own.
"We expect him to make a full recovery," Ark Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation said. "What a survivor!"

title: Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast
text:
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean.
The hurricane’s center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened Sunday to 120 mph (195 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane.
That’s not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.
By Sunday afternoon, Simon’s eye was moving northwest about 45 miles (75 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.
Forecasters say powerful winds will sweep from Mexico’s western coast to the Sierra Madre
Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon’s center, meaning the entire area between Mexico’s western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.
“We’re expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect,” Papin said. “They’re also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that’s likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells.”
The hurricane center on Sunday said Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches (20 centimeters), in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.
“Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches (76 centimeters) are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco,” the center said in its latest advisory. “This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any on-going flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain.”
Mexico’s president urges residents to stay sheltered
As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to the social platform X on Sunday to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
“Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety,” she wrote.
Hotel worker says residents learned from major hurricane in 2002
Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he could not go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people’s concerns about the hurricane comforting.
“It happened to us before. It hit us years ago,” Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. “People didn’t expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we’re different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won’t let it happen again.”
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.
Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city’s boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
“The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!” police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco’s capital.
“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” Villarreal said. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”
___
This article has been edited to correct the spelling of Philippe Papin’s name.

title: The UMaine System is becoming an ‘AI leader.’ Some students and staff are wary.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For Jared Fairfield, enrolling in graduate school at the University of Southern Maine this fall was a big personal and financial decision, one he said he’s still wrestling with.
That’s why the 36-year-old social work student was so jarred when he received artificial intelligence-generated feedback from a professor on the first assignment in his psychology methods course.
“For the person who is supposed to be the authority, the intellectual guide, to use ChatGPT, was very disorienting,” Fairfield said.
But when Fairfield raised concerns about what he saw as unethical AI use, he said his professor responded candidly that he had used it, and pointed to a recent announcement from the university system’s leader about its investment in an AI tool that would “help strengthen teaching and research.”
That interaction came shortly after the University of Maine System, to which USM belongs, rolled out access to ChatGPT Edu for all students, staff and faculty through a $1.4 million, two-year contract with the company OpenAI. The tool is now available to 30,000 individuals across the system, although “whether and how they use it will be entirely up to them,” per the system’s announcement.
His professor’s behavior, as Fairfield came to understand it, was fine. The professor later sent an email to every student in Fairfield’s class, telling them to expect that all responses would be “augmented with AI.”
“In a commonsense way, that’s probably not a good thing to be doing in a graduate-level course,” Fairfield said. “But he wasn’t doing anything that he couldn’t do.”
As of Oct. 8, more than 3,700 people across the system have signed up for an account, which comes with data privacy protections and cannot be used to train OpenAI’s models. Leaders describe the contract as a success, and critical to “preparing students for the modern workforce.”
But many in the system, including students, staff and faculty, seem skeptical of the deal — and AI’s place in higher education broadly.
As the technology becomes more ubiquitous in workplaces and universities across the country, the University of Maine System has embraced its place in the technological transition and describes itself as a “national AI leader.”
Ryan Low, formerly the system’s chief financial officer, received an additional title of Vice Chancellor of AI Integration last year and has taken the helm of that transformation. He said there haven’t been any surprises so far with the rollout, and that there has been strong interest in the ChatGPT Edu trainings offered by the system.
But some individual faculty and staff members have concerns about the impact on student learning, and many have raised issues with the purchase, which was made with unbudgeted funds, amid financial struggles in the university system.
“To see the system prioritize software contracts while cutting the hours and jobs of the human beings who keep these universities running sends a deeply troubling message about UMS fiscal priorities,” said Sara Abronze, president of the system’s professional staff union.
HOW THE CONTRACT CAME TO BE
In fall 2024, the system convened an AI Working Group — made up of university presidents, administrators, one trustee, one professor and one student — to develop a strategy on artificial intelligence’s implementation in the system.
Their final report, released in August 2025, concludes that, “strategic, deliberate investment now” will determine whether the system becomes a leader in the AI transformation or is “left reacting to it.” The group offered several recommendations, including that the system purchase a single AI tool that could be accessible to everyone.
People across the system were already using AI through personal, less-secure accounts. More than 12,600 students, 700 faculty members and 1,335 staff members already had a free or paid ChatGPT account, according to system data about the number of sign-ups associated with an @maine.edu email address.
Faculty surveys conducted by the working group at the flagship University of Maine and the University of Maine at Presque Isle found that a majority of professors were willing to use AI tools if they were easily accessible.
The system put out a public request for proposals in the early spring, and received four: one from OpenAI, and three from Gemini, Google’s chatbot product, from different sellers.
“It was a really easy decision that had nothing to do, in this case, with the difference between ChatGPT and Claude or Gemini, and really just came down to cost,” Low said.
Although the working group recommended paying for the tool with a per-credit hour fee of $18 to $20, faculty had concerns, and the system decided to pay instead with unbudgeted investment income.
The system announced the deal in May, and began rolling it out as an option for faculty, staff and students before the start of the semester. As of Oct. 8, about 8.8% of students, 22% of faculty and 30% of staff have made ChatGPT Edu accounts through the system.
Low said things are playing out roughly as anticipated, and he expects the numbers to increase throughout the semester.
SOME SKEPTICAL, SOME EXCITED
Americans are now more skeptical about AI than they are excited about it, according to an August study from the Pew Research Center. This is increasingly true of young people, 55% of whom now say they’re more concerned than excited about AI’s growing use in daily life, amid shocking headlines about leaders warning of the potential dangers of the technology.
At the same time, Americans increasingly use AI at work. More than half of U.S. employees say they use AI on the job, according to a July survey by Gallup, and 65% of employees at organizations that have implemented AI say it has improved their productivity and efficiency.
While many faculty members are excited about AI, others feel the university is jumping on the latest trendy bandwagon in higher education.
The union representing professional staff surveyed its members anonymously this summer, and out of 137 responses, about 69% disagreed that ChatGPT would have a positive impact on their work or productivity. More than 80% were extremely dissatisfied with the way the university communicated with staff about the contract, and nearly 90% said they were dissatisfied with the decision to spend $1.4 million on the product.
Paula Gerstenblatt, a professor of social work at USM, said AI has no place in her classroom. She said she’s invested in walking students through the iterative process of learning.
“I need to know where they are in their writing, in their critical thinking,” Gerstenblatt said. “If you’re using a tool like AI, it’s going to polish it up, and I don’t know where you are.”
She also doesn’t buy the system’s argument that AI familiarity is critical for entering the workforce; in her field, she said, employers want multi-faceted and civically engaged thinkers.
But the sentiment ranges across disciplines. Amir Kordijazi, an industrial engineering professor at USM who studies AI’s applications in manufacturing, said he supports the contract because he wants higher education to be at the forefront of AI innovation, and make sure the technology is developed in ways that benefit the public.
“Given the pace of this transformation, I don’t believe our educational institution can afford to remain on the sidelines,” Kordijazi said. “In fact, I believe they have a responsibility to take a leading role.”
Kordijazi said all of his students are using AI, so he has a responsibility to educate them on how to use it.
That’s not the situation for Erin Bertoni, a social work grad student at UMaine, who said there’s universal skepticism among her cohort.
Bertoni said she’s not anti-AI, but does have concerns about the specific deal (she cited OpenAI being sued for violating copyrights and investigated for allegedly misleading shareholders) and the system’s communications around it.
“We’re paying a lot of money for education, and we’re getting watered down education,” Bertoni said. “I think it really hinders academic integrity and learning, the capacity to learn.”
Bertoni said she’s not sure she would have chosen UMaine today, following the contract.
The editorial board of The Maine Campus, the university’s student newspaper, called for greater transparency in the AI acquisition process in a September piece, and said the contract calls into question the system’s concern for academic integrity.
“To the professors who have strict AI policies in their classes and view using it as cheating, this program could seem like an endorsement for that behavior by the university,” the board wrote.
UNIVERSITY SYSTEM BULLISH ON DEAL
Low said from his perspective, the deal has been “a very, very transparent process.” The working group gave regular public updates to the board of trustees, which were livestreamed, and held a public request for proposals.
Samantha Warren, the system’s spokesperson, said the system never received critical public comments about AI from students during trustee meetings, and have heard less pushback than expected. Low said the student representatives to the board, and to individual university AI task forces, didn’t share any concerns.
Warren said she can’t think of another voluntary resource that has been adopted by so many students so quickly.
Faculty seem to be adapting to the change, too. Just last week, after many rounds of discussion, USM’s faculty senate passed a policy that, among other things, will require professors to disclose all AI use to students, and permit students to opt out of being graded with AI.
It was a controversial debate and took several rounds of voting to resolve, said Shelton Waldrep, the faculty senate member who drafted the policy.
The proposal will go to the president and provost now, who have 30 days to approve it, before it can take effect.
There is no system-wide policy; it’s up to each individual university to set its own guidelines.
FUTURE OF CONTRACT UNKNOWN
UMS is not the first nor the largest university system to invest in AI on this scale.
The California State University System paid $17 million in 2025 to give all 523,000 of its students, faculty and staff access to ChatGPT Edu amid a financial crisis; this year, faculty asked the system not to renew the contract, but it did. The University of Colorado reached a three-year, $2 million-per-year agreement for its 100,000 students, staff and faculty, which has also garnered pushback.
But UMaine, the flagship university, is facing a $19 million budget shortfall. Faculty and staff reacted with apprehension about the new expenditure given that they have been told to expect layoffs to address the school’s financial woes.
“I see that and I think: How many of my colleagues could we retain for a million and a half a year?” biology and ecology professor Jacquelyn Gill said at the time. “Which of those is more important?”
Abronze, the staff union president, said many in her unit have serious fears that the system will replace their jobs with AI. She sent a letter to Low in May, sharing those worries and requesting more information about the contract. They met over the summer, but she was disappointed by his answers.
Warren, the spokesperson, said the system’s investments have won them national recognition. The system expects the contract will allow the universities to recruit students and faculty, and anticipates it will draw increased philanthropic and federal funding. She cited an ongoing application to the National Science Foundation for UMaine and other partners to expand AI literacy across the state.
Low said it’s too early to know if the system will extend the agreement with Open AI, or how they might fund it if so. He said they’ll do a survey this fall, and another at the end of the two-year period, and present those findings to trustees to decide if they will continue.
The contract includes options for three additional one-year extensions, the first of which would cost $693,665. Any financial process would happen publicly in board of trustee meetings. But if the system does extend the contract, it may need to look at funding it through a fee to students.

title: Troy Jackson’s sound bites won’t be enough
text:
Jacob Posik is the political director of Maine Civic Action and the director of legislative affairs of Maine Policy Institute.
There is a fundamental difference between sounding like you know what you’re talking about and knowing what you’re talking about. In last week’s first U.S. Senate debate, Troy Jackson brought the sound bites. Sen. Susan Collins brought the substance.
This likely wasn’t shocking to anyone who’s used to hearing Jackson fumble over his words or make a fool of himself while commanding the Maine Senate.
For much of the debate, while Jackson seemed determined to land the next punch, deliver the next rehearsed line or manufacture the next campaign clip, Collins did something much less flashy but far more important. The senator demonstrated that she, unlike Jackson, understands how government works, how policy is made and the responsibilities of the office she holds.
As the debate went on, this distinction became impossible to ignore. Jackson was quick with accusations but thin on details. And when the conversation moved beyond simple political rhetoric and into the mechanics of how policy is made, his lack of substance and shallow intellectual depth became painfully obvious. The contrast was striking.
Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly returned to familiar attacks against President Donald Trump and Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Regardless of the question, he seemed more interested in delivering his next rehearsed one-liner than offering substantive answers about the challenges facing Maine families.
This kind of political rhetoric might generate applause at a campaign rally comprised of a small smattering of Graham Platner leftovers, but it’s hardly a substitute for knowledge or competence when it comes to a U.S. Senate debate.
Perhaps the most embarrassing moment came during an exchange about healthcare, when Jackson appeared to confuse the responsibilities associated with Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement.
Jackson criticized Collins for failing to increase Medicaid reimbursement rates for Maine hospitals, suggesting that her position as chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee magically gave her the authority to address the issue.
The problem? Jackson revealed he fundamentally misunderstands how the program operates and which level of government is in charge of reimbursement.
Collins correctly explained that Medicaid reimbursement rates are established by states within federal requirements. Maine has the authority to adjust those rates, meaning Jackson was criticizing Collins for something that falls substantially within the responsibilities of state government. Hopefully the irony isn’t lost on anyone.
Jackson has spent the better part of 20 years as a fixture in Augusta politics. He served as president of the Senate for six years, one of the most powerful positions in state government, helping to oversee the very legislative institution responsible for determining Maine’s healthcare policies and funding priorities.
Instead of increasing those rates to help the people he pretends to care about, Jackson and his allies went on bloated spending sprees in budget after budget. They provided oodles in subsidies to their friends in the “affordable” housing and “clean” energy worlds. They gave out “free” community college on your dime and “free” school lunches to the children of millionaires.
Yet there he stood, trying to blame Collins for a responsibility that largely belongs to the state government he once led for six years. For someone seeking promotion to the U.S. Senate, that’s an embarrassing display of ignorance.
This exchange also exposed a broader weakness of Jackson’s. It’s easy to criticize Washington for the problems Maine faces; it’s much more difficult to explain how we should solve those problems.
Based on Jackson’s statements during the debate, all of Maine’s problems would cease to exist overnight if Trump was no longer president or Brett Kavanaugh no longer served on the Supreme Court. His performance suggested he believes political outrage can substitute for legislative effectiveness.
To be clear, Collins’ record is not beyond criticism. Her decisions deserve scrutiny, and all Maine voters are entitled to question her judgment on any vote she’s cast while serving as our senator.
But meaningful criticism requires more than repeating the same accusations, delivering rehearsed insults or hoping the audience overlooks the absence of substantive policy knowledge.
More than anything, the debate demonstrated why experience and competence matter. Collins came prepared to discuss the responsibilities of government and defend her legislative record. Troy Jackson came prepared to attack Trump, Kavanaugh and deliver campaign slogans.
One candidate demonstrated the knowledge necessary to govern. The other demonstrated a meager ability to campaign.
If Jackson hopes to convince Mainers that he belongs in the U.S. Senate, he will need to offer considerably more than political theater.
Susan Collins didn’t just win the first debate. She gave Maine’s former Senate president a much-needed lesson in how government actually works.

title: Pope Leo XIV says he will undergo surgery in the coming days. Here’s why
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery “in the coming days” to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate.
The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo’s expected recovery time from surgery would be a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
The Vatican didn’t say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it.
A nodule can be benign or malignant
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
“Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.
“When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis,” he said.
If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview.
“It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It’s unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, “doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it.”
He thanked the faithful “for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”
Surgery to be at the pope’s hospital
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Francis’ illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope’s health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days.
This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted.
A nodule doesn’t mean cancer but should be investigated
Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn’t mean lung cancer. And in fact “a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer.”
But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. “The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule,” he said in an interview.
Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said.
“In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery,” he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications.
Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking.
Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage “the aim … is curative,” he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy’s private Sky TG24.
“When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere,” he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.
“Being physically fit and healthy is certainly an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery,” he added.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, for Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days.” In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.

Barry reported from Milan; AP reporter Danica Kirka contributed from London.
