title: In central Maine, communities struggle to find, keep animal control officers
text:
When Dexter “Buzz” Bridges stepped down as animal control officer in six central Maine towns in September, he left some of them with a problem.
With low pay and regular recertification requirements, town officials say animal control has high turnover and filling the position isn’t easy. The state’s Animal Welfare Program’s website shows more than 20 Maine towns currently have no ACO listed.
That highlights a chronic problem for many Maine communities. State law requires them to have animal control officers certified by the state’s Animal Welfare Program to deal with disease, animal abuse and aggressive or abandoned pets.
Without an animal control officer, problems like rabies fall to local law enforcement or to municipal officials, straining resources. And without other options, residents sometimes take disputes over pets into their own hands.
Town officials say a regional or state animal control program would help lighten the burden the current system places on towns by creating full-time benefited positions. As it stands, rural ACOs string together low-paid roles across sometimes more than 10 towns to make a living.
THE CERTIFICATION ISSUE
The state gives new animal control officers six months to get certified once they’re hired and requires them to continue their training every year to maintain certification.
Bridges, who worked in Chesterville, Mercer, Rome, Norridgewock, Smithfield and Strong, has been working as an uncertified animal control officer for years. According to the state, he enrolled in recertification coursework in November 2023, but never completed it.
Until a Rome resident began complaining about Bridges in September and reported his status to the towns, most of them said they weren’t aware he was uncertified.
The Animal Welfare Program does not routinely send individual lapsed certification notices to municipalities or ACOs, said Jim Britt, director of communications for the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, which houses the Animal Welfare Program.
The state database shows 87 towns have an ACO marked as “uncertified.” Because some towns share ACOs, more than 50 individual ACOs are uncertified, either because they were recently hired and are completing certification or because their certification lapsed, violating the requirement.
Town officials are expected to verify their ACOs’ certification status annually, Britt said, and promptly address any lapses.
Norridgewock Town Manager Richard LaBelle said small municipalities are generally forgiving of certification lapses because of the nature of the animal control business.
“Not that it makes it right or makes it appropriate, but folks just aren’t lining up at the door to help with stray animals and animal neglect and things like that,” LaBelle said.
LaBelle said the Animal Welfare Program is broken and he doesn’t see things improving.
“The state continues to put regulations and rules out on municipalities with no support, and this is one of those cases where you’re seeing it,” LaBelle said. “It’s a glaring example.”
Bridges, who is running for election in House District 58, encompassing Belgrade, Fayette, Mount Vernon, New Sharon, Rome and Vienna, said it’s a hard job. He was stretched thin, and he was bitten once. But he thinks he’s uniquely suited to animal control: he’s good with animals and good with people. He said that’s not easy to find.
He said he wasn’t aware his certification had lapsed until last month.
A state report said the state informed Bridges of the lapse multiple times, but when a reporter requested a record of those notifications, Britt wrote that “the Animal Welfare Program does not routinely send individual certification-lapse notices to municipalities or ACOs.”
Bridges said he resigned from his posts when he learned about the issue. “It was a heartbreak for me,” he said.
LOW PAY AND LOW APPEAL
Bridges’ experience working across multiple towns is not unique.
Carrie Faloon is an animal control officer for around three dozen Piscataquis County communities and unorganized territories. She started working in animal control while she was also a home health care worker because she loves animals.
Faloon realized she couldn’t do both jobs when she was getting ACO calls in the middle of a shift, so she moved away from home care and started taking on more towns.
There is no typical day — she might get five calls, she might get 18. More and more, she’s dealing with complaints about abandoned pets as the cost of living and veterinary care has increased.
She’s also handling feral cat colonies, which pose risks to public safety in the forms of rabies, parasites, rapid reproduction and car accidents.
Many of Faloon’s calls end in visits to animal shelters contracted by the towns.
Peri Starr, who works at the Franklin County Animal Shelter, said without animal control officers, chaos abounds. ACOs serve as a legal authority for people to call about strays or animal abuse, and she said having someone knowledgeable on the job helps.
Most of Faloon’s municipalities pay her per call, so her yearly take-home pay varies. She said one year she might make $10,000 and the next she might make $20,000.
Across his six towns, all of which paid a flat rate, Bridges made around $20,000 a year, plus mileage in some cases, town reports show.
LaBelle said he was frustrated when Rome residents began digging into Bridges, leading to his resignation.
“This is what pushes people from their willingness to work in local government,” LaBelle said. “It’s unfortunate. We see it across all municipalities … being reasonable and achieving compliance at the end of the day is the goal, not being punitive.”
Rebecca Rasmussen, first select person in Smithfield, said she was embarrassed when she learned ACO Bridges’ certification had lapsed. To her, it highlighted a problem in municipal government as a whole.
“Things are so fragmented. Most employees … are part time. The jobs are piecemeal, and so communication breaks down,” Rasmussen said. “It’s hard to retain people. It’s hard to recruit people and its hard to even know what’s happening … we’re all trying to afford, basically, to maintain our own municipality when in some ways its not sustainable.”
Strong Town Clerk Amanda Coolong said she doesn’t anticipate any issues with replacing Bridges — the town’s previous ACO worked for years and people have already applied.
But in Mercer, first selectboard member Ricky Parlin said Bridges was the latest in a string of ACOs who have filled the position in the last six and a half years.
“I just wish the state would lax on some of these rules and regulations that they have to make it easier,” Parlin said. He said it’s “extremely hard” to find new animal control officers.
In recent years, Mercer raised its ACO stipend hoping to keep somebody in the job, Parlin said. In 2025, Mercer budgeted $2,400 for its ACO.
“It’s a lot of money for the number of calls that he has,” Parlin said. “But it’s not much money for a guy that has to be around 24/7.”
Officials in Mercer, Rome and Norridgewock have recently hired an animal control officer who currently serves, Manchester, New Sharon and Starks, according to the Animal Welfare database.
SEARCHING FOR A FIX
Joel Greenwood, executive director of the Kennebec County Council of Governments, has heard from municipalities about their struggles. He thinks a regional program could help.
About a year ago, KVCOG started a regionalized code enforcement service, after towns struggled to find and keep part-time code enforcement officers who often worked part time for multiple towns.
Now, KVCOG employs two full-time code enforcement officers, with stable jobs and benefits, who contract out to towns in the region. So far, Greenwood said it has been a big success, and he thinks it could work for animal control, too.
When KVCOG first started the code enforcement program, he said there was often a trust within municipalities that code enforcement officers would stay up to date with their certifications — much like in animal control — but no one ever knew whose job it was to check. Now, its KVCOG’s job.
In the meantime, rural towns, shelters and ACOs are doing their best to keep feral cat populations at bay and handle pet disputes. Faloon is on the board for the Maine Animal Control Association, a private organization that helps educate ACOs on certification requirements and gives trainings.
She encourages new ACOs to get in touch with the association, and to get into the field for the right reasons.
“You can’t go into it for the money because there is no money,” Faloon said. “You have to go into it because you love animals.”

title: Obituary: John “Jack” Tyler Kidder III
text:
SACO – John “Jack” Tyler Kidder III of Saco, Maine, passed away peacefully on Oct. 3, 2026 at Maine Medical Center after a brief illness. He was surrounded by his loving family, and a beautiful sunset blessed the moment.
Jack was born March 6, 1944, in Rumford, to Dorothy and John Kidder Jr. He was raised in Rangeley and attended high school at Fryeburg Academy, where he jumped for the Fryeburg Academy ski team even though he was, ironically, afraid of heights. He attended Husson College, where he earned a degree in Business Administration in1966.
Jack built a very successful career as an Independent Insurance Adjuster. He began at GAB in 1967, but when they asked him to move to New Jersey, he declined because he wanted to raise his family in Maine. So, in 1974, in the basement of their home on Colonial Acres in Westbrook, he founded Colonial Adjustment, Inc.
He was highly regarded and influential in the field for four decades. He was best known for building trustworthy and lasting relationships and served as president of the National Association of Independent Insurance Adjusters from 2009 to 2010. He retired in 2014, when his son Scott assumed the role of president.
Jack lived an incredibly full and meaningful life. He was an avid hunter and angler and greatly enjoyed spending time in his home region of Rangeley, where his father and grandfather were registered Maine Guides, a family tradition his son Steven proudly continues today.
He also enjoyed skiing, especially on his home mountain, Saddleback, where he was locally known as one of the first four people to ski the mountain before it opened in the late 1950s. Jack kept that connection to the woods, the water, and the slopes alive throughout his life, introducing his children, grandchildren, and many friends to the activities he loved in the area he so deeply treasured.
Jack met the love of his life, Barbara, in 1994, and they soon became virtually inseparable. They married on March 1, 1997, and enjoyed a beautiful and loving life together. Early on, they enjoyed yearly visits to Aruba and spent weekends at their beloved camp in Rangeley. In more recent years, Papa Jack and Granny were truly happiest in their cozy home in Saco, with their beloved dogs, Annie and Teddy and more often than not, with a Red Sox, Bruins, or Patriots game playing on the TV.
Jack’s family and friends were always his priority, and they all loved him dearly. Those who knew him well will always remember his charisma, storytelling, sense of humor, warm smile, and devotion to his family. He was kind, generous, and loyal. He was a man of his word and as honest as the day was long. If Jack Kidder shook your hand, you had a friend for life whom you could forever count on. To say that he will be deeply missed is a massive understatement.
He is survived by his devoted wife, Barbara; his children, Steven Kidder (Joyce Gauthier), Scott Kidder (Erica), and Amy Gray (Will); his grandchildren, Corey, Carly, Jack, Sam, Cora and Megan.
He was predeceased by his parents John Kidder Jr. and Dorothy Kidder.
A Celebration of Life will be held on Saturday, Oct. 24 from 1 to 4 p.m. at DiMillo’s Floating Restaurant, 25 Long Wharf, Portland — forever one of Jack’s favorite spots.
Burial will be a private family graveside service in Rangeley.
Funeral arrangements are being handled by Dennett, Craig and Pate Funeral Home, Saco.
In lieu of flowers, please consider making a donation to Fryeburg Academy, in Jack T Kidder III’s name.
745 Main St.
Fryeburg, ME 04037

title: Car wash attendant’s small gestures make big impact on boy with autism
text:
Car wash attendant’s small gestures make big impact on boy with autism in New Hampshire
For most families, a trip to the car wash is just another errand. For 5-year-old Liam, it is the main event.
Liam has autism, and his mother, Crystal Albrecht, co-founder of the Albrecht Foundation, said finding an activity all her children enjoy can be difficult. ScrubaDub in Salem, New Hampshire, has become one of the family’s favorite destinations.
“When we first started doing this, it was just a way to get out of the house,” Albrecht said. “Having a son with autism, it’s really difficult to find a place that we could go where everybody would have fun. This became one of those spots.”
The children pile into the car, Albrecht grabs a coffee, and the family heads to the car wash hoping one employee in particular is working.
His name is Benjamin Pineiro, but the family knows him as Ben.
Pineiro greets customers, hands out treats, and uses a marker to draw characters such as Mickey Mouse and Minnie Mouse on vehicle windows. The colorful creations give children something to enjoy before entering the car wash.
“While working here, I realized some people are scared of the car wash,” Pineiro said. “I just wanted to give them something to look forward to while they’re here.”
For Liam and his family, Pineiro’s drawings and friendly greetings have become a meaningful part of each visit.
“It truly touches my heart, to the point where I felt so compelled to write something and send something in,” Albrecht said. “It sits with me even after we leave.”
In May, Albrecht wrote to ScrubaDub to explain how much Pineiro’s kindness meant to her family.
“The small gestures may seem minor during the course of a busy workday, but for families like ours, they are not small at all,” she wrote. “They create moments of happiness and connection that stay with us long after we leave.”
Her message had an emotional impact on ScrubaDub’s staff.
“We were tearing up in the office,” said Alex Paisner, the company’s director of people and culture. “We had a couple of people crying.”
Paisner’s grandparents founded ScrubaDub in 1966. He said stories such as Liam and Pineiro’s reflect the kind of customer service the family-owned business strives to provide.
“On the surface level, it’s tough to be passionate about washing cars,” Paisner said. “To be able to change lives by making that positive impact on people is fantastic.”
Pineiro said he did not know about Liam’s autism or understand how much his actions meant to the family until he learned about Albrecht’s message.
“It made me feel really good,” he said.
Until recently, Pineiro and Liam had known each other only through a car window. The two finally met face to face during one of the family’s visits.
“I think you’re my favorite customer I’ve ever had,” Pineiro told Liam.
Pineiro said seeing Liam outside the vehicle was special, particularly when the boy held his hand.
“We don’t share words all the time,” Pineiro said. “I’m glad he feels safe with me here.”
For Pineiro, it takes only two minutes, a marker and a little extra care to turn an ordinary errand into something extraordinary.
“I think some people underestimate the power of being nice to someone,” he said.
Albrecht hopes the story reminds others that even brief moments of kindness can have a lasting effect.
“You never know what’s going on in the car,” she said. “You never know what that smile or that acknowledgment might do for somebody.”

title: Bernie Sanders Joins Troy Jackson for Rally in Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Several hundred people gathered in the Agora Center in downtown Lewiston for a Troy Jackson Senate campaign rally with Senator Bernie Sanders on Sunday.
The rally featured local Lewiston speakers including Mayor Carl Sheline, former city council member Safiya Khalid, and fired CMMC nurse Katie Grinnell, as well as Jackson endorser David Sullivan, General Vice President of the Eastern Territory for the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM). Former Maine state senator Jackson, the Democratic candidate for the Senate in Maine, then spoke, followed by a speech by Vermont senator Bernie Sanders.
Jackson is up against 30-year senator Susan Collins in a tight race that could determine the Senate majority.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington,” Jackson said in his speech. “She tells us that she’s one of the most powerful people in the U.S. Senate. So I think that Maine has the right to ask, ‘Well, what the hell did she do with [that power]?’”
Collins has faced criticism in Maine for her close relationship with President Donald Trump at a time when some view the Trump administration as not doing enough to combat affordability issues. At a debate between the two Senate candidates on Oct. 6, Collins said she had played a crucial role in getting tariffs on road salt reduced for Mainers, to which Jackson responded, Mainers “can’t eat road salt.”
That quote was commonly referenced at the rally.
“Now, don’t get me wrong, we do need road salt here in our great state,” Khalid said in her speech. “After all, we do have our winters. But as Troy Jackson said, we cannot eat road salt, nor can we pay our rent with road salt, nor can we pay medical bills with road salt.”
Early in his speech, Jackson thanked Sanders for being there, commending the Vermont senator’s stance on affordability, a major campaign issue for Jackson.
“Even before Bernie ran for president in ‘16, he’s been willing to say something that shouldn’t really be that controversial: working people built this country,” Jackson said. “And working people want to have the government work for them.”
Sanders spent much of his speech on the idea of affordability.
“There is a reason why working class people die six years earlier than the rich, and it’s not just the healthcare,” Sanders said. “It is the stress that they have to deal with every day, wondering how the hell they’re going to survive. And it is not a radical idea to say that in the richest nation in the history of the world, that should not be happening.”
Jackson has built his campaign around being a lifelong member of the working class, and he spoke frankly about his intent to center Maine’s working class in his campaign and beyond.
“It’s different towns, different struggles, but it’s the same damn truth,” Jackson said of his experiences with Mainers on the campaign trail. “People are working harder than ever just to keep their heads above water.”
A major point for Sanders was reminding the audience that the results of November’s election will reverberate past Maine.
“This election is much more than either of those candidates. It’s about holding Trump accountable and ending Republican control over the United States Senate,” Sanders said. He spoke about issues such as ICE involvement in communities, Medicaid cuts, the Iran war, AI, climate, and wealth distribution, saying, “we will not reverse those policies if Republicans retain control over the Senate.”
Jordan Wood, former congressional and senatorial candidate cheering from the front row, jumped in this race himself in August before dropping out and supporting Jackson.
“It’s an easy decision for me,” Wood said about his enthusiastic support of Jackson. “I’ve gotten to know him really well. We campaigned together for a year… in this exact room, demonstrating against ICE when they invaded Lewiston, [and] I walked the picket line with him in Bath and in Fort Kent.”
Local speakers focused on Lewiston-related issues. Sheline, who is also up for reelection, mentioned Central Maine Medical Center’s recent nurse strike and unionization, which resulted in the firing of 14 nurses.
“I know that our nurses will win their fight,” Sheline said. “And I believe that together, we can win ours, too. Donald Trump will go down as the worst president ever.”
Khalid mentioned how the Agora Center was also the site of an anti-ICE protest in January.
“Nearly 1,000 of us came together, standing against ICE and the fear that immigration enforcement was waiting in our communities,” Khalid said. “Look around this room, we were right here, and Troy Jackson stood with us right here on the stage.”
Jackson also spoke of Lewiston’s importance in his own political journey, mentioning how his stance on gun control changed in the wake of the Oct. 25, 2023 shooting.
“I’m a sportsman, and for a long time, I opposed some of the gun laws that people in my own party were willing to support,” Jackson said. “When 18 of our neighbors were murdered here, and I watched this community bury 18 people, those 18 funerals changed me because sometimes leadership means having the guts to admit that what you believed before isn’t good enough anymore.”
Bates students were present at the rally, some of whom are registered to vote in Maine. Many were drawn to the rally by Sanders’ presence.
“I think that having someone in office that would actually pass stricter legislation would be really, really encouraging and exciting,” Natalie Damer-Salas ‘28 shared. “I have voted in Georgia, but I felt like it was more important to vote in Maine for this election. It felt a bit closer.”
Others spoke of their desire to remain connected to the local community.
“I think for me, a big part of being a Bates student is being involved in Lewiston,” Misra Ahmed ‘28 said. “Even though I’m not voting in Maine this year in this election, I still wanted to get to know all the candidates.”
Philip Cook ‘30 wishes to be more involved in Lewiston as a newcomer.
“This is my first interaction really with Troy Jackson and his campaign,” Cook said. “But we’re now part of this community, and it is something I want to be passionate about and try to make a difference.”
Leaving the rally, students shared their enthusiasm about participating in this election.
“We’re both registered in Maine and terrified for the state of the country,” Alexa Terry ‘27 said about herself and Willow West ‘27, “It’s exciting to be in a place where there’s a candidate that I’m actually excited to vote for.”
For some students, this rally made the election more tangible, reminding them how they can remain involved close to home.
“I feel like coming here made me realize how incredibly important this specific election is,” West said. “It’s definitely inspired me to reach out to other people, make sure that they are aware of the dire importance of this election and what it means for the entire country and the working class especially.”

title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an ‘energy ceasefire’ but Kyiv says attacks continue
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.
“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.”
The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump’s ceasefire post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”
Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponizing winter.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin “had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet.’ We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world.”
He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC’s “This Week .”
On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
Trump spars with Zelenskyy
Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
Zelenskyy said in response to Trump’s comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
“Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.
“With all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader,” he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
Ukrainian strike on Russian data center triggers outages
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company’s services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.
Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.
“I’d press the ‘call’ button to contact them, but nothing happens,” he said. “There’s nothing I can do, so I’m just forced to cancel.”
Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. “Nothing worked,” he said.
Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a “direct impact” and weren’t just about “convenience.” He said they affected “healthcare, and everything else.”
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company’s major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.
Zaporizhzhia death toll rises to 23
Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia’s Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.
___
Blann reported from Kyiv, Ukraine, and Morton reported from London.

title: Obituary: Helen Mary Acheson
text:
LAKEWOOD RANCH, Fla. – Helen Mary Acheson, 62, passed away at home on Oct. 1, 2026, surrounded by her loving family after a heroic battle with ovarian cancer.
Born on Jan. 21, 1964 in Rochester, N.Y. to James M. Acheson and Carolyn (Mendros) Acheson, Helen grew up in Westbrook, Maine and graduated from Westbrook High School. She later became a certified reflexologist. As the headstrong, determined oldest of seven siblings, she quickly honed her caregiving and leadership skills—qualities that would define her relationships with people throughout her life.
Helen married Philip Rich in 1986, to whom she was married for 29 years. They settled in Windham where they raised their children: Jordan, Christopher, and Emily. The children attended Westbrook schools where Helen became a devoted advocate for the school department’s esteemed music program.
Throughout her life starting in high school, Helen was a compassionate personal caregiver for individuals facing severe, life-limiting conditions. She strived to ensure those in her care maintained their comfort, integrity, and dignity. Her fierce protection of her loved ones earned her the nickname “Hurricane Helen.”
Helen had a lifelong love for travel. She felt most at peace in nature, especially by the water, and found immense joy in camping, hiking, kayaking and exploring the outdoors. She passed this enthusiasm on to everyone around her, taking countless cross-country road trips, and inviting friends and family to experience her favorite places and beyond, including the coast of California and the lakes, mountains, and coast of Maine.
Helen faced her devastating 2025 ovarian cancer diagnosis with tremendous strength, undergoing aggressive treatments, with an unwavering commitment to her family, especially her beloved baby grandson, Aiden (aka her handsome), who was the light of her life.
Helen was predeceased by her father, James M. Acheson, stepfather, Conrad Bellerose; treasured son, Christopher Rich, and son-in-law, Eric Voss.
She is survived by her son and daughter-in-law, Jordan and Meagan Rich and grandson, Aiden, of Winter Garden, Fla.; daughter, Emily Rich, formerly of Los Angeles, Calif.; partner John Bellerose; and cherished dogs, Pudge and Maisie. She is also survived by her mother, Carolyn (Mendros) Bellerose, stepmother, Ann Acheson; six siblings, Julianna Acheson Holmdahl (Lars), James Acheson, Marion Acheson-Silver (Richard Silver), Elizabeth Heasly (Gabe), Katherine Kerkam (Ted) and Daniel Acheson (Katie); her uncle, William Acheson (Peg); as well as many nieces and nephews; great-nieces and nephews; and wonderful friends.
The family will have a private celebration of Helen’s life next summer at their home in Pemaquid Harbor, Maine.

title: Longtime school bus driver fired after stopping to let student rescue injured kitten
text:
HARFORD COUNTY, Md. (WJZ) - Parents in a rural Maryland community are rallying behind a school bus driver who was fired after she stopped to let a student rescue an injured kitten.
Cynthia Morgan, 67, worked as a school bus driver in the Harford County Public Schools district for 11 years. She was recently removed from her route after she let a North Harford Elementary School student get off the bus to pick up an injured kitten. Morgan says being fired devastated her.
Parents like Carolyn Kalambihis say they understand the safety concerns but believe removing Morgan from her route was excessive. Video recorded on the rural Heaps School Road shows little traffic, a detail parents say is important to understanding what happened.
“We live in North Harford, so it’s very rural back here. She wouldn’t have done it, you know, let a child get off the bus to get a kitten if it was a more high-traffic road,” Kalambihis said.
She says Morgan has been driving her kids to school for five years, and they absolutely love her.
“She is an angel. She’s the most caring person. Every year at the beginning of the school year, she buys every child on the bus school supplies. She buys them gifts for Christmas, every holiday, birthdays. She’s given them birthday cards, all out of her own pocket,” Kalambihis said.
Now, Kalambihis and other Harford County parents are circulating a petition that calls for Morgan to be allowed to return to her route.
“We just feel the way that it was handled was not appropriate,” Kalambihis said. “We feel that termination was a little excessive, an overreaction by the Department of Transportation through HCPS. I think it could have been handled in a lot of other ways.”
Kalambihis said she believes Morgan understands that allowing a student off the bus was a mistake.
“It’s definitely a concern for safety. There is no question that it was a mistake,” Kalambihis said. “It shouldn’t have happened. I believe she knows that and understands and, looking back, knows she made a mistake and should not have done what she did.”
Harford County Public Schools said Morgan was employed by an independent contractor, not directly by the school district. However, the district is responsible for certifying drivers who transport students for its schools.
“Certification and decertification are not always based on a single factor but often involve consideration of multiple circumstances and requirements,” the district said in a statement. “Student safety remains our top priority, and all certification decisions are made with that responsibility in mind.”
The district declined to comment on Morgan’s specific situation.

title: Maine’s elections are getting crazy expensive. Where does the money go?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The most expensive advertisement of Maine’s campaign season so far begins like this: “Augusta politician Troy Jackson: While his family cashed in, you paid the price.”
A man narrates for 30 tensely soundtracked seconds over quotes pulled from years-old news articles, blaming the former Maine Senate president and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate for higher taxes. It’s a classic attack ad.
At the end, the narrator lowers and hastens his voice.
“Pine Tree Results PAC is responsible for the content of this advertising” — all $2.2 million of it, according to a federal campaign finance filing.
A different group, SRCP Media Inc., developed the spot and bought space on the airwaves for it — not Pine Tree Results PAC.
This is a pretty normal arrangement. SRCP Media is one of the premier conservative campaign advertising firms in the country. It’s based in a waterfront office building in Alexandria, Virginia, just across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.
This year in Maine, with a potentially Senate-tilting election at the top of the ballot, plus a hotly contested House race and an open governor’s seat to boot, campaigns and outside groups have dropped hundreds of millions of donor dollars to persuade voters to fill in their preferred ballot bubble.
So far, the eye-watering total exceeds $300 million, according to the ad tracking service AdImpact. But little of the campaign money meant to convince Maine’s electorate is actually being spent on Maine companies.
Not all of the cash spent this cycle has shown up in federal financial reports, which are filed quarterly. But as of the last reports from late September, it’s clear that a relatively small percentage of campaign spending comes home to Maine broadcasters or other advertisers.
Instead, well over half is going to D.C.-area consultants and firms like SRCP Media, a Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram analysis of the data found. Only about 8% is spent in Maine.
Between a relative lack of locally based campaign expertise and the explosion of money available to campaigns and PACs, the modern election has turned into an expensive game of D.C.-area consultant chess, experts say.
Ben Coolidge Gagnon, a veteran of two Maine gubernatorial campaigns, said this small state’s campaigns can only grow so big before they run out of places to spend money. Sara Gideon’s record-fundraising 2020 U.S. Senate campaign, he noted, still has millions left in the bank.
“So where does all that money go in the future?” Coolidge Gagnon said. “More consultants.”
WHERE THE MONEY GOES
While they can sometimes get candidates in trouble, donations are the backbone of modern campaigns. Without millions from donors, candidates wouldn’t be able to pay staff, and outside groups couldn’t buy ads.
Most of those donations come from outside of Maine. In federal races this cycle, about 83% of Maine candidates’ donations have come from other states, according to the campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets.
The spending of that money mostly happens outside of Maine, too.
This year, more than $67 million has gone to Virginia, Maryland and the District of Columbia, where media firms and PACs operate in close proximity to Washington’s halls of power. Pennsylvania-based firms have raked in another $10.5 million.
In federal races, only 3.4% of the money has been spent in Maine. About a quarter of consulting costs went to Maine, and a staggeringly low 0.2% of advertising costs went to Maine firms.
Money is also flowing out of Maine even in the races for governor and state Legislature, where representatives are sent to Augusta, not Capitol Hill.
About 37% of electioneering spending for state offices has gone to the nation’s capital or its bordering states, while about 20% has gone to Maine-based companies.
Generally, campaigns were most likely to keep their money in Maine when paying for food, events and travel. Polling and advertising spending happened almost entirely outside of this state.
THE ELECTIONS BUSINESS
Coolidge Gagnon got his start in politics in 2014 on Mike Michaud’s gubernatorial campaign, and later worked for the Maine Democratic Party and on the finance team in Janet Mills’ first gubernatorial run.
He’s watched the elections industry explode in recent years, jet-fueled by the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission decision, which has allowed super PACs to independently raise and spend without limits.
Maine has mostly been left on the outside of that boom, Coolidge Gagnon said, and the reason is simple: this state only has three statewide elections, for governor and its two U.S. senators. It’s difficult to get experience here, and it’s not particularly lucrative to stay.
Massachusetts, by contrast, elects six executive officers and its two U.S. Senators in statewide elections. New York has six statewide elections. North Carolina has 34.
Consulting firms based elsewhere have more races to draw from, Coolidge Gagnon said, and political operatives “will hop state to state anyway” to follow big campaigns and big money.
Richard Schlackman, who has been in political advertising and consulting all over the country since the 1970s, said spending tens of millions of dollars across state lines is par for the course. All of the incentives point toward spending more.
“What you have to understand — if things are going well, your side gives you more money to keep it going well,” he said. “If things are going bad, your side gives you money to destroy the other side.”
It’s simply more profitable to center on Washington, D.C., or New York, Schlackman said — that’s where all of the power players are, and the big names with connections.
Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general and Republican nominee for that state’s competitive U.S. Senate seat, said outright that D.C. consultants had taken control of his message during a fundraiser this last month, Politico reported: “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.”
“They get more of that money,” Schlackman said of D.C. operatives. “That doesn’t mean you’re getting a better ad.”
WHO GETS THE MONEY?
There’s a scene in the early 2000s television series, The West Wing, where the fictional president’s chief of staff and prospective campaign manager, Bruno Gianelli, negotiate Gianelli’s pay.
“Fifteen percent of the ad buys,” Gianelli says. “You’re gonna say 10, so why don’t we just say 13?”
That scene holds pretty true to how campaign advertising consultants get paid today, Schlackman said — consultants develop the ad and charge a percentage of the total cost to place the ad on TV. For some, there’s a monthly retainer fee.
That makes consultants some of the biggest winners of expensive election seasons like this one in Maine.
“The money’s in the buy for these TV consultants,” Schlackman said.
In Maine’s state elections, campaigns and PACs regularly report their books to the Maine Ethics Commission. Federal races have similar requirements. But those public reports don’t always tell the whole story, Coolidge Gagnon said, especially on advertising.
State filings show less than $600,000 has been spent on advertising, but gubernatorial candidates’ spots have been blasting through TVs and radios for months.
While the state campaign finance guidebook recommends that groups record the final vendor — for an ad, that’s usually a TV station or social media company — campaigns and PACs often only report the first payee: the media consulting firm they used to develop and place the ad.
“They want to give the least amount of information as they legally have to,” Coolidge Gagnon said. “There’s a competitive advantage of people knowing where the buys are going.”
Campaigns and other groups can subscribe to services like AdImpact, which track ad spending, to get a bit more information. But those services cost thousands of dollars, and the Press Herald analysis didn’t find any Maine campaigns had subscribed to AdImpact.
The election cycle has long been a boon to TV and radio stations that get paid to air candidates’ ads, said Tim Moore, the CEO and president of the Maine Broadcasters Association, in an interview this summer. This year’s been no different, he said. Anyone watching or listening can vouch for that.
But while that money does help stations pay their employees and support a healthy broadcasting ecosystem, it also ebbs and flows. Off years don’t produce the same kind of political spending.
Plus, he said, stations sometimes have to hand over profits to their owners, wherever they may be.
New York-based Democratic political consultant Roy Moskowitz said Maine is a relatively cheap state to advertise in, especially compared with where he operates. Maine only has two congressional districts and three TV markets, where customers get the same channels and ads. New York City has more than a dozen congressional districts and two dozen cable advertising zones.
On the one hand, that means it’s pretty easy to buy advertising space here, he said. On the other, the relatively low cost, Moskowitz said, means there are fewer Maine-based media firms because it’s not worth it for businesses to set up shop here.
Plus, the advertising landscape is changing.
While Maine voters, who skew older, are easy to reach on broadcast television, Moskowitz said consultants see streaming services like Hulu and Apple TV and social media as the most effective forms of political advertising. It’s easier to target specific consumers based on their beliefs and habits through those platforms, he said.
More streaming-based advertising only promises to further shift money away from Maine and toward D.C.-based consulting firms and California-based media conglomerates.
And at some point, Coolidge Gagnon said, there’s only so much advertising to buy and so many people to hire.
When Maine’s ad breaks fill up and rosters bloat, there’s still millions left over.

title: The grave consequences of politicizing science
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Laura Ligouri is founder and chief external strategy officer of Mindbridge, a Maine-based nonprofit organization that uses psychology and neuroscience to support work on human rights and democratic resilience.
Democracy is more than a system for electing leaders. At its core, it is a system designed to protect human dignity and freedom by distributing power, safeguarding fundamental rights and holding those in authority accountable to the people they serve.
Democracies accomplish this not through elections alone, but through a network of independent institutions that help ensure decisions are guided by evidence, law and professional expertise.
Among these institutions are an independent judiciary, a free press, a professional civil service and an independent scientific enterprise. Each serves a distinct role, but together they make it more difficult for any individual or political movement to consolidate power by controlling how reality is defined, interpreted or communicated.
It’s no coincidence that a 2026 report by Freedom House warns that independent institutions are facing increasing political pressure both globally and within the United States. This is why the scientific community is right to be alarmed by the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules.
The concern is not simply that political actors may exert greater influence over scientific funding decisions. The deeper concern is the political capture of institutions that produce knowledge.
The proposed changes to federal research funding are often framed as a dispute over science. In reality, they reflect something much broader: a struggle over power. Throughout history, political movements have sought not only to win elections, but to shape the institutions that determine how society understands truth, expertise and reality itself.
Political power, however, is rarely consolidated through coercion alone. More often, power is secured by persuading ordinary citizens that independent institutions no longer deserve their trust. As the OECD notes, declining trust in public institutions undermines democratic governance by weakening citizens’ confidence in the institutions responsible for informing, protecting and representing them.
Appeals to patriotism, morality, tradition or partisan allegiance transform institutional disputes into questions of identity — framing universities, scientists, journalists or judges not as independent arbiters, but as adversaries in a larger political struggle.
This strategy is effective not because people abandon reason, but because it taps into psychological processes that have shaped human survival for thousands of years. We like to think of ourselves as rational decision-makers, carefully weighing evidence before reaching conclusions. In reality, we are motivated reasoners. Our brains evolved not primarily to discover objective truth, but to help us survive within groups.
For most of human history, survival depended on remaining connected to trusted communities. As a result, our emotions, identities and group affiliations often shape what we believe long before conscious reasoning begins. Under conditions of uncertainty or perceived threat, these tendencies become even more pronounced. We increasingly look to those we identify with for cues about whom to trust, what to fear and which version of reality to accept.
Once scientific questions become tied to political identity, evidence itself begins to function differently. It is no longer evaluated primarily for its accuracy, but for what accepting or rejecting it communicates about who we are and where we belong. Scientific claims become badges of group membership rather than invitations to inquiry.
Viewed through this lens, the debate over the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to federal grantmaking rules is about far more than research funding.
Here in Maine, Sen. Susan Collins recently expressed concern that the proposal would allow political appointees to override scientific merit review, undermining the longstanding principle that federally funded research should be evaluated on scientific merit.
When political ideology begins shaping which scientific questions receive support and which findings receive legitimacy, science ceases to function as an independent check on power.
The deeper concern is that proposals like this risk embedding those dynamics within the institutions themselves, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which political influence further erodes public trust, and declining trust becomes justification for even greater political influence. Any and all guardrails that intervene on such processes from taking place are no longer present.
Democracies depend upon citizens having access to trusted sources of information and shared mechanisms for evaluating competing claims. In an era of social media, misinformation and declining institutional trust, that premise can feel increasingly difficult to sustain. Yet that is precisely why independent institutions committed to evaluating evidence through transparent, accountable processes have never been more important.
For states like Maine, where scientific research serves small and rural communities and supports major regional employers, the consequences extend well beyond academia. Federal research funding helps drive discoveries that lead to new medical treatments, fuels Maine’s growing life sciences economy, creates high-skilled jobs and trains the next generation of scientists, physicians and innovators at institutions such as the University of Maine, The Jackson Laboratory, MaineHealth, MDI Biological Laboratory and the University of New England.
Research leaders have warned that growing uncertainty surrounding federal funding threatens not only scientific discovery, but also the economic vitality, workforce development and medical advances upon which communities across Maine increasingly depend.
Importantly, history suggests that democratic institutions are rarely weakened all at once. More often, they are gradually reshaped through a series of changes that each appear limited in scope, administrative in nature or justified by immediate political concerns. Viewed in isolation, any one change may seem relatively insignificant. Viewed together, they can fundamentally alter how democratic societies determine what is true.
This is why the debate surrounding the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions matters, even to those who will never apply for a federal research grant. The proposal is not simply about science funding. It is about whether one of democracy’s most important safeguards — the independent evaluation of evidence — remains insulated from political loyalty or becomes increasingly subject to it.
Protecting scientific independence is about far more than protecting science. It is about safeguarding one of democracy’s most essential foundations: our collective ability to distinguish evidence from ideology, truth from propaganda and scientific process from political loyalty.

title: DOJ says it’s investigating whether White House TV pool’s coverage halt violated antitrust law
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday.
Emily Covington, a spokesperson for the department, said group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law. “The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws,” she said.
The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC.
The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that cover the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports — a type of free speech, pillar of American democracy.
Last month’s developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump’s efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over the days-long ban. It was lifted after a judge handed the three news organizations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday.
Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ regional director of the Americas, on Saturday criticized the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”
___
Taxin contributed to this report from Santa Ana, California.

title: 2-year-old ‘fighting for her life’ after suspect stabs toddler, her mom in random attack
text:
PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WJAR) - A 2-year-old Rhode Island girl is fighting for her life after she and her mother were stabbed in an attack police say was completely random.
Amaalia Javier and her 2-year-old daughter were waiting for the girl’s siblings to get off a school bus Wednesday afternoon when Providence Police say 46-year-old Nelson Blanco attacked them. The incident was caught on surveillance cameras.
Jessie Palmer, a certified nursing assistant, was also waiting for the school bus in a car with her own child when she heard a scream and saw the suspect attacking the victims. She claims Blanco went after the toddler first, and Javier tried to step in.
“He pushed her out of the way because she tried to shield the baby with her body, and he pushed her out of the way and stabbed her and then went back to the baby,” Palmer said.
Palmer and other bystanders intervened before the suspect ran off. While some people chased after him, Palmer worked to keep the 2-year-old alive.
“I helped the baby out the carriage, and when I saw she was bleeding, I put her to the floor and was putting pressure,” Palmer said. “Another lady… came and helped me apply the pressure, and then, the baby stopped breathing. So, we had to stop performing CPR and breathing for the baby until the ambulance came.”
The toddler remained in intensive care Thursday, and Providence Police Col. Oscar Perez said she is “fighting for her life.” Her mother has been released from the hospital and is focused on her daughter’s condition, friends say.
Blanco was arraigned Thursday on several charges stemming from the stabbing, including felony assault with a dangerous weapon. Police say he admitted to the attack, which they say was completely random. There was no known connection between the suspect and the victims.
“That man’s evil and what he did was wrong, and I don’t even think jail’s enough punishment for him,” Palmer said.
Court records show Blanco’s criminal history dates back decades and includes a 2003 case in which he was charged with stabbing two 7-year-old children.

title: Who Is Nidal Hasan? Army Major Faces Execution by Firing Squad
text:
Who Is Nidal Hasan? Fort Hood Killer Faces First Military Execution in Decades
Nidal Hasan is a former U.S. Army major who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas.
Hasan was sentenced to death in 2013 for the attack, which targeted fellow service members at the military installation.
More than a decade later, his scheduled execution is drawing renewed attention as officials consider how it will be carried out.
What Did Nidal Hasan Do?
On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood, a major U.S. Army installation in Texas. The shooting killed 13 people and injured 32 others.
READ MORE: These Five States Have Produced the Most Serial Killers
Hasan, who was serving as an Army psychiatrist at the time, was arrested following the attack. He was later convicted by a military jury and sentenced to death.
When Is Nidal Hasan's Execution?
Hasan's execution is scheduled for Dec. 3, according to the Pentagon, and is expected to be carried out by firing squad.
If carried out, it would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 and the first military execution by firing squad since 1945.
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he had not yet decided whether the execution would be livestreamed.
"He was vicious, he was violent," Trump told reporters at the White House. He added that showing the execution might deter others from committing similar acts, but said he would make the final decision.
Fox News Digital previously reported that Trump approved the use of an Army firing squad following a recommendation from War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

title: 'Other Mommy' tops the box office with $27.5M; 'The Social Reckoning' opens to $5.5M
text:
The Jessica Chastain horror “Other Mommy” topped the North American box office this weekend with a bigger audience than expected, while “The Social Reckoning” got off to a lackluster start.
‘Other Mommy’ is another win for horror
“Other Mommy,” released by Universal Pictures, earned $27.5 million in its first few days in 3,365 theaters, according to studio estimates on Sunday. The movie, about a sinister supernatural creature that terrorizes a young girl who thinks it’s her mother, got dismal reviews from both critics and audiences. It also joins the ranks of “Megalopolis” and “Hereditary” with a D+ CinemaScore.
But with a production budget of around $19 million, it’s also another win for the horror genre and producer Blumhouse Atomic Monster, which was behind “Backrooms” and “Obsession.” “Other Mommy” opened in 50 international markets as well, boosting its global debut to $45.2 million.
Jim Orr, Universal’s head of domestic distribution, noted that the audience gender divide was evenly split and about 2/3 were between 18 and 34 years old.
“No matter how you look at it, everybody turned out for it. It wasn’t just one particular demographic,” Orr said. “That usually is a very good sign.”
‘The Social Reckoning’ fails to connect
“The Social Reckoning,” the weekend’s other big release, was not as lucky, earning an estimated $5.5 million from 2,606 North American theaters. Aaron Sorkin wrote and directed the film about a Facebook whistleblower who leaked incriminating documents to a Wall Street Journal reporter.
Sixteen years ago, “The Social Network,” which Sorkin wrote and David Fincher directed, opened to over $22 million and went on to gross over $224 million worldwide, receiving eight Oscar nominations and winning three. A similar fate might be a stretch for “The Social Reckoning,” which stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White and Jeremy Strong and received mixed-to-negative reviews from critics. Audiences gave it a B- CinemaScore. According to reports, the Sony Pictures release cost around $30 million to produce, not accounting for marketing and promotion.
Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends, said October is a time when studios take chances and it doesn’t always work out.
“These movies that are topical in nature, sometimes they resonate with the culture, sometimes they don’t,” said Dergarabedian. “You don’t always know what’s going to connect with audiences.”
He compared “The Social Reckoning” to “Digger,” which fell 60% in its second weekend.
The overall box office is still up
“The Social Reckoning” opened behind several holdovers as well. The Anne Hathaway psychological thriller “Verity” took second place with $11.5 million, down 64% from its opening weekend. In third place, “Resident Evil” added $8.4 million, bringing its domestic total to $138.5 million. The Brad Pitt survival thriller “Heart of the Beast” took fourth with $7.1 million.
Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey ” also made an encore appearance in the top 10 in its 13th weekend in theaters where it was back in 12 IMAX 70 mm locations. It added $2 million from 560 North American theaters, bringing its domestic total just shy of $623 million.
Several high-profile films opened in limited release this weekend as well. The Cannes Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” debuted on four screens this weekend where it made $124,000. Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary “Musk,” which runs nearly four hours, made $68,900 from four locations. And Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” made $85,716 from six locations through Sunday.
The annual domestic box office crossed the $8 billion mark on Friday and is up over 19% from last year. According to Rentrak, that’s about 8% behind 2019.
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Other Mommy,” $27.5 million.
2. “Verity,” $11.5 million.
3. “Resident Evil,” $8.4 million.
4. “Heart of the Beast,” $7.1 million.
5. “The Social Reckoning,” $5.5 million.
6. “Forgotten Island,” $4.5 million.
7. “Primetime,” $4 million.
8. “Digger,” $3.2 million.
9. “Angel and the Badman,” $2.1 million.
10. “The Odyssey,” $2 million.

title: Obituary: Sally A. Hinkley
text:
TURNER – Sally A. Hinkley, 87, a resident of Turner, passed away peacefully, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at her home, with her loving family by her side. She was born on Nov. 4, 1938, in Lewiston, the daughter of Norman A. Parks, Sr. and Alice (Creamer) Parks. She was a 1957 graduate of Edward Little High School in Auburn.
On Aug. 17, 1957, at the East Auburn Baptist Church, she married Donald True Hinkley of Turner. They enjoyed 63 years together before his passing on June 23, 2021.
Sally worked as a substitute teacher for MSAD 52 in the Turner, Leeds and Greene Schools. Sally was also a 4-H Leader for many years. She enjoyed snowmobiling, quilting, and going to her camp in Eustis. Don and Sally were snowbirds for 13 years, living winters at their second home, in DeLand, Fla. where she loved socializing with everyone.
Sally is survived by her three children, Suzanne Denis and husband Paul of Clay, N.Y., Rebecca Elsman and husband Steve of Hartford, and Michael Hinkley and wife Julie (Lowell) of DeLand, Fla.; 17 grandchildren; 33 great-grandchildren; her brother and sister-in-law, Norman and Laura Parks, Jr. of Buckfield, her brother-in-law, Russell A. Hinkley, Sr. of Turner, her sister-in-law, Arlene Samson of Turner; and many nieces and nephews.
She was predeceased by her parents; infant daughter, Shelia Hinkley; grandson, Scott Hinkley; her sister and brother-in-law, Pamela and Floyd Richardson, her brother-in-law, Joseph Samson, her sister-in-law, JoyCe Hinkley; and several nieces and nephews.
A funeral service will be held at 11 a.m. on Friday, Oct. 16, at the First Universalist Church of Turner Center, 450 Turner Center Road (Route 117), Turner. Interment at South Turner Cemetery, Upper Street, in Turner.

title: Carr crash radio appearance by Sen. Collins
text:
When I lived in Maine, I worked hard against Susan Collins’ election to the United States Senate. Over the years, however, I have come to grudgingly admire her avowed commitment to avoiding name-calling and personal attacks. Collins is a dignified presence in an arena that is increasingly undignified. It was disappointing, therefore, to hear her on “The Howie Carr Show,” broadcast from Gorham on Sept. 25.
Carr, as anyone who listens regularly to his show knows, revels in name-calling and personal attacks. He often refers to immigrants as “cholos,” describes foreign countries as “Third-World hellholes,” and rates women on their looks. Indeed, in a segment that aired just before Collins appeared, he made some very misogynistic comments about the lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, who apparently does not meet his beauty standards.
Carr has been around for many years, and everyone is aware of his shtick. Collins should be ashamed of appearing on this show.
David Scannell
Bedford, N.H.

title: Indian Island man slain in Washington County shooting
text:
A 41-year-old Indian Island man was killed in a Saturday night shooting in Down East Maine, police said.
Police received a report of a shooting around 9:30 p.m. on Peter Dana Point Road on the Passamaquoddy reservation, where they found Cory Fields dead.
State Police, the Indian Township Police Department, Indian Township Fire Rescue, the Passamaquoddy Tribal Warden Service and the Washington County Sheriff’s Office all arrived at the scene.
An autopsy the next day by the Office of Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta found Fields died from gunshot wounds, the Maine State Police said.
Jeremy Stevens, 46, of Indian Township, was arrested for murder and taken to Washington County Jail, police said.
The chiefs of the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy tribes issued a joint statement expressing “shock and deep sadness” over the killing.
“Our hearts are with the family and loved ones of the individual who lost their life, and with the entire Wabanaki community as we grieve this devastating loss,” the statement from Chief Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik, Kirk Francs of the Penobosot Nation, and William Nicholas Sr., Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk said.

title: Bernie Sanders joins Troy Jackson for ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour in Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With Election Day about three weeks away, Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is in Maine this weekend, drumming up support for Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson.
The three-stop ‘Solidarity Forever’ tour kicked off in Bangor Saturday night at the Cross Insurance Center.
“Whether Troy wins or not can determine who controls the Senate and the future of the United States of America,” said Sanders during his remarks. “So, I am running around the country and others are doing the same for two goals. Number one, we’ve got to stop Trump. We got to make sure Democrats gain control over the House and the Senate, but that is not enough. We got to make sure that when Democrats do have control over the House and the Senate, they have the guts to stand up to their campaign contributors and fight for an agenda that works for working families.”
Former Maine Senate President Jackson said his priorities include protecting and expanding Social Security, supporting unions and schools, and Medicare for All.
“Look, I’ve had the honor of having some power in Maine. And for 20 years, I’ve tried to remember one thing: It was never mine. You gave it to me. My job was to use it for you. And if you send me the United States Senate, that’s exactly what I’m going to do,” Jackson said during Saturday’s rally.
Jackson responded to criticism from Collins’ campaign, saying: “They’re not going to make me ashamed of where I’ve come from. They’re not going to make me ashamed of my family. They’re not sure as hell going to stop me for fighting for yours.”
He also addressed the current senator’s record and allegations of corruption.
“Senator Collins has had 30 years in Washington. She claims to be one of the most powerful people in the Senate. And what I know is where were you when we needed you the most?” Jackson questioned. “I don’t take corporate PAC money or trade tax dollars for donations, and unlike our senator, I don’t owe Donald Trump anything.”
Speakers joining Jackson and Sanders at Saturday’s rally included Erin Oberson, co-president of the Maine State Nurses Association, and Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance.
Saturday night’s rally marked the first stop of the Solidarity Forever tour. Jackson and Sanders are scheduled to travel to Lewiston and Biddeford on Sunday.

title: County Runners Capture Four Team Titles in Big Saturday of Cross Country
text:
County Cross Country: Houlton, Caribou and Presque Isle Bring Home Team Titles
Aroostook County runners put together a dominant Saturday on two different courses, bringing home four team championships along with several individual victories at the Red Riot Challenge in Orono and the Pendale’s meet in Hermon.
Houlton/GHCA captured both the varsity boys and JV girls team titles at the Red Riot Challenge. At Pendale’s, Caribou won the varsity boys competition and Presque Isle claimed the varsity girls title.
Individually, Houlton/GHCA’s Malachi Witmer, Caribou’s Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves all crossed the finish line first in their respective varsity races.
Red Riot Challenge
Houlton Boys Put Four Runners in the Top Five
Houlton/GHCA controlled the varsity boys 4,000-meter race, placing four runners among the first five finishers and winning the team championship with 35 points.
Malachi Witmer led the way, winning the race in 13:22.20.
Wyatt Quint finished third in 13:39.71, Logan Witmer was fourth at 13:40.40 and Brayden Drake followed in fifth with a time of 13:41.60.
Stephen Cormier completed Houlton/GHCA's scoring five in 23rd place at 15:59.20.
The Shires finished 17 points ahead of second-place George Stevens Academy. Orono was third with 61.
Lucas McPhee added a 29th-place finish for Houlton/GHCA in 16:59.80.
Fort Kent's Jaxson Saucier was 30th overall with a time of 17:00.30.
Houlton JV Girls Earn Perfect Team Score
Houlton/GHCA also swept the scoring positions in the JV girls race to finish with a perfect 15 points.
Charlotte Estabrook won the 4,000-meter race in 20:00.94.
Dalylah Mincey finished second at 22:48.95, Kaley Whitman was fourth at 25:09.28, Alaina Locker finished sixth at 25:48.28 and Sandra Quinlan rounded out the scoring in eighth.
Burlock Leads County JV Boys
Houlton/GHCA's Victor Burlock was the top County finisher in the JV boys race, placing fourth in 18:53.38.
Pendale's Meet
Caribou Goes 1-2-3 to Win Boys Team Championship
Caribou grabbed the first three individual places in the varsity boys 5,000-meter race and went on to win the team title with 33 points.
Pierce Gorneault took the individual victory in 16:45.00.
Tewolde Stewart followed in second at 17:24.95, while Peyton Gorneault completed the Vikings' 1-2-3 sweep with a third-place finish in 18:00.59.
Xander Jamieson finished 13th and Alex Searles was 14th to complete Caribou's scoring five.
Micah Menifield finished 17th and Isaac Brissette was 20th.
Caribou finished 36 points ahead of second-place Presque Isle.
Presque Isle Boys Take Second
Presque Isle packed four runners into the top 12 on the way to second place with 69 points.
Jeremy Charette led the Wildcats with a fourth-place finish in 18:02.30.
Connor Meile placed ninth at 18:28.24, Geonni Guevara was 11th in 18:58.76 and Henry Clayton finished 12th at 19:01.52.
Matthew Demarest completed the Wildcat scoring in 35th place.
Central Aroostook freshman Carlson Rolon also turned in a strong race, finishing 26th in 21:36.85.
Graves Wins, Presque Isle Claims Girls Team Title
Caribou's Emma Graves earned the individual victory in the varsity girls 5,000-meter race, crossing the line in 19:23.22.
Presque Isle then used a deep pack behind Graves to win the team championship.
Aleah Rideout led the Wildcats with a runner-up finish in 19:58.19, followed immediately by Lillian Johnson in third at 20:06.15.
Taylor York placed seventh in 20:55.44 and Marie Johnston was 10th at 22:19.55.
Meredith House finished 16th to complete Presque Isle's scoring five and give the Wildcats 31 points.
Caribou finished second with 42 points.
Behind Graves, Jenna Strid placed fifth, Isabella Albert was eighth, Gloria Dionne finished 17th and Anna Haley was 23rd.
Jade Clayton finished 18th for Presque Isle, while Lydia Bragdon was 26th.
Caribou Sweeps Top Four in JV Boys
Caribou also dominated the front of the JV boys race.
Isaac Goodwin won in 19:46.29, followed by teammates Emerson Langworthy in second, Wesley Thomas in third and Jimmy Norelli in fourth.
Presque Isle Places Two in JV Girls Top Four
Presque Isle freshmen Ashton Hughes and Macyn Morton finished third and fourth in the JV girls race.
Hughes crossed the line in 25:17.55, with Morton just behind at 25:21.86.
Washburn's Eleanora Streeter finished fifth in 26:51.15, while Presque Isle's Ellie Blackstone and Grace Hilton placed seventh and eighth.
Saturday's results gave County runners a strong finish to another busy weekend, with team championships for Houlton/GHCA, Caribou and Presque Isle and individual victories from Witmer, Gorneault, Graves, Estabrook and Goodwin.
