title: Oxford County sheriff candidates cite finances, public trust, accountability as top issues
text:
Three longtime law enforcement officers are running for election as sheriff of Oxford County on Nov. 3.
Incumbent Christopher R. Wainwright, 55, of Dixfield, a Republican, is seeking a third term. He is being challenged by sheriff’s deputy Justin M. Brown, 47, of Hartford, who is not enrolled in any party, and Paris police patrolman and school resource officer Timothy L. Holland, 69, of Peru, a Democrat.
The three men have 107 years of law enforcement experience among them: Brown, 26; Holland, 45-plus; Wainwright, 36.
Wainwright beat Brown to retain the sheriff position in 2022.
Brown is one of three Oxford County deputies to file complaints against Wainwright for alleged retaliation after reporting unlawful or improper conduct by Wainwright and cooperating with a county-ordered investigation that led county commissioners to petition Gov. Janet Mills for his removal in February 2024.
Wainwright said he is limited by law in discussing employees, but he is “confident that the facts will speak for themselves through the process.”
The candidates recently responded to questions about their qualifications, goals and what they see as challenges.
They all stressed the need for careful budget management, reducing unnecessary costs, and using taxpayer’ resources efficiently. They also acknowledge the need to to address department staffing, improve recruitment and retention of deputies and corrections officers, and rebuild internal morale and teamwork.
A central theme is rebuilding public trust and restoring professional standards through honest communications, operational transparency, and accountability to the community.
Voters will cast their ballots Nov. 3 and the winner will begin serving Jan. 1, 2027, for a four-year term.
REGIONAL JAIL PROPOSAL
The candidates weighed in on whether a proposed regional jail would be worth exploring to better serve inmates, work more efficiently, share costs of staffing and other expenses.
When a jail is overcrowded counties pay to board inmates at another facility for $95 or more a day per inmate. Sheriffs in Androscoggin, Franklin and Oxford counties presented the idea in October 2025 and only Androscoggin and Franklin favored hiring a consultant to see if the idea is feasible.
Holland said he does not support a regional jail initiative, while Brown and Wainwright favor exploring the option to see if it would save money and be beneficial to Oxford County taxpayers.
“Considering the lack of jail funding currently, I would like to sit down with officials from Oxford County to explore options which could work for our taxpayers,” Holland wrote.
“I do believe a regional jail is worth exploring but there needs to be a more comprehensive
study completed to determine what the long-term cost would be and what the impact to the
citizens of Oxford County would be,” Brown said. 
Wainwright said he has already begun working with Franklin County Sheriff Scott Nichols Sr. and Androscoggin County Sheriff Eric Samson “to look at whether a regional facility could provide a more sustainable and cost-effective way to meet our correctional needs.”
“The key for me is that we have to make decisions based on facts, numbers, and what is best for the taxpayers we serve,” he said.
GOALS
“My goal is to continue building on the progress we have made and ensure the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office is prepared to meet the needs of our communities for years to come,” Wainwright wrote. They have already made improvements, he said, including returning the county jail to a full-service facility after being required by a previous governor to be a 72-hour holding facility, which proved to be inefficient, costly to taxpayers, and unable to adequately meet the needs of those in custody.
Holland’s goals include rebuilding the team to “restore trust and accountability to our communities.” He cited “community policing by way of increased deputy visibility within the communities. Maximize the use of resources within the organization.”
Brown wrote that among his goals is to” build an agency that citizens and employees can trust again,” along with establishing measurable outcomes and providing public reports showing progress.
WHAT’S THE BIGGEST CHALLENGE?
Holland believes the biggest challenge facing the sheriff is budgeting, along with an appropriately staffed department with a critical eye on labor contracts to work within taxpayer capabilities.
He cited “accountability to taxpayers by gaining their trust through transparency of operations.”
Brown said the biggest challenge is providing quality service across the large, rural area while maintaining the resources required to address substance abuse and the opioid epidemic.
“Staying focused on these issues with rising costs requires a delicate balance of
maintaining a responsible budget while providing the service our residents expect and deserve,” he wrote.
“One of our biggest challenges is keeping up with the growing demands being placed on law enforcement,” Wainwright wrote. “Our deputies are responding to an increasing number of calls involving mental health, substance use, and other complicated instances that often require more than traditional law enforcement alone.”
He said he would also continue to focus on trying to get the state to pay its fair share of operating county jails instead of having to ask taxpayers to pick up more of the cost.
All three candidates said they plan to work with the three county commissioners to make sure department needs are met and maintain open lines of communication and fiscal responsibility.
ABOUT THEM
Brown said he has continued to advance his education to better serve county residents during his decades of service. His education and experience, he said, has helped him prepare to the lead the Sheriff’s Office.
Holland said he has the “experience to take on the challenges of which Oxford County presents and along with my leadership team will be ready on Day 1 to take command. I will not be an absentee in the Sheriff’s Office,” he wrote.
Wainwright said he is proud of what the Sheriff’s Office and jail staff have accomplished to strengthen the department. He started his career when he was 19 and has served as sheriff for the past eight years.

title: Obituary: Claire Delisle Levine
text:
WESTBROOK – Claire Delisle Levine, of Westbrook, Maine, passed away on Oct. 5, 2026, at the age of 87, leaving behind a lifetime of love, cherished memories, and a family who meant everything to her.
Born on March 22, 1939, Claire was a devoted mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and friend whose kindness, warmth, and generous spirit touched the lives of everyone fortunate enough to know her.
Above all else, Claire was a mother. Raising her three children as a single mom, she worked tirelessly and made countless sacrifices to ensure they were loved, cared for, and provided with every opportunity she could give them. She often put her own needs aside for the sake of her children, never asking for recognition or anything in return. Her strength, determination, and unconditional love were the foundation of her family and will forever remain a part of her legacy.
Throughout her life, Claire worked in professional offices and the grocery industry, where she was known for her friendly personality and genuine interest in others. She had a special way of connecting with people and developed many lasting friendships along the way. To Claire, the people she met were never just coworkers or customers; they were friends.
Claire found happiness in life’s simple pleasures. She loved spending time at the beach, especially Pine Point, where the ocean breeze and peaceful surroundings brought her joy. Her garden was another special place, providing countless hours of enjoyment and a beautiful reflection of her nurturing spirit. She also had a particular fondness for butterflies, whose delicate beauty brought her happiness.
Her love extended beyond her family to her beloved furry companions, who received the same affection, tenderness, and unconditional devotion she so freely gave to everyone she loved.
Claire is survived by her three children, Stephen Levine, Susan Fossett (Greg), and Peter Bloxam (Michelle); her five beloved grandchildren, Meghan, Jimmy, Kristin, Alec and Katie; and six great-grandchildren. Each held a special place in her heart, and her greatest happiness came from knowing she was surrounded by the love of her family.
Claire’s life was not defined by material things or grand accomplishments, but by the love she gave, the sacrifices she made, and the countless lives she touched through simple acts of kindness. She taught her family the meaning of strength, compassion, perseverance, and unconditional love, not merely through words, but through the example she set every day.
She gave so much of herself to those she loved and asked for so little in return. Her love was her greatest gift, and her family will carry that gift with them forever.
Claire will be deeply missed, lovingly remembered, and forever held in the hearts of those who knew and loved her.

title: Auburn school comes together for canine cause, motivated by comfort dog Luna
text:
Every Monday, Wednesday and Friday since the start of the school year, students and faculty at Auburn’s Franklin Alternative School have run — or walked — in the surrounding High Street neighborhood to prepare for a 5K race. The event not only supported a favorite school cause but ended up bringing them together and teaching lessons in ways they never expected.
“So many of our students face barriers when it comes to being part of their community. Sometimes they are tangible — poverty, abuse, instability — and sometimes in their heads — anxiety, depression — but all of those barriers send the message to kids that they don’t belong. A 5K is such a simple thing but it’s an event that has a strong sense of community,” said Principal Melissa McLeod.
Despite the rigors of a 5K, the students didn’t need much convincing right from the start, McLeod said, because the 5K benefited the organization behind the school’s beloved comfort dog, Luna.
And as far as McLeod was concerned, it didn’t matter that there ended up being more walking than running as training for the 5K progressed, because it was all about the effort and the cause.
“A lot who wanted to run are now walking,” McLeod joked last week, before eight school staff and 22 students lined up Oct. 4 for Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford.
Franklin School is an alternative learning environment that students at risk of not graduating can choose to attend. It serves about 100 students from Lewiston and Auburn. In the eight years McLeod has served as principal, the school has always had a wait list, she said.
The school secured a $125,000 grant two years ago from The John T. Gorman Foundation, a philanthropic organization in Maine, to pilot trauma-informed programming that can bolster academic achievement and social outcomes.
McLeod said the school implemented an aerobic movement program three times a week as part of the wellness side of the grant. She explained that academic research shows that movement not only helps regulate a person’s nervous system, but can help improve academic performance.
The addition of training for a 5K felt like a perfect way to implement that exercise, she said. And the staff idea to do the Moxie’s Memorial 5K was a great motivator: The event raises funds for the nonprofit that brought Franklin Alternative’s comfort dog Luna into the school’s life.
Every student and staff member who could participate, did, and they were out of the building every Monday, Wednesday and Friday to train. The staff had a lot of fun with it, McLeod said, and some even started lifting weights.
“One thing I emphasized to staff is that if we are going to get the kids to do this, we have to show enthusiasm, and there ended up being a lot more than we thought,” she said.
Luna has become a staple to Franklin Alternative School. She has a distinctive personality and free reign through the school’s hallway. McLeod said Luna helps the students immensely. If students, or even staff, are having a difficult day, they can spend some time cuddling with Luna to lift their spirits. At the end of the day, Luna goes home to McLeod and her family.
Luna has also made an impact on the greater Auburn school community. McLeod jokes that if she goes anywhere with Luna, it will take twice as long because everyone wants to pet her.
Luna came to Franklin School from Mission Working Dogs, which hosts the Moxie’s Memorial 5K in Oxford. The organization breeds, raises and trains service dogs for disabled veterans and civilians who are suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, or mobility issues, while also providing comfort dogs to hospitals and schools.
Christy Gardner, an Auburn Edward Little High School graduate, was injured in 2006 while serving as a sergeant in the U.S. Army Police Military in Asia. After returning to Maine, Gardner adopted her service dog, Moxie, in 2010 and in 2020 founded Mission Working Dogs.
Auburn Police Department’s comfort dog, Benny-Bud, also came from Mission Working Dogs.
Gardner said after the 5K event Oct. 4 that it was “awesome” to have the Franklin students and Luna participate in the race.
“They brought great attitudes and smiles to the event. We love our partnership with their school and the difference therapy dog Luna brings to the environment there,” Gardner said.
McLeod said she knows it sounds cliché, but participating with students and staff in an event like the one this past weekend reinforces the feeling of family that the school has.
Often, students at Franklin Alternative School arrive needing more than just academics, they need a support system. The combination of physical movement training for the recent 5K and the new statewide cellphone ban have strengthened that bond, McLeod said.
“We have these kids who are always walking around the city, but now they’re forced to walk with adults and other kids. They are all talking to each other, and they’re still at school so they can’t have their phones. It’s forcing the kids to be more social with adults and it’s been great, just walking around chatting,” she said.
Several teachers, including Stevie Dunton, a special education teacher, got involved in the 5K. He said he is not a runner, but he wanted to show his students that they could do whatever they put their minds to.
Melissa Anderson, a social worker, said Luna is an integral part of the support system at Franklin. Anderson herself is a new member of the “Franklin family” and being a part of the training for the 5K and seeing the success of the students was meaningful to her.
“The conversations that grew out of morning walks and the confidence built through this opportunity were truly wonderful to observe and be a part of,” said Anderson.
Moving forward, staff at Franklin Alternative School will continue to remind their students that they have a sense of belonging in the community, whether they are training together or bonding in the classroom with Luna, especially in the light of conversations around youth and the gun violence Lewiston is experiencing.
“Kids who are told that they don’t have value and don’t belong in their communities have no incentive to protect their streets or contribute in positive ways. They also have no incentive to hold each other accountable. We will continue to encourage our kids at Franklin to be a part of their world and will open any doors we can to get them passage into their community,” McLeod said.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Emily Duggan can be reached at eduggan@sunjournal.com

title: The story of how a German tourist ended up mistaking Bangor for San Francisco
text:
This story was originally published in October 2020.
Erwin Kreuz, a genial, unassuming 49-year-old Bavarian brewery worker, was quite pleased to be making his first trip overseas from his native Germany, when he boarded a World Airways flight from Frankfurt to San Francisco in early October 1977.
His arrival in the City by the Bay was delayed, however, by an unplanned two-week layover in Bangor, during which he thought he had landed in San Francisco — a mix-up that ended up changing Kreuz’s life, making national headlines, and becoming a part of local Bangor lore.
Kreuz’s plane, a charter flight that made regular trips between Germany and San Francisco, had stopped to refuel at Bangor International Airport. After the plane landed, a flight attendant woke Kreuz from a nap and apparently wished him a pleasant visit to San Francisco — because she was getting off her shift and wouldn’t see him again, not because he’d actually reached the California city.
Kreuz, however, assumed he’d arrived at his intended destination and got off the plane and went through customs.
Despite there being no Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz or Haight-Ashbury district, Kreuz spent four days wandering the Bangor region, assuming he was in San Francisco — or, at least, a suburb of it. The prevalence of Chinese restaurants in Bangor — which San Francisco is famous for — made him think that perhaps he just hadn’t found the city center yet. The fact that Kreuz hardly spoke English only made things more confusing.
Eventually, Kreuz asked a cab driver, in his limited English, to take him to the San Francisco city center. The cab driver informed him that San Francisco was 3,000 miles away, and that he was in Bangor, Maine.
Luckily, the cab driver knew someone who spoke German — Gertrude Romine, who with her husband ran a German restaurant in Old Town. He drove Kreuz to the restaurant, and Romine explained to the hapless traveler where he was.
A Bangor Daily News reporter was contacted, and after the story ran in the paper, Kreuz became a local celebrity, practically overnight.
Over the course of the next few weeks, Kreuz was given the red carpet treatment. He was given the key to the city by the Bangor City Council, he was named an honorary member of the Penobscot Indian Nation and the Old Town Rotary Club, and he had a meeting with Gov. James Longley. He met Andre the Seal, the famed harbor seal adopted by the Rockport harbormaster, who gave Kreuz a kiss. Kreuz celebrated his 50th birthday while he was in Bangor, and by his own request, he had his birthday party at a local McDonald’s.
He reportedly received three marriage proposals, and a couple in the Aroostook County town of St. Francis gave Kreuz an acre overlooking the St. John River, in the hopes that he’d return to Maine to live. Kreuz reportedly paid taxes on the land until at least 1984.
The story made its way into the national spotlight when Kreuz was featured in Time Magazine, and in a segment on “The Today Show” on NBC, with Tom Brokaw lauding Bangor’s generosity of spirit in how the city treated the wayward German. German news magazines Der Spiegel and Stern reported on it in his home country of West Germany.
“I think people really bought into the fun of it, and they didn’t make fun of him. They really embraced him,” said Bangor historian Richard Shaw. “I think it says a lot about Mainers. He took to us, and we took to him.”
Magnus Stark, a photographer and marketing director for the Penobscot Theatre Company, became fascinated by the Kreuz story several years ago, and has researched it to try to find out more about Kreuz himself — what his life in Germany was like, and what ended up happening to him after his last trip to Maine in 1979.
Stark said Kreuz grew up in what became East Germany, and escaped into West Germany after World War II. He was an accomplished beer brewer, and also made and sold cheese. He had a kind of happy-go-lucky attitude, Stark says, that served him well as he was squired about on his unintentional Maine vacation.
“I totally feel for this guy, because I remember when I first moved to Bangor, and I didn’t know what I was getting myself into, and I kind of had to go with it,” said Stark, a native of Norway (the country, not the Maine town) who moved to Bangor in 2012. “It actually reminds me of how I felt when I first moved to the states in ‘79.”
When people in San Francisco got wind of Kreuz’s story, the San Francisco Examiner flew him out to the city for another round of celebrity treatment. He met the mayor, George Moscone, was given a tour of Chinatown, and was the guest of honor at a rodeo at the Cow Palace. When he finally boarded a flight to return to Germany, he wore a sign reading “Please let me off in Frankfurt.”
The following year, in October 1978, Kreuz was invited back to Bangor for a few more weeks as the guest of honor for the grand opening of the Bangor Mall, cutting the ribbon on the brand-new shopping complex. Upon returning to Germany, however, Kreuz’s luck started to run out.
He’d taken many extra weeks of vacation time in order to visit the U.S., something his employer did not approve of. Kreuz also reportedly wanted to be compensated for the public appearances the brewery had him do to capitalize on its employee’s fame. And when Kreuz reportedly told a newspaper that he actually preferred to drink a competing brewery’s beer, that was the last straw. He was fired that winter.
Kreuz returned to Bangor a third time, in March 1979, to look for work. The opportunities available, however, were not so great.
“When he came back the third time, he kind of thought he’d be getting a job in Bangor,” Stark said. “And when he goes to the mall to see what’s available, the only job they offered him was as a janitor. I think, to Erwin, he was kind of like, ‘I’m a brewmaster, I’m a cheesemonger and I make good money doing it.’ It wasn’t what he wanted. And so he went back to Germany.”
According to the BDN, Kreuz was not bitter about his situation, and was instead grateful for his experiences in Maine. Very little is known about Kreuz’s life after he returned to Germany for the last time. Stark, in all his research, hasn’t even been able to find out if he’s alive or dead, though if Kreuz is still alive he’d be 93 years old. He did not have any children, apparently, and Stark hasn’t been able to find any other family members.
Ironically, if Kreuz’s memorable journeys had happened more recently, he undoubtedly could have found a more gratifying job at one of Maine’s more than 150 craft breweries, rather than as a janitor at the Bangor Mall.
“Think of all the employment to come his way later, with all of Maine’s microbreweries,” Shaw said. “He supposedly quipped during a meeting with the governor that he kept his youthful looks by consuming 23 glasses of beer a day.”

title: AP Top 25 poised for new No. 1 after Oklahoma upsets Texas
text:
Georgia is poised to take over the No. 1 spot in the AP Top 25 after pulling out a 20-17 win against No. 6 Alabama. But the Bulldogs won’t be the only team on the move after a wild week of upsets.
Oklahoma stunned Texas in the Red River Rivalry, UCLA pulled off a road upset against Oregon, South Carolina routed Florida and Kentucky delivered another overtime thriller, this time against LSU.
Stick around for projections, voter Q&A and live updates when the latest rankings drop at 2 p.m. EDT.
Here’s what to know:
Bulldogs on the rise: Georgia is set to take over No. 1 for the first time since 2024 after a hard fought road win over Alabama.
Down goes Texas: The Longhorns fell to a struggling Oklahoma team in the Red River Rivalry on Saturday afternoon, leaving the No. 1 spot in the poll up for grabs.
Fumble fest in Oregon: The No. 13-ranked Ducks turned over the ball seven times in a 17-15 upset loss to UCLA. Oregon lost five fumbles and backup quarterback Dylan Raiola threw two interceptions before being benched for Brock Thomas.
Georgia appears set to rise to No. 1 after Oklahoma upsets Texas
By MAURA CAREY
Georgia is poised to take over the No. 1 spot in the AP Top 25 after pulling out a 20-17 win against No. 6 Alabama. But the Bulldogs won’t be the only team on the move after a wild week of upsets.
Oklahoma stunned Texas in the Red River Rivalry, UCLA pulled off a road upset against Oregon, South Carolina routed Florida and Kentucky delivered another overtime thriller, this time against LSU.
Stick around for projections, voter Q&A and live updates when the latest rankings drop at 2 p.m. EDT.
Here’s what to know:
1. Bulldogs are on the rise: Georgia is set to take over No. 1 for the first time since 2024 after a hard fought road win over Alabama.
2. Down goes Texas: The Longhorns fell to a struggling Oklahoma team in the Red River Rivalry on Saturday afternoon, leaving the No. 1 spot in the poll up for grabs.
3. Fumble fest in Oregon: The No. 13-ranked Ducks turned the ball over seven times in a 17-15 upset loss to UCLA. Oregon lost five fumbles and backup quarterback Dylan Raiola threw two interceptions before being benched for Brock Thomas.
Who decides the rankings?
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
AP Top 25 voters are writers and broadcasters who cover college football.
AP employees do not vote, but they do choose the voters, and they seek wide representation from all over the country. This season, there are 69 voters.
The focus begins with voter representation in states with a Bowl Subdivision school, and the total number of voters from each state increases with the number of FBS teams. There are also spots reserved for national voters.
The AP allows broad latitude for voters to determine their rankings. They are urged to base their votes on performance, not reputation or preseason speculation (except, of course, for the always provocative preseason poll); to avoid regional bias, for or against; to pay attention to head-to-head results; and to make significant changes if desired.
Upheaval on tap for Top 25
By DAVE ZELIO
Six teams in the AP Top 25 lost over the weekend, which always portends a shakeup in the rankings.
But it’s who lost that suggests today’s poll is going to get an overhaul: No. 1 Texas, No. 6 Alabama and No. 10 LSU all went down, pretty much guaranteeing a new team at the top of the rankings. No. 2 Georgia is a likely candidate.
Amid the intrigue is how far voters will drop Texas (which lost in overtime against its archrival) and Alabama (which lost by 3 points to Georgia after at least one controversial decision by the officiating crew).
There may be some new faces, too. Teams like Wake Forest, Northwestern and Kentucky all have 1 loss each and stirring victories on their resumes already.

title: Egypt’s Fayoum mummy portraits to travel abroad for first time after restoration
text:
Egypt’s Fayoum mummy portraits to travel abroad for first time after restoration
Egypt unveiled Sunday a restored version of the “Tondo of the Two Brothers,” a prized 2nd-century painting from the famed Fayum portraits.
Related video: Sylvester Stallone digs into painful memories and the making of ‘Rocky’ in memoir ‘The Steps’
Specialists from Rome worked alongside conservators from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir — where the collection is usually kept — for three weeks to restore the artwork, officials said at a press conference.
Fayum mummy portraits were painted primarily on thin wooden panels and placed over the faces of the deceased within mummy wrappings, combining Egyptian funerary traditions with artistic influences from the wider Greco-Roman world.
Egypt will lend a major part of the collection to a temporary exhibition in Rome, marking the first time it will travel abroad.
“The restoration of the Tondo of the Two Brothers is an important example of what can be achieved through international cooperation in the preservation and study of cultural heritage,” said Sherif Fathy, Egypt’s minister of tourism and antiquities. “Egypt and Italy share deep historical and cultural ties, and this project brings together Egyptian and Italian expertise to preserve an exceptional work of art for future generations.”
Experts describe the painting as unusual because of its circular shape and its depiction of two people instead of one, and rank it among the most vivid surviving portraits from Roman-era Egypt. It was painted using a technique in which pigments are mixed with molten wax, and restorers were able to recover the features of the brother on the right.
Aly Abdel Halim, director general of the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir, said the conservation required careful intervention because both the wooden support, damaged by termites, and the painted surface were fragile.
The portraits will be featured in an exhibition in Rome from November to May 2027.
Tomaso Radaelli, chairman of MondoMostre, the exhibition’s organizer, said it will bring together more than 110 objects, including painted panels, funerary shrouds, masks, marble portraits, plaster casts and ancient jewelry.

title: Some in Florida and Alabama without power as Isaias moves north to Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic
text:
Nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power early Sunday as remnants of Isaias moved north, where widespread moderate to heavy rainfall was expected across the central Appalachians and mid-Atlantic region.
Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the southeastern U.S., especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service. That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops.
Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage.” The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building’s insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about.
In Florida’s Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from 4 to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city’s fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Along Alabama’s Gulf Coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.
President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after earlier doing the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.
The U.S. Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm.
The National Weather Service said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155 mph (250 kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a Category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning Sunday to parts of southwestern Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California.

title: 1 in 100 wheelchairs and scooters are mishandled by U.S. airlines
text:
1 in 100 wheelchairs and scooters are mishandled by U.S. airlines
For every hundred wheelchairs or scooters damaged enplaned in cargo compartments on airlines, one is mishandled.
The U.S. Department of Transportation publishes a monthly report which includes the number of wheelchairs and scooters mishandled by airlines. Last year, almost 10,000 wheelchairs or scooters were mishandled, meaning they were lost, delayed, damaged or stolen.
From January through July of this year, more than 511,000 wheelchairs and scooters have boarded domestic flights for airlines with at least 0.5% of total domestic passenger revenue. More than 5,500 of those were mishandled.
Frontier Airlines had the highest rate of mishandling wheelchairs and scooters from January through July 2026 at 1.52%.
The mishandled wheelchair and scooter rate includes bags lost by branded codeshare partners of the carriers. For example, the United Airlines network includes flights that were marketed by them but operated by a different airline.
U.S. airlines have only been required to report the number of wheelchairs and scooters mishandled since the passing of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018.
People who use wheelchairs are not typically able to use it on a plane because of the size of the aisle. Instead, they will use a smaller aisle chair provided by the airline to transport the traveler to the plane and bring their device as close to the gate as possible upon landing.
For domestic flights, if a wheelchair is damaged, the airline must cover the original cost of the device, according to the Department of Transportation.
Wheelchairs can be damaged or lost in the process, for example, when larger, 400- or 500-pound power wheelchairs must be transported in the cargo compartment.
But there are also difficulties for people with disabilities being moved and lifted in confined spaces by people who are not properly trained, according to Paralyzed Veterans of America’s Chief Policy Officer, Heather Ansley.
"This leads to injuries. It leads to people being dropped in the process," Ansley said. "There's a very big human toll that is really hidden in helping people get on the aircraft."
There are a couple ways people can submit disability-related complaints about air travel. One is through the Department of Transportation and the second is through the airline. 
People looking for compensation or a refund would have to file the complaint with the airline, Ansley said.
Both disability-related complaints submitted to DOT and to the airlines have grown over the past few decades. For DOT complaints, the number more than doubled from before COVID-19 to 2022.
There were 43,451 disability-related complaints filed to airlines directly in 2024, the most recent data available. That accounts for more than five complaints per 100,000 enplaned passengers, which is more than triple the rate 20 years prior.
The growing problems have lead to the "Wheelchair Rule" finalized by DOT in December 2024, the end of President Joe Biden's administration. This included a deadline of June 2026 for airline employees and contractors who assist passengers with disabilities to take a training course.
Certain provisions of the Wheelchair Rule, however, have since been delayed from being enforced until April 2027. These include rules on the frequency of refresher training, pre-departure notifications to passengers about their device being loaded onto the plane and reimbursing a passenger the fare difference if they have to take a different flight.
The enforcement of a training requirement related to accessible bathrooms on planes was also delayed.
Five major airlines supported a lawsuit by Airlines for America in February 2025 which challenged the rule from the Department of Transportation. The Trump administration has delayed the rule enforcement multiple times, most recently stating the intent to revisit the regulations under a "Wheelchair Rule II."

title: Week Ahead in Washington: Oct. 11
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will travel to Ohio and Alaska this week to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, while Vice President JD Vance is set to campaign in Texas.

title: Villages evacuated as flash flood from Budhi Gandaki river hits northern Nepal
text:
Villages evacuated as flash flood from Budhi Gandaki river hits northern Nepal
Residents along the Budhi Gandaki river in north central Nepal evacuated on Sunday as flash flooding destroyed homes and other structures in the area.
Video: Flooding in Nepal
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority evacuated villagers and warned others to move to safer areas while remaining on alert until late Sunday.
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
The disaster management agency is trying to determine the cause of the flash flood in the Budhi Gandaki river, which merges into the Trishuli river and is a key waterway near the capital Kathmandu.
Videos on social media show houses and sheds being swept away by the swollen river flowing between tall mountains. It was not immediately clear how many of the small villages in the mountainous area were impacted. Social media posts indicate the government warning prompted an evacuation in Arughat, a riverside town on the highway connecting Kathmandu to other parts of the country.
Nepal is still recovering from a devastating flood in August along the mountainous Nepal-China border that left more than 1,400 people dead and thousands more missing.
The office of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Monday announced an end to search and rescue operations for additional victims. Authorities will instead concentrate on recovery including restoration of roads and bridges cut off by floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made aid deliveries difficult.
The government estimates the rebuilding effort will cost $4.77 billion. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed.

title: 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
text:
139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti
At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via phone.
“What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.”
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.”
“The local authorities did their best,” Coissac said, “but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.”
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock, where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
“They're all in a state of shock,” Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. “I tried to talk to some of them, but it's very difficult.”
Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.
At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.
Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
“This is a devastating loss of life,” said Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.”
In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.
Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project.
“No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.”
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

title: Trump urges Sen. John Fetterman to switch parties
text:
Trump urges Sen. John Fetterman to switch parties and become a Republican
President Donald Trump openly encouraged Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania to switch parties and become a Republican just weeks before the midterm elections could reshape control of Congress.
Video above: Fetterman appears in RNC video, introducing McCormick at convention
"I'd love to see him as a Republican," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday as he returned to Washington from a rally in Tennessee. "He does better as a Republican than he does as a Democrat."
The comments were among the most direct overtures by Trump to woo Fetterman into the GOP, a matter of growing importance as the party could lose its Senate majority in next month's elections. With his everyman appeal, Fetterman was a Democratic star when he was first elected to the Senate in 2022. But during his time in Washington, he has split with Democrats on issues ranging from immigration to Israel, leading to speculation that he might switch parties.
A representative for Fetterman didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Fetterman has repeatedly rejected the notion of becoming a Republican, writing in The Washington Post in May that he would be a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." His relationship with fellow Democrats became more tenuous after he recorded a video for the Republican midterm convention last month praising his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Republican Dave McCormick, suggesting there were extremists in his party.
Video below: Pennsylvania senators, Fetterman and McCormick, address White House Correspondents' Dinner shooting
"I'm always going to stand with America," Fetterman said in the video. "I'm always going to reject the extremes and socialism and that anti-American way of life."
Such flirtations with the GOP could make it extremely difficult for Fetterman to win the Democratic nomination for another term in the Senate, a prospect Trump raised on Saturday as he encouraged the party switch.
Democrats need to pick up four seats to retake the Senate majority, a once remote prospect that remains challenging for the party. But Trump's unpopularity and the economic fallout from the Iran war have intensified headwinds for the GOP, making Democrats more bullish about a path to Senate control.
If Democrats picked up the four seats for a 51-seat majority, that could potentially put Fetterman in an influential position, reducing the incentive to switch parties.
The last senator whose party switch affected control of the chamber was Jim Jeffords of Vermont, who left the GOP in 2001 to give Democrats a narrow majority. Former Pennsylvania Sen. Arlen Specter's decision to abandon Republicans in 2009 helped Democrats achieve a supermajority.
Sloan reported from Cedar Rapids, Iowa

title: Death Notice: Byron L. West
Sunday Photos: October 11th, 2026
An 18-year investment pays off: Maine’s first ‘Alfond babies’ head to college
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gregory W. Powell is executive chairman of the Harold Alfond Foundation.
Eighteen years ago, the Harold Alfond Foundation made an investment of $500 in hundreds of babies born in central Maine. In so doing, we invited their families to invest along with us.
This fall, that long-term investment is paying off as these “Alfond babies,” now young
adults, are stepping onto college campuses and into postsecondary training programs for
the first time.
This milestone moment affirms something we at the Harold Alfond Foundation have long believed: that even a modest investment in a child’s future can fundamentally change their aspirations and trajectory.
Our founder, Harold Alfond, believed that every Maine child deserved an opportunity to
excel in life and that higher education in all its various forms would enhance each child’s
future. And along with it, our state. 
Harold knew, what the research now confirms and our federal government has come to realize, that children with higher education savings, no matter how modest, are more likely to enroll in and complete higher education. And that investing early in life was best as it strengthened the aspirations for success in life of parents and their children as the value of their financial investment grew over time.
And so, in 2008, we established the Alfond Scholarship Foundation, and with its terrific help began investing $500 in a college savings account for every child born in a handful of
central Maine communities whose parents opened a NextGen 529 savings account.
Building on the success of that early pilot, we then took the program statewide in 2009. Today, every baby born in Maine automatically receives a $500 Alfond Grant, which is invested on their behalf in the state’s NextGen 529 college savings program.
Since the program’s inception, our $500 grants have been awarded to and invested for more than 184,000 Maine children. Thanks to the stock market, together with our grants and the contributions of Maine families who opened their companion accounts, and matching grants by the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME), total savings for higher education now exceeds $813 million.
For our oldest and first grant recipients who have started college this fall, that $500 grew to nearly $2,500. That’s five times the original grant, funds that they are now using tax-free for higher education expenses whether for a Harvard degree or trade certifications,
apprenticeships or licensing exams.
But $500, even with compound investment returns over time, was never meant to single-
handedly fund higher education. Rather, the Alfond Grant was intended as a spark to build aspirations and confidence as well as to inspire every family to join us and start actively saving for their children’s futures.
Today, a third of Maine families with an Alfond Grant have joined us and taken the critical step of opening their own companion NextGen 529 account where they are investing additional funds for their child’s education. That is where I want to focus our attention here.
If your child has received our $500 grant and you have not yet opened a NextGen 529 account, we encourage you to join us and do so. You do not need to start big. You can open a NextGen account for your child alongside the Foundation’s $500 Alfond Grant without making an initial contribution. And you can invest money into your child’s account when you are ready and in many cases receive generous additional contributions from FAME, our state’s nationally recognized NextGen 529 provider.
In the last autumn of Harold Alfond’s life, I sat with him at his camp as he looked over the lawn and lake where his great grandchildren, now off to school, had played and swam in the summer sun. We imagined how the future of every Maine child might be shaped with a $500 investment for higher education. And how with even the most modest of family contributions and the compounding of investment returns over 18 years, our children and our state would be better for it.
Harold knew he would never meet the young adults, once newborns, who headed off to college this fall. But he loved this state and he said, “Let’s do it.”
So this fall, we are celebrating the first of our Alfond babies, now young adults off to college. We are celebrating with their families, who had the foresight to open a NextGen 529 account for their children.
To those students and their families: congratulations! And to the families whose children
will follow, we hope the Alfond Grant and saving for higher education will be part of your
journey, too. An investment in your children today that opens the door to their greater
opportunity tomorrow.

title: Six senators demand Trump administration 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Six senators demand Trump administration 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Related video above: Trump says Ukraine should "get a new leader" after striking diesel deal with Russia
Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.
“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote.
The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said.
Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.
“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.”
He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.
“This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said.
Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump.
Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day.
Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S.
“The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said.
Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

title: Senators urge Trump administration to reverse Russian diesel plan to lower fuel prices
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.
Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.
“The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote.
The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there’s a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.
“We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said.
Trump’s announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”
Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president’s action would be in violation of U.S. law.
“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.”
He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.
“This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said.
Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump.
Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day.
Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S.
“The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said.
Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.
—-
Associated Press writer Mae Anderson in New York contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine steps up strikes on Russia's tech infrastructure, damaging third data center in 4 days
text:
Ukraine steps up strikes on Russia’s tech infrastructure, damaging third data center in 4 days
A Ukrainian drone attack shut down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the company said Sunday, the third strike on its facilities in four days as Kyiv widens its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia.
Related video: Trump announces deal with Russia in attempt to lower diesel prices
The attack on the data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across Yandex's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine's strikes on data centers follow Russian attacks on data hubs in Ukraine.
"As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.
The strike came a day after President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said Saturday.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back, writing on X Saturday night that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence and had the backing of Ukrainians.
"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.
Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, Ivan Fedorov, the former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council, said Sunday. The death toll from Saturday's attack stood at 20, including four children, he said. More than 30 people were wounded, he said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

title: Obituary: Mark F. Kemmerle
text:
BRUNSWICK – Mark F. Kemmerle, 78, passed away on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026.
He was born in Scranton, Pa. on Sept. 1, 1948, the first child of Llewellyn and Alice Kemmerle.
Mark always carried a book with him–as he aged, two books, including a collection of crossword puzzles which he and his wife Toni enjoyed tackling together. He listened to music at full volume while cooking dinner, often over the objections of his loving family. He kept detailed logs of the movies he watched, sometimes over 400 films a year, and wrote spirited emails to his brother Peter and daughter Karen debating the merits of different auteurs. He loved nothing more than spending seven hours of his Sunday watching Red Zone during the NFL regular season with his dutiful son-in-law Adam. He took great joy in reminiscing about his formative years at Brown University, especially with his daughter and fellow alumna, Allison. Mark and family made a yearly pilgrimage to Stratford, Ontario, to attend the Shakespeare festival, where he enjoyed dozens of plays and ate copious amounts of pad thai. In his later years, he proved a devoted grandfather; his granddaughter Nora loved to hear him read stories with a different voice for each character.
During his long, eventful life, he lived in Pennsylvania, Ohio, Rhode Island, Indiana, and Florida, but he considered himself a Mainer and lived in Brunswick with his family for the past 29 years.
Mark is survived by his wife, Toni Kemmerle; and his three children, Karen, Michael, and Allison; by his loving brother and sister, Peter and Anne, and their families; by his sons-in-law, Adam Shuler and Andrei Barbu; and by the grandchildren he loved so much, Nora and George Barbu.
Mark fought a short but hard battle with pancreatic cancer. His wife Toni and sister Anne nursed him through his final illness, while his daughter Karen and her partner Adam came to support and love him.
A celebration of life will be held in summer 2027.
Mark was a lifelong advocate for disability rights and served as the director for the Maine Developmental Services Oversight and Advisory Board for five years. He ensured his son Michael received an education, proper benefits, and a dignified life, so in lieu of flowers or gifts, please donate to the Independence Association in Brunswick.

title: Land trusts secure 1,800 acres in Somerset County along Appalachian Trail
text:
Two land trusts have secured a 1,843-acre parcel southeast of Moxie Pond and along the Appalachian Trail in a remote part of Somerset County, in what they called “a win for both people and nature.”
The Trust for Public Land, a national organization, and the Northeast Wilderness Trust, based in Vermont, announced last month their acquisition of the Moxie Pond Wilderness Preserve.
The deal with timberland management company Weyerhaeuser closed thanks to a $3.2 million fundraising effort, the organizations said in a news release.
It was supported by private dollars from individual donors and foundations, after federal funds originally set aside for the acquisition fell through. The groups worked together on fundraising; the Northeast Wilderness Trust is the property owner and steward.
The preserve will serve as a buffer for a 5-mile stretch of the Appalachian Trail at the start of the 100-Mile Wilderness, the land trusts said. Both groups say protecting lands around the trail is a priority.
The new ownership will also guarantee an important regional snowmobile and ATV trail through a permanent easement conveyed to the state, said Lynnette Batt, a Farmington-based senior project manager with the Trust for Public Land.
The preserve will also offer public access for hunters, although Northeast Wilderness Trust has some restrictions on its properties, including a prohibition on predator hunting.
It adds to more than 20,000 acres of adjacent conserved land. The area is a mixture of federal, state and privately owned parcels, some of which the Trust for Public Land was involved in protecting.
The new preserve includes 37 acres of wetlands, 3 miles of brook trout streams and a mile of some of the last remaining undeveloped shoreline along Moxie Pond, in its southeast corner. The land lies in Bald Mountain Township T2 R3, an unorganized territory a few miles east of Caratunk, as the crow flies.
The property is to be managed as “wildland,” the land trusts said. That will entail a passive management approach called “rewilding” in which forests grow old.
“The project strikes a careful balance with Maine’s diversity of human and nonhuman stakeholders in mind, securing existing access while safeguarding more than 1,800 acres of forest that, as they rewild, will act as core habitat for wildlife and will naturally evolve into a future old-growth forest,” said Jon Leibowitz, president and CEO of Northeast Wilderness Trust, in a statement. “The Preserve offers something to love to every Mainer who cherishes this precious landscape.”
Alex Littlejohn, director of conservation for Weyerhaeuser, called the project a “compelling conservation opportunity.”
The Trust for Public Land had originally been planning to acquire the land on behalf of the National Park Service. It entered into a purchase contract with Weyerhaeuser in 2023, Batt said.
The nonprofit was lined up to receive a $2.1 million grant from the federal Land and Water Conservation Fund, and the land would have become part of the Appalachian National Scenic Trail.
But before final approval, federal officials added a new, last-minute requirement that local and state governments express their lack of objection for a round of land acquisition projects funded through the program.
In this case, the relevant local governing authority was the Somerset County Board of Commissioners. Three of five commissioners refused to sign off on a “no objection letter,” citing their qualms about the federal government taking over Maine’s land and the prohibition of hunting and other strict regulations the National Park Service imposes on its land.
“We had strong local support, so we felt good about moving forward with the project with a different avenue,” Batt said in an interview by telephone Thursday. “Northeast Wilderness Trust, last fall, stepped in to help us pivot the project to private funding.”
Mark Leathers, president of the Lake Moxie Camp Owners Association, was among those who urged the commissioners not to derail the project. Leathers, also a forester and master Maine guide, asked the commissioners to leave politics out of their decision and consider the people who live near the proposed project.
“This is one parcel in Maine where the ecological, recreational, and aesthetic values far outweigh the timber value,” Leathers said in a statement shared by the land trusts. “My family has savored this view almost at a spiritual level for six generations, since 1929, and now it will be preserved forever.”

title: Obituary: Neil Michael Brochu
text:
SACO – Neil Michael Brochu, 40, was born on July 19, 1986, in Portland, and passed away on Sept. 25, 2026. He leaves behind family who loved him deeply, friends who will miss him dearly, and memories that will bring both laughter and tears to all who were fortunate enough to know him.
Neil grew up in southern Maine and attended schools in Saco and Falmouth, where he played football during his high school years. From an early age, he developed a strong work ethic, a love of learning new skills, and an appreciation for the simple things in life.
A graduate of culinary school at NECI, Neil began his professional life as a chef in Portland, and Boston, Mass. He developed a passion for cooking that remained with him throughout his life. Never one to shy away from hard work or a new challenge, Neil went on to build a career in property management and the trades. He became a skilled carpenter, electrician, and all-around handyman – a true jack-of-all-trades who took pride in working with his hands, solving problems, and providing for the people he loved.
Of all the roles Neil held throughout his life, none meant more to him than being a father.
His daughter, Amelia Athearn Brochu, affectionately known as “Mimi,” was the center of his world. Neil lived to be her dad. Whether they were drawing, painting, hiking, or exploring the beautiful outdoors surrounding their home in Eugene, Ore., he cherished every opportunity to spend time with her.
Some of Neil’s happiest moments were found in the simplest routines. Drawing on his love of cooking, he delighted in preparing breakfast for Amelia each morning, carefully cutting fresh fruit, making oatmeal from scratch, or cooking eggs and bacon – whatever Mimi happened to want that day. For Neil, being a father was not simply about the big moments or special occasions. It was about being present, sharing experiences, and finding joy in caring for his little girl.
Outside of work and family, Neil had a passion for fitness and loved spending time in the gym. Music was an important part of his life, as were movies, video games, and the seemingly endless collection of movie quotes he enjoyed sharing with those closest to him. He had a sense of humor that could turn an ordinary conversation into a memorable one, and he appreciated the kind of laughter that comes from years of shared experiences and inside jokes.
Neil never measured his life by material possessions or outward appearances. He found satisfaction in honest work, meaningful relationships, and the simple pleasures of everyday life. He was happiest when he had something to work on, someone to laugh with, or an opportunity to spend time with the people he loved.
To his family, Neil was much more than the sum of his accomplishments. He was a son, a father, a brother, and a friend. To his brothers, he was a best friend – a companion through years of laughter, music, movies, and the countless ordinary moments that, in the end, become extraordinary memories.
Neil will be remembered for his hardworking spirit, his humor, his many talents, and, above all, the tremendous love he had for his daughter and family.
Neil is survived by his beloved daughter, Amelia; his brothers Matt Brochu, Lex Goduti, and Ian Goduti; his parents, Shannon Goduti and Dave Brochu; his stepfather, Richard Goduti; his countless nieces and nephews; extended family and friends, who will continue to honor his memory and carry his love with them.
His absence leaves a space that cannot be filled, but his memory will live on in the stories told, the laughter shared, the music played, and the everyday moments that remind those who loved him of the man they were so fortunate to know.
Perhaps nowhere will his legacy be more meaningful than in the life of his beloved Mimi, who will always carry with her the love of a father who found his greatest happiness in being hers.
Neil will be deeply loved, profoundly missed, and never forgotten.
A memorial service will be held at 3 p.m., on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the new Conroy-Tully Walker Funeral Home, 300 Allen Ave., Portland with a celebration to continue at Bruno’s at 4 p.m.
To view Neil’s Memorial Page or to share an online condolence, please visit http://www.ConroyTullyWalker.com.
In lieu of flowers or gifts, a fund has been established for his daughter, Amelia. Donations may be made through https://everloved.com/life-of/neil-brochu/.

title: 1 killed in Gray turnpike crash after driver swerves to avoid deer
text:
One person was killed in a crash Friday night on the Maine Turnpike and three others were injured when a driver apparently swerved to avoid hitting a deer.
According to Maine State Police spokesperson Shannon Moss, troopers responded to the crash at mile marker 60 in Gray at 11:47 p.m.
The initial investigation indicates that the driver of a 2010 Honda Fit, Megan Stuart, 31, of Auburn, was traveling north when she swerved to avoid the deer. The vehicle hit the median-side guardrail and spun 180 degrees to face oncoming traffic.
A 2016 Chevrolet Malibu, also traveling north, crashed head-on into the Fit, Moss said in a statement.
Stuart was taken to Maine Medical Center with non-life-threatening injuries. A passenger in the Fit, Soda Mao, 38, of Auburn, was pronounced dead at the scene.
The driver and passenger in the Malibu suffered minor injuries, Moss said.
Police shut down the turnpike to clear the scene for about 20 minutes, and one lane was closed for about two hours.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Death Notice: Sally A. Hinkley
Obituary: Robert Kidder Stewart
text:
CUMBERLAND FORESIDE – Robert Kidder Stewart lived a life defined by adventure, generosity, authenticity, stewardship, and a deep love for his family and the natural world. He followed his own path with curiosity and purpose, leaving behind a legacy that will endure for generations.
Bob passed away peacefully, surrounded by love, on July 21, 2026, at the age of 85. Born in Boston, Mass. on Oct. 12, 1940, to Charles and Louise Stewart, he was raised in Weston alongside his older brother, Tim, and older sister, Mary.
Bob attended Noble and Greenough High School and Brown University. During his junior year at Brown, he traveled to Alaska, where he studied the wilderness, deepening a lifelong connection to nature and exploration.
At Brown, Bob met his beloved Janet Louise Johnson, who was attending Wellesley College. They married on June 27, 1964, and built a life together rooted in love and family that spanned nearly 60 years.
After briefly working as a stockbroker in Rhode Island, Bob and Janet moved to Maine, where he joined the Stewart family blueberry and canning business. He became an invaluable leader and trusted friend to the loyal employees who helped make the company successful.
Throughout his life, Bob embraced every opportunity to explore and challenge himself. He rowed the coast of Maine, kayaked the waters of Maine and Canada, cycled through Spain and Portugal, hiked mountains from Maine to Scotland and countless places in between, and ran thousands of miles. If there was an adventure to be had, Bob wanted to experience it.
He even earned his hot air ballooning license and flew small aircraft. His love of the sea led him to bring the historic schooner Sylvina W. Beal to Portland, where he ran the vessel and offered cruises along the Maine coast. Bob lived fully and authentically, following his passions and building a life shaped by exploration.
Bob was also an avid reader and prolific writer. He became remarkably knowledgeable across an extraordinary range of subjects. He wrote poems, stories, and even a children’s book. He had a wonderful wit and keen sense of humor, bringing these qualities to his conversations.
Bob and Janet shared a love of travel that took them all around the world. In later years, they treasured time in Bermuda with their family, creating cherished memories with their children and grandchildren.
Bob’s greatest passion was conservation. He believed the land was not something to possess, but something to protect and pass on. He dedicated himself to preserving forests, mountains, islands, and wildlife habitat throughout Maine and neighboring Canada.
One of Bob’s proudest conservation achievements was Puzzle Mountain in western Maine. In 2005, he donated 485 acres to the Mahoosuc Land Trust, including all three summits of Puzzle Mountain and five miles of the Grafton Loop Trail. The land became the Stewart Family
Preserve at Puzzle Mountain, helping preserve one of Maine’s most treasured landscapes and its connection to the Appalachian Trail. Through Bob’s generosity and vision, generations of hikers will continue to explore these mountains, enjoy their breathtaking views, and connect with the natural world he loved so deeply.
His conservation work extended across the Bay of Fundy, where he donated Little Mowat Island and protected additional islands through conservation easements.
Bob’s generosity extended beyond the land. During years of traveling to Kerala, India, he formed meaningful relationships within local communities and helped build a school for a community that did not previously have one.
As Janet’s health declined due to Alzheimer’s, they found joy in walks together along Pratt’s Brook in Yarmouth. After Janet passed away in May, 2024, Bob honored those memories by donating natural sitting stones along the path for others to rest and enjoy the peaceful surroundings they had loved.
Even in the final week of his life, Bob remained focused on conservation. He told his family he wanted one of his remaining islands donated and protected for future generations-a final reflection of the way he lived.
Above all else, Bob’s greatest legacy was his family. He is survived by his children, Robert Stewart Jr. and Jennifer Stewart Guay; their spouses, Jamie Geier and Norman Guay; and his beloved grandchildren, Kaitlyn Guay, Charlie Stewart, Logan Guay, and Zachary Stewart.
Bob was an active and engaged Papa who took great joy in his grandchildren, attending hockey games, rock climbing competitions, and the many moments that filled their lives. He was proud of the people they were becoming and loved being part of their journeys.
Bob lived life on his own terms, guided by curiosity, conviction, generosity, and love. His legacy lives on through the family he cherished and through the mountains, islands, and communities forever changed by his vision and stewardship.
A Celebration of Bob’s life will be held Saturday, Nov. 7, from 1 to 3 p.m. at The Portland Country Club. All who knew and loved Bob are welcome.
Please visit http://www.jonesrichandbarnes.com to leave condolences for the Stewart family and share a memory of Bob.
