title: UMaine’s role in pay-to-play scheme deserves a closer look
text:
ProPublica’s investigation into Sen. Susan Collins’ pay-to-play practice raises serious concerns about complicity on the part of the University of Maine and damage to the university’s research mission.
In addition to wood composites, to what extent has research at Maine’s institution been dependent on the senator’s largesse and to what extent has this largesse been determined on the senator’s need for campaign funds? To what extent does the research that the university embraces reflect the senator’s priorities and to what extent are those priorities in the best interests of Maine people and Maine students? To what extent have the senator’s priorities corrupted the university?
It beggars belief that the university’s administration did not understand Sen. Collins’ pay-to-play strategy, and the university’s claim of innocence should be thoroughly investigated.
ProPublica has played its part, and Maine’s media should now play theirs.
Tony Brinkley
Professor of English (retired), University of Maine
Bangor

title: Maine Sen. Susan Collins signs letter to Trump opposing Russian diesel imports
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Sen. Susan Collins has joined five other senators Sunday in signing a letter to President Donald Trump opposing the purchase of Russian diesel amid rising fuel costs.
Trump announced Friday in a social media post that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin struck a deal over the phone that would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia to the United States. An additional 500,000 tons would be supplied in November, with an addition 4 million to follow, Trump wrote.
Three Republican senators — Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, John Curtis of Utah and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — also signed the letter with Collins. Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and and Connecticut’s Richard Blumenthal also signed.
“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia,” Collins said in a statement provided Sunday by a spokesperson. “I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following.”
Trump’s announcement came a few weeks after Congress passed legislation in an effort to cut revenue Russia receives from oil and gas to finance its war against Ukraine. The legislation imposes tariffs on some Russian oil and natural gas importers, with exceptions for countries that import 15% or less.
The six lawmakers also noted in the letter that Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.
“Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the lawmakers wrote. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.”

title: Downtown Bucksport Thai and sushi eatery plans to expand and add ramen
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Just over a year since they opened a new restaurant on Bucksport’s Main Street, the couple behind Chalee Thai-Sushi are planning to expand their menu and add dine-in seating in an adjacent office building.
Chalee Chaikaew and Vee Napapornipat, who also own the Siam Sky Thai food restaurant in Blue Hill, announced their plans and purchase of 54 Main St. on Friday. Chaikaew is the chef at the Bucksport establishment, which has an extensive menu including sushi offerings and Thai cuisine like pho noodles and curry dishes.
The current location is a take-out, but many customers want to dine in, sometimes eating on her sofa, according to Napapornipat.
“We need to do something to make people more comfortable,” she said.
The expanded restaurant would bring more dining options to the center of Bucksport, which has seen transitions in the last two years with new arrivals and the recent departure of Stowaways Town Tavern for Blue Hill.
The couple won’t have a timeline for their Bucksport project until plans are reviewed by the town, according to Napapornipat.
Chaikaew and Napapornipat are originally from Bangkok and opened their Blue Hill restaurant in 2018, followed by Siam Sky 2 in Ellsworth two years later. They sold the latter business to a friend last year, mainly to pursue a location they could own rather than lease, the Ellsworth American reported at the time. The Ellsworth spot has been renamed ThaiConic.
In Bucksport, they plan to add a walkway connecting the two buildings and turn the ground floor of 54 Main St. into a “spectacular dining area” with counter service, the couple wrote in a Facebook post Friday.
The existing building will be used for food preparation and storage.
The couple also thanked their employees and community for support of the growing business.
“I never dream about success, I WORK for it !!” their Facebook post read. “I can be patient and wait for anything, but there is one thing I simply cannot wait for: eating the most delicious ramen with a rich, flavorful broth at Chalee Thai sushi and ramen.”
54 Main St. currently houses an accounting firm, which Napapornipat said plans to move into another downtown building.

title: 58th annual Fall Foliage Festival supports coastal Maine history
text:
BOOTHBAY, Maine (WABI) - There was lots of red, orange and gold at one coastal Maine this weekend with businesses from all over helping to support an important piece of history. Autumn colors were in full swing at the 58th annual Fall Foliage Festival, held at the Boothbay Railway Village Museum.
The 35-acre museum was founded in 1964 by Maine preservationist George McEvoy, who had a passion for locomotives.
“There is over 100 years of Maine history here. It’s not your average museum where families come and kids can’t run free. It’s there’s a lot of hands on and we do a ton of community events throughout the year,” said Lori Reynolds, Marketing and Event Coordinator for the Boothbay Railway Village Museum. much history from around the state that has ended up here for permanent archival.”
The festival helps to support the museum, with around a hundred vendors spanning from Boothbay to other regions of Maine.
“I have been coming here for 25 years with my pickles and jam. It’s been a lot of fun. I’m seeing a lot of familiar faces from over the years. A lot of people look for me specifically here, and it’s always great to see them come in and remember their favorite flavors,” said vendor Sarah Brewer of Slice O’Country.
“We like the historical context and hearing the train going around and seeing the steam and everything from the train,” said Renee Brown of Misty Mountain Farm, “We like looking at all of the different historical buildings and everything they have on display.”
“The Boothbay Town Hall is the real original Boothbay building town hall that was built in 1847, and they moved it here and they moved a lot of buildings here,” said Reynolds.
Organizers say it was also a great day for families to get out during peak foliage season.
“We’ve always had that beautiful foliage view while we’re enjoying the festival. Being outdoors in the nice crisp fall air, we have hot cider here, we have tons of great food, that whole vibe of just enjoying fall in New England,” said Reynolds.

title: Dixfield man drowns while kayaking in Roxbury
text:
A Dixfield man died after apparently falling out of his kayak Saturday on Ellis Pond in Roxbury, officials said.
The Maine Warden Service was notified shortly after 4 p.m. of a possible drowning.
Shawn Noyes, 20, had been kayaking with his family, Lt. Dan Menard wrote Sunday in a Maine Warden Service news release.
Noyes was seen in the water attempting to swim to a nearby island, when he disappeared and was feared drowned.
The air temperature Saturday was in the mid-50s and the water temperature would have been even colder. A person entering water at such temperatures would experience cold water immersion syndrome, which can lead to a loss of motor control within minutes.
The Maine Warden Service conducted a search Saturday evening with the help of the Roxbury, Mexico and Rumford fire departments.
Noyes’s kayak and life jacket were recovered from the pond.
 On Sunday, the Maine Warden Service dive team recovered Noyes’s body; he was not wearing a life jacket. The Maine Warden Service said everyone should wear life jackets while recreating
on the water.
